AP-3 (delta, a beta subunit, a mu subunit and a sigma subunit) is a cytosolic vesicle coat that is recruited to endosomal membranes by the GTP-bound form of the small GTPase ARF1, captures transmembrane cargo bearing dileucine- and tyrosine-based sorting signals, and polymerises into a tubular carrier that delivers that cargo to lysosomes and to lysosome-related organelles. Unlike the closely related AP-1 and AP-2 complexes, AP-3 does not require a clathrin lattice: its coat is built from rows of AP-3 arches cross-linked by ARF1 dimers. Within the complex, delta is the subunit that carries the primary ARF1 contact - two interfaces on its N-terminal HEAT-repeat trunk, both needed for the complex to stay on membranes - and, through a hinge in its long disordered linker, a dedicated binding site for the longin domain of the SNARE VAMP7, which AP-3 transports only when VAMP7 is engaged in a cis-SNARE complex. Delta also contributes, with the sigma subunit, to the dileucine cargo pocket. Delta is the only large subunit of AP-3 that is not duplicated in vertebrates: the ubiquitous complex uses beta-3A and the neuron-specific complex beta-3B, but both contain delta, so delta loss removes both forms. Characterised cargoes include LAMP1 and LAMP2, CD63, tyrosinase and TYRP1, VAMP7, CLN3, the zinc transporters ZnT2 and ZnT3, phosphatidylinositol-4-kinase type II alpha and, postsynaptically, AMPA receptors in complex with stargazin. Loss of delta-adaptin causes pigment-granule, platelet dense-granule, lytic-granule and synaptic-vesicle defects: it underlies the Drosophila garnet eye-colour mutant, the mouse mocha mutant, and human Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 10, in which oculocutaneous albinism and a platelet storage-pool defect are accompanied by neutropenia, impaired cytotoxic lymphocyte degranulation, seizures, neurodevelopmental delay and hearing loss.

AP4B1 encodes the beta-1 subunit (beta4-adaptin) of the heterotetrameric adaptor protein complex 4 (AP-4), which consists of epsilon (AP4E1), beta4 (AP4B1), mu4 (AP4M1), and sigma4 (AP4S1) subunits. Unlike clathrin-associated AP-1, AP-2, and AP-3 complexes, AP-4 forms a non-clathrin coat on vesicles departing from the trans-Golgi network (TGN). AP-4 mediates signal-dependent sorting and export of transmembrane cargo proteins from the TGN to endosomal compartments and pre-autophagosomal structures, recognizing YXXOE-type sorting signals. Key cargoes include ATG9A (autophagy machinery), APP (amyloid precursor protein), DAGLB (endocannabinoid synthesis), SERINC1/3 (lipid scramblases), Sortilin (lysosomal enzyme trafficking), and AMPA/delta-2 glutamate receptors (neuronal polarity). The beta4 subunit contains an N-terminal trunk domain involved in complex assembly and a C-terminal ear (appendage) domain that recruits the accessory protein tepsin through a conserved hydrophobic binding site. AP-4 complex assembly requires the AAGAB chaperone, which stabilizes subunits and prevents proteasomal degradation. AP-4 plays critical roles in autophagosome biogenesis (via ATG9A trafficking), lysosome function (via Sortilin), neuronal polarity (via glutamate receptor sorting), and axonal endocannabinoid signaling (via DAGLB). Loss of AP-4 function results in cargo retention at the TGN and impaired autophagy, particularly affecting axonal compartments in neurons. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in AP4B1 cause spastic paraplegia type 47 (SPG47), part of the AP-4 deficiency syndrome characterized by severe intellectual disability, progressive spasticity, and structural brain abnormalities including thin corpus callosum.

AP4E1 encodes the epsilon large subunit of the heterotetrameric AP-4 adaptor complex. AP-4 forms a nonclathrin coat on the cytoplasmic face of the trans-Golgi network and sorts membrane proteins into transport carriers. The epsilon N-terminal trunk contributes to the complex core and binds activated ARF1 for membrane recruitment, while its C-terminal ear binds the accessory protein tepsin. These interactions support coat assembly and cargo transport in coordination with the mu4 cargo-recognition subunit.

AP4M1 encodes mu4-adaptin, the medium (mu) subunit of adaptor protein complex 4 (AP-4), a heterotetramer of epsilon (AP4E1), beta-4 (AP4B1), mu-4 (AP4M1) and sigma-4 (AP4S1) that forms a non-clathrin coat on the cytosolic face of the trans-Golgi network. Within the complex, mu4 is the cargo-recognition subunit: its C-terminal mu homology domain (residues 184-452) binds short sorting motifs in the cytosolic tails of transmembrane proteins, with a signal preference of its own rather than the canonical YXXPhi specificity of the mu subunits of AP-1, AP-2 and AP-3, and with a binding surface whose location on the domain differs from theirs. Recruitment of AP-4 to trans-Golgi network membranes is ARF-dependent and brefeldin A-sensitive, and mu4 itself binds ARF1 directly and independently of its nucleotide state. The physiological cargo established by both targeted and unbiased approaches is ATG9A, the only multispanning membrane protein of the core autophagy machinery: AP-4 exports ATG9A from the trans-Golgi network to the peripheral cytoplasm, and when AP-4 is lost ATG9A is retained at the Golgi, autophagosome formation is impaired, and axons accumulate swellings and aggregates. Additional AP-4-dependent cargoes include the amyloid precursor protein, whose mu4-bound YKFFE motif routes it from the trans-Golgi network to endosomes and so limits amyloidogenic processing, and SERINC1/SERINC3. Accessory factors tepsin, RUSC1/2 and the FTS-Hook-FHIP complex act with the coat; mu4 binds the Hook1 and Hook2 coiled-coil domains directly, coupling AP-4 and its ATG9A cargo to dynein-dependent perinuclear positioning. In neurons AP-4 restricts cargo, including AMPA receptor-TARP complexes, to the somatodendritic domain, and in polarized epithelia it participates in basolateral sorting. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in AP4M1 cause spastic paraplegia 50, a childhood-onset complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability, microcephaly and progressive spasticity, one of the four genetically equivalent forms of AP-4 deficiency syndrome.

AP4S1 encodes sigma4-adaptin, the single small subunit of adaptor protein complex 4 (AP-4), an obligate heterotetramer that also contains the large adaptins epsilon (AP4E1) and beta4 (AP4B1) and the medium adaptin mu4 (AP4M1). AP-4 assembles a non-clathrin coat on the cytosolic face of the trans-Golgi network, where the small GTPase ARF1 and membrane cargo recruit it cooperatively, and packages a defined set of transmembrane proteins into vesicles that leave the TGN for peripheral and axonal compartments. Its best-characterised client is ATG9A, the lipid scramblase required for autophagosome biogenesis; the amyloid precursor protein, SERINC1 and SERINC3, sortilin, and AMPA and delta-2 glutamate receptors have also been reported as AP-4-dependent, and the accessory proteins tepsin, RUSC1 and RUSC2 link AP-4 vesicles to microtubule motors. Within the complex sigma4 is the architectural subunit: the epsilon trunk wraps around it to build the central core, the two large adaptins cannot associate in its absence, and loss of sigma4 destabilises all four subunits, abolishes complex assembly and abolishes tepsin recruitment to membranes. Unlike the sigma subunits of AP-1, AP-2 and AP-3, sigma4 has no demonstrated role in recognising dileucine sorting signals; in AP-4 the tyrosine-based and non-canonical cargo signals are read by mu4. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in AP4S1 cause spastic paraplegia 52, one of four genetically distinct but clinically indistinguishable forms of AP-4 deficiency syndrome, a childhood-onset complex hereditary spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability, progressive lower-limb spasticity and developmental brain malformations. Heterozygous carriers are unaffected.

APC is a large, multidomain tumor suppressor that coordinates beta-catenin turnover and cytoskeletal organization. Its central repeats bind beta-catenin and its SAMP motifs engage AXIN in the cytoplasmic destruction complex, helping recruit and present beta-catenin to kinases and ubiquitination machinery. Its C-terminal regions bind microtubules, associate with microtubule-end proteins and directly recruit actin monomers to nucleate filaments. These activities contribute to cell polarity, migration and accurate mitosis. APC also binds regulatory partners, including Asef-family nucleotide-exchange factors, whose autoinhibition it can relieve. APC occupies cytoplasmic, cortical, junctional and nuclear pools; truncating variants disrupt several of these separable functions and underlie familial adenomatous polyposis and many sporadic colorectal cancers.

XIAP is a cytosolic and nuclear inhibitor-of-apoptosis protein with three BIR domains and a C-terminal RING E3 ubiquitin-ligase domain. Its BIR2/linker and BIR3 elements directly inhibit active apoptotic caspases, while its RING domain ubiquitinates pathway-specific substrates in apoptosis, NOD1/NOD2 innate immune signaling, Wnt/TLE transcriptional control, copper homeostasis, and interferon regulation.

BIRC5 (survivin) is a member of the inhibitor of apoptosis (IAP) family that functions primarily as an essential component of the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC). Despite its historical name "apoptosis inhibitor survivin," contemporary evidence establishes that survivin's best-characterized and evolutionarily conserved function is in mitotic regulation, not apoptosis inhibition. As a CPC component, survivin associates with Aurora B kinase, INCENP, and borealin to regulate chromosome alignment, kinetochore-microtubule attachment, spindle midzone assembly, and cytokinesis. The protein localizes dynamically during mitosis: to centromeres during prometaphase/metaphase, to the spindle midzone during anaphase, and to the midbody during cytokinesis. While survivin has been implicated in anti-apoptotic activity, this appears to be indirect and context-dependent, likely mediated through interactions with XIAP and sequestration of SMAC/DIABLO, rather than direct caspase inhibition. Unlike other IAP family members, survivin lacks the full RING domain required for direct caspase ubiquitination. Expression peaks at G2/M phase and is largely absent from most normal adult tissues but highly overexpressed in cancers.

Apolipoprotein B is the persistent lipid-binding scaffold of triglyceride- and cholesterol-rich lipoproteins. Hepatic apoB100 forms the structural framework of VLDL and remains on IDL and LDL as the particles are remodelled in circulation. Intestinal RNA editing produces the shorter apoB48 product, which supports chylomicron assembly and persists in chylomicron remnants. Nascent apoB acquires lipid in the endoplasmic reticulum with assistance from microsomal triglyceride transfer protein and is exported as lipoprotein cargo. ApoB100 also presents LDL-receptor recognition surfaces that couple lipid carriage to particle clearance. ApoB48 lacks the canonical apoB100 LDLR-binding region; apoE can instead mediate remnant recognition. Intracellular quality-control pools coexist with the principal extracellular carrier role.

Apolipoprotein E is a secreted exchangeable apolipoprotein that associates with plasma, interstitial, and central-nervous-system lipoprotein particles. Through amphipathic lipid-binding domains and receptor-binding activity, APOE mediates cholesterol and phospholipid efflux, high-density lipoprotein particle formation/remodeling, and receptor- or proteoglycan-dependent clearance of chylomicron remnants, VLDL, IDL, LDL, and HDL particles. APOE is produced prominently by liver and by astrocytes and other glial cells in brain, where it supports lipid redistribution among cells. APOE also binds amyloid-beta, tau, immune receptors, extracellular matrix proteoglycans, and other partners, but these disease- or context-linked activities are secondary to its core lipid-transport and lipoprotein-clearance roles.

Apolipoprotein L1 is a membrane-active component of human serum trypanosome lytic factors. It circulates on lipoprotein particles and acts after uptake by susceptible trypanosomes, disrupting parasite membrane ion homeostasis. Mature human APOL1 forms cation-selective channels after acidic membrane association and subsequent neutralization. Its carboxy-terminal region is recognized by the trypanosome serum resistance-associated protein, which counteracts host killing. Loss of circulating APOL1 can compromise innate protection against normally non-human-infective trypanosomes. APOL1 is expressed in multiple tissues, including pancreas, lung, prostate, liver, placenta and spleen. Its coding risk haplotypes G1 and G2 are associated with increased susceptibility to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and other forms of nondiabetic kidney disease. The relationship between cell-intrinsic renal injury and its circulating host-defense activity remains an active mechanistic question.

Amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP) is a type I transmembrane glycoprotein that undergoes regulated proteolytic processing to generate soluble ectodomains, membrane-tethered C-terminal fragments, amyloid-beta peptides, and the APP intracellular domain. Full-length APP acts at the neuronal cell surface and in secretory/endocytic compartments, where it contributes to cell adhesion, synaptogenesis, neurite outgrowth, axonogenesis, and interactions with extracellular matrix ligands. Alternative splice isoforms differ in inclusion of the Kunitz protease inhibitor domain, giving APP751/770 protease-inhibitor activity that is absent from neuronal APP695. APP and amyloid-beta fragments bind transition metals, especially copper and zinc, linking the ectodomain and cleavage products to metal homeostasis and redox biology. In Alzheimer disease, familial APP variants and APP dosage alter amyloidogenic processing and the production or aggregation of amyloid-beta species.

Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT; EC 2.4.2.7) is the cytosolic enzyme of the purine salvage pathway that catalyzes the transfer of the phosphoribosyl group of 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP) to adenine, producing AMP and diphosphate. This single-step reaction recycles free adenine - notably the adenine released as a byproduct of polyamine biosynthesis, as well as adenine of dietary origin - into the adenine nucleotide pool at lower energetic cost than de novo synthesis. APRT is a homodimer belonging to the type I purine/pyrimidine phosphoribosyltransferase family and, like other type I PRTases, uses a magnesium-PRPP complex; it is expressed ubiquitously and acts in the cytosol. Loss of APRT function causes adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency (APRTD), an autosomal recessive disorder in which unsalvaged adenine is instead oxidized by xanthine dehydrogenase to the highly insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (2,8-DHA); precipitation of 2,8-DHA in the urinary tract and renal parenchyma produces 2,8-DHA nephrolithiasis, crystalline nephropathy, and progressive renal failure.

The androgen receptor (AR; NR3C4) is an intracellular steroid receptor with an N-terminal transcriptional activation domain containing a polymorphic polyglutamine tract, a zinc-finger DNA-binding domain and a C-terminal ligand-binding domain. Full-length AR recognizes androgens, moves between cytosolic and nuclear pools, binds regulatory DNA and recruits context-dependent coactivators or corepressors to control transcription. It supports male sexual differentiation, reproductive function and tissue-specific androgen responses. Alternative products, including AR-V7, can alter ligand dependence and transcriptional behavior. The disordered activation domain supports molecular condensation as one mode of receptor assembly. Loss-of-function variants cause androgen insensitivity, whereas expansion of the CAG-encoded polyglutamine tract causes spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy. Dysregulated AR signaling, including altered abundance, ligand responses and splice products, contributes to prostate cancer progression.

A-Raf (ARAF) is one of the three RAF-family serine/threonine protein kinases (with BRAF and RAF1/CRAF) that act as MAP kinase kinase kinases in the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK/ERK) cascade. It has an N-terminal RAS-binding domain and cysteine-rich C1-like domain (CR1), a Ser/Thr-rich regulatory region carrying the inhibitory 14-3-3 site Ser-214 (CR2), and a C-terminal protein kinase domain (CR3). In resting cells ARAF is held in an autoinhibited cytosolic complex with 14-3-3 proteins and the HSP90/CDC37 chaperone; RAS-GTP recruits it to the plasma membrane, where Ser-214 dephosphorylation (by PP2A or the SHOC2-MRAS-PP1C complex) and side-to-side homo- or heterodimerization with BRAF or CRAF activate it to phosphorylate the activation loops of MEK1/MEK2 (MAP2K1/MAP2K2). ARAF is the least catalytically active RAF paralog, but it sustains RAS-driven ERK signalling in some contexts and can confer resistance to BRAF/CRAF-selective inhibitors. A fraction of ARAF localises to mitochondria, where it restrains apoptosis largely independently of its kinase activity, notably by sequestering the pro-apoptotic kinase MST2. Activating somatic ARAF mutations occur in lung adenocarcinoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and central conducting lymphatic anomaly. A short splice isoform (DA-Raf1) lacking the kinase domain acts as a dominant-negative RAS antagonist.

ARC (activity-regulated cytoskeleton-associated protein, Arg3.1) is a neuronal immediate-early gene product that is, structurally and functionally, a domesticated retrotransposon capsid protein. Its 396-residue chain folds into two lobes whose arrangement matches the capsid domain of retroviral Gag polyproteins, and tetrapod Arc genes derive from a vertebrate lineage of Ty3/gypsy retrotransposons; fly Arc genes come from a separate insect lineage of the same element family, so the two are convergent domestications rather than orthologues of a single cellular ancestor. The protein does two things that reflect that ancestry. First, it self-assembles. A short helical coil in the N-terminal domain drives oligomerisation beyond the dimer stage, and the assembled protein forms double-shelled capsids roughly 32 nm across that encapsidate RNA. RNA is required for efficient assembly, and the RNA taken up is not sequence-selective - abundant transcripts are packaged roughly in proportion to their abundance, with Arc's own mRNA prominent because it is abundant where Arc is made. Neurons release these capsids in extracellular vesicles; recipient neurons endocytose them, and the delivered mRNA reaches the cytoplasm where it can be translated on demand. Arc is therefore a vehicle for intercellular RNA transfer in the nervous system. Second, Arc weakens synapses. Induced within minutes of strong activity and delivered as mRNA to stimulated dendritic regions, the protein accumulates at the postsynaptic density and the lateral margins of dendritic spines, anchored to the membrane by palmitoylation of an N-terminal cysteine cluster rather than by a transmembrane segment. There it binds endophilin 2/3 and dynamin 2 through separate regions and accelerates clathrin- and dynamin-dependent endocytosis of AMPA-type glutamate receptors into early endosomes. Losing Arc raises surface AMPA receptor levels and slows their internalisation; raising Arc does the reverse. This single mechanism underlies the late, protein-synthesis-dependent phase of long-term potentiation, metabotropic-receptor long-term depression, homeostatic downscaling of synaptic strength during chronic inactivity, and the consolidation of long-term memory. Targeting is paradoxical and deliberate: CaMKII-beta in its calmodulin-free state recruits Arc preferentially to synapses that have fallen silent, so the protein prunes the weak rather than the active. A separate nuclear pool, controlled by a dedicated localisation signal, retention domain and export signal, raises promyelocytic leukaemia body formation and lowers GluA1 transcription, giving the same downscaling by a transcriptional route. During cerebellar development Arc mediates the final stage of climbing-fibre synapse elimination. Both activities depend on the same interface. Mutating the seven-residue oligomerisation motif abolishes capsid formation and also blocks Arc-facilitated endocytosis; CaMKII phosphorylation of the Gag N-lobe disrupts the same surface and switches high-order assembly off. Protein levels are held brief by ubiquitination - by RNF216/Triad3A at two adjacent lysines, and by UBE3A - so that the signal is transient. Outside the nervous system, Arc is confined to skin-migratory dendritic cells, where it accelerates migration through myosin II-dependent actin dynamics and thereby shapes T-cell activation.

Arginase-1 is a cytosolic, manganese-dependent ureohydrolase that converts L-arginine and water to L-ornithine and urea. This homotrimeric enzyme contains a binuclear manganese cluster in each subunit and catalyzes the terminal step of the hepatic urea cycle, regenerating ornithine for nitrogen disposal. In human granulocytes it is stored in granules and can be released extracellularly, where arginine depletion suppresses T-cell proliferation and cytokine production. Granulocyte ARG1 also contributes to fungicidal activity; arginine depletion within the phagolysosome has been proposed as its antimicrobial mechanism. Loss-of-function variants cause arginase deficiency with hyperargininemia and progressive neurological disease.

ARL3 (ADP-ribosylation factor-like 3) is a small Arf-family GTPase that acts as a cargo-release factor for lipidated ciliary proteins. In its GDP-bound form it is inactive. Inside the cilium it is loaded with GTP by its ciliary guanine nucleotide exchange factor ARL13B. ARL3-GTP binds the lipid-binding carrier proteins PDE6D (PDEdelta, for farnesylated/prenylated cargo such as INPP5E, GRK1, PDE6 subunits) and UNC119A/B (for myristoylated cargo such as NPHP3, transducin-alpha, cystin). This binding releases the cargo, so that lipidated proteins are deposited in the ciliary membrane. Because ARL13B is ciliary and the GTPase-activating protein RP2 is concentrated at the ciliary base and in the cytoplasm, ARL3 activity is polarized: cargo is released inside the cilium and the carriers are recycled after RP2 stimulates GTP hydrolysis. ARL3 also binds ARL2BP/BART and the BART-like protein CFAP36/BARTL1 through its N-terminal amphipathic helix. It is found in the cilium (prominently the photoreceptor connecting cilium), at centrosomes, on mitotic spindles and midbodies, at the Golgi, and in the cytoplasm and nucleus. ARL3 depletion impairs cytokinesis in HeLa cells. ARL3 variants cause Joubert syndrome and inherited retinal dystrophy, and mouse Arl3 loss causes photoreceptor degeneration and renal cysts.

ARL6IP1 (also known as ARMER) is an ER membrane-shaping protein that contains reticulon-like hairpin transmembrane domains. Its primary function is generating positive membrane curvature to promote and stabilize tubular ER formation. ARL6IP1 binds to atlastin (ATL1) and recruits the inositol 5-phosphatase INPP5K to ER tubules. Loss of ARL6IP1 shifts ER architecture from tubules to sheets. In neurons, it is essential for smooth ER integrity within axons, coupling ER organization to mitochondrial dynamics at distal axon ends. Mutations cause autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 61 (SPG61). The anti-apoptotic activity initially reported (hence the "ARMER" name) is likely a secondary consequence of its role in ER homeostasis rather than a direct apoptosis regulatory function.

ARPC1B is the p41-Arc WD-repeat subunit of the seven-subunit Arp2/3 complex. It supports regulated branched actin-network assembly and cortical actin organization, including WASP-stimulated polymerization in human B cells. ARPC1B-containing complexes have distinct activation and disassembly properties from ARPC1A-containing complexes. ARPC1B is enriched in hematopoietic cells and is a major ARPC1 isoform in platelets. Biallelic loss causes immunodeficiency with inflammatory disease and congenital thrombocytopenia, with defects in platelet and immune-cell actin organization.

ARSA (arylsulfatase A; cerebroside-sulfatase, EC 3.1.6.8) is a lysosomal enzyme that removes sulfate from sulfatide to produce galactosylceramide and sulfate. Saposin B presents the lipid substrate, while a catalytic formylglycine residue derived from Cys69 and an active-site calcium ion support hydrolysis. ARSA also desulfates other sulfated glycosphingolipids, including lactosylceramide sulfate. It matures in the endoplasmic reticulum and is delivered through the mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathway to acidic degradative compartments. Deficient ARSA activity causes sulfatide storage and the demyelinating disorder metachromatic leukodystrophy.

ARSB (arylsulfatase B; N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase) is a lysosomal enzyme that removes 4-sulfate groups from N-acetylgalactosamine residues during degradation of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate. A calcium-containing active site and a catalytic formylglycine residue support sulfate-ester hydrolysis. ARSB matures through the secretory pathway and reaches lysosomes through mannose-6-phosphate-dependent delivery. Its effects on sulfated glycans can influence extracellular matrix properties and cell behavior. Deficient ARSB activity causes mucopolysaccharidosis VI (Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome).

ARSL (arylsulfatase L, formerly ARSE) is a glycosylated sulfatase that acts in the Golgi lumen. It promotes removal of the 4-O-sulfate from chondroitin sulfate chains during proteoglycan maturation, linking glycan sulfation to cartilage and bone development. Its full physiological substrate range remains incompletely defined. Activity depends on a conserved catalytic cysteine that undergoes formylglycine maturation. ARSL also hydrolyzes artificial aryl-sulfate substrates. Pathogenic loss of function causes X-linked recessive chondrodysplasia punctata, with abnormal cartilage development and skeletal mineralization.

ASAH1 encodes acid ceramidase, a soluble lysosomal N-terminal nucleophile hydrolase that cleaves ceramide into sphingosine and a free fatty acid at acidic pH. A glycosylated precursor undergoes autocleavage into disulfide-linked alpha and beta subunits, exposing catalytic Cys143 at the beta-subunit N terminus. Mannose-6-phosphate-dependent trafficking delivers the enzyme to the endolysosomal system, where saposin D facilitates access to membrane ceramide. Acid ceramidase shapes cellular ceramide and sphingosine pools; substrate preferences depend on ceramide structure and assay conditions. Cellular studies also support glycosphingolipid deacylation when lysosomal glycosidases are deficient. Secreted and nuclear pools occur in particular settings, including an interaction with the nuclear receptor SF-1 in adrenocortical cells. Pathogenic ASAH1 variants cause a spectrum including Farber disease and spinal muscular atrophy with or without progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

ASCL1 (Achaete-scute homolog 1, also known as MASH1/hASH1) is a proneural basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor that functions as both a classical transcriptional activator and a pioneer factor capable of accessing closed chromatin. It binds E-box motifs (CANNTG, particularly CACCTG) as a heterodimer with E-proteins (TCF3/E12/E47, TCF4) to activate neuronal and neuroendocrine gene programs. ASCL1 plays essential roles in neuronal differentiation, neuronal fate commitment, and neuroendocrine cell development. It is a master regulator of the SCLC-A (neuroendocrine) subtype of small cell lung cancer and directly activates targets including INSM1, MYT1, DLL1, and DLL3 (Notch pathway modulators). ASCL1 protein stability is regulated by CDK2-CyclinA2 phosphorylation, HUWE1-mediated ubiquitination, and protection via E-protein heterodimerization.

Argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) is a cytosolic homotetramer that catalyzes the reversible cleavage of argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. It acts downstream of argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1) in the urea cycle and supplies arginine in other tissues. Catalytic sites contain contributions from multiple ASL subunits, allowing some combinations of defective alleles to recover activity through intragenic complementation. ASL also provides structural support for nitric oxide synthase (NOS) assemblies involving ASS1, the arginine transporter SLC7A1/CAT-1 and HSP90. This role supports efficient use of extracellular arginine for nitric oxide production independently of ASL-mediated arginine synthesis; the NOS isoform and assembly context vary by tissue. Pathogenic variants cause argininosuccinic aciduria, a urea-cycle disorder with hyperammonemia and hepatic, neurological and vascular manifestations that can persist despite ammonia control. Impaired nitric oxide production contributes to vascular dysfunction but does not explain every manifestation.

GET3 (ASNA1; also known as TRC40 and arsenite-stimulated ATPase) is the central cytosolic ATPase of the GET/TRC pathway for post-translational targeting of tail-anchored (TA) membrane proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). It is a homodimeric P-loop NTPase of the ArsA/ArsA-like ATPase family. GET3 selectively recognizes and binds the single C-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) of newly synthesized TA proteins in the cytosol, receiving them via the BAG6/UBL4A/GET4 pre-targeting and bridging machinery (and from the cochaperone SGTA), and shields the hydrophobic TMD as a soluble carrier/chaperone. ATP binding drives the homodimer into a closed state that captures the substrate; the GET3-TA complex then docks at the ER-membrane receptor-insertase formed by GET1/WRB and CAMLG/GET2, and ATP hydrolysis triggers TA release for insertion into the lipid bilayer, after which GET3 returns to the cytosol for another round. GET3 is thus the targeting factor and TMD chaperone of the pathway, not the membrane insertase itself. It was originally isolated as the human homolog of bacterial ArsA, an arsenite/antimonite-stimulated ATPase, but its physiological role is TA-protein biogenesis. Loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal recessive, rapidly progressive infantile dilated cardiomyopathy. GET3 acts predominantly in the cytoplasm and transiently at the ER membrane.

ASNS is a cytosolic enzyme that makes L-asparagine from L-aspartate, glutamine and ATP. Its N-terminal glutaminase domain supplies nitrogen to the C-terminal synthetase domain, coupling glutamine hydrolysis to asparagine formation; human structural studies support a homodimer. The enzyme supplies asparagine for cellular metabolism and growth. Its expression responds to nutrient availability, and particular cancer-cell experiments link ASNS to survival during glucose deprivation and some drug treatments. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause asparagine synthetase deficiency, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, developmental impairment and seizures.

ASPA is a zinc-dependent aspartoacylase that hydrolyzes the amide bond of N-acetyl-L-aspartate, producing acetate and L-aspartate. Its soluble catalytic activity contributes directly to aspartate and acetate metabolism. The enzyme also accepts selected other N-acyl-L-aspartates in vitro. Its active site lies between an N-terminal metallohydrolase-like domain and a C-terminal domain that shapes substrate access. ASPA is expressed in brain white matter, where loss of its activity causes Canavan disease, a leukodystrophy with white-matter degeneration.

ASS1 encodes argininosuccinate synthase, a predominantly cytosolic homotetrameric ligase that catalyzes the ATP-dependent condensation of L-citrulline and L-aspartate to form argininosuccinate, AMP and diphosphate. Argininosuccinate is then cleaved by ASL to produce arginine and fumarate. ASS1 therefore directly supports hepatic nitrogen disposal through the urea cycle and L-arginine synthesis in other tissues. In endothelial cells, regeneration of arginine from citrulline supports nitric oxide production by nitric oxide synthase. ASS1 activity can be regulated by protein interactions and acetylation, including CLOCK-dependent modification associated with circadian ureagenesis. Peripheral mitochondrial association has been reported in rodent tissues, and nuclear localization has been demonstrated in particular human cell contexts. Pathogenic ASS1 variants cause autosomal recessive citrullinemia type I.

ATF4 (Activating Transcription Factor 4) is a bZIP transcription factor that serves as the central effector of the Integrated Stress Response (ISR). Under basal conditions, ATF4 translation is suppressed by upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in its 5'UTR. Upon cellular stress (ER stress, amino acid deprivation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial stress), phosphorylation of eIF2alpha by stress-sensing kinases (PERK, GCN2, HRI, PKR) leads to preferential translation of ATF4. In the nucleus, ATF4 heterodimerizes with other bZIP transcription factors (CHOP/DDIT3, C/EBP family members, CREB, ATF3) via its leucine zipper domain and binds to cAMP response elements (CRE) and C/EBP-ATF response elements (CARE/AARE) to activate transcription of stress-responsive genes involved in amino acid metabolism (ASNS, SLC7A11), redox homeostasis, autophagy, and apoptosis. ATF4 also plays non-stress roles in osteoblast differentiation and bone development.

ATF6 is a basic leucine zipper transcription factor synthesized as a type II endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein. During ER stress, the precursor moves to the Golgi, where MBTPS1 and MBTPS2 cleave it to release the N-terminal transcription factor. The released product enters the nucleus, binds ER-stress response regulatory DNA and activates genes encoding chaperones, folding machinery and components of ER-associated degradation. ATF6 also induces XBP1 transcription, coordinating branches of the unfolded protein response. Biallelic pathogenic ATF6 variants cause achromatopsia with impaired cone function and foveal development.

ATIC (bifunctional purine biosynthesis protein; AICAR transformylase / IMP cyclohydrolase, also known as PURH) is a cytosolic homodimeric enzyme that catalyzes the final two steps of de novo purine (IMP) biosynthesis. Its AICAR transformylase activity (EC 2.1.2.3) transfers a formyl group from 10-formyltetrahydrofolate to 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR), producing 5-formamido-AICAR (FAICAR); its IMP cyclohydrolase activity (EC 3.5.4.10) then cyclizes FAICAR to inosine 5'-monophosphate (IMP) plus water. The two catalytic activities reside on a single polypeptide in all species studied, with the IMP cyclohydrolase activity in the N-terminal MGS-like region (approximately residues 1-198) and the AICAR transformylase activity in the C-terminal region (approximately residues 199-592); the transformylase active site is formed at the dimer interface. The cyclohydrolase step is essentially irreversible and drives the otherwise unfavorable overall conversion of AICAR to IMP toward completion. Because the transformylase step is folate-dependent, ATIC is a pharmacological target of antifolates: the AICAR-transformylase activity is inhibited by methotrexate polyglutamates and pemetrexed and by nonclassical antifolates developed for tumor suppression, and elevated AICAR (as with the AMPK-activating AICA-riboside) reflects this node in folate/purine metabolism. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ATIC cause AICA-ribosiduria, an extremely rare autosomal-recessive inborn error of purine biosynthesis characterized by profound intellectual disability, epilepsy, dysmorphic features and congenital blindness, with massive urinary excretion and tissue accumulation of AICA-riboside/AICA-ribotide.

ATM is a large phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-related protein serine/threonine kinase that coordinates cellular responses to DNA double-strand breaks. Recruitment and activation linked to the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex enable phosphorylation of checkpoint and repair proteins, including p53, H2AX and CHEK2, helping coordinate cell-cycle arrest, DNA repair and damage-induced cell fate decisions. ATM also regulates telomere maintenance and responds to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Its predominant nuclear activity is complemented by regulated extranuclear pools, including ATM associated with the cytosolic surface of peroxisomal membranes during ROS signaling.

ATP1A1 encodes the catalytic alpha1 subunit of the sodium/potassium ATPase, a widely expressed P-type ion pump in the plasma membrane. Its transmembrane ion-binding sites and cytoplasmic ATPase domains couple ATP hydrolysis to export of three sodium ions and import of two potassium ions. Alpha1 assembles with a beta subunit and can associate with FXYD regulatory proteins. This electrogenic exchange maintains sodium and potassium gradients that support membrane potential, cell-volume control and secondary transport. Membrane polarity and partner-dependent regulation vary between tissues.

ATP1A2 encodes the catalytic alpha2 subunit of the sodium/potassium ATPase. In association with beta subunits, it uses ATP to export sodium and import potassium across the plasma membrane. Its ion gradients support excitability, muscle calcium handling and glial neurotransmitter clearance. Loss of pump function is associated with familial hemiplegic migraine and related neurological phenotypes.

ATP1A3 encodes the catalytic alpha3 subunit of the sodium-potassium pump, a multipass plasma-membrane P-type ATPase that couples ATP hydrolysis to sodium export and potassium import. Alpha3 assembles with a beta subunit and can associate with an FXYD regulatory protein. Its activity sustains ion gradients and membrane potential in neurons and other expressing cells. Disease-associated variants can impair pump activity or stability, producing neurological disorders. Cardiac glycosides inhibit the pump, and pathological amyloid assemblies can bind alpha3 and disrupt neuronal ion homeostasis.

ATP2B2 encodes plasma membrane calcium ATPase 2 (PMCA2), a multipass P-type pump that uses ATP hydrolysis to export calcium from the cytosol. Its ATP-dependent phosphorylation cycle helps restore low cytosolic calcium after cellular activity. Alternative splicing of the first intracellular loop and C-terminal regulatory region changes targeting and regulation. In sensory hair cells, PMCA2 exports calcium from stereocilia into endolymph, helping restore calcium levels after mechanotransduction. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants can cause autosomal dominant deafness 82 (DFNA82); other variants have been described as hearing-loss modifiers. Calmodulin regulates the pump through its cytoplasmic regulatory region.

ATP5F1E is the epsilon subunit of the F1 catalytic head of mitochondrial ATP synthase (Complex V, F1Fo-ATP synthase), a nuclear-encoded 51-residue protein. Together with the gamma and delta subunits it forms the central stalk that rotates inside the alpha3beta3 catalytic head, coupling proton translocation through the membrane Fo sector to ATP synthesis in F1. Epsilon is a structural, non-catalytic subunit: it does not itself carry out ATP synthesis but is required for assembly and biogenesis of the F1 part, including incorporation of subunit c into the c-ring rotor. The complex is embedded in the mitochondrial inner membrane, with the F1 head projecting into the matrix. In vivo the enzyme synthesizes ATP driven by the proton-motive force generated by the respiratory chain; its ATP-hydrolase activity is only an artificial in-vitro reversal. Loss-of-function variants (e.g. p.Tyr12Cys) cause mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency, nuclear type 3, presenting with lactic acidosis, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, and peripheral neuropathy.

ATP6V1A encodes the catalytic A subunit of the V1 peripheral domain of the vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (V-ATPase), the principal ATP-driven proton pump of eukaryotic cells. The V1 domain hydrolyzes ATP; subunit A forms three catalytic AB heterodimers that together with subunit B create the hexameric ring responsible for ATP hydrolysis, whose energy is transduced via a central rotor to drive proton translocation through the membrane-embedded V0 domain. V-ATPase is the primary source of organellar acidification in all eukaryotes, acidifying lysosomes, endosomes, the Golgi apparatus, and secretory vesicles; in specialized cells it is also found at the plasma membrane. ATP6V1A is expressed ubiquitously, with high expression in the skin and neurons. In neurons, V-ATPase plays additional roles in neurotransmitter loading into synaptic vesicles and in regulating synaptic transmission. Through its role in lysosomal acidification, V-ATPase (with subunit A as catalytic core) is required for activation of mTORC1 by amino acids at the lysosomal surface, for intracellular iron homeostasis via endosomal transferrin processing, and for autophagic flux. De novo heterozygous ATP6V1A mutations cause a developmental encephalopathy with epilepsy (IECEE3), while biallelic loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive cutis laxa type 2D (ARCL2D).

ATP6V1B1 encodes the B1 isoform of the non-catalytic B subunit of the V-ATPase V1 sector. B1 supports assembly and operation of the ATP-driven proton pump rather than independently hydrolyzing ATP or forming a proton pore. In renal epithelia, B1-containing pumps at the apical membrane contribute to urinary acidification and systemic acid-base balance. B1 is also expressed in the cochlea and endolymphatic sac, and pathogenic variants cause distal renal tubular acidosis with sensorineural hearing loss. Its conserved nucleotide-binding property is inferred from related B subunits, while disease-associated B1 variants can disrupt complex assembly and trafficking.

ATP6V1B2 encodes the non-catalytic B subunit (brain isoform, B2) of the V1 peripheral domain of the vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (V-ATPase). The V1 complex hydrolyzes ATP to power proton translocation through the membrane-embedded V0 domain. Three non-catalytic B2 subunits alternate with three catalytic A subunits (ATP6V1A) to form the catalytic AB heterohexameric ring of V1. ATP6V1B2 is the ubiquitously expressed isoform of the B subunit, in contrast to the kidney-specific B1 isoform (ATP6V1B1). V-ATPase acidifies lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi, and secretory vesicles in all cell types; in specialized cells including renal intercalated cells and melanocytes, it is found at the apical plasma membrane and in melanosomes respectively. ATP6V1B2 can partially compensate for ATP6V1B1 in renal intercalated cells under baseline conditions but not under conditions of acid load. Dominant mutations in ATP6V1B2 cause two allelic syndromes: DDOD (dominant deafness-onychodystrophy syndrome, MIM:124480) and Zimmermann-Laband syndrome type 2 (ZLS2, MIM:616455).

ATP6V0C encodes the 16 kDa proteolipid subunit c of the V0 domain of vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase). This small (155 amino acid) integral membrane protein with four transmembrane helices is a core structural component of the proton-conducting c-ring rotor. Nine copies of ATP6V0C assemble with one copy of ATP6V0B (subunit c'') to form the complete c-ring within the V0 membrane domain. The c-ring rotates during ATP hydrolysis by the V1 domain, enabling proton translocation across membranes via a conserved glutamate residue (E139) that serves as the proton-binding site. ATP6V0C-containing V-ATPases acidify lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi, synaptic vesicles, and secretory granules, and in specialized cells (osteoclasts, kidney intercalated cells) also function at the plasma membrane. ATP6V0C is the binding target of the V-ATPase inhibitor bafilomycin A1. Heterozygous pathogenic variants in ATP6V0C cause early-onset epilepsy with or without developmental delay (EPEO3, OMIM 620465).

ATP6V0A1 encodes the a1 isoform of the V0 membrane sector of the vacuolar H+-ATPase. It is a multi-pass membrane subunit that helps assemble the proton-translocation sector of V-ATPase complexes on endolysosomal, synaptic vesicle, secretory vesicle, melanosomal, and specialized plasma membranes. By contributing to ATP-driven proton transport, ATP6V0A1 supports acidification of lysosomes, endosomes, synaptic vesicles, and related organelles; pathogenic variants impair endolysosomal acidification and cause severe neurodevelopmental disease with synaptic and autophagy defects.

ATP6V0A4 encodes the a4 isoform of the membrane-integral a subunit of the V-type proton ATPase V0 sector. The protein is a multi-pass V-ATPase component that helps couple ATP hydrolysis in the V1 sector to proton translocation through V0. It is especially important in renal acid-base physiology, where a4-containing pumps are targeted to apical membranes of intercalated cells and other nephron segments to support urinary acidification, and it is also expressed in the inner ear where loss of function can contribute to sensorineural hearing loss. Like other V-ATPase a subunits, ATP6V0A4 participates in acidification of membrane-bounded compartments and specialized extracellular-facing membranes, with its best-supported human roles centered on kidney proton secretion and V-ATPase assembly/coupling.

ATP6AP1 encodes Ac45, a single-pass glycoprotein accessory subunit of the vacuolar H+-ATPase. Ac45 remains within the membrane V0 sector, where its contacts with other subunits support pump assembly and stability. Its assembly and compartment-targeting roles contribute to endolysosomal acidification and specialized secretory functions. In human hepatocytes it also localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum and ER-Golgi intermediate compartment. The lysosomal V-ATPase complex couples amino-acid availability to Ragulator/Rag-dependent mTORC1 signaling. Its cytosolic C-terminal tail also promotes Rheb GTP loading in biochemical and cellular experiments, a mechanism reported as unconventional GEF activity and linked to growth-factor-dependent mTORC1 signaling. Pathogenic ATP6AP1 variants cause an X-linked glycosylation disorder with immunodeficiency, hepatopathy and variable neurological features.

ATP7A is an ATP-driven Cu(I)-transporting P-type ATPase that supplies copper to secretory-pathway cuproenzymes and promotes cellular copper export. It resides predominantly at the trans-Golgi network under basal conditions and undergoes copper-responsive cycling through vesicular compartments and the plasma membrane. Copper delivery supports the activity of enzymes involved in pigmentation, catecholamine metabolism and connective-tissue maintenance, as well as neuronal copper homeostasis.

ATP7B is a P1B-type copper(I)-transporting ATPase (EC 7.2.2.8) that uses ATP hydrolysis to move cytosolic copper into the secretory and vesicular pathways. At the trans-Golgi network it supplies copper for secretory cuproproteins, including ceruloplasmin. Elevated copper promotes redistribution to post-Golgi compartments, where copper sequestration and subsequent exocytosis contribute to copper detoxification and biliary elimination. Six amino-terminal heavy metal-associated domains receive copper from ATOX1 and participate in regulation of the transport cycle; the transmembrane CPC motif is essential for transport. ATP7B localization varies with cell type, copper conditions and protein product. Loss of ATP7B function causes Wilson disease (MIM:277900), with impaired copper homeostasis and progressive copper accumulation, particularly in liver and brain.

ALDH7A1 (antiquitin) is a homomeric NAD+-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase. It oxidizes alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde (AASA), which equilibrates with delta-1-piperideine-6-carboxylate (P6C), to alpha-aminoadipate in L-lysine degradation. Mitochondrial and cytosolic forms are characterized, with an additional nuclear pool. The enzyme also oxidizes medium-chain and lipid-peroxidation-derived aldehydes and can use betaine aldehyde as a substrate. Stress-regulated membrane recruitment supports local NADH production: at Golgi membranes NADH inhibits BARS-dependent carrier fission, and membrane ALDH7A1 supports AIFM2/FSP1-mediated ferroptosis protection while also consuming reactive aldehydes. ALDH7A1 supplies NADH and promotes FSP1 recruitment; FSP1 performs quinone reduction. Human enzyme structures and solution studies connect active tetramer formation to catalysis. Biallelic pathogenic variants impair AASA oxidation to varying degrees, causing substrate accumulation and pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy associated with P6C-mediated inactivation of pyridoxal phosphate.

ATRX is a nuclear SNF2-family ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler. Its full-length protein combines an N-terminal ADD histone-recognition domain with a C-terminal ATPase motor. The ADD domain recognizes H3K9 trimethylation in the context of an unmethylated H3K4, and interactions with HP1 and other chromatin proteins aid targeting. Together with DAXX, ATRX organizes H3.3-containing chromatin at repetitive genomic regions, including pericentric and telomeric sites. The ADD domain also binds the histone-fold region of macroH2A, and ATRX limits macroH2A chromatin accumulation at selected loci. ATRX also protects susceptible genomic regions during replication. The PIP motif contributes to protection against genome-wide replication stress, whereas ATPase activity suppresses telomeric single-stranded DNA in tested human-cell contexts. Dependence on DAXX varies with the chromatin context and endpoint. These activities support chromatin organization and genome stability. Pathogenic germline variants cause ATR-X syndrome, while somatic ATRX loss is associated with alternative telomere maintenance in some tumors.

KIF1A encodes a neuron-specific kinesin-3 (Unc-104 subfamily) motor. An N-terminal motor domain with neck coil is followed by a regulatory CC1-FHA-CC2 region that controls autoinhibition and dimerization, and a C-terminal cargo-binding region ending in a PH domain. Activated KIF1A dimers move rapidly and processively toward microtubule plus ends, carrying synaptic vesicle precursors down the axon to presynaptic sites and transporting dense core vesicles in axons and dendrites, where Ca2+/calmodulin enhances cargo binding and scaffolds such as liprin-alpha and TANC2 capture vesicles at synapses. In radial glial progenitors of the developing cortex, KIF1A acts at the nuclear surface to drive basally directed interkinetic nuclear migration, opposing dynein-driven apical movement. Heterozygous and biallelic KIF1A variants cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder, spanning spastic paraplegia (SPG30), hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy (HSN2C), and NESCAV syndrome with intellectual disability, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy.

AUH is a mitochondrial methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase of the crotonase superfamily. It catalyzes the reversible hydration of 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA during leucine degradation. The protein forms a hexamer and also binds AU-rich RNA sequences through a positively charged surface. In human cells, AUH associates with mitochondrial RNA and ribosomes; altered AUH abundance perturbs mitochondrial protein synthesis. The physiological compartment and RNA targets of the classical AU-rich transcript-binding activity remain unresolved. A secondary itaconyl-CoA hydratase activity has been attributed to AUH in the mitochondrial C5-dicarboxylate pathway. Loss of its leucine-pathway activity causes 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type 1.

AXIN1 (Axis inhibition protein 1) is a cytosolic scaffold protein that serves as the core component of the beta-catenin destruction complex, which also includes APC, GSK3B, and CK1. AXIN1 coordinates the phosphorylation and subsequent ubiquitination of beta-catenin, thereby negatively regulating the canonical Wnt signaling pathway. Key functional domains include: an N-terminal tankyrase-binding motif, an RGS domain for APC binding, a GSK3B-binding helix (aa 383-400), a beta-catenin binding region, and a C-terminal DIX domain that mediates polymerization and formation of cytoplasmic condensates ("degradasomes"). AXIN1 is regulated by tankyrase-mediated ADP-ribosylation followed by RNF146-dependent ubiquitination and degradation. Loss-of-function mutations in AXIN1 are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma due to aberrant Wnt pathway activation. AXIN1 also has secondary roles in TGF-beta signaling (promoting Smad7 degradation via Arkadia) and JNK signaling, and participates in the AXIN1-HIPK2-TP53 complex upon UV irradiation.

AXIN2 (conductin) is a nonenzymatic scaffold of the cytosolic beta-catenin destruction complex. It organizes beta-catenin with APC and regulatory kinases, promoting beta-catenin phosphorylation and subsequent ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal turnover. Induction of AXIN2 by beta-catenin/TCF establishes negative feedback on canonical Wnt signaling. AXIN2 also occurs in nuclei and at centrosomes in defined cellular contexts; centrosomal AXIN2 coordinates GSK3-dependent beta-catenin phosphorylation to restrain premature centrosome separation. Changes in AXIN2 signaling contribute to developmental phenotypes, including tooth agenesis, and to tumor susceptibility.

B4GALT1 is a manganese-dependent, type II membrane glycosyltransferase of CAZy family GT7, with a lumen-facing catalytic domain concentrated in trans-Golgi cisternae. It transfers galactose from UDP-galactose in a beta-1,4 linkage to terminal N-acetylglucosamine residues on glycoproteins (EC 2.4.1.38), supporting complex N-glycan maturation. It also forms N-acetyllactosamine from free N-acetylglucosamine (EC 2.4.1.90) and can use selected glycolipid acceptors. In lactating mammary cells, a 1:1 complex with alpha-lactalbumin promotes glucose binding and enables lactose synthesis (EC 2.4.1.22). Alternative initiation produces long and short forms differing by a 13-residue cytoplasmic extension. Both can localize to the Golgi; the long form also contributes to a cell-surface pool, with relative targeting dependent on cellular context. Catalytically active soluble enzyme is found in human body fluids. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause B4GALT1 congenital disorder of glycosylation. The p.Asn352Ser hypomorph has reduced activity and is associated with altered serum glycoprotein glycans and lower LDL cholesterol and fibrinogen concentrations.

B4GALT7 encodes a 327-residue, manganese-dependent type-II Golgi membrane glycosyltransferase of the GT7 family. Its lumen-facing catalytic domain transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to xylose attached to a serine of a proteoglycan core protein, forming a beta1,4 linkage. This first galactose is the second sugar of the shared tetrasaccharide linker used to assemble chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin proteoglycans. Defective linker synthesis impairs proteoglycan glycanation and extracellular-matrix organization; biallelic pathogenic variants cause a spondylodysplastic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

BAAT is the human bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase (EC 2.3.1.65), the enzyme that catalyzes the final conjugation (amidation) step of bile-acid synthesis. It transfers the bile acid moiety from its CoA thioester (a bile-acyl-CoA such as choloyl-CoA or chenodeoxycholoyl-CoA, generated upstream by the bile acyl-CoA synthetase SLC27A5) onto the amino group of glycine or taurine, producing the glyco- and tauro-conjugated bile acids that constitute the major secreted and biliary forms. A single monomeric enzyme carries out conjugation with both glycine and taurine. Catalysis uses a Cys-235/Asp-328/His-362 charge-relay (catalytic triad) characteristic of the C/M/P thioester hydrolase (alpha/beta hydrolase) family, with Cys-235 as the nucleophile that forms a covalent bile acid-enzyme intermediate. The same active site confers a secondary bile-acyl-CoA thioesterase/hydrolase activity (choloyl-CoA hydrolase, EC 3.1.2.27); in vitro the recombinant enzyme also hydrolyzes long- and very long-chain acyl-CoAs and conjugates fatty acids to glycine. BAAT is a liver-enriched enzyme localized to the peroxisome and the cytosol (endogenous hepatocyte enzyme is predominantly peroxisomal, with a cell-type-dependent cytosolic pool). Loss-of-function variants cause familial hypercholanemia (FHCA3), an autosomal-recessive bile-acid conjugation defect marked by accumulation of unconjugated bile acids, fat malabsorption, fat-soluble-vitamin deficiency, and growth failure.

BAG3 is a human BAG-family co-chaperone that coordinates Hsp70-family and small heat-shock proteins. Its BAG domain regulates Hsp70 nucleotide exchange, while its IPV motifs recruit small heat-shock proteins including HSPB8 and HSPB1. This modular organization supports chaperone-assisted folding and routes damaged clients toward selective autophagy. BAG3 also couples Hsp70-associated cargo to dynein for transport to aggresomes. It acts mainly in the cytoplasm and at muscle Z-discs, where it helps maintain protein integrity under mechanical stress. Stress-dependent nuclear localization supports HSF1 regulation, and BAG3 can modulate cell survival in specific contexts.

BAR/IMD domain-containing adapter protein 2 (IRSp53) is a curvature-sensitive membrane-cytoskeleton adaptor that couples plasma membrane shape to actin remodeling. The protein contains an N-terminal I-BAR/IMD domain that senses and generates negative membrane curvature by binding PI(4,5)P2-rich membranes, a central CRIB/proline-rich region for small GTPase (Rac1/Cdc42) coupling, and a C-terminal SH3 domain that recruits actin nucleation-promoting factors (WAVE, N-WASP, Eps8, Mena/VASP). IRSp53 integrates Rho-family GTPase signaling with actin network assembly to drive filopodia, lamellipodia, and membrane ruffles, and is held in an autoinhibited conformation by 14-3-3 binding to a phosphorylated region between the CRIB and SH3 modules. The protein is enriched at plasma membrane protrusions and at sites of negative membrane curvature, where it couples membrane shape to a Rac1/Arp2/3 actin burst that restores the membrane's resting topography. In neurons it is a postsynaptic density protein that binds PSD-95, PSD-93 and the Shank scaffolds and drives dendritic spine morphogenesis; loss of function disrupts cortical neuronal migration, and variants that break the autoinhibited state cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.

BAP1 is a ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase with an active-site cysteine and a major role in chromatin regulation. In nuclear PR-DUB complexes, ASXL proteins activate BAP1 to remove monoubiquitin from histone H2A lysine 119. Engagement with nucleosomal DNA, histones and ubiquitin establishes substrate recognition. This reaction regulates transcription, with activating or repressive consequences depending on the locus and cellular context. BAP1 also deubiquitinates nonhistone proteins, including the nuclear transcriptional coregulator HCFC1 and the endoplasmic-reticulum calcium channel ITPR3. Its regulated nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution connects these substrate-specific activities to cell growth, genome maintenance and cell-death responses. Germline and somatic BAP1 variants are associated with tumor predisposition and, for some germline missense variants, neurodevelopmental disease.

BARD1 is the BRCA1-associated RING-domain protein that combines nuclear chromatin recognition with regulation of DNA repair. Its N-terminal RING forms a heterodimer with BRCA1, while its ankyrin repeats and tandem BRCT domains recognize nucleosomes bearing unmethylated H4K20 and damage-induced H2A ubiquitin marks. This recognition recruits and positions the BRCA1–BARD1 complex on post-replicative chromatin. BARD1 contributes to the complex's ubiquitin ligase activity toward C-terminal H2A lysines; BRCA1 supplies the demonstrated E2-binding interface. Through separate DNA-binding and RAD51 contacts, the heterodimer promotes homologous DNA pairing and stimulates DNA-end resection machinery during homologous recombination. BARD1 also participates in context-dependent regulation of RNA processing, protein stability and cell survival.

BBS1 is a subunit of the BBSome, a membrane-trafficking coat composed of BBS1, BBS2, BBS4, BBS5, BBS7, TTC8/BBS8, BBS9 and BBIP1. Its N-terminal beta-propeller binds GTP-loaded ARL6, helping recruit the complex to membranes. BBS1 also associates with cytoplasmic regions of signaling receptors, including Smoothened, Patched1 and the leptin receptor. These contacts contribute to cargo recognition and the regulated composition of ciliary membranes. BBS1 has cytoplasmic, centrosomal and ciliary pools and supports ciliary trafficking in sensory and other ciliated cells. Loss of BBS1 disrupts receptor trafficking and cilium function and causes Bardet–Biedl syndrome.

BBS2 is a structural subunit of the BBSome, an eight-protein complex that supports membrane-protein trafficking at cilia. BBS2 associates with BBS7 through a coiled-coil interface and contacts BBS9 through its C-terminal helical region, linking these subunits within the assembled complex. BBSome function supports ciliary signaling and the maintenance of sensory cells, including retinal photoreceptors. BBS2 is found in cytoplasmic and ciliary compartments. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and some variants are associated with nonsyndromic retinitis pigmentosa.

BBS4 is a tetratricopeptide-repeat protein and a subunit of the BBSome, an eight-subunit complex involved in the localization of membrane proteins at cilia. It occurs at centriolar satellites, centrosomes and ciliary structures. BBS4 interacts with PCM1 and the dynactin subunit DCTN1/p150-glued, supporting recruitment or retention of pericentriolar proteins and the organization of centrosomal microtubules. Its cooperation with DISC1 helps position PCM1 and associated proteins such as ninein near centrosomes. Within the BBSome, BBS4 contributes to ciliary trafficking and connects the complex with satellite proteins including CEP131 and CEP290. These functions have different requirements across cargoes and cell types; BBS4 loss does not prevent every form of cilium formation or ciliary protein transport. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause a Bardet-Biedl syndrome ciliopathy with retinal, metabolic and other organ involvement.

BBS5 is a subunit of the BBSome, an eight-protein complex involved in ciliary membrane-protein trafficking. It contains two pleckstrin-homology-like domains and binds phosphoinositides in isolated-protein assays. BBS5 occurs in the cytoplasmic BBSome and at ciliary membranes and basal bodies. In human retinal pigment epithelial cells, BBS5 supports cilium formation and entry of the BBSome into cilia. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause Bardet-Biedl syndrome, with variable retinal degeneration, obesity, polydactyly, renal abnormalities and other manifestations.

BCAT2 is a pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase (EC 2.6.1.42). It reversibly transfers the amino group of leucine, isoleucine or valine to 2-oxoglutarate, producing glutamate and alpha-ketoisocaproate, alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate or alpha-ketoisovalerate, respectively. The mitochondrial homodimer initiates BCAA catabolism upstream of the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex; the reverse reaction regenerates amino acids from existing ketoacid skeletons. PLP binds at the active site, and a nearby CXXC motif influences substrate positioning. BCAT2 is broadly expressed, with high abundance in muscle. A shorter splice product, PP18b, occurs in the cytosolic fraction of human placenta and is distinct from the paralog BCAT1. Biallelic loss of BCAT2 activity causes hypervalinemia and hyperleucine-isoleucinemia.

BCKDHA encodes the alpha subunit of the mitochondrial branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. Two BCKDHA and two BCKDHB chains form its E1 enzyme, which decarboxylates the ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine and reductively acylates the lipoyl group carried by DBT. BCKDHA contributes residues that bind thiamine diphosphate and associated metal ions at the shared active site. DBT subsequently transfers the acyl group to CoA, and DLD reoxidizes the reduced lipoyl group. This coupled reaction constitutes the committed oxidative step of branched-chain amino acid catabolism in the mitochondrial matrix, downstream of transamination. BCKDK and PPM1K regulate the complex through reversible phosphorylation of the E1 alpha subunit. Phosphorylation of precursor Ser337, corresponding to mature-chain Ser292, disrupts recognition of the DBT lipoyl domain and reductive acylation more strongly than the initial decarboxylation reaction. Biallelic damaging BCKDHA variants cause maple syrup urine disease type 1A.

BCKDHB encodes the beta subunit of the mitochondrial branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. Two BCKDHB and two BCKDHA chains form its E1 enzyme (EC 1.2.4.4), whose shared active sites decarboxylate the ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine and reductively acylate the lipoyl group of DBT. The beta chain contributes cofactor-binding and catalytic residues at the alpha-beta interface, as well as contacts for a structural potassium ion. E1 tetramers and DLD dimers associate with a 24-subunit cubic DBT core. DBT transfers the acyl group to CoA, and DLD reoxidizes the reduced lipoyl group. This coupled oxidation is the committed step of branched-chain amino acid catabolism in the mitochondrial matrix, downstream of transamination. Reversible phosphorylation of the alpha subunit regulates the assembled enzyme. Biallelic damaging BCKDHB variants cause maple syrup urine disease type 1B; loss of the beta subunit can also destabilize the alpha subunit.

BCL10 is a noncatalytic immune signaling adaptor with an N-terminal caspase recruitment domain. Activated CARD-containing proteins, including CARD9, CARD11 and CARD14, nucleate BCL10 assemblies that recruit and organize MALT1 and downstream signaling machinery. These cytoplasmic and membrane-associated CARD-BCL10-MALT1 complexes promote canonical NF-kappaB activation through regulated ubiquitin and kinase signaling. BCL10 self-association also provides a platform for MALT1 activation. The adaptor supports antigen-receptor responses in lymphocytes and selected innate responses, with dependence varying by receptor and cell type. Biallelic loss of BCL10 causes combined immunodeficiency, whereas dysregulated expression or activating signaling assemblies can contribute to lymphoma. Nuclear localization, transcriptional coactivation and effects on apoptosis occur in particular experimental or pathological contexts.

BCL2 is a membrane-associated regulator of cell survival. Its BH3-binding groove recognizes proapoptotic ligands and BAX, restraining mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome-c release and downstream caspase activation. BCL2 occurs at mitochondrial, endoplasmic-reticulum and nuclear-envelope membranes, with additional context-dependent pools. At the endoplasmic reticulum it inhibits IP3-receptor calcium release and binds BECN1 to limit autophagy; mitochondrial BCL2 can also inhibit AMBRA1-dependent autophagy. Cleavage or binding of Nur77 can expose a proapoptotic BCL2 state. Purified BCL2 has channel-forming capacity in reconstituted membranes, while its physiological use remains unresolved.

BCL2L1 encodes Bcl-2-like protein 1 (also called Bcl-x), a member of the Bcl-2 family that regulates apoptosis. CRITICAL ISOFORM BIOLOGY: Alternative splicing produces two functionally ANTAGONISTIC isoforms: (1) Bcl-xL (Q07817-1, 233 AA) is anti-apoptotic and inhibits BAX/BAK-mediated mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization; (2) Bcl-xS (Q07817-2, 166 AA) is pro-apoptotic, lacks BH1/BH2 domains, and can heterodimerize with Bcl-xL to inhibit its function. Most GO annotations refer to Bcl-xL, the dominant isoform. The annotation GO:0043065 "positive regulation of apoptotic process" likely reflects Bcl-xS function or IBA inference error. Beyond apoptosis, Bcl-xL regulates ATP synthase efficiency, calcium signaling, and autophagy.

BCS1L is a mitochondrial inner-membrane AAA ATPase that promotes respiratory complex III assembly by moving the folded Rieske iron-sulfur domain of UQCRFS1 from the matrix to the intermembrane-space side and enabling client incorporation into the membrane complex. Its N-terminal transmembrane helix anchors a matrix-facing region containing a BCS1-specific domain and a C-terminal AAA domain. The Bcs1-family motor forms a heptameric ring whose nucleotide-dependent conformational changes couple ATP utilization to protein translocation. BCS1L also associates with LETM1 and contributes to mitochondrial network organization. Pathogenic variants cause complex III deficiency, GRACILE syndrome and Bjornstad syndrome.

BDH1 is the mitochondrial NAD+-dependent D-beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.30), a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family enzyme anchored to the matrix side of the mitochondrial inner membrane. It catalyses the reversible interconversion of the two principal ketone bodies, (R)-3-hydroxybutanoate + NAD+ <=> acetoacetate + NADH + H+. This single reaction serves two opposite physiological directions: it is the terminal step of hepatic ketogenesis, producing beta-hydroxybutyrate (the main circulating ketone body), and the initiating step of ketolysis in peripheral tissues (heart, brain, skeletal muscle), regenerating acetoacetate for downstream oxidation. BDH1 is a lipid-dependent enzyme that requires phosphatidylcholine as an allosteric activator for full activity, and it assembles as a homotetramer. It is highly expressed in liver and mitochondria-rich oxidative tissues, where it is central to ketone-body homeostasis and the use of ketone bodies as an alternative energy substrate during fasting, prolonged exercise, or carbohydrate restriction.

Beclin-1 is the central scaffold subunit of class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3KC3/VPS34) complexes that generate phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) for autophagosome biogenesis and endocytic trafficking. BECN1 forms two mutually exclusive complexes: PI3KC3-C1 (with ATG14L) for autophagosome nucleation, and PI3KC3-C2 (with UVRAG) for endosome maturation and endocytic trafficking. The protein contains an N-terminal BH3 domain (aa 108-127) that binds BCL2/BCL-XL to regulate autophagy, a coiled-coil domain (CCD; aa 144-269) for dimerization and partner binding, and a C-terminal BARA/ECD membrane-binding domain. BECN1 is a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor and is essential for autophagy initiation through its adapter function in assembling PI3KC3 complex components.

BIN1 (amphiphysin II) is a peripheral membrane and cytoskeletal adaptor whose N-BAR domain binds phospholipids, senses membrane curvature and deforms membranes into tubules. Alternative splicing changes its membrane-targeting and interaction regions, giving neuronal, muscle and more widely expressed forms distinct properties. BIN1 membrane shaping is central to skeletal-muscle T-tubule organization and contributes to endocytic membrane remodeling. Its SH3 domain recruits partners including dynamin, while CLAP-containing forms interact with clathrin-associated machinery. Contacts with actin, nesprins and CLIP170 link membranes and the nuclear envelope to the cytoskeleton. Additional interactions with MYC, tau, intracellular clusterin and BACE1 connect particular BIN1 forms to growth regulation and neuronal protein trafficking. Pathogenic BIN1 variants that disrupt membrane deformation or dynamin recruitment cause centronuclear myopathy.

BLM is a RecQ-family ATP-dependent DNA helicase that moves with 3-prime-to-5-prime polarity and remodels branched DNA structures during genome maintenance. Its helicase, RecQ C-terminal and HRDC regions recognize and process duplex overhangs, replication forks, Holliday junctions, D-loops and G-quadruplex DNA. In the BLM–TOP3A–RMI1–RMI2 complex, BLM drives convergent branch migration and TOP3A removes the resulting DNA entanglement, promoting non-crossover recombination products. BLM also cooperates with DNA2 and EXO1 during DNA-end resection and with shelterin-associated proteins during telomeric DNA processing. It can anneal complementary DNA strands, an activity that cooperates with unwinding during fork remodeling. Nuclear BLM is enriched at repair-associated chromatin and PML nuclear bodies, with localization changing through the cell cycle and after DNA damage. Loss of BLM causes Bloom syndrome and a marked increase in sister-chromatid exchange and chromosome instability.

BMP4 is a secreted, disulfide-linked growth factor of the TGF-beta superfamily. Proteolytic maturation of its precursor produces a ligand that engages type I and type II BMP receptor complexes, initiating receptor-mediated SMAD1/5/8 signaling and context-dependent noncanonical responses. Co-receptors and extracellular antagonists modulate receptor use and signal strength, while the prodomain can bind fibrillin matrix components. BMP4 directs cell-fate choices and tissue patterning in many embryonic organs and regulates proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation according to cell type, developmental stage and signaling environment.

BMP6 is a secreted growth factor of the TGF-beta superfamily. Its processed ligand engages BMP type I and type II receptor complexes to initiate SMAD1/5/8-dependent and context-dependent noncanonical signaling. It promotes osteogenic differentiation and regulates hepatic hepcidin expression, connecting extracellular signaling with systemic iron balance. BMP6 can form an active heterodimer with BMP2 in experimental systems, and erythroferrone limits BMP6-containing ligand activity by binding extracellular ligand. Receptor use and cellular outcomes depend on tissue context.

BMPR1A (ALK3) is a single-pass cell-surface BMP receptor with an extracellular ligand-binding domain and an intracellular serine/threonine kinase domain. It recognizes BMP-family ligands in complexes with type II receptors; activation of its kinase couples extracellular signals to receptor-regulated SMADs. Ligand preference and output depend on receptor partners and cellular context. This signaling supports skeletal and cardiovascular development, differentiation and hepatic hepcidin regulation. BMPR1A also supplies type I receptor signaling in the AMH pathway during Müllerian-duct regression.

BMPR2 is a single-pass type-II bone morphogenetic protein receptor with an extracellular ligand-binding domain and an intracellular serine/threonine kinase. At the plasma membrane it participates in BMP ligand/type-I/type-II receptor complexes and phosphorylates type-I receptors, which relay signals to R-SMADs and other effectors. Ligand and receptor composition shape the response, including BMP9/10 signaling in vascular endothelium and BMP-dependent mesenchymal differentiation. These pathways contribute to pulmonary vascular homeostasis, cartilage and bone development, and context-dependent control of proliferation and survival. The canonical 1,038-residue product has a long cytoplasmic tail that binds regulatory proteins; a named 530-residue splice product lacks most of that tail. Activin-A reception is also documented in a defined gonadotrope-like cell context. Disease-associated variants can alter surface trafficking, kinase signaling and endothelial behavior. Some disease-associated mutants produce p38 responses absent from wild-type receptor in the tested cell context.

BNIP3 (BCL2/adenovirus E1B 19 kDa protein-interacting protein 3; NIP3) is an atypical BH3-only member of the BCL-2 family and the paralog of BNIP3L/NIX. It is a tail-anchored membrane protein with a C-terminal transmembrane helix that inserts it into the mitochondrial outer membrane and also the endoplasmic reticulum; the same helix drives stable homodimerization. Its N-terminal cytosolic region contains an LC3-interacting region (LIR), through which BNIP3 binds Atg8-family proteins and acts as a selective autophagy receptor that delivers mitochondria (mitophagy) and ER (ER-phagy) to autophagosomes. BNIP3 is strongly induced by hypoxia through HIF-1. Together with NIX it is required for hypoxia-induced autophagy, partly because its atypical BH3 domain releases Beclin 1 from BCL-2. BNIP3 also takes part in Mieap/SPATA18-dependent intramitochondrial quality control (MALM) and inhibits OPA1-mediated fusion. When overexpressed or under some stresses it promotes cell death, typically necrosis-like death through opening of the permeability transition pore and loss of membrane potential rather than classical cytochrome c/caspase apoptosis. Basal BNIP3 levels are kept low by SCF(FBXL4)/PPTC7-dependent ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover.

BNIP3L (NIX) is a tail-anchored, atypical BH3-containing member of the BNIP3/NIP3 family that is inserted into the mitochondrial outer membrane via its C-terminal transmembrane helix, with its N-terminal disordered region facing the cytosol. Its principal, conserved function is as a selective autophagy (mitophagy) receptor: an LC3-interacting region in the cytosolic domain binds Atg8-family proteins (LC3 and GABARAP/GABARAPL1/GABARAPL2), tethering mitochondria to the forming autophagosome and driving their programmed autophagic clearance. This is most prominent during terminal erythroid/reticulocyte maturation and other developmentally programmed or stress-induced episodes of mitochondrial turnover. NIX also participates in non-canonical mitochondrial quality control through ROS-dependent interaction with SPATA18/MIEAP, and under hypoxia it is induced by HIF and promotes pro-survival macroautophagy via its atypical BH3 domain. Although first described as a pro-apoptotic BCL-2-family protein, its effects on cell death are context-dependent and direction-dependent (it can both promote and inhibit cell death) and act largely through mitochondrial membrane permeability/necrosis rather than classical cytochrome-c/caspase apoptosis. Beyond mitochondria, NIX can independently localize to peroxisomes and act as a selective autophagy receptor for their clearance (pexophagy), broadening its cargo selectivity. NIX abundance is held in check by constitutive ubiquitin-mediated turnover: an SCF(FBXL4) ubiquitin ligase complex at the mitochondrial outer membrane, with the phosphatase PPTC7 as a cofactor, degrades NIX (and BNIP3) to restrain basal mitophagy, while hypoxia/HIF signaling induces NIX transcription. NIX is also exploited by several viruses, which hijack NIX-mediated mitophagy to degrade mitochondrial antiviral signaling components.

Dystonin is a plakin-family cytolinker whose alternative products connect cytoskeletal networks with cellular attachment structures and intracellular transport machinery. Epithelial BP230 links keratin intermediate filaments to hemidesmosomal membrane proteins and supports keratinocyte polarity and directional migration. Larger muscle and neuronal forms contain different combinations of filament-binding domains. Their functions include structural coupling at muscle Z-discs, microtubule association and regulation, and dynactin-associated retrograde transport in neurons. Product-specific domain composition and localization give these forms distinct functional capacities.

BRAF encodes a RAF-family serine/threonine protein kinase (EC 2.7.11.1) that is the canonical mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAP3K) of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signaling cascade.
