In quiescent cells BRAF is autoinhibited by an intramolecular interaction between its N-terminal regulatory region and the C-terminal kinase domain. Mitogenic stimulation generates GTP-loaded RAS, which binds the BRAF RAS-binding domain (RBD), relieves autoinhibition, and recruits BRAF to the plasma membrane. Activation requires side-to-side dimerization — BRAF homodimers and, most potently, BRAF-RAF1 (CRAF) heterodimers — stabilized by 14-3-3 proteins and the HSP90/CDC37 chaperone system. Activated BRAF phosphorylates and activates MAP2K1/MAP2K2 (MEK1/MEK2), the committed step that propagates mitogenic signaling through ERK1/ERK2 to control proliferation, differentiation and survival. BRAF localizes to the cytoplasm/cytosol and to the plasma membrane in its active RAS-bound state. It is a major oncogenic driver: the V600E activating mutation, which renders the kinase constitutively active as a RAS-independent monomer, is recurrent in melanoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, colorectal cancer, hairy-cell leukemia and other tumors, and germline BRAF mutations cause cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome.

BRCA1 is a nuclear tumor-suppressor protein that organizes DNA damage responses and homologous-recombination repair through several distinct molecular activities. Its N-terminal RING domain engages ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes in a ligase heterodimer with BARD1, modifying nucleosomal histones and other substrates; ubiquitin linkage and substrate specificity depend on the E2 and biochemical context. Tandem C-terminal BRCT repeats recognize phosphorylated protein motifs, while a central DNA-binding region and protein-interaction interfaces cooperate with BARD1 to promote DNA-end resection and recruitment of repair factors. BRCA1-containing assemblies also influence damage checkpoints, transcriptional regulation and context-dependent centrosome and metabolic responses. Pathogenic germline variants cause hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.

BRCA2 is a predominantly nuclear genome-maintenance protein that promotes homologous recombination by binding RAD51 and single-stranded DNA and assembling productive RAD51 filaments on RPA-coated DNA. Its BRC repeats, DNA-binding regions and C-terminal RAD51-binding region coordinate this mediator activity with partners including PALB2 and DSS1. RAD51 performs the DNA strand-exchange reaction, which BRCA2 stimulates. BRCA2 also stabilizes RAD51 at reversed replication forks to protect nascent DNA from nucleolytic degradation, a role distinct from fork reversal itself. Its recombination functions extend to telomere maintenance and meiosis. Pathogenic variants cause BRCA2-related cancer predisposition, while biallelic variants can cause Fanconi anemia complementation group D1.

Biotinidase (BTD; EC 3.5.1.12) is a secreted glycoprotein that hydrolyses biocytin and small biotinyl-peptides, releasing free biotin for reuse. It acts in biotin salvage after the breakdown of biotin-dependent carboxylases and in the utilization of dietary biotinyl compounds. The human serum enzyme belongs to the carbon–nitrogen hydrolase superfamily, with a nitrilase-like catalytic domain. Alternative products differ at their amino termini; the secretory form is well established, whereas the identity and activity of a proposed mitochondrial pool remain unresolved. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause biotinidase deficiency, with secondary impairment of biotin-dependent carboxylases and neurological and cutaneous manifestations. Early biotin supplementation can prevent neurological damage, providing the rationale for newborn screening.

BTK is a Tec-family nonreceptor protein tyrosine kinase that couples immune-receptor activation to intracellular signaling. Its PH domain recognizes phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate and recruits a cytosolic pool to membrane signaling assemblies. In B cells, BTK phosphorylates and activates PLCgamma2 within the BLNK-organized receptor pathway, supporting calcium mobilization, NF-kappaB signaling, activation and differentiation. BTK also phosphorylates substrates in innate immune pathways, including DDX41 and NLRP3, with outputs that depend on cell type and stimulation. SH2/SH3-mediated interactions organize signaling partners, and a smaller pool can shuttle through the nucleus. Loss of functional BTK causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

BUB1B encodes BUBR1, a mitotic checkpoint protein that restrains chromosome segregation and helps establish stable kinetochore–microtubule attachments. In the mitotic checkpoint complex with BUB3, MAD2 and CDC20, BUBR1 uses degron-like motifs and its N-terminal TPR domain to inhibit APC/C substrate recognition and ubiquitination, delaying anaphase. A separate kinetochore function uses its central KARD region and LxxIxE motif to recruit PP2A-B56; this positions phosphatase activity to balance mitotic kinase signaling, promote chromosome alignment and facilitate checkpoint silencing. Human BUBR1 has a C-terminal kinase-like domain with important noncatalytic functions, while intrinsic kinase activity remains disputed because positive and negative biochemical studies use different constructs and assay conditions. BUBR1 is predominantly cytoplasmic in interphase, accumulates at mitotic kinetochores and can redistribute along the anaphase spindle. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome 1, characterized by chromosome-segregation errors and developmental abnormalities.

BUB3 is a 328-residue WD40-repeat protein that folds into a seven-bladed beta-propeller and functions as a non-catalytic adaptor in the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC). It forms constitutive, mutually exclusive 1:1 complexes with the checkpoint kinases BUB1 and BUB1B (BubR1), each of which binds the top face of the propeller through a short GLEBS motif. During prometaphase the BUB1-BUB3 complex is recruited to unattached or tensionless kinetochores because BUB3 directly reads MPS1/TTK-phosphorylated MELT repeats of the outer-kinetochore protein KNL1; BUB3 is therefore required for kinetochore localisation of BUB1 and, downstream, of BUBR1, MAD1-MAD2 and CDC20, and it builds the platform on which the kinetochore catalyses conversion of MAD2 to its CDC20-bound closed form. A second BUB3 pool, bound to BUBR1, is incorporated with MAD2 and CDC20 into the soluble mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC), the diffusible inhibitor that binds APC/C-CDC20 and blocks ubiquitination of securin and cyclin B until every chromosome is bioriented; within the MCC, BUB3 is a peripheral, flexibly attached subunit that supports BUBR1 rather than contacting the APC/C directly. Through its BUB1 partnership BUB3 also promotes the establishment of stable end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments and chromosome congression. Its abundance and kinetochore loading are supported by the GLEBS-motif protein ZNF207/BuGZ, it binds the dynein light chain DYNLT3, and it is ubiquitinated by UBR5 to release the MCC from the APC/C during checkpoint silencing. BUB3 is nuclear in interphase and is also required for SAC function and accurate homologue segregation in oocyte meiosis I.

EGLN1 (PHD2) is an Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent prolyl hydroxylase that couples oxygen availability to HIF-alpha stability. It hydroxylates proline residues in HIF-alpha oxygen-dependent degradation domains, enabling recognition by the VHL ubiquitin-ligase machinery and subsequent proteasomal turnover. The enzyme acts in cytosolic and nuclear pools; its chemistry, rather than the downstream ubiquitination or proteolysis, is the oxygen-sensitive step. Additional neuronal studies connect PHD2-dependent hydroxylation to postsynaptic protein turnover and stress responses. Pathogenic EGLN1 variants cause familial erythrocytosis.

C1QA is the A chain of the secreted complement recognition protein C1q. Six copies each of the A, B and C chains assemble into collagen-like stalks and heterotrimeric globular heads. The A-chain globular module binds immunoglobulins, and assembled C1q recognizes clustered IgG or IgM on target surfaces. Within the C1 complex, this recognition couples to activation of the associated C1r and C1s proteases and initiation of the classical complement cascade. C1QA also contributes to recognition of altered-self surfaces and receptor-mediated immune regulation by assembled C1q, including phosphatidylserine recognition and CD33 signaling. In mouse models, C1qa-dependent complement activity participates in synaptic remodeling and glial responses.

C1QB encodes the B chain of the secreted complement recognition protein C1q. Six copies each of the A, B and C chains assemble into six collagen-like stems ending in heterotrimeric globular heads. The B-chain globular module recognizes immunoglobulins, while its collagen-like region helps recruit the C1r/C1s protease tetramer. These recognition and assembly functions initiate the classical complement pathway without conferring protease activity on C1QB. As part of intact C1q, the B chain also contributes to phosphatidylserine recognition and inhibitory immunoreceptor signaling. Complement-dependent synaptic remodeling has been demonstrated in rodents; these studies generally test the assembled C1q system rather than an autonomous B-chain activity.

CFAP410 (C21ORF2/LRRC76) is a leucine-rich-repeat protein associated with the serine/threonine kinase NEK1. It is found at ciliary basal bodies and photoreceptor connecting cilia, with an additional cytoplasmic pool. Its C-terminal domain forms a tetrameric helical bundle in vitro. Loss of CFAP410 or disease-associated variants disrupt primary-cilium formation and function in human cellular models, including motor neurons. Depletion also reduces homologous-recombination reporter repair, although the repair-specific molecular contribution of the CFAP410–NEK1 complex remains unresolved. Biallelic variants cause retinal ciliopathies with variable skeletal involvement, and some variants are associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

C3 is a secreted central component of the complement system whose proteolytic and chemical processing creates functionally distinct effectors. Activated C3b uses an internal thioester to attach covalently to nearby surfaces, provides a nonenzymatic platform for complement convertases, and marks targets for recognition by complement receptors. Further processing produces iC3b and C3d-containing fragments that connect opsonic recognition to phagocytes and B-cell co-receptors. Soluble C3a activates the G-protein-coupled receptor C3AR1 and elicits context-dependent inflammatory responses. These activities support microbial defense and removal or remodeling of tagged material; complement-dependent neural pruning and metabolic effects of the distinct C3a-desArg product depend on experimental and tissue context.

TIMMDC1 (TIM17 domain-containing protein 1; also known as C3orf1/M5-14) is a multi-pass integral protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane and a member of the Tim17/Tim22/Tim23 preprotein-translocase / membrane-insertase-like superfamily. It functions as a chaperone/assembly factor for mitochondrial Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase), where it acts during the mid-stage, MCIA-associated construction of the membrane arm of the enzyme. It transiently associates with incompletely assembled Complex I intermediates (including the ~315 kDa iron-sulfur/membrane-arm subcomplex) together with other assembly factors such as NDUFAF3, NDUFAF4, TMEM126B and the MCIA complex (ACAD9, NDUFAF1, ECSIT), and dissociates once the mature holoenzyme is formed; it is therefore not a stable structural subunit of the Complex I holoenzyme. TIMMDC1 is broadly expressed with enhanced levels in heart and skeletal muscle. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal-recessive mitochondrial Complex I deficiency (nuclear type 31, MC1DN31).

ERLIN2 (SPFH2, ER lipid raft-associated protein 2) is a single-pass type II endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein with a lumenal SPFH/prohibitin (band 7) domain, belonging to the band 7/mec-2 (stomatin-prohibitin-flotillin) family. It associates with lipid-raft-like domains of the ER membrane and functions as a scaffold rather than an enzyme. ERLIN2 forms a large ring-shaped heteromeric complex with its homolog ERLIN1 (SPFH1); the ERLIN1/ERLIN2 complex binds inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) tetramers and, together with the ER ubiquitin ligase RNF170, mediates the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of activated IP3Rs, controlling calcium signaling. ERLIN2 also promotes sterol-accelerated ERAD of HMG-CoA reductase through an AMFR/gp78-containing ubiquitin ligase complex (with TMUB1 bridging ERLIN2 to gp78), and it binds cholesterol and restricts SREBP activation by associating with the SCAP-SREBP-Insig machinery, thereby negatively regulating cholesterol and fatty acid biosynthesis. Through these activities it recruits and binds multiple ER ubiquitin ligases (RNF170, AMFR/gp78, SYVN1, RNF139, RNF185/RNF5). Loss-of-function variants in ERLIN2 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG18A/SPG18B) and a recessive intellectual disability syndrome.

Carbonic anhydrase II is a soluble zinc-dependent enzyme that rapidly and reversibly interconverts carbon dioxide and water with bicarbonate and protons. Its cytosolic catalysis supports intracellular pH control and the supply or removal of substrates coupled to epithelial acid-base transport. Human enzyme structures and mutational kinetics define the catalytic zinc environment and proton-transfer network. CAII can associate with the cytosolic face of membrane transport proteins, although direct binding and substrate-channeling interpretations depend on the transporter and assay. It also displays arylesterase and cyanamide-hydration activities in vitro. Biallelic CA2 deficiency causes osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification.

CA5A encodes carbonic anhydrase VA, a zinc-dependent enzyme imported into the mitochondrial matrix after cleavage of an N-terminal targeting peptide. It catalyzes reversible interconversion of carbon dioxide and bicarbonate. Its bicarbonate production supplies mitochondrial carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 and biotin-dependent carboxylases, linking this reaction to nitrogen disposal and intermediary metabolism without catalyzing their downstream reactions. Human loss-of-function variants can impair enzyme activity or stability and cause episodes of hyperammonemia and associated metabolic disturbances, particularly early in life.

Carbonic anhydrase 8 (CA8/CARP VIII) is a soluble carbonic-anhydrase-family protein that lacks the canonical zinc-dependent carbon dioxide hydration activity. Human CA8 carries Arg116 at a position occupied by a zinc-coordinating histidine in active family members. CA8 binds the cytoplasmic regulatory region of the endoplasmic-reticulum calcium-release channel ITPR1 and can reduce IP3 sensitivity and IP3-evoked calcium release. It is abundant in cerebellar Purkinje cells, and biallelic pathogenic variants cause congenital cerebellar ataxia with variable neurodevelopmental impairment.

CaBP2 is an EF-hand calcium-binding protein that regulates voltage-gated calcium channels in sensory cells. Its inhibition of CaV1.3 inactivation supports sustained presynaptic calcium entry and sound encoding at inner-hair-cell synapses. Calcium binding and membrane association support this regulatory role. Mouse ortholog studies support a role in retinal signal transmission. CaBP2 is expressed as long and short splice isoforms, L-CaBP2 and S-CaBP2.

CACNA1B encodes the pore-forming alpha1B subunit of the N-type, high-voltage-activated calcium channel CaV2.2. Its four homologous transmembrane repeats form voltage sensors and a calcium-selective pore. In neuronal plasma membranes, depolarization opens the channel and calcium entry couples electrical activity to neurotransmitter release. Beta and alpha2delta auxiliary subunits influence channel expression and gating, while presynaptic partners and phosphorylation pathways regulate the alpha1B subunit. The channel is sensitive to omega-conotoxins, including the pore blocker ziconotide. Biallelic variants predicted to cause loss of function underlie autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and non-epileptic hyperkinetic movements (NEDNEH); impaired calcium influx and synaptic transmission are the proposed disease mechanism.

CACNA1C encodes the pore-forming alpha1C subunit of CaV1.2, an L-type high-voltage-activated calcium channel. Its voltage sensors and calcium-selective pore convert plasma-membrane depolarization into calcium entry. In cardiac muscle this current contributes to the action potential and triggers ryanodine-receptor-mediated calcium release for contraction; in smooth muscle and neurons it links electrical activity to calcium-dependent responses. Beta and alpha2delta subunits regulate channel expression and gating, while calmodulin and other intracellular partners control inactivation and local signaling. Extensive alternative splicing changes gating, surface expression and pharmacology. Pathogenic variants can alter current density, selectivity or inactivation in different directions, producing cardiac and neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

CACNA1D encodes the pore-forming alpha1D subunit of CaV1.3, an L-type voltage-gated calcium channel. Calcium entry through the channel couples membrane depolarization to electrical and secretory responses. Its relatively negative activation range within the L-type family supports sinoatrial pacemaking and calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release from cochlear inner hair cells, with additional functions in neurons and endocrine cells. Beta and alpha2delta subunits regulate channel expression and gating, and intracellular partners organize local signaling. C-terminal alternative splicing changes activation and calcium-dependent inactivation. Loss-of-function variants can impair hearing and sinoatrial-node function, whereas activating variants can perturb adrenal and neuronal calcium signaling.

CACNA1E encodes the alpha1E pore-forming subunit of the R-type voltage-gated calcium channel CaV2.3. Its four homologous transmembrane domains couple membrane depolarization to calcium entry, with auxiliary subunits modulating channel properties. CaV2.3 acts in neuronal membranes to support calcium-dependent signaling and synaptic transmission, and also contributes to calcium entry in endocrine cells. Alternative splicing produces three named human protein products. Pathogenic variants can alter channel activation and inactivation and cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; enhanced channel activity is established for several tested variants rather than for every disease allele.

CACNA1F encodes the pore-forming alpha1 subunit of the CaV1.4 L-type voltage-gated calcium channel. Calcium entry through CaV1.4 couples retinal membrane voltage to neurotransmitter release and supports visual signaling. Its C-terminal splice variants differ in voltage-dependent activation, calcium-dependent inactivation and modulation by CaBP4. Pathogenic variants cause X-linked incomplete congenital stationary night blindness, cone-rod dystrophy and Aland Island eye disease; the molecular effects include altered splicing, predicted loss of channel function and experimentally demonstrated changes in gating.

CACNA1G encodes CaV3.1, the pore-forming subunit of a T-type calcium channel. Its four repeated membrane domains contain voltage sensors and the calcium-selective pore. Opening at relatively negative membrane potentials permits calcium entry across the plasma membrane and contributes to electrical excitability and rhythmic firing in neurons and cardiac nodal cells. Alternative splicing diversifies channel products. Dominant variants can perturb channel gating: the recurrent adult-onset ataxia-associated R1715H variant shifts voltage dependence, whereas particular de novo variants associated with severe childhood cerebellar disease increase window current and slow inactivation.

Alpha-2/delta-1, the founding member of the four-gene mammalian alpha-2/delta family and an auxiliary subunit of high-voltage-activated calcium channels. The single precursor is cleaved and disulphide-linked into an extracellular alpha-2 chain and a membrane-attached delta chain, and the mature protein is tethered to the outer face of the plasma membrane through a GPI anchor; its extracellular region carries VWA (with a MIDAS motif) and Cache domains. Assembled with a pore-forming CaV1 or CaV2 alpha-1 subunit and a cytoplasmic CaV-beta subunit, it raises calcium-current density and shifts voltage-dependent activation to more negative potentials, largely by increasing the number of channels at the cell surface rather than by conducting ions itself. It is expressed in skeletal and cardiac muscle T-tubules, in vascular smooth muscle, and broadly in neurons, where it concentrates at presynaptic terminals. It is the high-affinity binding site for the gabapentinoid drugs gabapentin and pregabalin. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause an early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, and missense variants have been associated with short-QT and Brugada-like cardiac syndromes. Two further roles are proposed and contested. The first is that alpha-2/delta-1 is the neuronal thrombospondin receptor that drives excitatory synaptogenesis; a conditional triple knockout of presynaptic alpha-2/delta-1, -2 and -3 found synapse development, active-zone ultrastructure and transsynaptic alignment intact and reassigned presynaptic alpha-2/delta to setting synaptic gain through Munc13-1, while astrocyte-conditioned-medium experiments continue to support a postsynaptic thrombospondin-1 receptor role. The second is that alpha-2/delta-1 forms a gabapentin-sensitive complex with NMDA receptors, independently of calcium channels, and promotes their synaptic trafficking in chronic pain; this model rests almost entirely on work from a single laboratory and has not been independently replicated.

CACNB2 encodes the voltage-dependent L-type calcium channel subunit beta-2 (CaVbeta2), an essential cytosolic auxiliary subunit of high-voltage-activated Ca2+ channels. The protein contains a conserved SH3-HOOK-guanylate kinase (GK) module that binds the alpha-interaction domain (AID) in the I-II linker of the pore-forming alpha1 subunit with nanomolar affinity. CaVbeta2 promotes proper channel trafficking to the plasma membrane and modulates voltage-dependent activation/inactivation kinetics of CaV1.x/CaV2.x channels. Multiple splice variants (beta2a-beta2e) differ in their N-termini, with beta2a being palmitoylated for membrane anchoring and beta2e capable of nuclear translocation. CaVbeta2 also mediates beta-adrenergic regulation of cardiac L-type channels through interaction with the RGK GTPase Rad.

SLC25A20 is the mitochondrial carnitine/acylcarnitine carrier (also called carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase, CACT/CAC), an integral multi-pass protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane belonging to the mitochondrial carrier (SLC25) family. It catalyzes the electroneutral exchange (antiport) of long-chain O-acyl-L-carnitines for free L-carnitine across the inner membrane, and at lower rates the uniport of free carnitine. This activity is the central step of the mitochondrial carnitine shuttle: carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1) on the outer membrane converts acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine, SLC25A20 imports the acylcarnitine into the matrix while exporting free carnitine, and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 (CPT2) on the matrix face of the inner membrane regenerates acyl-CoA for fatty acid beta-oxidation. SLC25A20 is thus essential for delivering long-chain fatty acids into the matrix for energy production, especially during fasting and metabolic stress. Loss-of-function variants cause carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency, a severe autosomal-recessive long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorder presenting mostly in the neonatal period with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia, cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrhythmia, and high mortality.

CAD is a multifunctional cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the first three steps of de novo pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis. Its glutamine-dependent carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase II module uses glutamine, bicarbonate and ATP to produce carbamoyl phosphate; its aspartate carbamoyltransferase module forms carbamoylaspartate; and its zinc-dependent dihydroorotase module cyclizes this intermediate to dihydroorotate. Subsequent reactions catalyzed by DHODH and UMPS produce UMP. CAD forms oligomeric assemblies and couples nucleotide supply to growth through allosteric and phosphorylation-dependent regulation, including S6K-mediated phosphorylation. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause CAD deficiency, a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy associated with impaired pyrimidine production and depleted glycosylation precursors. Clinical studies report uridine responsiveness, and human CAD-knockout complementation distinguishes damaging from functional variants.

CALM1 encodes calmodulin, a small calcium-sensor protein with four EF-hand calcium-binding sites. Human CALM1, CALM2 and CALM3 share the canonical calmodulin protein sequence, while their disease-associated variants and gene regulation remain distinct. Calcium-dependent conformational changes and target binding enable calmodulin to activate enzymes such as CaMKII and calcineurin and to regulate ion channels. Calmodulin supplies regulatory activity rather than the kinase, phosphatase or channel-pore activity of its partners. It acts in soluble pools and in partner-associated membrane and intracellular complexes. In cardiac cells, its control of CaV1.2 inactivation and RyR2 calcium release links calcium sensing to electrical and contractile function; pathogenic CALM1 variants can disrupt these interactions and cause severe arrhythmia.

CALM2 encodes calmodulin, a small EF-hand calcium sensor whose canonical protein sequence is identical to those encoded by CALM1 and CALM3. Calcium-dependent conformational changes and target association couple intracellular calcium signals to activation of enzymes such as CaMKII and calcineurin and to regulation of ion channels. Calmodulin supports CaV1.2 calcium-dependent inactivation and controls RyR2-mediated calcium release; it also regulates potassium channels through distinct target interactions. Soluble cytoplasmic and nuclear pools exchange with membrane- and organelle-associated complexes. CALM2 variants can cause severe cardiac arrhythmia, including long-QT syndrome, through altered calcium sensing and channel regulation. The same protein also participates in cell-cycle and synaptic signaling, with gene-specific expression and dosage contributing biological context.

Calmodulin-3 is a small EF-hand calcium sensor that binds target proteins and couples changes in intracellular calcium to enzyme and ion-channel regulation. Human CALM1, CALM2 and CALM3 share the canonical calmodulin protein sequence, while their transcriptional regulation and disease variants are gene-specific. Calcium-dependent conformational changes enable calmodulin to activate CaMKII-family kinases and calcineurin and to modulate nitric-oxide synthases. Channel-associated calmodulin regulates calcium-dependent inactivation of voltage-gated calcium channels and sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release through RyR2, linking calcium sensing to cardiac electrical activity and contraction. CALM3 variants can disrupt these regulatory interactions and cause severe arrhythmia. Cytoplasmic, membrane-associated, nuclear and mitotic pools reflect recruitment to different target complexes.

Calreticulin (CALR) is the soluble endoplasmic reticulum-luminal lectin chaperone that, together with the membrane-bound paralog calnexin, constitutes the central calnexin/calreticulin cycle of ER glycoprotein quality control. Its globular lectin domain binds monoglucosylated N-glycans (Glc1Man9GlcNAc2) on nearly all nascent glycoproteins, while its extended proline-rich P domain recruits the oxidoreductase ERp57 (PDIA3) and the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin B to promote folding, oligomeric assembly, and retention of incorrectly folded glycoproteins, triaging terminally misfolded clients toward degradation. Calreticulin is a major high-capacity, low-affinity calcium-binding protein that regulates ER calcium storage and homeostasis. It is a key chaperone in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I peptide loading complex, where it stabilizes peptide-receptive MHC I and couples optimal epitope selection to glycan processing. Beyond the ER, calreticulin has well-documented secondary roles: a cell-surface and extracellular "eat-me" signal that promotes phagocytic clearance of apoptotic and stressed cells (immunogenic cell death), C1q/complement interactions, and additional context-specific cytosolic and nuclear activities.

CAMK2A encodes the alpha subunit of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, an intracellular serine/threonine kinase enriched at excitatory neuronal synapses. Calcium-bound calmodulin relieves autoinhibition, and intersubunit Thr286 autophosphorylation can sustain activity after calcium falls. Alpha subunits form homo- and heteromeric CaMKII assemblies and couple synaptic calcium signals to phosphorylation and association of glutamate-receptor complexes and other targets. These activities support synaptic potentiation and dendritic-spine development. Alpha-specific perturbations also influence presynaptic release and endocannabinoid signaling in rodent models. Human pathogenic variants can disrupt catalytic regulation, target association and neuronal development; their effects are variant dependent.

CAMLG (CAML; calcium-modulating cyclophilin ligand; also GET2) is an integral endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein with a large cytoplasmic N-terminal region and three C-terminal transmembrane helices. Together with WRB (GET1), it constitutes the mammalian ER membrane receptor for the cytosolic ATPase TRC40/GET3, forming the GET (guided entry of tail-anchored proteins) insertase complex. This complex captures newly synthesized tail-anchored membrane proteins from TRC40/GET3 in the cytosol and mediates their post-translational insertion into the ER membrane. CAML is the mammal-specific subunit (not homologous to yeast Get2) and forms a heterotetramer with WRB stabilized by phosphatidylinositol binding; CAML and WRB are mutually dependent for correct membrane integration and stability. CAML was originally identified as a cyclophilin-B-binding protein that elevates intracellular calcium and activates NF-AT signaling in T cells, and it has additional reported roles in B cell survival, EGFR recycling, and stabilization of the E3 ligase RNF122. Biallelic variants cause an autosomal recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG2Z) characterized by a neurological phenotype and defective membrane trafficking.

Calpain-3 (CAPN3/p94) is an intracellular calcium-dependent cysteine endopeptidase enriched in skeletal muscle. It binds titin and undergoes rapid, regulated autolysis, coupling proteolytic activity and changing sarcomeric localization to muscle maintenance and adaptation. Mouse genetic and biochemical studies also support a nonproteolytic contribution to the organization of sarcoplasmic-reticulum-associated proteins and calcium release. Other experimental contexts implicate CAPN3 in myoblast reserve-cell formation, selective signaling-protein turnover, and Def/UTP25-associated nucleolar p53 turnover. These activities depend on cell context and the CAPN3 construct or isoform examined. Pathogenic human CAPN3 variants cause calpainopathy, including recessive and dominant limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

Calpain-5 is a non-classical calcium-regulated cysteine protease with a calpain catalytic core and a C-terminal C2 domain. It occurs in intracellular soluble and membrane-associated pools; C2-domain residues and S-acylation contribute to membrane association. Full-length human CAPN5 undergoes calcium-dependent autoproteolysis. Pathogenic variants cause neovascular inflammatory vitreoretinopathy, but their biochemical effects depend on the variant and experimental construct. Candidate interaction partners and in-vitro substrates have been reported; the physiological substrates and pathways underlying its retinal function remain incompletely defined.

ALX1 (CART1) is a paired-like homeodomain transcription factor that recognizes regulatory DNA and can activate or repress transcription depending on the promoter and cellular context. It acts in the nucleus and is enriched at developmental regulatory chromatin in human cranial neural crest cell models. ALX1 contributes to craniofacial mesenchymal and skeletal patterning; biallelic human variants cause frontonasal dysplasia, while mouse and zebrafish studies resolve additional lineage and developmental-stage requirements. In responsive human epithelial and ovarian cancer models, ALX1 promotes SNAI1 expression and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Its sequence recognition and transcriptional activity are established, whereas native oligomeric stoichiometry and the physiological roles of many high-throughput interaction partners remain less well resolved.

CASK is a multidomain intracellular scaffold and protein kinase of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase family. Its L27, PDZ, SH3 and guanylate-kinase-like regions organize membrane-associated protein complexes, including neurexin-, syndecan- and LIN7-containing assemblies. Its N-terminal kinase domain catalyzes protein phosphorylation without requiring magnesium; this activity is distinct from the inactive C-terminal guanylate-kinase-like domain. CASK occupies cytoplasmic, membrane and context-dependent nuclear pools and contributes to neuronal function and development. Pathogenic CASK variants cause X-linked neurodevelopmental disorders, including microcephaly with pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia and intellectual disability with or without nystagmus.

CASP1 (caspase-1; interleukin-1 beta converting enzyme, ICE) is the prototypical inflammatory caspase, a cysteine-dependent aspartate-specific endopeptidase of the clan CD peptidase family. It is expressed mainly in monocytes, macrophages and other immune cells and is synthesized as an inactive cytosolic zymogen comprising an N-terminal caspase-recruitment domain (CARD), a large (p20) catalytic subunit bearing the His/Cys catalytic dyad, an interdomain linker, and a small (p10) subunit. The active enzyme is a heterotetramer of two antiparallel p20/p10 heterodimers. Caspase-1 is the effector protease of canonical inflammasomes: cytosolic pattern-recognition receptors (NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRC4/NAIP, AIM2, pyrin) assemble, directly or through the bipartite adaptor ASC/PYCARD, into platforms that cluster procaspase-1 via homotypic CARD-CARD interactions, driving proximity-induced autoproteolysis and activation. Once active, caspase-1 cleaves the precursors of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 into their mature, secreted, receptor-binding forms, and cleaves gasdermin-D to release its pore-forming N-terminal fragment, which permeabilizes the plasma membrane to drive the lytic, proinflammatory cell death pyroptosis and the release of mature IL-1 family cytokines. Caspase-1 also processes additional substrates (including caspase-7, cGAS, sphingosine kinase 2 and ZNFX1) and contributes to apoptosis in some overexpression and disease contexts. It acts in the cytosol and is central to innate immune defense against microbial infection and to the pathology of autoinflammatory diseases.

CASP10 is a tandem-death-effector-domain initiator caspase recruited by FADD to Fas/CD95 and TRAIL death-inducing signaling complexes and to related cytosolic death platforms. Proximity-induced CASP10 activation generates an Asp-directed cysteine endopeptidase that can mature downstream caspases; prodomain-only isoforms can instead scaffold NF-kappaB signaling, and a CASP10-c-FLIP(L) protease complex has a survival role in myeloma cells by cleaving BCLAF1 to restrain autophagic cell death.

CASP14 encodes caspase-14, a unique non-apoptotic cysteine protease essential for keratinocyte terminal differentiation and cornification. Unlike other caspases involved in apoptosis, CASP14 functions specifically in the formation of the epidermal barrier by cleaving filaggrin to generate natural moisturizing factors and facilitating nuclear degradation during cornification. The protein is expressed in suprabasal layers of the epidermis and is critical for maintaining skin hydration and barrier function.

CASP3 (caspase-3; apopain/CPP32/Yama) is the principal executioner cysteine-aspartic protease of apoptosis in human cells. Synthesized as an inactive zymogen, it is activated by proteolytic cleavage by initiator caspases (CASP8, CASP9, CASP10) and granzyme B into a heterotetramer of two p17/p12 heterodimers with a catalytic cysteine. It is a cysteine-type endopeptidase (EC 3.4.22.56) that cleaves substrates strictly after aspartate residues, with a preferred Asp-X-X-Asp recognition motif. During the execution/demolition phase of apoptosis it cleaves hundreds of cellular substrates, including PARP1, the ICAD/DFF45 inhibitor of the CAD/DFF40 DNA-fragmentation nuclease, cytoskeletal and junctional proteins, and numerous signaling proteins, thereby dismantling the dying cell and promoting phosphatidylserine exposure for efferocytosis. Beyond classical apoptosis, caspase-3 cleaves gasdermin-E (GSDME/DFNA5) to switch cells to pyroptosis, processes cytokines such as IL-18, and restrains innate antiviral signaling by cleaving cGAS, MAVS, IRF3, and NF-kB subunits. It also has non-lethal roles, contributing to differentiation programs (e.g., erythroid, keratinocyte, neuronal) through limited substrate cleavage. Caspase-3 acts mainly in the cytoplasm/cytosol but its active form is also found in the nucleus during apoptosis; its activity is restrained by inhibitors including XIAP and BIRC6 and by S-nitrosylation of the catalytic cysteine.

Calsequestrin-2 is an acidic calcium-storage protein of the cardiac sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium-dependent assembly into oligomers and polymers supports its high-capacity buffering of luminal calcium. Association with the ryanodine-receptor release complex couples this reservoir to regulated calcium release for cardiac contraction. CASQ2 variants can disturb calcium storage, polymerization or release-complex regulation. Biallelic pathogenic variants and certain heterozygous variants cause catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, with variant-dependent mechanisms and penetrance. The protein supplies calcium buffering and regulatory interactions; the ryanodine receptor supplies the ion-conducting pore.

CASR encodes the calcium-sensing receptor, a class C seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor that functions as a homodimer. Its extracellular Venus flytrap and cysteine-rich domains sense extracellular calcium and transmit ligand-dependent conformational changes to the transmembrane domains. Calcium sensitivity is modulated by amino acids and other ligands. Coupling to Gq/11 and Gi/o pathways regulates phosphoinositide signaling, intracellular calcium responses and cyclic AMP in a cellular-context-dependent manner. In parathyroid and renal tissues, this sensing system helps regulate parathyroid hormone secretion and systemic calcium balance. Receptor folding, dimerization, glycosylation and regulated delivery to the cell surface influence signaling capacity. Loss-of-function and gain-of-function variants alter the calcium set point and underlie familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism and autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, with severity and inheritance depending on the variant and allelic context.

Caveolin-1 is an oligomeric membrane protein that forms the membrane-embedded structural framework of caveolae together with CAV2 and cavin partners. Its tightly associated protomers support a stable coat that can insert into the cytoplasmic membrane leaflet. Separate interactions organize selected receptors, channels and trafficking proteins, while direct inhibition of nitric-oxide synthase provides a defined enzyme-regulatory activity. Partner recruitment and regulatory direction depend on the cellular context, phosphorylation and relative protein abundance. The alpha and beta products arise from alternative translation initiation. Biallelic loss of CAV1 causes generalized lipodystrophy, and heterozygous variants are associated with incompletely penetrant pulmonary arterial hypertension; evidence for dominant lipodystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is more limited.

Caveolin-3 is the muscle-enriched caveolin isoform and an oligomeric component of the caveolar coat at the sarcolemma. Together with cavins, it organizes membrane microdomains and coordinates recruitment and trafficking of selected proteins. Its interactions with dysferlin and MG53 connect caveolar organization to muscle membrane repair. Channel-specific assemblies regulate calcium currents and potassium-channel surface turnover, including recruitment of NEDD4-2 to hERG. Disruption of caveolin-3 abundance or trafficking can impair muscle membrane organization and cause caveolinopathy.

EF-hand calcium-binding protein of the mitochondrial intermembrane space and the principal regulatory subunit of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter. MICU1 sits on the intermembrane-space face of the inner membrane, peripherally associated with the MCU/EMRE pore, and forms disulfide-linked heterodimers with MICU2 or MICU3 (and, in skeletal muscle and kidney, MICU1-MICU1 homodimers). Binding of Ca2+ to the EF-hands of the dimer, with high affinity and strong cooperativity, switches the uniporter between a closed and an open state: below the threshold MICU1 occludes the pore and prevents constitutive Ca2+ leak into the matrix, and above it MICU1 stimulates flux, so that mitochondria respond to cytosolic Ca2+ transients rather than to resting Ca2+. Loss of MICU1 causes constitutive matrix Ca2+ loading, excess reactive oxygen species and sensitisation to apoptotic stress, and in humans causes a myopathy with learning difficulties and extrapyramidal signs. Whether the low-Ca2+ state reflects physical pore occlusion or allosteric potentiation of MCU was disputed, with recent patch-clamp and divalent-free flux measurements favouring occlusion. MICU1 also has functions that do not require the uniporter: it localises to the inner boundary membrane and cristae junctions, interacts with MIC60 and CHCHD2, and is required for MICOS complex assembly and normal cristae architecture, and Micu1-null lethality is not rescued by removing MCU or EMRE. A further uniporter-independent role has been proposed, in which Ca2+-dependent MICU heterodimers scaffold a metabolon coupling glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase to succinate dehydrogenase/complex II; this is a recent single-laboratory claim and is not yet independently corroborated.

CBL (c-Cbl) is a cytoplasmic RING-type ubiquitin E3 ligase and signaling adaptor that is recruited to activated tyrosine-kinase complexes. Its N-terminal tyrosine kinase-binding module recognizes selected phosphotyrosine motifs, while a linker and RING domain recruit an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme; Tyr371 phosphorylation helps relieve autoinhibition. Its proline-rich region binds SH3-domain adaptors, and phosphorylated CBL can itself recruit SH2-domain partners. CBL ubiquitinates receptors and associated signaling proteins, contributing to receptor trafficking and attenuation of growth-factor signals. Ubiquitination can also regulate signaling without accelerating degradation: CBL and CBLB redundantly modify ligand-engaged LAG3, enabling its inhibitory activity in T cells. CBL can act through noncatalytic interactions as well, with context-dependent effects on survival signaling. It acts in the cytosol and on the cytoplasmic side of membrane-associated complexes. Germline CBL variants cause a Noonan-like disorder with variable predisposition to juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia; disease-associated linker/RING variants can disrupt ubiquitination and receptor trafficking.

SERPINH1 (Serpin H1, better known as HSP47, also called colligin / gp46) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, collagen-specific molecular chaperone. Although it belongs to the serpin superfamily by fold, it is non-inhibitory and does not act as a protease inhibitor. In the ER lumen HSP47 binds specifically to the folded triple-helical region of procollagen, stabilizing the nascent triple helix, preventing local unfolding and premature aggregation, and serving as a quality-control factor in collagen biosynthesis. HSP47 accompanies procollagen from the ER to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment/cis-Golgi, where the lower pH triggers its release; it then recycles back to the ER through its C-terminal RDEL retrieval signal. It is heat-shock inducible. Loss-of-function variants cause autosomal-recessive osteogenesis imperfecta type X (OI10), underscoring its essential role in collagen maturation.

Human cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) is a PLP-dependent, heme-containing enzyme that catalyzes condensation of L-serine with L-homocysteine to form cystathionine, the first step of transsulfuration toward cysteine. It also uses cysteine with homocysteine to generate cystathionine and hydrogen sulfide. The principally cytoplasmic enzyme has a C-terminal regulatory region that binds S-adenosylmethionine and controls activity and stability; its reduced heme can bind NO and CO and modulate catalysis. CBS forms oligomeric assemblies, and human full-length protein can form regulated filaments. A sumoylated fraction has also been detected at the nuclear scaffold. Biallelic CBS deficiency causes classical homocystinuria through impaired homocysteine metabolism.

KRIT1 (CCM1) is a non-enzymatic adaptor of endothelial cells built from an N-terminal pseudo-Nudix domain, three NPX(Y/F) motifs, four ankyrin repeats and a C-terminal FERM domain. In its closed form the first NPAY motif binds the FERM domain; ICAP1 (ITGB1BP1) binding to that motif opens the protein, and KRIT1 competes with the beta1 integrin tail for ICAP1, relieving ICAP1 suppression of integrin activation. KRIT1 binds microtubules, and GTP-loaded Rap1 binding to the FERM F1/F2 lobes releases it from microtubules to PI(4,5)P2-containing plasma membrane at cell-cell junctions. There the FERM domain binds the cytoplasmic tail of the transmembrane protein HEG1, and the third NPX(Y/F) motif binds the PTB domain of CCM2, anchoring the KRIT1-CCM2-PDCD10 complex at VE-cadherin-based adherens junctions. Junctional KRIT1 stabilizes cell-cell contacts, suppresses RhoA/Rho kinase signaling and, through CCM2, restrains MEKK3-KLF2/4 signaling, keeping the endothelium quiescent and polarized; it also influences FOXO1/SOD2-dependent ROS homeostasis. Loss-of-function variants cause autosomal dominant cerebral cavernous malformations type 1.

CCND1 encodes cyclin D1, a 295-residue, non-catalytic D-type cyclin that couples mitogenic signalling to cell-cycle commitment. Its cyclin box binds CDK4 or CDK6 to form a serine/threonine kinase holoenzyme in which cyclin D1 supplies the activating conformational change and the substrate specificity; the assembled complex phosphorylates the retinoblastoma family pocket proteins RB1, RBL1 and RBL2 in G1, releasing E2F transcription factors and licensing the G1/S transition, after which cyclin E-CDK2 completes RB inactivation. Cyclin D1 itself has no kinase activity. Its abundance, rather than its intrinsic activity, is the regulated variable: RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling induces CCND1 transcription while PI3K-AKT supports translation and complex assembly, and CIP/KIP proteins (p21, p27) promote holoenzyme assembly and carry it through the nuclear membrane into the nucleus. At the G1/S boundary, GSK3-dependent phosphorylation of Thr286 drives XPO1-mediated nuclear export followed by ubiquitination - chiefly by CRL4(AMBRA1), and by SCF(FBXO4), SCF(FBXO31) after DNA damage, APC/C-CDC27 and UHRF2 - and proteasomal degradation, while USP2 deubiquitination and FBXO32-mediated K27-linked ubiquitination stabilise it. Beyond the kinase, cyclin D1 has CDK-independent activities as a transcriptional corepressor: tethered by INSM1 it delivers HDAC1/HDAC3 to the NEUROD1 and insulin promoters, and it restrains the androgen receptor and NRF1. Cyclin D1 is nuclear, cytoplasmic and nuclear-membrane associated, is required in a tissue-restricted way for retinal and pregnancy-associated mammary development, and is a prominent oncogene: it is amplified or overexpressed in many carcinomas and is placed under immunoglobulin-locus control by t(11;14)(q13;q32) in mantle-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma.

Cyclin D2 is a noncatalytic regulatory subunit of cyclin-dependent kinases that couples growth signals to G1 progression and entry into S phase. Its association with CDK4 or CDK6 promotes retinoblastoma-family protein phosphorylation by the kinase subunit, relieving restraint on cell-cycle progression. Cyclin D2-containing complexes redistribute between the cytoplasm and nucleus, with nuclear-envelope and chromatin-associated populations observed during cell-cycle entry. Cyclin D2 abundance is controlled by ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis. Pathogenic CCND2 variants cause megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-polydactyly-hydrocephalus syndrome 3.

CCNE1 encodes cyclin E1, a regulatory subunit of the cyclin-dependent kinase CDK2. Cyclin E1 binds and activates CDK2, driving phosphorylation of key substrates such as RB1 to promote the G1/S transition of the cell cycle and commitment to S-phase entry. Cyclin E1 itself has no catalytic activity; its role is to confer substrate specificity and temporal activation on CDK2. The protein is predominantly nuclear and its abundance is tightly regulated by SCF-FBXW7-dependent ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, triggered by phosphodegron motifs phosphorylated by CDK2 and GSK3. CCNE1 amplification and overexpression are frequent in cancers, particularly high-grade serous ovarian cancer (~22% of TCGA cases), where they drive replication stress and genomic instability.

CD14 is a leucine-rich-repeat glycoprotein expressed mainly by monocytes and macrophages (weakly by granulocytes). It exists as a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored protein on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, concentrated in lipid rafts, and as a soluble form in plasma and other body fluids produced by release of the anchored protein or secretion of an anchor-less form. Its bent LRR solenoid carries an amino-terminal hydrophobic pocket that binds acylated microbial molecules. CD14 accepts monomeric bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from LPS-binding protein (LBP) and transfers it to the TLR4-MD-2 complex, forming with TLR4 and MD-2 the LPS receptor complex; it similarly delivers di- and triacylated lipopeptides to TLR2-TLR6 and TLR2-TLR1 heterodimers and binds lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan. Because it lacks a transmembrane and cytoplasmic domain, CD14 does not itself transmit signals across the membrane, but it greatly sensitises cells to low ligand concentrations. Membrane CD14 is also required for LPS-induced TLR4 dimerization and for Syk/PLCgamma2-dependent endocytosis of TLR4, which enables TRIF-dependent interferon production from endosomes. Soluble CD14 confers LPS responsiveness on CD14-negative cells such as epithelial and endothelial cells. CD14 also binds apoptotic cells and mediates their recognition and clearance by macrophages without triggering inflammation. Mice lacking CD14 are resistant to endotoxic shock.

CD19 is a single-pass membrane glycoprotein of B lymphocytes that organizes signaling at the B-cell surface. It associates with CD21/CR2 and CD81 in a co-receptor complex, and its phosphorylated cytoplasmic tail recruits signaling proteins, including PI3K regulatory subunits and GRB2. This noncatalytic adaptor function adjusts the sensitivity of antigen-receptor signaling and supports effective humoral immune responses. Biallelic loss of CD19 function can cause antibody deficiency despite the presence of mature circulating B cells.

CD28 is the prototypic T cell co-stimulatory receptor (signal 2) that synergizes with TCR engagement (signal 1) to enable full T cell activation. It is a ~44 kDa disulfide-linked homodimer of the immunoglobulin superfamily, containing an extracellular IgV-type domain with a conserved MYPPPY motif that mediates binding to its ligands CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) on antigen-presenting cells. CD28 is expressed on nearly all human CD4+ T cells and a substantial fraction of CD8+ T cells. Upon ligation, the cytoplasmic tail recruits signaling molecules via three key motifs: YMNM (binds PI3K p85 subunit and GRB2), PRRP (recruits ITK leading to PLCgamma1 and SLP-76/GADS engagement), and PYAP (binds Lck and assembles PKC-theta at the synapse). These converge on NF-kB, AP-1, and NFAT transcriptional programs and mTOR-dependent metabolic reprogramming to drive IL-2 production, T cell survival, proliferation, and effector differentiation. The inhibitory receptor CTLA-4 competes for the same B7 ligands with higher affinity, providing a critical negative regulatory checkpoint. Inherited CD28 deficiency causes susceptibility to HPV-related verrucosis (IMD123). CD28 localizes to the immune synapse at the T cell-APC interface, where it accelerates Lck recruitment to TCR microclusters and lowers the TCR activation threshold.

CD3D encodes CD3 delta, a single-pass type I membrane glycoprotein that supplies structural and signaling functions within the T cell antigen receptor complex. Its extracellular immunoglobulin-like domain and transmembrane helix form a CD3 delta-epsilon heterodimer that supports assembly of the receptor. Its cytoplasmic tail contains one immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif, providing a phosphorylation-dependent signaling interface. Human CD3 delta is present in both alpha-beta and gamma-delta TCR-CD3 complexes. The clonotypic TCR chains recognize ligand, while the associated CD3 chains couple recognition to intracellular signaling. CD3D supports T cell receptor signaling and thymocyte development; biallelic loss-of-function variants cause immunodeficiency 19, a form of severe combined immunodeficiency.

CD3 epsilon is a single-pass membrane subunit of the T-cell antigen-receptor complex. Its extracellular and transmembrane contacts assemble CD3 gamma-epsilon and delta-epsilon heterodimers with the clonotypic receptor, while its cytoplasmic basic region, proline-rich sequence and ITAM recruit signaling proteins including LCK, NCK, ZAP70 and SYK. CD3 epsilon coordinates these interactions without intrinsic kinase activity. Ligand recognition by the clonotypic chains is thereby coupled to T-cell signaling; CD3 epsilon also receives an inhibitory input from ITPRIPL1 and participates in LAG3-associated regulation of the receptor. CD3E disruption causes immunodeficiency 18, a T-B+NK+ severe combined immunodeficiency.

CD3G encodes CD3 gamma, a single-pass signaling subunit of the T cell antigen receptor. Its extracellular immunoglobulin-like domain pairs noncovalently with CD3 epsilon, and extracellular and transmembrane contacts help organize the receptor complex. Human alpha-beta and reconstituted gamma-delta TCR complexes contain this gamma-epsilon module. The cytoplasmic tail carries one ITAM whose phosphorylation permits signaling-effector recruitment, including ZAP70, while a separate dileucine sorting signal engages endocytic adaptors and helps control receptor internalization. CD3 gamma promotes normal surface receptor abundance and efficient ligand- or PKC-stimulated trafficking; some mature human T cells retain surface receptors and constitutive internalization without it. Biallelic defects cause variable immunodeficiency, sometimes accompanied by autoimmunity and altered regulatory-T-cell function.

CD247 (CD3 zeta) is a single-pass membrane signaling subunit of T-cell antigen receptors and selected activating immune receptors. It forms a disulfide-stabilized zeta homodimer whose transmembrane contacts assemble the TCR-CD3 complex; human CD247 also forms homo- or mixed dimers with FcRgamma in CD16A receptor complexes. Its cytoplasmic tail carries three ITAMs, which become docking sites for ZAP70 after phosphorylation by Src-family kinases, coupling receptor engagement to intracellular signaling without intrinsic kinase activity. Receptor recognition specificity is supplied by the assembled ligand-binding subunits. CD247 occupies plasma-membrane and intracellular trafficking pools, with receptor composition and adaptor usage varying by lymphocyte type and species.

CD4 is a single-pass type I cell-surface glycoprotein of the immunoglobulin superfamily, expressed on helper and regulatory T cells and, in human, also on monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and NK cells. Its ectodomain comprises four immunoglobulin-like domains, D1 to D4. The membrane-distal D1 domain binds a non-polymorphic concavity formed by the alpha-2 and beta-2 domains of MHC class II molecules, with Phe43 of CD4 inserting into that pocket; the interaction is of remarkably low affinity, so CD4 contributes not by independent ligation but by being co-recruited to a peptide-MHC class II complex that the T cell receptor is already engaging. On the cytoplasmic face, two cysteines in the short CD4 tail together with two cysteines in the LCK unique region coordinate a single Zn2+ ion in a zinc clasp, so that CD4 carries the Src-family kinase LCK and delivers it to the TCR-CD3 complex, where LCK phosphorylates the CD3 ITAMs and initiates the ZAP70-LAT-PLCG1 cascade. Palmitoylation of the membrane-proximal cysteines plus LCK association concentrate CD4 in plasma-membrane rafts and contribute to receptor and PKC-theta clustering at the immunological synapse, and D4-mediated dimerization is required for stable class II binding. CD4 thereby sets the sensitivity and the avidity threshold of class II-restricted recognition, which shapes thymic selection into the CD4 lineage and the subsequent helper T cell response, including IL-2 production. Outside T cells, MHC class II ligation of CD4 on human blood monocytes triggers MAPK- and Src-kinase-dependent differentiation into mature macrophages, a role absent in mouse monocytes, which do not express CD4. When the TCR and CD4 engage the same agonist peptide-MHC class II, their cytosolic juxtamembrane regions become proximal within a compact TCR-CD3-pMHCII-CD4 macrocomplex, and in resting T cells CD4 accumulates at microvillar tips in an LCK-dependent manner. A short CD4 isoform that retains D4, the transmembrane segment and the tail but lacks the distal domains still binds LCK yet cannot bind HLA class II. Loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal recessive CD4 deficiency (immunodeficiency 79) with recalcitrant HPV warts and, in a cohort of seven patients, no detectable CD4+ T cells but an expanded population of TCR alpha-beta CD4-CD8- double-negative cells with helper-like phenotypes that partly substitute for the missing compartment. CD4 is additionally the primary cellular receptor for HIV-1: the same D1 surface binds the envelope glycoprotein gp120 and triggers the conformational change that exposes the CCR5/CXCR4 site, and HIV-1 Nef and Vpu in turn down-regulate CD4 by clathrin-mediated endocytosis and ER-associated degradation.

CD79A (Ig-alpha) is a type I membrane protein that forms the signaling heterodimer of the B-cell antigen receptor with CD79B (Ig-beta). Its extracellular and transmembrane regions help assemble and express the receptor complex, while its cytoplasmic immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif provides phosphorylation-dependent docking sites for intracellular signaling proteins. Antigen recognition is supplied by the associated membrane immunoglobulin; CD79A contributes signal transmission and receptor organization rather than intrinsic kinase activity. This receptor unit supports B-cell development, activation and survival. Loss-of-function variants can disrupt the pro-B to pre-B transition and cause autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia. An alternative splice transcript lacks part of the extracellular region.

CD79B (Igβ) is a type I transmembrane signaling subunit of the B-cell antigen receptor. It forms a disulfide-linked heterodimer with CD79A that associates with membrane immunoglobulin, supports receptor assembly and surface expression, and couples antigen recognition to intracellular signaling through immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs. The paired CD79 chains also support receptor-directed antigen trafficking to late endosomal processing compartments, facilitating MHC class II presentation. Ig-beta enhances Ig-alpha phosphorylation in chimeric-receptor experiments, although the underlying recruitment or protection mechanism is unresolved. Biallelic CD79B defects cause autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia 6; the hypomorphic G137S allele impairs heterodimer assembly and receptor surface expression, with a leaky block in B-cell development.

Codanin-1 is an intracellular regulator of histone-chaperone availability. It binds ASF1A and ASF1B through multiple interaction elements, including histone-mimicking helices, and sequesters them away from histones and downstream partners. Its predominant cytosolic activity limits ASF1 access to the nucleus and thereby regulates histone supply for chromatin assembly. Codanin-1 also binds and stabilizes CDIN1; its C-terminal region stimulates CDIN1 RNA exonuclease activity in purified assays. The physiological RNA substrates and the relationship between these activities remain unresolved. Biallelic CDAN1 variants cause congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type I with abnormal erythroblast chromatin.

CDC14A is a cysteine-dependent protein phosphatase with a strong preference for proline-directed phosphoserine substrates. Centrosomal and cytoplasmic CDC14A dephosphorylates drebrin and regulates actin-dependent primary cilium growth, while other protein substrates connect it to cell-cycle regulation. Its intracellular distribution varies with cell state and protein form and includes centrosomal, cytoplasmic and nuclear pools; in vertebrate sensory hair cells it also occupies kinocilia and stereocilia. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause hearing loss, sometimes accompanied by male infertility. Catalytic competence and intracellular targeting can be separable, with the C-terminal region contributing to functions required for hearing.

CDC20 (p55CDC) is the mitotic coactivator of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), the multisubunit cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase that drives the metaphase-to-anaphase transition and mitotic exit. CDC20 has no catalytic activity of its own: its N-terminal C-box, KILR motif and C-terminal IR tail dock it onto the mitotically phosphorylated APC/C (APC8/CDC23 and APC3/CDC27), where it relieves APC1 auto-inhibition, enhances E2 recruitment and, through its C-terminal WD40 beta-propeller, recognises D-box, KEN-box and ABBA degrons on substrates. APC/C-CDC20 polyubiquitinates securin (PTTG1) and cyclin B1, releasing separase to cleave cohesin and inactivating CDK1, and also targets cyclin A, NEK2A, KIF18A, BUBR1, USP22, FBXO31 and AXIN2. CDC20 is the direct target of the spindle assembly checkpoint: unattached kinetochores catalyse its incorporation into the mitotic checkpoint complex (BUBR1-BUB3-CDC20-MAD2), in which MAD2 and BUBR1 occupy its degron receptor sites and block E2 access so that APC/C stays inactive until all chromosomes are bioriented; APC/C-mediated ubiquitination of MCC-bound CDC20, opposed by USP44 and promoted by p31comet, then dissolves the MCC and reactivates the ligase. CDC20 is synthesised from G1/S, peaks in mitosis, is regulated by BUB1 phosphorylation and SIRT2 deacetylation, and is degraded at the M/G1 transition when CDH1/FZR1 takes over APC/C activation. It localises to kinetochores, spindle poles/centrosomes and the mitotic cytosol. In oocytes, APC/C-CDC20 executes homologue disjunction at the meiosis I metaphase/anaphase transition, and biallelic CDC20 loss-of-function variants cause oocyte maturation arrest and female infertility (OZEMA14). In rodent postmitotic neurons a centrosomal Cdc20-APC pool additionally regulates dendrite morphogenesis and presynaptic differentiation.

CDC42 is a small Rho-family guanine-nucleotide-binding protein that couples extracellular and intracellular signals to changes in cell architecture. Its GTP-bound state engages effectors such as WASP-family proteins, PAK kinases and PAR6 polarity complexes; intrinsic GTP hydrolysis, accelerated by GTPase-activating proteins, returns it toward an inactive GDP-bound state. Spatial control of this cycle at membranes regulates actin organization, filopodial protrusion and cell polarity. Cytosolic and organelle-associated pools support context-dependent trafficking and mitotic functions. Alternative products differ at their C termini, including sequences involved in lipid modification and membrane targeting.

CDC45 is a nuclear replication factor that forms the CMG helicase with the MCM2–7 motor and the GINS complex. It contributes the architecture needed for productive DNA unwinding and remains associated with the replication machinery during DNA synthesis. Purified human CDC45 also binds single-stranded and branched DNA. Its RecJ-related fold has lost the conserved nuclease active site, and ATP-driven unwinding is a property of the assembled CMG complex. Biallelic hypomorphic CDC45 variants cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome and craniosynostosis, linking impaired replication capacity to developmental growth defects.

LRBA is a large BEACH-domain membrane-trafficking scaffold that cycles among cytosolic, trans-Golgi, endosomal, and other endomembrane pools. ARF-family GTPases recruit LRBA to the trans-Golgi network and Rab4-positive endosomes, where it supports endosomal traffic and endolysosome homeostasis. In activated and regulatory human T cells, LRBA routes the inhibitory receptor CTLA4 toward Rab11 recycling compartments and away from lysosomal degradation, thereby maintaining CTLA4 abundance and immune homeostasis. LRBA also participates in ATG9A-vesicle delivery to damaged mitochondria during phagophore growth and PINK1/Parkin mitophagy. In activated human B cells, LRBA binds the regulatory RIIalpha and RIIbeta subunits of protein kinase A and can act as an activation-dependent A-kinase anchoring protein. Biallelic LRBA loss causes an immunodeficiency and autoimmunity syndrome with impaired B-cell activation, plasmablast formation, immunoglobulin secretion, and CTLA4-dependent immune regulation. The LRBA PH-BEACH tandem forms an integrated structural unit, but its PH domain did not bind phospholipids in direct assays. Two reviewed protein isoforms exist, without evidence that the established trafficking or anchoring functions are isoform-specific.

E-cadherin is a classical, calcium-dependent cell-surface adhesion protein prominent in epithelial tissues. Its five extracellular cadherin repeats form adhesive contacts with cadherins on neighboring cells, while its cytoplasmic tail associates with catenins and connects the adhesion complex to the cortical cytoskeleton. These interactions organize and stabilize adherens junctions and help maintain epithelial architecture. E-cadherin undergoes regulated endocytosis, recycling and proteolytic shedding, allowing junction strength and surface abundance to change during tissue remodeling. Loss or alteration of its adhesive function contributes to developmental defects and to the invasive behavior of several epithelial cancers.

Cadherin-11 is a type II classical cadherin that mediates calcium-dependent homophilic cell adhesion, particularly in mesenchymal cells. Its extracellular cadherin repeats engage cadherin molecules on adjacent cells, while the canonical cytoplasmic tail recruits catenins at adherens junctions. These contacts coordinate cell organization and collective movement. A truncated splice isoform modulates the intact protein, and proteolytic release produces an extracellular fragment. CDH11 dysfunction perturbs craniofacial development; osteoblast and valve-cell studies also connect its adhesive role to tissue formation and remodeling.

CDH2 encodes N-cadherin, a classical single-pass transmembrane cadherin. Its extracellular cadherin domains bind cadherins on neighboring cells to mediate calcium-dependent adhesion, while its cytoplasmic tail binds catenins that organize and stabilize adherens junctions. This adhesive architecture supports tissue integrity and the development and organization of neural and cardiac tissues. Neural stem-cell anchorage, synaptic organization and axon growth are specialized contexts of this adhesion system. De novo variants affecting the extracellular or cytoplasmic domains are associated with a multisystem developmental disorder that includes callosal, cardiac, ocular and genital abnormalities.

P-cadherin (cadherin-3) is a type I classical cadherin that mediates calcium-dependent homophilic cell-cell adhesion. Its extracellular cadherin domains recognize P-cadherin on adjoining cells, while its intracellular region associates with beta-catenin in adhesive junctions. It is expressed in epithelial compartments including basal cells and hair follicles. P-cadherin supports follicular keratinocyte proliferation, maintenance of the hair growth phase and follicular pigmentation through context-dependent signaling relationships. Biallelic CDH3 defects cause sparse hair with progressive macular dysfunction, and can also cause ectodermal dysplasia with limb abnormalities.

CDK4 (cyclin-dependent kinase 4) is a 303-residue serine/threonine protein kinase of the CMGC group, CDC2/CDKX subfamily (EC 2.7.11.22), and the catalytic subunit of the cyclin D-CDK4 holoenzyme. It is catalytically inactive as a monomer and is activated by binding a D-type cyclin (CCND1, CCND2 or CCND3) together with phosphorylation of the activation-loop residue Thr172; activity is opposed by the INK4 inhibitors (p16/CDKN2A, p15/CDKN2B, p18/CDKN2C, p19/CDKN2D) and modulated by the CIP/KIP proteins (p21/CDKN1A, p27/CDKN1B, p57/CDKN1C), which both promote complex assembly and, at higher stoichiometry, inhibit. Before assembly CDK4 is chaperoned by Hsp90-Cdc37. In early-to-mid G1 the cyclin D-CDK4 complex phosphorylates the retinoblastoma-family pocket proteins RB1/pRb, RBL1/p107 and RBL2/p130, relieving their repression of E2F transcription factors and thereby licensing E2F-dependent gene expression and the G1/S transition; cyclin E-CDK2 subsequently completes RB hyperphosphorylation. Additional substrates include SMAD3, FOXM1 and RUNX2. CDK4 is cytoplasmic when uncomplexed; the cyclin D-CDK4 complex assembles in the cytoplasm, accumulates at the nuclear membrane and translocates into the nucleus at the G1/S transition, where it colocalizes with RB1, and is also detected in nucleoli and heterochromatin. Together with its paralog CDK6, CDK4 is the dedicated metazoan G1 cyclin-dependent kinase. It is a major oncology drug target: CDK4 amplification and activating mutations occur in cancer, the germline R24C variant causes familial melanoma, loss-of-function variants cause autosomal-recessive primary microcephaly, and CDK4/6 inhibitors are established therapies in HR-positive breast cancer.

CDK5 encodes a proline-directed serine/threonine kinase activated by CDK5R1/p35, CDK5R1/p25, and CDK5R2/p39 family regulators, with major functions in neuronal development, neurite and axon growth, cytoskeletal and dendritic-spine dynamics, synaptic vesicle cycling, synaptic plasticity, and p25-linked neurodegenerative apoptosis as a stress/disease context. Human CDK5 also regulates induced neuronal autophagy through phosphorylation of SH3GLB1/endophilin B1. Beyond the nervous system, CDK5 partners with cyclin B1 in proliferating cells and is active during mitosis, where it acts as a canonical CDK-cyclin kinase required for mitotic fidelity.

CDKN1B encodes p27Kip1, a largely disordered Cip/Kip-family regulator that binds cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases. Its N-terminal inhibitory region folds on cyclin–CDK complexes and restrains CDK2 activity and the G1/S transition. p27 also bridges cyclin D1 and CDK4; the assembled complex can remain inhibited, while tyrosine phosphorylation, particularly at Tyr74, alters the inhibitory contact and permits substrate-dependent CDK4 activity. Nuclear and cytoplasmic p27 pools are regulated by phosphorylation, transport and ubiquitin-dependent turnover. Cytoplasmic interactions with RhoA and stathmin link p27 to actin and microtubule regulation, with effects on motility that depend on cell context. Loss or misregulation of p27 disrupts proliferative restraint and contributes to endocrine and other tumors.

CDKN1C encodes p57Kip2, an intrinsically disordered CIP/Kip-family inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases. Its N-terminal inhibitory region restrains cyclin-CDK activity and cell-cycle progression. Predominantly nuclear p57 coordinates proliferation with differentiation and development, with additional context-dependent effects on transcription and protein interactions. CDKN1C is an imprinted locus expressed predominantly from the maternal allele. Loss-of-function variants can cause Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, whereas IMAGe-associated variants in its PCNA-binding region increase growth suppression. Mouse studies establish roles in lens, skeletal, renal, placental and other organ development, with tissue-dependent compensation by p27.

CDKN2A encodes distinct tumor-suppressive proteins through alternative first exons and reading frames. The 156-residue p16INK4A protein (P42771) is an ankyrin-repeat inhibitor that binds CDK4 and CDK6, limits cyclin D-dependent kinase activity and restrains RB-dependent progression from G1 into S phase. Nuclear and cytoplasmic p16 pools contribute to control of proliferation and stable arrest in senescence contexts. The unrelated p14ARF protein (Q8N726-1) instead regulates the MDM2–p53 pathway. These proteins share a locus but do not share a primary sequence or interchangeable biochemical functions.

CEBPA encodes C/EBPalpha, a basic leucine-zipper transcription factor that recognizes cis-regulatory DNA as a homodimer or heterodimer and coordinates differentiation with proliferative restraint. Its N-terminal regulatory regions and interacting transcription factors shape promoter-specific activation and repression. C/EBPalpha drives granulocytic and adipocyte gene programs and contributes to differentiated functions in liver and lung. The p42 and N-terminally truncated p30 products share the C-terminal DNA-binding and dimerization region but differ in regulatory potency; an N-terminally extended product is associated with nucleolar rDNA regulation. C/EBPalpha also associates with cell-cycle regulatory proteins, linking transcriptional control to cell-cycle arrest in a product- and phosphorylation-dependent manner. Disruptive CEBPA variants impair myeloid differentiation and predispose to acute myeloid leukemia.

Centromere protein F (CENP-F, mitosin) is a very large (~3100 aa) coiled-coil protein that is farnesylated at its C-terminal CAAX motif and whose abundance is cell-cycle regulated: it accumulates in the nucleus (nuclear matrix) during S and G2, and is degraded after mitosis. In late G2/prophase CENP-F is recruited to nuclear pore complexes by direct binding of its C-terminal leucine-zipper region to the NUP133 beta-propeller, where it acts as an adaptor that recruits the NudE-family proteins NDE1 and NDEL1, and through them LIS1 and cytoplasmic dynein-dynactin, to the nuclear envelope. This NUP133-CENP-F-NDE1/NDEL1 chain keeps centrosomes tethered to the nucleus at mitotic entry and, in radial glial progenitors of the developing cortex, drives the dynein-dependent apical (G2) phase of interkinetic nuclear migration. After nuclear envelope breakdown CENP-F becomes a component of the outer kinetochore (fibrous corona), recruited via BUB1 and CENP-E, where its two terminal microtubule-binding domains couple kinetochores to dynamic, including depolymerizing, microtubule ends, and where it again recruits NDE1/NDEL1-LIS1-dynein; it contributes to stable kinetochore-microtubule attachment, chromosome congression and accurate segregation, and through a direct interaction with NDE1 it limits dynein-mediated stripping of corona proteins. CENP-F is also found at spindle poles (by dynein-mediated poleward transport), the spindle midzone and midbody, and at cytokinesis it is recruited by the Miro GTPases to mitochondria to promote their microtubule-based redistribution into daughter cells. In ciliated cells it localizes to the mother-centriole subdistal appendages, basal body and axoneme. Biallelic truncating CENPF variants cause Stromme syndrome, a ciliopathy-like disorder with intestinal atresia, ocular anomalies, microcephaly and renal defects. CENP-F has additionally been reported to bind RB-family proteins and to repress ATF4 transactivation.

CEP250, also called C-Nap1, is a large coiled-coil centrosomal protein concentrated at the proximal ends of parental centrioles. It forms cohesive assemblies and anchors components of the centrosomal linker, maintaining interphase centriole proximity and organizing the centrosomal accumulation of linker proteins. Its association with the centrosome changes during the cell cycle and is regulated by phosphorylation, including modification by NEK2. Human CEP250 variants are associated with retinal and auditory disease; experimental ciliary phenotypes depend on cell type and perturbation context.

Cofilin-2 is an actin-binding protein enriched in striated muscle that promotes filament severing and depolymerization. Its direct interaction with actin changes filament organization and supports turnover of sarcomeric thin filaments. Cofilin-2 localizes to the muscle actin cytoskeleton, including the Z-disc region, and interacts with muscle LIM protein, which modulates its activity. Human CFL2 variants can cause congenital myopathy with abnormal actin accumulation and sarcomeric organization.

CFTR is a membrane anion channel of the ATP-binding cassette protein family. Phosphorylation and ATP-dependent conformational cycling regulate its pore, which conducts chloride and bicarbonate down their electrochemical gradients. Its ATPase activity controls gating rather than pumping anions against a gradient. At epithelial apical membranes, CFTR supports salt, fluid and bicarbonate transport; tissue-specific consequences include airway surface hydration, pancreatic and intestinal secretion, and sweat-duct salt handling. Cytosolic terminal and regulatory regions engage trafficking adaptors, chaperones and regulatory proteins. The channel cycles through biosynthetic and endosomal compartments, and misfolded forms can be retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and eliminated through quality-control pathways. Pathogenic variants cause cystic fibrosis; the common F508del variant disrupts folding and cell-surface delivery, reducing epithelial anion secretion.

Choline acetyltransferase catalyses transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline, producing acetylcholine.
