It supplies the neurotransmitter in cholinergic neurons, including motor-neuron terminals, and is essential for normal neuromuscular transmission. Human CHAT produces proteins with distinct N-terminal extensions. The common smaller enzyme is principally cytoplasmic and can shuttle through the nucleus; the larger primate product is enriched in neuronal nuclei. Nuclear ChAT can affect choline-transporter expression in human neuronal cells, although the molecular connection remains unresolved. Pathogenic variants impair acetylcholine synthesis and can cause congenital myasthenic syndrome with episodic apnea.

CHD2 is a nuclear ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler with tandem chromodomains and an SNF2-family motor. It binds DNA and histones, uses ATP hydrolysis to organize nucleosomes, and regulates chromatin accessibility and histone H3.3 occupancy. Its recruitment can depend on lineage-specific transcription factors or, at DNA breaks, PARP1-generated poly(ADP-ribose). These chromatin activities contribute to gene-expression programs during development and to an accessible environment for nonhomologous end joining. Human CHD2 haploinsufficiency alters cortical interneuron development and is associated with developmental disorders and epilepsy. MyoD-dependent recruitment supports myogenic chromatin marking before differentiation in mouse cells; FOSL1-associated recruitment supports a distinct transcriptional program in human glioma cells.

CHD3 (Mi-2alpha) is an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler that changes nucleosome positioning and DNA accessibility. It forms CHD3-containing NuRD assemblies and contributes remodeling activity alongside the histone-deacetylase subunits. Its tandem PHD fingers recognize histone H3 tails, with sensitivity to their modification state. CHD3 acts mainly on nuclear chromatin and can support either transcriptional repression or activation in a target- and cell-dependent manner. Human stem-cell studies link CHD3-dependent chromatin accessibility to cranial neural crest specification. A smaller centrosomal pool associates with pericentrin and contributes to centrosomal protein retention and spindle organization. Pathogenic CHD3 variants can alter ATPase activity or its coupling to remodeling and cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent speech and language impairment.

CHD4 (Mi-2beta) is an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler that engages nucleosomal DNA and histones to change nucleosome positioning and accessibility. It is a remodeling subunit of CHD4-containing NuRD assemblies and also forms the ADNP/HP1-associated ChAHP complex. DNA-binding regulators and chromatin readers recruit these assemblies to selected genomic regions, where CHD4 supports context-dependent transcriptional repression and, in other settings, transcriptional competence. HDAC subunits provide the associated deacetylation activity. Nuclear CHD4 also supports local transcriptional control and homologous recombination at DNA lesions. Developmental consequences include regulation of erythroid gene expression and neuronal maturation. A smaller cytoplasmic and centrosomal pool associates with pericentrin, with behavior distinct from CHD3. Pathogenic CHD4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder.

CHKA (choline kinase alpha) is a cytosolic, Mg2+-dependent small-molecule kinase that catalyzes the first committed step of the CDP-choline (Kennedy) pathway of phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis: the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of choline to phosphocholine (EC 2.7.1.32). The same active site also phosphorylates ethanolamine to phosphoethanolamine (EC 2.7.1.82), contributing to phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis, although choline is the strongly preferred substrate. The enzyme belongs to the choline/ethanolamine kinase family and adopts a protein-kinase-like fold; it is active as a homodimer and can also form heterodimers with choline kinase beta (CHKB), with dimerization required for catalytic activity. CHKA is broadly expressed and is frequently over-expressed in human cancers (breast, lung, colon, glioblastoma), where elevated phosphocholine makes it an oncometabolic drug target. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants that reduce choline kinase activity cause an autosomal-recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and microcephaly. One splice isoform additionally relocalizes to lipid droplets upon glucose deprivation and, after AMPK phosphorylation and KAT5 acetylation, adopts a moonlighting protein-tyrosine kinase activity toward perilipins PLIN2/PLIN3.

CHM encodes Rab escort protein 1 (REP1), a soluble Rab-binding protein that couples Rab geranylgeranylation to membrane delivery. REP1 presents Rab substrates to the RABGGTA–RABGGTB catalytic machinery, remains associated with prenylated Rab products and delivers them to intracellular membranes. It also inhibits GDP release from Rab proteins in biochemical assays. Its defining work is substrate recognition and escort rather than autonomous geranylgeranyl-transfer chemistry. A cytosolic pool supports this trafficking cycle; nuclear localization has also been reported, with its functional significance unresolved. Loss of REP1 causes choroideremia, linking defective Rab processing and trafficking to retinal degeneration.

CHN1 encodes alpha-chimaerin Rac GTPase-activating proteins that promote GTP hydrolysis on Rac and restrain Rac-dependent cytoskeletal signaling. The alpha2 product contains an N-terminal SH2 domain in addition to a lipid-responsive C1 region and a C-terminal GAP domain; alpha1 has a different N terminus. Alpha2 associates with Eph receptors and couples guidance cues to spatially regulated Rac signaling in developing axons. Mouse and chick studies establish roles in growth-cone responses and motor-axon trajectory selection, while human dominant gain-of-function variants cause Duane retraction syndrome and strengthen Rac inactivation. Cytosolic alpha2 can redistribute toward membranes after stimulation. In human alpha2, C1-dependent diacylglycerol recognition helps control membrane recruitment, while intramolecular contacts restrain ligand access.

CHRM1 encodes the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor, a class A (rhodopsin-like) seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor. It is the most abundant muscarinic receptor in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, where it is located on the plasma membrane of the somatodendritic compartment of pyramidal neurons, and it is also expressed in sympathetic ganglia and exocrine glands. Binding of acetylcholine to the orthosteric site activates the receptor, which couples preferentially to heterotrimeric Gq/11 proteins; Gq/11 alpha subunits then stimulate phospholipase C-beta, generating inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing intracellular calcium and activating protein kinase C. Downstream consequences include suppression of the M-type potassium current and resulting neuronal depolarization, slow excitatory postsynaptic potentials, induction of immediate-early transcription factors, and stimulation of non-amyloidogenic secretion of amyloid precursor protein derivatives. M1 signaling supports hippocampal long-term potentiation and cortex-hippocampus-dependent memory, and is required for seizure induction by muscarinic agonists in mice. The receptor undergoes agonist-induced internalization and down-regulation together with Gq/G11.

CHRNA1 encodes the alpha1 subunit of the skeletal-muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Two alpha1 chains join beta1, delta and either fetal gamma or adult epsilon to form a ligand-gated cation channel at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction. Alpha1 contributes acetylcholine-recognition interfaces and pore-gating elements that convert motor-neuron transmitter release into endplate depolarization and muscle contraction. The assembled receptor also conducts calcium, with permeability influenced strongly by the complementary subunits. Pathogenic variants can impair receptor expression or alter gating and agonist affinity, causing congenital myasthenic syndromes; severe biallelic defects can cause fetal akinesia. Human splice products differ: the P3A-containing alpha+ product was not incorporated into functional receptors in the tested heterologous system.

CHRNA4 encodes the alpha4 subunit of neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Alpha4 commonly assembles with beta2 into pentameric acetylcholine-gated cation channels, contributing ligand-recognition interfaces and the shared transmembrane pore. Receptor activation depolarizes neurons and can modulate presynaptic transmitter release. The two major alpha4beta2 stoichiometries differ in agonist sensitivity, conductance and calcium permeability; accessory subunits further alter receptor behavior. Alpha4-containing receptors occur in somatodendritic and presynaptic compartments and respond to nicotine. Pathogenic pore-domain variants can alter receptor behavior and cause autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy.

CHRNB1 encodes the beta1 subunit of the skeletal-muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Beta1 contributes a pore-lining transmembrane helix and allosteric gating elements to a heteropentamer containing two alpha1 subunits, delta and either fetal gamma or adult epsilon. Acetylcholine binding at alpha1 interfaces opens the assembled cation channel at the neuromuscular postsynaptic membrane, depolarizing muscle and initiating contraction. Beta1 pore mutations can prolong channel activation and cause slow-channel congenital myasthenic disease. The function of the N-terminally shortened alternative beta1 product remains unresolved.

CHRNB2 encodes the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor β2 subunit, an integral plasma-membrane component of heteropentameric ligand-gated cation channels. β2 contributes pore-lining helices and the complementary face of agonist-binding interfaces. In receptors such as alpha4β2, subunit composition and stoichiometry tune acetylcholine sensitivity, desensitization, conductance and calcium permeability. These receptors mediate neuronal excitation and modulate transmitter release, with circuit-dependent effects on attention, nicotine responses and development of visual connections. Pathogenic variants can alter channel gating and are associated with sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy.

CHRNG encodes the gamma subunit of the fetal skeletal-muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Gamma assembles with two alpha1 subunits, beta1 and delta to form a postsynaptic cation channel that couples acetylcholine release to muscle excitation and prenatal movement. Gamma contributes to the pore, gating architecture and the complementary side of an acetylcholine-binding interface; fetal receptors have greater agonist sensitivity and longer openings than adult receptors in which epsilon replaces gamma. The human gamma-containing receptor conducts calcium as a small fraction of its inward current. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause fetal akinesia and lethal or nonlethal multiple pterygium phenotypes. The developmental replacement by epsilon explains why surviving individuals may lack ongoing postnatal myasthenia. Functional effects of the alternative product replacing residues 117–169 with lysine remain unresolved.

CHST3 encodes chondroitin 6-O-sulfotransferase 1, a type II Golgi membrane enzyme that transfers sulfate from PAPS to C6 of N-acetylgalactosamine residues in chondroitin chains. This reaction shapes extracellular and cell-surface chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans. CHST3 also sulfates galactose C6 in keratan sulfate as a lower-efficiency secondary activity. Biallelic loss of CHST3 activity causes skeletal dysplasia with joint dislocations and progressive spinal involvement.

CLCN5 encodes ClC-5, a voltage-dependent chloride:proton exchanger concentrated in renal epithelial endosomal membranes. Coupled ion transport supports proximal-tubule handling of filtered proteins and solutes, and pathogenic loss of function causes Dent disease. ClC-5 also occupies Golgi and plasma membrane pools whose abundance depends on cell context and trafficking partners, including KIF3B and TMEM9-family proteins. Its cytoplasmic CBS-domain region recognizes ATP, ADP and AMP. The physiological consequences of nucleotide occupancy and the distribution of the two human protein products remain incompletely resolved.

CLCN7 encodes ClC-7, a member of the CLC family that functions as an electrogenic 2Cl(-)/1H(+) antiporter (exchanger) rather than a passive chloride channel. It resides in the membranes of late endosomes and lysosomes, and in osteoclasts it localizes to the ruffled border bounding the resorption lacuna. ClC-7 forms an obligate heteromeric complex with the accessory beta-subunit OSTM1, which is required for ClC-7 protein stability and transport activity. By coupling chloride flux to the outwardly directed proton gradient, ClC-7 provides the counter-ion movement that allows the V-ATPase to acidify the lysosomal lumen and the osteoclast resorption space, and it raises luminal chloride concentration. Loss-of-function variants cause osteopetrosis (recessive OPTB4 and dominant Albers-Schonberg OPTA2) together with lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration, whereas certain gain-of-function variants cause a distinct hypopigmentation, organomegaly and delayed-myelination syndrome.

CLDN14 encodes claudin-14, a four-pass membrane protein that forms structural strands of epithelial tight junctions. Its self-association and interactions with other claudins restrict paracellular permeability, supporting the inner-ear barrier and regulated renal calcium handling. In model junctions, claudin-14 can form a barrier on its own and replace claudin-16 within claudin-19-containing strands. Its cytoplasmic C-terminal motif binds PDZ domains. Human loss-of-function variants cause recessive nonsyndromic deafness, while renal expression is responsive to calcium-sensing pathways.

CLN3 (battenin) is a multipass endolysosomal membrane protein whose loss causes juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. It conducts chloride and contributes to lysosomal ion balance and degradative function. A detailed trafficking study identified cytosolic-region binding to active Rab7 and RILP, linking CLN3 to the positioning and trafficking of late endosomal compartments. CLN3 deficiency also disrupts lipid distribution, lysosomal metabolite clearance and neuronal physiology. Cellular lipid-binding and transport observations complement these roles, while the exact mechanism of glycerophosphodiester clearance and proposed soluble glycolipid transfer remains unresolved.

CLN5 is a glycosylated lysosomal lipid enzyme that promotes bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) formation and has cysteine-dependent palmitoyl-thioester hydrolase activity. Its endogenous thioester substrates remain unidentified, and its contribution to cellular BMP pools depends on the extracellular lipid environment and other lysosomal enzymes. CLN5 passes through the secretory pathway as a processed precursor and occupies the lysosomal lumen and luminal membrane surface. Cellular studies connect it to Rab7 activation and retromer-dependent recycling of lysosomal sorting receptors. Loss of CLN5 causes a neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis with progressive neurodegeneration.

CLN6 is a multipass endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein involved in the delivery of newly synthesized lysosomal enzymes. Together with CLN8, it recruits enzyme precursors at the ER, while CLN8 subsequently accompanies cargo toward the Golgi. CLN6 forms homodimers and exposes luminal regions involved in recruitment. Its deficiency impairs lysosomal degradative capacity and causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, with progressive neurological and visual dysfunction. Secondary cellular observations include altered lipid distribution and lysosomal pH.

CLN8 is an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein with distinct cargo-receptor and lipid-acyltransferase activities. Together with CLN6 it recruits newly synthesized lysosomal enzymes, engages COPII coat machinery and escorts selected enzymes toward the Golgi before returning to the ER through a C-terminal retrieval signal. CLN8 also transfers acyl groups from acyl-CoA to lysophosphatidylglycerol to form bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate, contributing to cellular BMP pools. Loss of CLN8 disrupts lysosomal enzyme delivery and lipid balance and causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis with progressive neurological decline.

CLPP is the serine-protease subunit of mitochondrial ClpXP. After import into the matrix, mature CLPP subunits assemble proteolytic rings whose active sites face an enclosed chamber. CLPX docks to CLPP and uses ATP to recognize, unfold and translocate protein substrates; CLPP cleaves the delivered polypeptides. Oligomeric stability and activity depend on the preparation and activation state. This division of labor supports mitochondrial protein turnover and quality control. Mouse studies implicate ClpXP in ERAL1 turnover during mitoribosome maturation and in renewal of respiratory complex I N-module proteins. Human biochemical experiments establish CLPP catalysis, CLPX coupling and activation by imipridone compounds. Phosphoserine-dependent substrate recognition is supplied by CLPX. Biallelic CLPP variants cause Perrault syndrome, with sensorineural hearing loss and ovarian dysfunction; tested variants affect catalytic activity, oligomerization or CLPX coupling differently. CLPP-dependent mitochondrial stress signaling varies by model: the worm ortholog contributes to the mitochondrial unfolded-protein response, whereas the tested mouse Dars2-deficient cardiac and human SPG7-depletion systems can mount the assayed response without CLPP.

CLTC encodes clathrin heavy chain 1 (CHC17), the major structural component of clathrin-coated vesicles. CHC17 forms triskelia composed of three heavy chains and three light chains that polymerize into polyhedral lattices at the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi network. The protein contains an N-terminal WD40-like beta-propeller domain (terminal domain) that serves as the primary adaptor binding site, seven clathrin heavy-chain repeat (CHCR) domains forming the leg, and a C-terminal hub/trimerization domain. Core functions include: (1) clathrin-mediated endocytosis at the plasma membrane via AP-2 adaptor interaction; (2) intracellular trafficking at the TGN via AP-1 and GGA adaptors; (3) mitotic spindle stabilization through TACC3/ch-TOG/clathrin complex formation at kinetochore fibers. Recent evidence (2024) suggests clathrin also actively constricts membrane pores during fission, beyond its traditional coat function.

CNGA1 is the pore-forming alpha subunit of the rod photoreceptor cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channel. Three CNGA1 subunits assemble with one CNGB1 subunit in the native channel at the rod outer-segment plasma membrane. Intracellular cGMP binding promotes pore opening and cation influx; the light-driven fall in cGMP closes the channel and reduces the rod dark current. CNGA1 can also form functional homomeric channels in expression systems. Human pathogenic variants can impair channel abundance, targeting or function and cause recessive retinitis pigmentosa.

CNGA3 is the ligand-binding and pore-forming alpha subunit of the cone photoreceptor cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channel. It assembles with CNGB3 in cone outer-segment membranes, where intracellular cGMP promotes cation entry; light-driven loss of cGMP closes the channel and contributes to the cone electrical response. Human reconstituted complexes contain three CNGA3 subunits and one CNGB3. CNGA3 can also form conductive homomers and respond less effectively to cAMP. Biallelic CNGA3 variants cause achromatopsia and related cone dysfunction. Ortholog studies additionally report neuronal, glial and sensory-tissue expression and context-dependent protein interactions.

CNGB1 encodes beta subunits of sensory cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels and the soluble glutamic acid-rich product GARP2. In rod photoreceptors, CNGB1 assembles with three CNGA1 subunits at the outer-segment plasma membrane, contributing to the pore, cGMP recognition, gating and channel targeting. Olfactory beta-containing channels assemble with CNGA2 and CNGA4 and couple cAMP signals to depolarizing cation currents under calcium/calmodulin feedback. Human CNGB1 variants cause recessive retinitis pigmentosa. The separate GARP2 product is inferred to restrain basal rod PDE6 activity from biochemical studies of its bovine ortholog.

CNGB3 is the beta subunit of the cone photoreceptor cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channel. It assembles with CNGA3 in a heterotetramer containing three alpha subunits and one beta subunit. CNGB3 contributes to the ion-conduction pathway, selectivity filter and cyclic-nucleotide-binding machinery, shaping ligand sensitivity and pore gating. Intracellular cGMP controls the cone membrane current during visual transduction. Pathogenic CNGB3 variants can disrupt channel function and cause achromatopsia or related cone disorders.

Cochlin is a secreted extracellular-matrix glycoprotein with an N-terminal LCCL domain and two von Willebrand factor A domains. Its collagen-binding and sulfated-glycan-binding capacities connect it to matrix organization and maintenance, especially in the inner ear. Pathogenic COCH variants can cause dominant progressive audiovestibular disease, while biallelic loss of function also impairs hearing. Proteolytic release of the LCCL region produces a distinct immune-active fragment that can aggregate bacteria and attract immune cells. Cochlin also influences cell shape in cultured human trabecular-meshwork cells.

COL10A1 encodes the alpha-1 chain of type X collagen, a secreted short-chain collagen produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes in presumptive mineralization zones of hyaline cartilage. Three chains assemble through their C-terminal NC1 domains into homotrimers that contribute to extracellular matrix organization during skeletal development. Type X collagen forms higher-order networks in vitro and associates with collagen fibrils in tissues. Its isolated human NC1 trimer binds calcium. Dominant pathogenic COL10A1 variants cause Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia.

COL11A2 encodes the alpha-2 chain of type XI collagen, a minor fibrillar extracellular matrix collagen. Full-length chains assemble with alpha-1(XI) and a COL2A1-derived alpha-3(XI) chain in collagen-XI heterotrimers, which participate in the organization of cartilage collagen fibrils. The protein is synthesized through the secretory pathway and acts in extracellular matrices. Human variants cause skeletal dysplasia and sensorineural hearing loss; human cartilage ultrastructure and mouse tectorial-membrane studies connect these phenotypes to altered fibril organization. Alternative splicing generates products that differ in sequence and length.

COL1A1 encodes the pro-alpha-1 chain of type I collagen, a major fibrillar component of extracellular matrices in bone, skin, tendon and many other connective tissues. Its C-terminal propeptide helps select and assemble collagen chains in the endoplasmic reticulum. Two alpha-1(I) chains usually associate with one alpha-2(I) chain, although alpha-1(I) homotrimers also form. Following secretion and propeptide removal by other proteins, mature collagen molecules assemble into fibrils that provide tensile support and organize the matrix. Collagen-I matrices also interact with extracellular proteins and influence cellular adhesion, migration and signaling. Pathogenic COL1A1 variants disrupt matrix quantity or architecture and cause osteogenesis imperfecta and other connective-tissue disorders.

COL1A2 encodes the proalpha2(I) collagen chain, a secreted precursor that associates with two proalpha1(I) chains to form the usual type I procollagen heterotrimer. Its C-terminal propeptide contributes to chain recognition and assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum. After secretion and propeptide removal, alpha2-containing collagen molecules assemble into extracellular fibrils that provide tensile support to bone, tendon, skin and other connective tissues. Mutations that disrupt chain folding, processing or assembly can cause osteogenesis imperfecta or Ehlers–Danlos phenotypes.

COL2A1 encodes the pro-alpha-1(II) collagen chain, a major structural component of cartilage and vitreous extracellular matrices. Alpha-1(II) chains assemble into type-II collagen homotrimers and also supply the alpha-3 chain of type-XI collagen. Following secretion and removal of propeptides by extracellular procollagen proteinases, collagen molecules assemble into cross-linked fibrils that organize and support the matrix. Alternative splicing produces forms with different N-terminal sequences and a shorter C-terminal product. Disruption of collagen-II abundance or architecture causes skeletal dysplasias and connective-tissue disease with ocular and auditory manifestations.

COL3A1 encodes the pro-alpha-1(III) collagen chain. Three chains assemble into type-III collagen, a fibrillar extracellular-matrix component that supports the architecture and mechanical integrity of skin, blood vessels and other connective tissues. Collagen III also acts as a receptor ligand: it can engage inhibitory LAIR1 on immune cells and the adhesion receptor ADGRG1/GPR56 in the developing nervous system. Its extracellular interactions couple matrix structure to cellular adhesion and signaling. Pathogenic variants disrupt collagen secretion, assembly or matrix incorporation and cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Alternative splicing produces a shorter chain whose complete physiological activity profile is less well characterized.

COL4A1 encodes the alpha1 chain of type IV collagen, a network-forming constituent of basement membranes. The NC1-containing chain combines with COL4A2 in alpha1(IV)2alpha2(IV) protomers; associations through the C-terminal NC1 and N-terminal 7S regions connect protomers into a matrix network. Peroxidasin-dependent sulfilimine cross-links stabilize adjoining NC1 domains. This network supports tissue architecture and vascular, renal and other basement membranes, and pathogenic COL4A1 variants can disrupt their organization and integrity. Proteolysis can release the NC1-derived fragment arresten, which interacts with endothelial cell surfaces and suppresses angiogenic responses in experimental fragment preparations. Alternative splicing also produces a shortened chain lacking the NC1 region. The collagen IV gene family extends beyond animals to the filasterean Ministeria vibrans, whereas organized basement membranes have a distinct and variable distribution among animal lineages.

COL4A3 encodes the alpha-3 chain of type-IV collagen, a secreted basement-membrane protein. It assembles with alpha-4 and alpha-5 chains into triple-helical protomers that associate through terminal domains to form a matrix network, particularly important in the glomerular basement membrane. Disruption of this architecture causes Alport-spectrum kidney disease and can affect hearing. Proteolytic release of its C-terminal NC1 region produces tumstatin, a fragment that binds integrins and inhibits endothelial proliferation and pathological angiogenesis in experimental systems. Alternative transcripts change or remove portions of the C-terminal region, so their assembly and fragment activities need not be equivalent.

COL4A4 encodes the alpha4 chain of type IV collagen, a secreted structural component of basement membranes. It assembles with alpha3 and alpha5 chains into collagen IV protomers whose terminal interactions organize the glomerular basement-membrane network. The collagenous region and C-terminal NC1 domain contribute to this architecture; COL4A4 variants are associated with thin-basement-membrane nephropathy and Alport-spectrum kidney disease. Isolated recombinant human NC1, termed tetrastatin, binds integrin alphaVbeta3 and inhibits melanoma-cell growth and invasion in experimental systems. A synthetic C-terminal peptide, QS-13, binds alpha5beta1 and reduces endothelial migration and experimental vascularization, a fragment activity distinct from the intact structural chain.

COL4A5 encodes the alpha-5 chain of type-IV collagen, a secreted component of basement-membrane networks. Alpha-5 participates in alpha3/alpha4/alpha5 and alpha5/alpha5/alpha6 collagen protomers, whose terminal-domain interactions support matrix architecture in tissues including the kidney, skin and intestine. Pathogenic COL4A5 variants cause X-linked Alport syndrome. Isolated recombinant human NC1 and a synthetic pentastatin peptide bind integrin in experimental assays and perturb pulmonary endothelial barrier function. The identity, physiological production and endogenous roles of naturally released bioactive fragments remain incompletely resolved; these isolated-fragment experiments do not establish or exclude the same activity in assembled collagen.

COL5A1 encodes the alpha1 chain of type V collagen, a secreted fibrillar matrix component that helps initiate collagen fibrils and regulate their diameter and organization. Alpha1(V) commonly assembles with alpha2(V) into type V heterotrimers that coassemble with type I collagen; tissue-specific V/XI hybrid assemblies also occur. Its retained N-terminal region interacts with matrix proteins and contributes to fibril organization and cell–matrix behavior, whereas the C-propeptide participates in precursor assembly before processing. Reduced or altered alpha1(V) disrupts connective-tissue architecture and causes classical Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, with skin, joint and ocular manifestations. Alternative splicing changes a segment of the C-terminal propeptide.

COL5A2 encodes the alpha-2 chain of type-V collagen, a secreted fibrillar extracellular-matrix protein. Its principal assembly contains two alpha-1(V) chains and one alpha-2(V) chain. Type-V collagen participates in heterotypic fibrils with type-I collagen and helps organize their architecture. The alpha-2 chain supports efficient incorporation of type-V collagen into the matrix; disruption of its structure alters fibril assembly and connective-tissue integrity, causing classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Its structural contribution is particularly important in skin and corneal connective tissue. The precursor passes through the secretory pathway before extracellular processing and matrix incorporation.

COL6A1 encodes the alpha1 chain of collagen VI, a secreted extracellular matrix protein with a short triple-helical region flanked by von Willebrand factor A domains. Alpha1(VI) assembles with other collagen VI chains into triple-helical units that form disulfide-linked dimers and tetramers and extracellular beaded microfibrils. The canonical complex contains alpha1(VI), alpha2(VI) and alpha3(VI); alternative long chains support additional assembly contexts. Collagen VI provides matrix architecture around cells and connects tissue mechanics with cell adhesion and survival. Pathogenic COL6A1 variants cause collagen VI-related muscular dystrophies, including Bethlem and Ullrich phenotypes.

COL6A2 encodes the alpha2 chain of collagen VI, a secreted extracellular matrix protein with a short collagenous region flanked by von Willebrand factor A domains. In canonical collagen VI, alpha2 associates with alpha1 and alpha3 chains; intracellular dimers and tetramers give rise to extracellular beaded microfibrils that support tissue architecture. The major 2C2 product and two shorter C-terminal splice products share their N-terminal and collagenous regions, but the assembly properties of the shorter products remain incompletely established. Collagen VI occurs around cells and in connective-tissue matrices, including muscle-associated matrix. Pathogenic COL6A2 variants cause collagen VI-related muscular dystrophies, including Bethlem and Ullrich phenotypes.

COL6A3 encodes the alpha3 chain of collagen VI, an extracellular matrix protein with an extended array of N-terminal von Willebrand factor A domains, a short collagenous region and C-terminal globular domains. Long alpha3 products associate with alpha1 and alpha2 chains to form collagen VI units that assemble into dimers, tetramers and extracellular beaded microfibrils. Specific N- and C-terminal regions support higher-order assembly and matrix deposition. Human recombinant N-terminal domains bind heparin and hyaluronan. Proteolytic processing releases C-terminal fragments, including C5/endotrophin; experimentally studied fragments differ from the intact matrix chain. Alternative splicing produces five recorded human products, two of which lack the collagenous and C-terminal regions. Pathogenic COL6A3 variants cause collagen VI-related muscular dystrophies.

COL7A1 encodes the alpha1 chain of collagen VII, the principal structural protein of anchoring fibrils at epithelial basement membranes. Three alpha1(VII) chains form a long interrupted triple helix flanked by NC1 and NC2 regions. NC1 binds matrix ligands, including fibrillar collagen I, collagen IV and laminin 332; C-terminal interactions organize antiparallel assemblies that mature into anchoring fibrils linking the basement membrane to underlying connective tissue. Human skin and reconstituted matrix experiments support this mechanical attachment function. Pathogenic variants cause dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, with fragile dermal–epidermal adhesion. The two annotated splice products differ by a 32-residue segment in the collagenous region; their individual assembly and binding properties have not been comprehensively compared.

COL9A1 encodes the alpha1 chain of collagen IX, a fibril-associated collagen with interrupted triple helices in cartilage and vitreous extracellular matrix. Alpha1(IX) assembles with alpha2(IX) and alpha3(IX), and the resulting heterotrimer associates with type II collagen fibrils and other matrix components. The long alpha1 chain exposes an N-terminal NC4 domain that binds heparin and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein. Recombinant NC4 can also inhibit terminal complement assembly. Alternative transcripts encode a shorter N-terminal form and a truncated product. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause recessive Stickler syndrome with ocular, auditory and skeletal manifestations.

COL9A3 encodes the alpha3 chain of collagen IX, a fibril-associated collagen with interrupted triple helices. It assembles with alpha1(IX) and alpha2(IX) in cartilage and vitreous extracellular matrix. Its collagenous and noncollagenous regions contribute to chain assembly, and alpha3(IX) forms covalent connections within the type II/type IX collagen network. These structural interactions help organize and stabilize the matrix. Pathogenic variants cause multiple epiphyseal dysplasia and recessive Stickler syndrome with skeletal, auditory and ocular manifestations.

COMP (thrombospondin-5) is a secreted, calcium-binding matrix glycoprotein that assembles through its N-terminal coiled-coil region into pentamers. It binds collagen and other matrix ligands and promotes early collagen fibril organization in cartilage, tendon and additional connective tissues. Integrin-dependent attachment and context-dependent survival and vascular effects extend its matrix role. Its calcium-binding repeats and C-terminal domain couple conformation to ligand interactions. Pathogenic variants disrupt matrix organization, secretion or cellular homeostasis and cause skeletal or tendon-associated disease. The shorter annotated splice product lacks most of the second EGF-like domain and a short adjacent segment.

COPG1 encodes the gamma-1 subunit (gamma-1-COP) of the heptameric coatomer (COPI) complex. COPI is a cytosolic protein complex that reversibly associates with Golgi membranes and is essential for retrograde vesicle-mediated transport from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The gamma subunit resides in the adaptor "F" subcomplex (gamma/zeta) that connects ARF1-GTP to the coat and participates in cargo selection and vesicle formation. COPG1 contributes to recognition of dilysine (KKxx/KxKxx) retrieval motifs on cargo proteins and interacts with KDEL receptors for retrograde trafficking of ER-resident proteins. Mutations in COPG1 cause immunodeficiency 128 (IMD128), characterized by recurrent infections and ER stress due to defective retrograde transport of KDEL-bearing chaperones.

COQ7 (also called CLK-1, the clock-1 homolog) is the mitochondrial di-iron hydroxylase that catalyzes the penultimate step of coenzyme Q (ubiquinone, CoQ10) biosynthesis. It hydroxylates the quinone 5-methoxy-2-methyl-3-(all-trans-polyprenyl)benzoquinone (demethoxyubiquinone, DMQ) at the C6 position, using NADH and O2, to give 3-demethylubiquinone, the substrate for the final COQ3-catalyzed O-methylation that produces CoQ. It has a ferritin-like fold with a carboxylate-bridged di-iron center (it binds two iron ions per subunit and is NOT a flavin- or heme-dependent enzyme); substrate binding mediates reduction of the diiron center by NADH and initiates molecular oxygen activation for hydroxylation. COQ7 is a peripheral inner-mitochondrial-membrane protein on the matrix face and is a component of the eukaryotic CoQ biosynthetic complex (COQ metabolon / synthome) together with COQ3, COQ4, COQ5, COQ6 and COQ9; the lipid-binding protein COQ9 binds COQ7 and presents the hydrophobic DMQ substrate to it. A distinct pool of uncleaved COQ7 localizes to the nucleus and chromatin, where it participates in a mitochondria-to-nucleus retrograde signaling program that modulates reactive oxygen species metabolism and the mitochondrial unfolded protein response independently of ubiquinone biosynthesis. In humans, loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency (COQ10D8) and distal hereditary motor neuronopathy (HMNR9); the clk-1/COQ7 ortholog influences lifespan in invertebrate and mouse models.

Coronin-1A is a 461-residue WD-repeat protein with a C-terminal coiled-coil region that mediates homotypic association. In leukocyte settings it binds actin and regulates cortical actin networks, including Arp2/3-dependent nucleation and remodeling that supports migration, phagocytosis and lytic-granule access. Its localization and association with actin depend on cellular context; bulk endogenous protein can occupy actin-independent pools. Human CORO1A deficiency causes severe or combined immunodeficiency with loss of peripheral T cells. Specialized signaling and vesicle-associated observations extend beyond its actin-related behavior, while the biochemical mechanisms and contributions of distinct protein pools remain incompletely resolved.

COX10 is a multipass mitochondrial inner-membrane enzyme that converts protoheme IX (heme b) and farnesyl diphosphate to heme O. This farnesylation is the first step of heme A biosynthesis; COX15 subsequently converts heme O to heme A. Heme A supplies the prosthetic groups of cytochrome c oxidase, so COX10 deficiency impairs the accumulation and assembly of respiratory complex IV. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency with variable neurological and systemic manifestations. Alternative splicing produces a shorter protein with an altered N terminus.

COX11 is a mitochondrial inner-membrane copper metallochaperone required for assembly of cytochrome c oxidase (respiratory chain complex IV). Anchored in the inner membrane by a single N-terminal transmembrane helix, it presents a conserved C-terminal copper-binding headgroup (CFCF motif; Cys217/Cys219) on the intermembrane space side. COX11 receives Cu(I) from the soluble intermembrane-space chaperone COX17 and specifically and directly delivers/inserts copper into the CuB site of the catalytic subunit MT-CO1 (COX1) during complex IV assembly; stable copper coordination is coupled to COX11 dimerization, supported by COX19. Loss of COX11 causes mitochondrial complex IV deficiency and, in humans, an autosomal recessive infantile-onset mitochondrial encephalopathy (MC4DN23).

COX15 is a multipass mitochondrial inner membrane enzyme that converts heme O to heme A by oxidation of its C8 methyl group to a formyl group. Heme A supplies the prosthetic groups of cytochrome c oxidase, linking this biosynthetic reaction to respiratory complex IV assembly and activity. Human COX15.1 partially restores heme A content and oxidase activity in deficient patient fibroblasts. Alternative splicing produces a 388-residue product with a different C terminus from the 410-residue displayed product; equal catalytic competence of the two products has not been established. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, including severe infantile cardiomyopathy and neurological disease.

Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 4 isoform 1 (COX4-1), the ubiquitously expressed nuclear-encoded regulatory subunit of mitochondrial Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). COX4-1 is a single-pass transmembrane protein of the inner mitochondrial membrane with a large matrix-facing regulatory domain and a C-terminal intermembrane-space segment that contacts COX2 to help shape the cytochrome c docking site. Although noncatalytic, COX4-1 is the primary regulatory subunit of Complex IV, carrying an allosteric ATP/ADP-binding site in its matrix domain that mediates feedback inhibition of CIV activity at high ATP/ADP ratios. Phosphorylation of Ser58 by intramitochondrial PKA (via the sAC-cAMP-PKA axis) prevents ATP binding and relieves this inhibition, acting as a rapid bioenergetic switch. COX4-1 participates in early assembly modules (COX4-COX5A) and contributes to Complex IV stability and respirasome (CI-CIII2-CIV) formation. A tissue-specific isoform, COX4I2, is expressed under hypoxia and in lung/brain, and isoform switching between COX4-1 and COX4-2 modulates oxygen affinity and redox signaling. Pathogenic COX4I1 variants (e.g., K101N, P152T) cause autosomal recessive Complex IV deficiency (MC4DN16) with growth failure, developmental regression, and chromosomal instability.

COX5A (cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5A, mitochondrial) is a nuclear-encoded, non-catalytic structural (supernumerary) subunit of mitochondrial respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX), the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain. Complex IV transfers electrons from reduced cytochrome c to molecular oxygen, reducing it to water, and pumps protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane to help generate the proton-motive force that drives oxidative phosphorylation. The catalytic redox centres (heme a, heme a3, Cu_A, Cu_B) reside in the three mtDNA-encoded core subunits MT-CO1, MT-CO2 and MT-CO3; COX5A is one of the eleven nuclear-encoded supernumerary subunits that surround and stabilise this catalytic core. The mature protein is a peripheral inner-membrane protein on the matrix side, produced from a precursor with a cleaved N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency (nuclear type 20), presenting with pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia and failure to thrive.

Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 6A1 (COX6A1) is the liver-type nuclear-encoded COX6A isoform and a supernumerary subunit of mitochondrial Complex IV. It is a single-pass inner mitochondrial membrane component of mature cytochrome c oxidase, with a structural/regulatory role rather than an independent redox catalytic activity. COX6A1 contributes to Complex IV-dependent electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation as part of the intact enzyme, and pathogenic variants cause recessive intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with Complex IV dysfunction.

COX6A2 (cytochrome c oxidase subunit 6A2, mitochondrial; also called cytochrome c oxidase polypeptide VIa-heart / VIA-muscle) is the heart- and skeletal-muscle-specific nuclear-encoded structural (supernumerary) subunit 6A of mitochondrial respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain. It is a small, single-pass protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane and is non-catalytic; the catalytic core of Complex IV is formed by the three mitochondrially encoded subunits MT-CO1, MT-CO2 and MT-CO3. COX6A2 sits at the monomer-monomer interface of the complex and contributes to Complex IV assembly, stabilization and dimerization, and to modulation of oxidative phosphorylation. COX6A1 is the ubiquitously expressed paralogous isoform, whereas COX6A2 expression is restricted to heart and skeletal muscle. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in COX6A2 cause an autosomal recessive, muscle-specific mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency (MC4DN18), presenting with infantile hypotonia and muscle weakness and, in some patients, respiratory insufficiency and cardiomyopathy, with reduced Complex IV levels and activity in skeletal muscle.

COX6B1 is an 86-residue nuclear-encoded, noncatalytic structural subunit of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase, complex IV. It associates with the intermembrane-space face of the inner-membrane complex and supports assembly and respiratory electron transfer. Its early assembly role depends on the mitochondrial redox environment, while its presence in the mature complex supports efficient oxidase activity. The precise connection to MT-CO2 maturation remains unresolved. Pathogenic substitutions of Arg20 cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency.

COX7B (cytochrome c oxidase subunit 7B, mitochondrial; polypeptide VIIb) is a small, nuclear-encoded structural subunit of mitochondrial respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX/CIV), the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain. Complex IV comprises a mitochondrially encoded catalytic core (MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3) that carries out the reduction of oxygen to water, together with nuclear-encoded supernumerary subunits, of which COX7B is one. COX7B is a non-catalytic subunit that surrounds and supports the catalytic core and contributes to assembly and stability of the holoenzyme; it is a single-pass protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane (matrix-facing N-terminus, transmembrane helix, intermembrane-space C-terminus) synthesized as an 80-residue precursor with a cleaved mitochondrial transit peptide. Through its role in Complex IV it participates in mitochondrial electron transport from cytochrome c to oxygen and in oxidative phosphorylation. In humans COX7B is X-linked, and deleterious mutations cause an X-linked disorder, linear skin defects with multiple congenital anomalies (LSDMCA2), within the microphthalmia-with-linear-skin-defects (MLS/MIDAS) spectrum, an unconventional mitochondrial disease with a prominent neurodevelopmental phenotype.

COX8A encodes cytochrome c oxidase subunit 8A, a small (69-aa precursor, 44-aa mature) nuclear-encoded, single-pass structural subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain). It is the ubiquitously expressed COX8 isoform and, in primates, the only COX VIII form. Complex IV has a catalytic core of three mitochondrially encoded subunits (MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3) that carry the redox centers (heme a/a3, Cu_A, Cu_B) surrounded by eleven nuclear-encoded supernumerary subunits, of which COX8A is the smallest. COX8A is non-catalytic: it does not itself perform cytochrome c oxidase chemistry but contributes to the structural integrity, assembly, and stability of the complex, which reduces molecular oxygen to water using electrons from cytochrome c and helps generate the transmembrane proton-motive force that drives ATP synthesis. The protein is anchored in the mitochondrial inner membrane by a single transmembrane helix. Loss-of-function variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 15 (MC4DN15), an autosomal recessive Leigh-like syndrome with epilepsy.

Ceruloplasmin is a secreted multicopper glycoprotein whose ferroxidase activity oxidizes Fe(II) to Fe(III), coupling extracellular iron handling to cellular iron homeostasis. Soluble plasma ceruloplasmin and membrane-associated forms provide different spatial contexts for this chemistry. Loss of ceruloplasmin causes tissue iron accumulation in aceruloplasminemia. Additional measured activities include glutathione-dependent peroxide reduction, cuprous-ion oxidation and inhibition of myeloperoxidase; stressed plasma ceruloplasmin also associates with the extracellular chaperone clusterin.

CPOX is an oxygen-dependent coproporphyrinogen-III oxidase that catalyzes successive oxidative decarboxylations of two propionate side chains to form protoporphyrinogen IX in heme biosynthesis. The characterized human enzyme is a homodimer and does not require a metal or organic cofactor. Its mitochondrial precursor is processed to a mature enzyme in the intermembrane space; rat fractionation additionally identifies a loosely inner-membrane-associated fraction. Pathogenic variants cause hereditary coproporphyria or harderoporphyria.

CPS1 is a mitochondrial ammonia-dependent carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase. It uses two ATP molecules to combine ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, supplying the first synthetic step of hepatic ureagenesis and an upstream precursor for intestinal citrulline production. N-acetylglutamate activates the enzyme through a C-terminal allosteric pocket, and catalysis requires magnesium and potassium. Its ancestral glutaminase-like region does not confer the glutamine-hydrolyzing reaction of CAD or bacterial two-subunit synthetases. CPS1 deficiency impairs nitrogen disposal and causes hyperammonemia. Additional cellular pools and context-dependent functions, including support of pyrimidine synthesis in particular lung cancers, coexist with its principal mitochondrial metabolic role.

CPT1A is a malonyl-CoA-sensitive carnitine acyltransferase of the mitochondrial outer membrane. It converts long-chain acyl-CoA and L-carnitine into acylcarnitine and CoA, supplying the carnitine shuttle and mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation. This catalytic entry step links lipid utilization to nutritional state; inherited loss of function causes CPT1A deficiency with impaired fasting adaptation and hypoketotic hypoglycemia. CPT1A also has experimentally demonstrated peptide-lysine succinyltransferase activity, including ENO1 modification, and a reported adaptor role recruiting ZDHHC4 to MAVS to sustain innate immune signaling. Its two human protein products differ at their C termini; equivalent full-length activity of both products has not been established.

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT2) is a mitochondrial carnitine O-acyltransferase associated with the matrix face of the inner membrane. It completes the carnitine shuttle by converting imported acylcarnitines and coenzyme A to acyl-CoA and free L-carnitine, providing substrates for mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. The reaction is reversible, and the enzyme also forms acylcarnitines from several medium- and long-chain acyl-CoAs. CPT2 is synthesized as a 658-residue precursor with an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence. Biallelic defects impair fatty acid oxidation and can cause severe neonatal or infantile disease or recurrent muscle symptoms, including rhabdomyolysis during metabolic stress.

CR2 (CD21) is a complement-fragment receptor expressed at the cell surface, with an extracellular array of complement-control repeats, a single membrane-spanning segment and a short cytoplasmic tail. It recognizes C3-derived ligands and participates in B-cell co-receptor complexes that amplify antigen responses. CR2 also binds CD23 and Epstein–Barr virus gp350/220; the latter interaction supports viral attachment and entry. Interferon-alpha and DNA interactions have been reported in defined experimental contexts. Four protein products differ within the extracellular region, while the N-terminal ligand-binding domains and membrane anchor are retained.

CRADD (RAIDD) is a nonenzymatic signaling adaptor that links death-domain-containing PIDD1 to caspase-2. Its C-terminal death domain assembles with the processed PIDD1 death-domain region, while its N-terminal CARD recruits caspase-2 through prodomain interactions. These contacts organize caspase-2 activation platforms involved in apoptotic signaling. Cytoplasmic and, after genotoxic stress, nucleolar platforms have distinct requirements for PIDD1. CRADD-dependent caspase-2 activation can also reinforce p53 signaling through MDM2 cleavage. Disruptive human CRADD variants impair neuronal apoptotic signaling and cause a cortical malformation syndrome. The shorter alternative product retains the CARD region but lacks the canonical death domain; its cellular function is unresolved.

CRB1 is a Crumbs-family membrane protein that helps organize the apical polarity architecture of retinal photoreceptors and Müller glia. Its canonical C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages PALS1/MPP5, linking CRB1 to a larger polarity assembly at the outer limiting membrane. CRB1 supports epithelial apicobasal organization and maintenance of retinal cell contacts; biallelic defects cause a spectrum of inherited retinal dystrophies. Alternative products differ in extracellular sequence, membrane topology and cytoplasmic tail, and tissue-specific Crb1 forms have distinct functions in experimental models. Mouse work also implicates Crb1 in intestinal and retinal epithelial barriers, while human CRB1–CRB2 association has been demonstrated without resolving whether the interaction acts between or within cells.

CREB1 (Cyclic AMP-responsive element-binding protein 1) is a nuclear bZIP transcription factor that binds as homo- or heterodimers to cAMP response elements (CRE; palindromic sequence TGACGTCA) in target gene promoters. The protein contains an N-terminal transactivation domain (with Q1-KID-Q2 regions) and a C-terminal basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain for DNA binding and dimerization. Phosphorylation of Ser-119 (Ser-133 in some numbering) by upstream kinases (PKA, CaMKs, AKT, RSKs, MSKs) promotes recruitment of coactivators CBP/p300 via the KID-KIX interaction, activating transcription. CRTC coactivators can also enhance CREB-dependent transcription independently of Ser-119 phosphorylation. CREB1 mediates cAMP-responsive gene expression in response to diverse stimuli including hormones, growth factors, and neuronal activity.

CREB-binding protein (CREBBP/CBP) is a transcriptional coregulator and protein lysine acetyltransferase that couples sequence-specific transcription factors to chromatin modification and transcriptional machinery. Its nuclear activities include acetylation of histones and nonhistone regulators and promotion of RNA polymerase II transcription, with repressive effects in particular regulatory contexts. It also modifies cytoplasmic substrates. Substrate-specific studies establish MRE11 lactylation during DNA repair and N-terminal ubiquitin-chain extension activity toward primed p53 in the cytoplasmic fractions studied. Multiple interaction domains support distinct protein assemblies rather than a single invariant complex. Pathogenic CREBBP variation causes Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome; the two protein products differ within the N-terminal recruitment region, and their functional equivalence is not established.

CRTAP (cartilage-associated protein) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lumen glycoprotein that is an essential, non-catalytic subunit of the collagen prolyl 3-hydroxylation complex, together with prolyl 3-hydroxylase 1 (P3H1/LEPRE1) and cyclophilin B (PPIB/CyPB). Within this ternary complex, P3H1 provides the catalytic prolyl 3-hydroxylase activity and PPIB the peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase activity, while CRTAP acts as a scaffolding/helper subunit required for complex assembly and stability. The complex 3-hydroxylates a single specific proline residue (Pro986) of the alpha1(I) and alpha1(II) fibrillar procollagen chains in the ER and also functions as a collagen-specific molecular chaperone/foldase that controls the rate of collagen triple-helix folding; delayed folding in its absence leads to overmodification of the collagen helix. CRTAP and P3H1 are mutually stabilizing: loss of either protein destabilizes the other. A minor fraction of CRTAP is secreted into the extracellular space/matrix. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta type VII, underscoring an essential role in collagen biosynthesis and skeletal development.

CRX is a paired-like homeodomain transcription factor expressed in retinal photoreceptors. It recognizes regulatory DNA and works with other transcription factors, including NRL and nuclear receptors, to control photoreceptor gene expression. Its activity supports photoreceptor differentiation and maintenance. Human retinal organoid and reporter experiments show activation of photoreceptor genes and context-dependent repression of other retinal programs. Pathogenic variants can disrupt DNA binding or transcriptional regulation and cause inherited retinal degeneration.

Cryptochrome-1 (CRY1) is a FAD-binding transcriptional repressor in the mammalian circadian clock that binds CLOCK:BMAL1 to inhibit E-box-driven transcription and regulate rhythmic gene expression; it also modulates metabolic and glucocorticoid signaling.

Cryptochrome-2 (CRY2) is a flavoprotein member of the cryptochrome/photolyase family that functions as a light-independent transcriptional repressor in the mammalian circadian clock. CRY2 heterodimerizes with PER proteins (PER1, PER2, PER3) and translocates to the nucleus where the PER-CRY complex inhibits CLOCK:BMAL1-driven transcription, forming the negative limb of the transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL). CRY2 retains a photolyase homology region with an FAD-binding pocket that serves as a regulatory hub for ubiquitin ligase recognition (FBXL3, FBXL21) and small-molecule stabilizers rather than for photoreception. CRY2 lacks DNA photolyase activity but can bind DNA weakly. CRY2 also inhibits protein phosphatase 5 (PP5) activity, interacts with nuclear receptors (glucocorticoid receptor, HNF4A) in a ligand-dependent manner, and contributes to glucose and glucocorticoid homeostasis. CRY2 stability is regulated by phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitination via SCF(FBXL3) and SCF(FBXL21) complexes, and by PER2-mediated protection from degradation.

CRYAB (alpha-crystallin B chain, also known as HSPB5) is a small heat shock protein that functions as a molecular chaperone with holdase activity. It binds partially denatured or destabilized proteins in an ATP-independent manner to prevent their aggregation, but unlike HSP70-family foldase chaperones, it does NOT actively refold substrates. CRYAB forms large polydisperse oligomeric complexes, typically of 10-40 subunits, and can hetero-oligomerize with CRYAA (HSPB4). The canonical sHSP architecture comprises a central alpha-crystallin domain (ACD) flanked by a variable N-terminal domain (NTD) and a short C-terminal domain (CTD); chaperone activity is tightly coupled to oligomeric assembly and dynamic subunit exchange (DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54647-7). A conserved N-terminal IXI-like motif (NT-IXI) engages the ACD hydrophobic groove, and perturbation of this motif transforms native assemblies into reversible elongated helical fibrils, as resolved by cryo-EM (DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54647-7). Stress-activated phosphorylation at Ser19/Ser45/Ser59 by p38 MAPK modulates oligomeric state; the p38-CRYAB(pS59) cascade is a stress-response module that can shift CRYAB condensates toward less dynamic, aggregate-prone states under pathological conditions (DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2024.109510, DOI:10.1172/jci163730). In the eye lens, CRYAB serves dual roles as a structural protein contributing to transparency and refractive index, and as a chaperone preventing aggregation of damaged crystallins. Outside the lens, it is highly expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscle where it associates with cytoskeletal elements including desmin intermediate filaments and titin at Z-bands and intercalated disks. CRYAB also functions as a mitochondrial chaperone and anti-apoptotic protein, binding pro-apoptotic factors Bax, Bcl-X(S), cytochrome c, and VDAC; the E105K mutation causing hereditary optic atrophy reduces these interactions and impairs mitochondrial OXPHOS assembly (DOI:10.1172/jci.insight.182209). CRYAB is secreted via extracellular vesicles and exerts paracrine effects including promotion of angiogenesis in cardiac contexts (DOI:10.1186/s13287-023-03468-4, DOI:10.1038/s42003-022-04402-9). Mutations in CRYAB cause myofibrillar myopathy, cataracts, dilated cardiomyopathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy, and hereditary optic atrophy.

CSF1R (CD115/c-FMS) is a class III receptor tyrosine kinase activated by CSF1 and IL34. The extracellular D2–D3 region contacts ligand, while CSF1-driven assembly brings two receptor ectodomains around one CSF1 dimer. Ligand-dependent assembly of the full-length cell-surface receptor activates tyrosine autophosphorylation and downstream signaling that controls mononuclear-phagocyte survival, proliferation and differentiation, including macrophage, microglial and osteoclast functions. CSF1R signaling also influences cell migration, tissue development and inflammatory responses. Pathogenic variants cause neurological and skeletal disorders. An alternative 306-residue product lacks the canonical transmembrane and kinase regions.

CSF2RA encodes the ligand-recognizing alpha subunit of the granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) receptor. Its membrane form binds GM-CSF and assembles with the common beta subunit CSF2RB to form a signaling receptor that supports myeloid-cell proliferation and activation through pathways including JAK-STAT. Alternative splicing produces forms with different cytoplasmic tails or extracellular and membrane regions, including a soluble ligand-binding receptor. Defective GM-CSF receptor responses can impair pulmonary surfactant homeostasis and cause hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

CSF2RB encodes the shared transmembrane beta chain of the human GM-CSF, interleukin-3 and interleukin-5 receptors. It cooperates with ligand-specific alpha chains to form cytokine-binding receptor assemblies, stabilize high-affinity interactions and couple extracellular engagement to associated JAKs and intracellular signaling proteins. This supports cytokine-dependent survival, proliferation and activation of hematopoietic cells. The beta chain has no intrinsic kinase domain. Disrupted receptor function can impair pulmonary surfactant homeostasis and is associated with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. Two sequence-defined products differ by a six-residue insertion in the extracellular region; their functional equivalence has not been established.

Casein kinase I isoform delta (CK1delta) is a constitutively active, monomeric serine/threonine protein kinase of the casein kinase 1 (CK1) family. It uses ATP and is magnesium-dependent, and is operationally defined as a "casein kinase" by its preference for acidic substrates; it performs both primed (phospho-directed) and unprimed phosphorylation. Its activity is autoinhibited by C-terminal autophosphorylation and reactivated by phosphatase (PP1)-mediated dephosphorylation. CK1delta is a central component of the circadian clock, phosphorylating PERIOD proteins PER1 and PER2 to control their stability and nuclear entry and thereby set circadian period; missense variants (e.g. T44A, H46R) reduce kinase activity and cause familial advanced sleep phase syndrome and familial migraine. CK1delta also phosphorylates Dishevelled (DVL2/DVL3) and other components to modulate Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, acts at the centrosome and Golgi to promote microtubule nucleation, Golgi organization and primary (non-motile) ciliogenesis, and regulates the mitotic spindle. It phosphorylates a large and diverse set of additional substrates including p53/TP53, MDM2, YAP1, HIF1A, TOP2A, connexin-43/GJA1, PKD2, eIF6, DCK and tau/MAPT, linking it to DNA-damage responses, Hippo signaling, vesicle trafficking and (via tau hyperphosphorylation) neurodegeneration. It localizes to the cytoplasm/cytosol, nucleus, centrosome, perinuclear region, spindle and spindle microtubules, Golgi apparatus, ciliary basal body and plasma membrane, with correct localization dependent on kinase activity.

CSNK2A1 encodes the catalytic alpha subunit of protein kinase CK2, a broadly expressed protein serine/threonine kinase that often recognizes acidic substrate sequences. It phosphorylates nuclear and cytosolic proteins, both as a catalytic subunit of alpha/beta CK2 assemblies and in alpha-subunit assays. Substrate phosphorylation regulates protein stability, DNA-damage signaling and repair, transcription-associated complexes, chaperone systems and translation. The outcome depends on the substrate and cellular context: CK2 can stabilize one protein while promoting degradation or inhibiting a regulatory interaction in another. The shorter N-terminally truncated product lacks part of the annotated kinase domain and has not been established as catalytically equivalent to the canonical product.

CSNK2B (casein kinase II subunit beta, CK2beta) is the non-catalytic regulatory subunit of protein kinase CK2 (casein kinase 2), a constitutively active, highly pleiotropic acidophilic serine/threonine kinase. The CK2 holoenzyme is a heterotetramer in which a CSNK2B beta dimer bridges two catalytic alpha subunits (CSNK2A1 and/or CSNK2A2); the beta subunits form a stable zinc-finger-mediated dimer that links the two catalytic subunits, which make no direct contact with each other. CSNK2B has no catalytic activity of its own. Within the holoenzyme it docks and stabilizes the catalytic subunits, raises basal catalytic activity, modulates substrate specificity and selectivity, and can recruit specific substrates and partners (e.g. via its C-terminal region and its KSSR protein-interaction pocket). CK2 phosphorylates hundreds of substrates bearing acidic residues C-terminal to the phosphoacceptor (consensus S/T-X-X-D/E), influencing transcription, translation, cell cycle, DNA repair, Wnt and other signaling, circadian rhythm, and apoptosis (its major recognized role being to counteract apoptosis). CSNK2B also has activities reported to be partly independent of CK2 catalysis, including negative regulation of cell proliferation and adaptor/scaffolding roles. It localizes predominantly to the nucleus and cytoplasm. In humans, de novo loss-of-function and missense variants cause Poirier-Bienvenu neurodevelopmental syndrome (POBINDS), an autosomal dominant disorder of seizures and intellectual disability, consistent with haploinsufficiency.

CSRP3 encodes muscle LIM protein (MLP), a striated-muscle protein with two LIM domains in its full-length form. MLP binds and cross-links actin filaments and interacts with alpha-actinin and telethonin at the Z disc, supporting sarcomere integrity and the mechanical behavior of cardiac muscle. Nuclear MLP associates with myogenic transcription factors, while a short splice product shows distinct interaction and differentiation effects. Altered MLP function is associated with cardiomyopathy.

Cystatin-B (stefin B) is a small intracellular inhibitor of papain-like cysteine proteases. It binds and inhibits cathepsins with enzyme-dependent affinities, limiting peptidase activity in the cytosol and nucleus. Its subcellular distribution changes with cellular differentiation, and nuclear CSTB can restrain cathepsin L-mediated protein processing. CSTB is also detected in extracellular fluids, vesicle preparations and extracellular matrix-enriched fractions, without an established constitutive secretion mechanism. A human-cell RNA capture screen identifies an additional mRNA-binding context whose physiological consequences remain unresolved. Loss of CSTB function causes Unverricht-Lundborg progressive myoclonus epilepsy.

NKX2-5 (CSX) is an NK-2 class homeodomain transcription factor, the vertebrate ortholog of Drosophila tinman, expressed in cardiac progenitors of the first and second heart fields and in embryonic and adult myocardium, as well as in spleen mesenchyme and pharyngeal/thyroid primordia. Its homeodomain binds NKE (TNAAGTG) elements in promoters and enhancers of cardiac genes such as NPPA/ANF, GATA4, MYL2 and miR-143/145; a C-terminal autorepressive domain makes it a modest activator on its own, and it activates or represses targets in combination with partner transcription factors, notably GATA4 and TBX5 (plus SRF/myocardin and coactivators such as FBLIM1/Cal and CAMTA2). Activity is modulated by casein kinase II phosphorylation and SUMOylation. In the mouse it is required for heart looping, ventricular myocyte specialization, second heart field/outflow tract development and formation of the atrioventricular node and conduction system in a dosage-dependent manner. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in humans cause secundum atrial septal defect with progressive atrioventricular conduction block, and also ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot and other congenital heart defects; variants are also associated with congenital asplenia and thyroid dysgenesis.

CTBP1 (C-terminal-binding protein 1) is a transcriptional corepressor that functions as a scaffold to nucleate multi-protein chromatin-modifying complexes. It lacks intrinsic DNA-binding activity and is instead recruited to target gene promoters by DNA-binding transcription factors (e.g. ZEB1/2, KLFs, BCL6, MECOM) that present PXDLS/PLDLS short linear motifs. Once recruited, CTBP1 assembles corepressor complexes containing HDAC1/2, LSD1/KDM1A, and RCOR1/CoREST to mediate transcriptional silencing through histone modification. CTBP1 contains a D-isomer-specific 2-hydroxyacid dehydrogenase-like domain with a Rossmann fold that binds NAD+/NADH, and NADH binding allosterically promotes dimerization/oligomerization critical for corepressor function, establishing CTBP1 as a metabolic/redox sensor in transcriptional regulation. CTBP1 also has roles in Golgi membrane fission (as CtBP1/BARS) and has been reported at presynaptic terminals in neurons. It is predominantly nuclear but shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm depending on cellular context.

Cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH; also CSE/CGL; EC 4.4.1.1) is a cytosolic, pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme that catalyses the second and final step of the transsulfuration pathway, converting the homocysteine-derived intermediate L,L-cystathionine into L-cysteine, 2-oxobutanoate and ammonia. It thereby channels methionine/homocysteine-derived sulfur into de novo L-cysteine biosynthesis, supplying cysteine for downstream metabolism including glutathione synthesis. The enzyme is a homotetramer with PLP bound covalently to Lys212 and is most highly expressed in liver. Beyond its canonical transsulfuration role, CTH is a major enzymatic source of the gaseous signaling molecule hydrogen sulfide (H2S): using L-cysteine and, at lower rates, L-homocysteine as substrates it produces H2S (together with pyruvate/2-oxobutanoate and ammonia), and in vitro also generates lanthionine and homolanthionine. Through H2S generation and by acting as a cysteine-protein sulfhydrase (persulfidating target cysteines on proteins such as GAPDH, PTP1B/PTPN1 and NF-kB RELA), CTH participates in vascular tone, smooth-muscle biology, inflammation and the ER stress response. Loss-of-function variants cause cystathioninuria, an autosomal recessive condition marked by elevated plasma/urinary cystathionine that is largely clinically benign.

CTLA4 (CD152) is an inhibitory immune receptor whose canonical protein is a single-pass type I membrane glycoprotein with an extracellular Ig-like V-type domain and a disulfide-linked homodimeric organization. It binds the B7 ligands CD80 and CD86 more strongly than the stimulatory receptor CD28, restricting their availability for T-cell costimulation. Ligand capture and transendocytosis remove B7 molecules from neighboring antigen-presenting cells, reducing responder T-cell activation and proliferation. CTLA4 is constitutively expressed in regulatory T cells and induced in activated conventional T cells. Much of the protein resides in intracellular vesicles and cycles to the surface. Its cytoplasmic YVKM motif regulates trafficking: phosphorylation of Tyr201 in the canonical precursor prevents AP-2 binding and favors surface retention. Heterozygous pathogenic CTLA4 variants cause immune dysregulation with autoimmunity, immunodeficiency and lymphoproliferation (IDAIL). CTLA4 is targeted by the blocking antibody ipilimumab, whereas the soluble CTLA4-Ig fusion abatacept exploits B7 binding to inhibit costimulation.

Alpha-E-catenin is a cytoplasmic adhesion protein that couples cadherin–catenin complexes to the actin cortex at adherens junctions. Its N-terminal region associates with beta-catenin or plakoglobin, while actin binding, force-dependent conformational changes and recruitment of vinculin and other cytoskeletal partners stabilize junctional linkage. Cytosolic alpha-catenin can oligomerize and influence actin organization, and cytoplasmic and nuclear pools are also found outside junctions. The shorter CTNNA1b product lacks the N-terminal beta-catenin-binding region.

CTNNB1 encodes beta-catenin, a 781-residue armadillo-repeat protein that connects cadherin-based cell adhesion with Wnt-responsive transcription. At adherens junctions, its armadillo-repeat groove binds cadherin cytoplasmic tails and its N-terminal region recruits alpha-catenin, linking the cadherin complex to the force-responsive actin-associated junctional machinery. A regulated cytoplasmic pool binds APC and AXIN in the destruction complex, where CK1/GSK3 phosphorylation enables beta-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination and turnover. Canonical Wnt signaling stabilizes beta-catenin and promotes its nuclear association with TCF/LEF factors and transcriptional coactivators, activating context-dependent target genes. It also binds nuclear receptors and other regulatory partners. Its C-terminal PDZ-binding sequence supports selected scaffold interactions, while a centrosomal pool participates in centriole cohesion. These molecular activities contribute to developmental patterning, tissue homeostasis and context-dependent proliferation or differentiation; stabilizing mutations and destruction-complex defects contribute to tumorigenesis.

CTNND1 encodes p120-catenin, an armadillo-repeat protein that binds cadherin cytoplasmic tails and controls cadherin surface stability. At adherens junctions it supports persistent cell-cell adhesion by protecting cadherins from turnover while allowing regulated junction remodeling. Cadherin-free long p120 products can restrain RhoA activation; cadherin engagement and phosphorylation modulate this regulation. Cytoplasmic and nuclear pools interact with signaling proteins and the transcription factor Kaiso. Alternative translation starts and splicing generate products with different N- and C-terminal sequences and distinct patterns of nuclear accumulation and effects on cell morphology.

CTNS encodes cystinosin, a seven-transmembrane PQ-loop family transporter of the lysosomal membrane that exports L-cystine, generated by lysosomal proteolysis, from the lysosomal lumen to the cytosol by proton symport, coupling cystine binding to protonation of a buried aspartate. Lysosomal sorting depends on a C-terminal GYDQL motif recognised by AP-3 and a second conformational motif; an alternatively spliced isoform (cystinosin-LKG) lacking GYDQL also reaches the plasma membrane. Cystinosin is also present in melanosomes and engages the Ragulator-Rag complex, linking lysosomal amino acid efflux to mTORC1 signalling. Biallelic loss of CTNS causes cystinosis, with intralysosomal cystine accumulation that damages kidney (renal Fanconi syndrome), eye and other organs.

CTPS1 is a glutamine-dependent CTP synthase that couples ATP consumption to the amination of UTP, supplying CTP for nucleotide and membrane-lipid synthesis. Its homotetrameric enzyme can assemble into regulated cytoophidia in the cytoplasm and nucleus; substrate-associated human filaments enhance catalytic activity. Increased CTP supply is particularly important for proliferation of activated lymphocytes. CTPS1 also catalyzes protein asparagine deamidation: modification of histone H1 facilitates subsequent acetylation and chromatin relaxation during DNA repair, while IRF3 deamidation limits interferon induction. These catalytic roles are regulated by cellular context and phosphorylation.

Cathepsin D is a lysosomal aspartic endopeptidase that cleaves internal peptide bonds during protein turnover. The human 412-residue precursor enters the secretory pathway and is processed to active single-chain and mature light/heavy-chain forms. Its two catalytic aspartates support acidic-compartment proteolysis, including degradation of defined substrates such as apolipoprotein E and internalized insulin. Cathepsin D also occurs in extracellular and secretory-granule compartments. Release from lysosomes into the cytosol can promote mitochondrial cytochrome-c release and caspase-dependent apoptosis.

CTSF encodes cathepsin F, a papain-family cysteine endopeptidase that hydrolyzes proteins in acidic compartments. Its 484-residue precursor contains a signal peptide and an unusually long proregion with a cystatin-like segment; processing releases the 214-residue catalytic chain. Cathepsin F acts in lysosomes and can also be secreted by macrophages. It can cleave the MHC class II invariant chain and apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins in defined experimental settings. Biallelic CTSF defects cause adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type B (CLN13).

CTSK encodes cathepsin K, a papain-family cysteine endopeptidase synthesized as a 329-residue secretory precursor and processed to a mature 215-residue enzyme. It acts in lysosomal compartments and after secretion, with a prominent role in osteoclast degradation of collagen-rich bone matrix. Its proteolysis extends to several extracellular matrix proteins, and glycosaminoglycans modulate its collagenolytic activity. Specialized thyroid pools also participate in thyroglobulin proteolysis and hormone liberation. Loss of CTSK function causes pycnodysostosis, characterized by impaired bone remodeling and brittle, dense bone.

Cubilin is a very large (~3623 aa) peripheral apical-membrane glycoprotein built from an N-terminal coiled-coil region, eight EGF-like domains and a cluster of 27 CUB domains. It has no transmembrane segment and is tethered to the apical plasma membrane through the transmembrane protein amnionless (AMN), with which it assembles into the cubam endocytic receptor (one CUBN trimer plus one AMN chain). Functioning as a non-enzymatic multiligand cargo receptor, cubilin binds the intrinsic factor-cobalamin (IF-B12) complex through its CUB5-8 domains in a calcium-dependent manner and, together with AMN and megalin (LRP2), mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis of ligands. In the ileum this drives intestinal absorption of dietary vitamin B12, while in the renal proximal tubule cubam reabsorbs abundant filtered proteins such as albumin, transferrin, vitamin-D-binding protein (GC), apolipoprotein A-I/HDL and hemoglobin. Ligands are delivered to endosomes and lysosomes for processing. Loss-of-function mutations in CUBN cause Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome 1 (megaloblastic anemia 1), characterized by selective intestinal B12 malabsorption with proteinuria, and C-terminal variants are associated with chronic benign proteinuria.
