Cullin-3 is the central scaffold of CRL3 ubiquitin ligase complexes. Its N-terminal region recruits BTB/POZ-containing substrate adaptors, while its C-terminal region engages RBX1 and the ubiquitin-transfer machinery. These assemblies control protein abundance through ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal turnover and also generate non-degradative ubiquitin signals that regulate mitosis, membrane trafficking and other substrate-specific processes. CUL3 acts in nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments, with regulated Golgi, membrane and mitotic pools. Adaptor choice couples the same scaffold to targets involved in oxidative-stress responses, cell-cycle control, receptor and metabolic signaling, and transcriptional regulation. The displayed 768-residue product and two shorter splice products differ in the N-terminal adaptor-binding region: the 744-residue product lacks residues 1–24 and the 702-residue product lacks residues 23–88 of the displayed sequence.

CXCR4 is a seven-transmembrane chemokine receptor that recognizes CXCL12 and activates heterotrimeric G-protein signaling, principally through Gi. This axis directs cell migration, including hematopoietic cell homing, and contributes to immune-cell positioning and developmental programs. Pathogenic CXCR4 variants cause WHIM syndrome, characterized by peripheral neutropenia despite retention of mature myeloid cells in bone marrow. The receptor signals at the plasma membrane and undergoes regulated internalization and endosomal sorting. Intracellular interactions with arrestins, cytoskeletal regulators and ubiquitin-system proteins control its signaling and trafficking. CXCR4 also participates in MIF signaling with CD74 and serves as a CD4-associated entry coreceptor for susceptible HIV strains. Alternative N-terminal products differ in expression and ligand responses.

CYB5A encodes cytochrome b5 type A, a small heme-containing electron carrier. Its membrane-bound form is anchored in the endoplasmic reticulum and exposes a cytoplasmic heme domain to redox partners. An alternatively spliced erythrocyte form lacks the membrane anchor and occurs in the cytosol. Cytochrome b5 supports lipid and steroid metabolism and the maintenance of reduced hemoglobin. Human CYB5A enhances CYP17A1 17,20-lyase activity; disruption can cause methemoglobinemia and impaired androgen synthesis. Electron donation and substrate-dependent conformational effects contribute to its interactions with P450 enzymes.

CYLD is a cytoplasmic USP-family deubiquitinase that removes K63- and Met1-linked ubiquitin chains from signaling proteins. Its catalytic domain, stimulated and recruited by SPATA2, edits receptor-associated ubiquitin scaffolds and regulates inflammatory and cell-death signaling. Its N-terminal CAP-Gly region also binds microtubules and interacts with HDAC6 to inhibit tubulin deacetylation independently of ubiquitin hydrolysis. These catalytic and noncatalytic activities connect CYLD with microtubule organization, cell-cycle progression and centrosomal functions. Loss of CYLD function predisposes to cutaneous adnexal tumors.

Cytochrome P450 11B1 (P450c11beta, steroid 11-beta-hydroxylase; EC 1.14.15.4) is a mitochondrial inner-membrane, heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase expressed in the zona fasciculata/reticularis of the adrenal cortex. It catalyses the final step of cortisol (glucocorticoid) biosynthesis, hydroxylating 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol, and also converts 11-deoxycorticosterone (21-hydroxyprogesterone) to corticosterone. Electrons for catalysis are delivered from NADPH through the mitochondrial adrenodoxin system (ferredoxin reductase FDXR and the [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin FDX1/FDX2). CYP11B1 is the glucocorticoid-branch paralog of CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase), with which it is more than 93% identical; unlike CYP11B2 it lacks efficient 18-oxidase activity and cannot generate aldosterone. It additionally 11beta-hydroxylates adrenal androgens (e.g. androstenedione, testosterone). Loss-of-function mutations cause 11beta-hydroxylase-deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia (adrenal hyperplasia 4), the second most common form of CAH, presenting with a hypertensive phenotype (from 11-deoxycorticosterone excess) and androgen excess.

CYP11B2 encodes aldosterone synthase, a heme-dependent cytochrome P450 associated with the mitochondrial inner membrane of adrenal zona glomerulosa cells. It converts deoxycorticosterone to aldosterone through sequential 11-beta hydroxylation, corticosterone 18-hydroxylation and subsequent 18-oxidation, using oxygen and electrons supplied through the mitochondrial adrenodoxin system. Aldosterone production links this catalytic activity to sodium, potassium and water balance. CYP11B2 also accepts other corticosteroid substrates, including demonstrated conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and further metabolism of cortisol to 18-oxygenated derivatives. Loss of CYP11B2 activity causes aldosterone synthase deficiency and salt wasting. The 503-residue precursor undergoes mitochondrial targeting and processing.

CYP17A1 (cytochrome P450c17; steroid 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20 lyase) is a microsomal, endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that sits at the central branch point of steroidogenesis. It is a single bifunctional enzyme with two catalytic activities on one polypeptide: (1) 17-alpha-hydroxylase (EC 1.14.14.19), which hydroxylates the C21 steroids pregnenolone and progesterone to their 17-alpha-hydroxy derivatives (precursors of the glucocorticoid cortisol), and (2) 17,20-lyase (EC 1.14.14.32), which cleaves the C17-C20 bond of the 17-alpha-hydroxy intermediates to generate the C19 androgen precursors dehydroepiandrosterone (from 17-alpha-hydroxypregnenolone) and androstenedione (from 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone), the committed step toward androgens and estrogens. The relative use of the hydroxylase-only versus hydroxylase-plus-lyase route determines whether steroid flux is directed to cortisol or to sex steroids. Catalysis is a cytochrome-P450 monooxygenase reaction using molecular oxygen, with two electrons supplied by NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase (POR); the 17,20-lyase activity additionally requires cytochrome b5, which acts as an allosteric effector that increases the lyase Vmax without direct electron transfer. The enzyme is predominantly expressed in the adrenal cortex and gonads. Loss-of-function of CYP17A1 causes combined 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency (a form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, MIM:202110), presenting with hypertension and defective sexual development; isolated 17,20-lyase deficiency (46,XY disorder of sex development) also occurs. CYP17A1 is a validated drug target: the inhibitor abiraterone blocks androgen synthesis in castration-resistant prostate cancer.

CYP19A1 (aromatase; cytochrome P450 19A1; P-450AROM; estrogen synthase; EC 1.14.14.14) is a microsomal, endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed step of estrogen biosynthesis: the aromatization of C19 androgens to C18 estrogens. In three sequential oxidations, each consuming one molecule of O2 and one of NADPH supplied via cytochrome P450 reductase (POR), it removes the C19 angular methyl group and aromatizes the steroid A-ring, converting androst-4-ene-3,17-dione (androstenedione) to estrone and testosterone to 17beta-estradiol; the first two steps are C19-methyl hydroxylations (19-hydroxy then 19-oxo/aldehyde) and the third, unique step is A-ring aromatization with C1-beta hydrogen abstraction, C10-C19 bond cleavage, and release of formic acid. The heme iron is axially coordinated by a conserved cysteine thiolate, and membrane anchoring via the hydrophobic N-terminal segment is required to give lipophilic steroid substrates access to the active site. Aromatase is the only vertebrate enzyme that makes estrogens from androgens. It is expressed via tissue-specific alternative promoters in the gonads (ovarian granulosa cells, testis), placenta, adipose tissue, brain, skin fibroblasts, and bone. Loss of function causes aromatase deficiency (virilization, tall stature from unfused epiphyses, and osteoporosis), whereas gain/overexpression causes aromatase excess syndrome (gynecomastia and precocity); aromatase is the pharmacological target of aromatase-inhibitor therapy (letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane) for estrogen-dependent breast cancer. Minor secondary activities include 2-hydroxylation of estrone and oxidation of dihydrotestosterone to 19-nor products.

CYP1B1 is a 543-residue, heme-dependent cytochrome P450 associated with the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane. With reducing equivalents supplied by NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, it oxidizes estrogens, retinoids, arachidonic acid and diverse xenobiotics. Human CYP1B1 preferentially forms 4-hydroxylated estrogens in studied enzyme systems and generates both hydroxylated and epoxidized fatty-acid products. It also converts fatty-acid hydroperoxides to oxo products through a distinct dehydration reaction demonstrated without added NADPH. These metabolic activities influence local redox balance and vascular and extracellular-matrix behavior; loss of function is associated with primary congenital glaucoma. Mitochondrial association has been demonstrated under induced conditions in mouse tissues, while its human physiological substrate and compartment contributions remain context dependent.

Cytochrome P450 21A2 (P450c21, steroid 21-hydroxylase; EC 1.14.14.16) is a heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum (microsomal) membrane, expressed predominantly in the adrenal cortex. It catalyses hydroxylation at carbon 21 of C21 steroids using molecular oxygen and electrons supplied by NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase (POR). It acts at the branch point of adrenal corticosteroid biosynthesis, converting progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) in the mineralocorticoid branch (feeding aldosterone synthesis) and 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol in the glucocorticoid branch (feeding cortisol synthesis), thereby supplying both the mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid arms of steroidogenesis. Loss-of-function variants cause 21-hydroxylase deficiency, the commonest cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (>90-95% of cases), producing cortisol and aldosterone deficiency with adrenal androgen excess across a spectrum from salt-wasting and simple-virilizing classic forms to non-classic late-onset disease; deleterious alleles arise largely by gene conversion with the adjacent CYP21A1P pseudogene.

CYP27A1 is a mitochondrial heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 that oxidizes the terminal side chain of cholesterol and several oxygenated sterols. Using electrons supplied through adrenodoxin and adrenodoxin reductase, it forms a side-chain alcohol and can carry out further oxidation to an aldehyde and carboxylic acid. These reactions supply bile-acid intermediates and contribute to cholesterol disposal. The precursor is imported into mitochondria and processed to a mature enzyme associated peripherally with the matrix face of the inner membrane. CYP27A1 also hydroxylates vitamin D3 at C25 and generates oxysterols with context-dependent signaling activities. Loss of CYP27A1 activity causes cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.

CYP27B1 (25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase) is a mitochondrial cytochrome P450, embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and supplied with electrons from NADPH through adrenodoxin reductase (FDXR) and adrenodoxin (FDX1). It catalyses the rate-limiting step of vitamin D activation, 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (calcidiol) to 1-alpha,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (calcitriol), the hormonal ligand of the vitamin D receptor; it also 1-alpha-hydroxylates 25-hydroxyvitamin D2 and 24R,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 and other CYP24A1 pathway intermediates. Its principal site of action for circulating calcitriol is the renal proximal tubule, where expression is induced by PTH and repressed by calcitriol and FGF23, but it is also expressed in keratinocytes, macrophages/dendritic cells, osteoblasts and other extrarenal cells where locally produced calcitriol acts in an autocrine/paracrine manner. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A (pseudovitamin D-deficiency rickets).

Cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (cytochrome P450 7A1), the rate-limiting, committed first enzyme of the classic (neutral) bile-acid biosynthesis pathway. It is a heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane that hydroxylates cholesterol at the 7-alpha position to yield 7-alpha-hydroxycholesterol, consuming molecular oxygen and reducing equivalents supplied by NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase. This 7-alpha-hydroxylation is the rate-controlling step that commits hepatic cholesterol to catabolism and bile-acid synthesis; the enzyme also 7-alpha-hydroxylates several oxysterols (for example 24-hydroxycholesterol and 4-beta-hydroxycholesterol) as a minor activity. CYP7A1 is expressed almost exclusively in liver, and its transcription is tightly, dynamically regulated: it is repressed by bile acids through FXR-dependent feedback and induced by conditions such as glucose and cholestyramine, allowing bile-acid output to be matched to physiological demand. Loss-of-function causes CYP7A1 deficiency, an autosomal disorder characterized by hepatic cholesterol accumulation, hypercholesterolemia and premature gallstones.

CYP7B1 is a 506-residue, heme-containing cytochrome P450 associated with the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. It uses electrons supplied through NADPH–cytochrome P450 reductase to 7-alpha-hydroxylate 25- and 26(27)-hydroxycholesterol, supplying intermediates for alternative bile-acid synthesis and oxysterol clearance. It also hydroxylates 3-hydroxy steroids including dehydroepiandrosterone and pregnenolone. Its product 7-alpha,25-dihydroxycholesterol activates the chemotactic receptor GPR183/EBI2; mouse studies establish a stromal ligand-producing role in B-cell positioning. Loss-of-function variants cause spastic paraplegia type 5A and, in severe cases, congenital bile-acid synthesis defect type 3 with neonatal liver disease.

CYP8B1 (sterol 12-alpha-hydroxylase; 7-alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one 12-alpha-hydroxylase; cytochrome P450 8B1; EC 1.14.14.139) is a liver-enriched, endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane heme-thiolate cytochrome P450. It is the branch-point enzyme of the classic (neutral) bile-acid synthesis pathway: as a monooxygenase using O2 and electrons from NADPH--cytochrome P450 reductase, it 12-alpha-hydroxylates 7-alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one and related C27 sterol intermediates (including 3-alpha,7-alpha-dihydroxy-5-beta-cholestan-26-oate/DHCA and, in vitro, chenodeoxycholate). Because 12-alpha-hydroxylation commits intermediates toward cholic acid rather than chenodeoxycholic acid, CYP8B1 sets the cholic-acid:chenodeoxycholic-acid ratio and thereby the hydrophobicity and cholesterol-solubilizing properties of the bile-acid pool. It is a single-pass, N-terminally anchored microsomal protein that coordinates its catalytic heme iron through a conserved axial cysteine.

DAG1 encodes dystroglycan, a cell-surface receptor that links extracellular matrix to the membrane-associated cytoskeleton. The 895-residue precursor enters the secretory pathway and undergoes SEA-domain self-processing into extracellular alpha-dystroglycan and transmembrane beta-dystroglycan, which remain noncovalently associated. Glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan binds laminins and other matrix ligands, including agrin and perlecan. Beta-dystroglycan anchors this ligand-binding surface in the membrane and engages cytoplasmic partners such as dystrophin, utrophin, ankyrin and CLASPs. This linkage supports basement-membrane organization and tissue integrity, with specialized roles at muscle membranes, glial interfaces and synapses. Glycan-dependent ligand binding, cytoplasmic-tail phosphorylation and proteolytic processing modify receptor behavior. Released alpha-derived material and intracellular beta-chain pools occur in specific contexts, including nuclear trafficking in cultured human cells.

DBT encodes the lipoylated E2 acyltransferase of the mitochondrial branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. It transfers the branched-chain acyl groups derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine from its lipoyl arm to coenzyme A. Its cubic 24-subunit core organizes the other catalytic components, while its mobile domain carries the lipoyl cofactor on Lys105 in precursor numbering and channels intermediates between active sites. The lipoyl-domain linker also docks regulatory proteins. The precursor is imported into mitochondria and processed to a mature matrix enzyme. Pathogenic DBT variants can impair complex activity and cause maple syrup urine disease.

DCC (deleted in colorectal cancer) is a single-pass transmembrane netrin receptor with extracellular immunoglobulin-like and fibronectin type III domains and a cytoplasmic signaling tail. Netrin-responsive DCC assemblies recruit intracellular effectors that regulate neuronal migration, axon extension and guidance. The receptor also associates with translation machinery and supports synaptic signaling in mature neuronal circuits. In the absence of netrin, its intracellular region can organize a caspase-dependent apoptotic signaling platform. This dependence-receptor behavior underlies its proposed role as a candidate tumor suppressor. Proteolytic processing distinguishes a membrane-retained proximal signaling region from a released distal tail.

Decorin is a small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP, 359 amino acids) consisting of a core protein (~40 kDa) with 12 leucine-rich repeats and a single attached chondroitin sulfate or dermatan sulfate glycosaminoglycan chain at Ser-34. Decorin plays two critical core functions in the extracellular matrix: (1) regulation of collagen fibrillogenesis, where it binds to collagen types I, II, III, and VI fibrils via its LRR domain to control fibril diameter, spacing, and assembly kinetics, and (2) sequestration and negative regulation of TGF-beta signaling, where it binds all three TGF-beta isoforms in the ECM to diminish their biological activity and exert anti-fibrotic effects. Additionally, decorin binds and modulates receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR, VEGFR2, and Met, triggering receptor internalization, autophagy induction in endothelial cells via Peg3, and suppression of angiogenesis. Decorin also binds fibronectin, thrombospondin-1, and other ECM components. The protein is secreted and localized to the extracellular matrix, with transient presence in Golgi lumen during biosynthesis and GAG chain modification. Decorin deficiency causes congenital stromal corneal dystrophy (CSCD), highlighting its essential role in collagen organization and tissue architecture.

DCTN1 encodes p150Glued, the largest subunit of dynactin, the multiprotein complex that activates cytoplasmic dynein-1. p150Glued forms, with DCTN2 and DCTN3, the shoulder of the Arp1-filament-based dynactin complex and projects a long coiled-coil arm ending in an N-terminal CAP-Gly and basic domain. Through these regions it binds dynein intermediate chain, microtubules (preferentially tyrosinated) and plus-end tracking proteins EB1 and CLIP-170, so that dynactin, together with a cargo adaptor such as BICD2 or HOOK3, converts dynein into an ultra-processive minus-end-directed motor and loads it at microtubule plus ends. Dynein-dynactin transports vesicles, endosomes, lysosomes, retromer carriers and other organelles, drives retrograde axonal transport, and pulls on the nuclear envelope in nuclear positioning, neuronal nucleokinesis and prophase nuclear envelope breakdown. In mitosis p150Glued localizes to kinetochores, spindle poles and the cell cortex, where cortical dynein-dynactin positions and orients the spindle. A separate centrosomal pool at mother-centriole subdistal appendages anchors microtubules and supports centriole cohesion and primary cilium formation. The neuron-enriched full-length isoform (with CAP-Gly domain) also acts directly on microtubules, promoting nucleation and suppressing catastrophe. CAP-Gly domain mutations cause Perry syndrome and distal hereditary motor neuronopathy, and DCTN1 variants are associated with ALS susceptibility.

DCX (doublecortin) is a neuronal microtubule-associated protein built from two tandem doublecortin (DC) domains followed by a serine/proline-rich C-terminal region. It is expressed in migrating and differentiating neurons of the developing central and peripheral nervous system and in adult neurogenic niches. DCX binds the microtubule lattice in the groove between protofilaments, selectively and cooperatively recognizing 13-protofilament microtubules; it promotes tubulin polymerization and nucleation of 13-protofilament microtubules in vitro and stabilizes microtubules against depolymerization. In cells it decorates the GDP lattice rather than growing plus ends, and is enriched in leading processes, growth cones and neurite tips. Phosphorylation by PKA, MARK/PAR-1 and other kinases lowers its microtubule affinity at the leading edge. In migrating neurons DCX outlines the perinuclear microtubule cage that converges on the centrosome and associates with LIS1 and dynein, supporting nucleus-centrosome coupling during nucleokinesis. DCX is required for radial migration of cortical neurons; loss-of-function variants cause X-linked lissencephaly in males and subcortical band heterotopia (double cortex) in females, many of which weaken microtubule binding.

DDB2 (DNA damage-binding protein 2, the p48 subunit of UV-DDB; XPE factor) is a nuclear protein built from an N-terminal helix-loop-helix that docks onto DDB1 and a seven-bladed WD40 beta-propeller that engages DNA. With DDB1 it forms the UV-damaged DNA-binding (UV-DDB) heterodimer, the UV-lesion sensor of global-genome nucleotide excision repair (GG-NER), which directly recognizes UV-induced photolesions, preferentially cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and 6-4 photoproducts (6-4PPs), as well as apurinic/abasic (AP) sites and short mismatches. The propeller flips the damaged bases into a binding pocket and kinks the duplex by roughly 40 degrees with local strand separation. By binding CPDs that are otherwise poorly recognized, DDB2 recruits and hands off the lesion to the XPC-RAD23B complex to initiate downstream NER. DDB2 also acts as the substrate-recognition receptor (a DCAF) of a CUL4-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase, CRL4(DDB2) (DDB1-CUL4A/CUL4B-RBX1), assembling on chromatin at sites of UV damage. This ligase ubiquitinates chromatin histones (notably H2A, and H3/H4), ubiquitinates XPC to modulate its DNA binding, and autoubiquitinates DDB2 itself to trigger its turnover; these ubiquitination events help remodel and open damaged nucleosomes and hand the lesion to XPC. DDB2 activity is tightly coupled to its modification state: monoubiquitination is compatible with damage binding, whereas polyubiquitination abolishes damaged-DNA binding and promotes proteasomal degradation, and XPC (assisted by centrin-2) competitively suppresses DDB2 ubiquitination to stabilize it for repeated rounds of repair. The ligase is regulated by NEDD8 conjugation and by the COP9 signalosome, and DDB2 protein levels are controlled by ubiquitination/deubiquitination (e.g., USP24, USP44), by PARP1-dependent stabilization, and by p53, which induces DDB2 expression. Loss-of-function mutations in DDB2 cause xeroderma pigmentosum complementation group E (XP-E), with UV sensitivity and skin-cancer predisposition.

DDC encodes aromatic-L-amino-acid decarboxylase, a cytosolic PLP-dependent homodimer that converts L-DOPA to dopamine and 5-hydroxy-L-tryptophan to serotonin. These reactions supply the catecholamine and serotonin/melatonin biosynthetic pathways. The cofactor forms an internal aldimine with Lys303 and helps organize the catalytic sites. DDC also associates with tyrosine hydroxylase and DJ-1 in dopaminergic cells and can interact with androgen receptor in prostate-cell assays. Biallelic loss of function causes aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase deficiency, an inherited neurotransmitter disorder with combined catecholamine and serotonin deficiency.

AltDDIT3 is a 34-amino-acid peptide encoded by the conserved upstream open reading frame (uORF) in the 5' leader of the DDIT3 (CHOP/GADD153) mRNA, whose main open reading frame encodes the stress-induced transcription factor CHOP; the uORF spans the junction of exons 1 and 2. Translation of this uORF is the best-understood activity at this sequence: in unstressed cells ribosomes translate the uORF, the nascent chain (through an Ile-Phe-Ile motif near its C terminus) stalls elongating ribosomes, and reinitiation at the downstream CHOP start codon is suppressed; during the integrated stress response, eIF2-alpha phosphorylation lets scanning ribosomes bypass the poor-context uORF start codon and translate CHOP. This repression is a cis property of the mRNA and of the translating nascent chain. Whether the released peptide has its own function is less clear. Translation-initiation ribosome profiling supports its synthesis, and when overexpressed as a GFP fusion in HeLa cells it is mainly nuclear with a cytoplasmic fraction, co-localizes with CHOP and co-immunoprecipitates with it; an independent study also found the peptide in a stable complex with CHOP. Untagged overexpression improved cell survival under 6-thioguanine stress in a pooled screen, but the mechanism and physiological relevance of these trans activities are unknown.

DDR2 is a single-pass cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinase that recognizes triple-helical collagen through an extracellular discoidin domain. Its cytoplasmic kinase converts collagen recognition into tyrosine phosphorylation and downstream signaling that regulates cellular responses to the extracellular matrix, including matrix remodeling and mesenchymal cell behavior. DDR2 signaling contributes to skeletal growth and tissue remodeling; inherited loss-of-function and activating variants produce distinct skeletal and connective-tissue disorders.

DDX11 is an ATP-dependent DNA helicase associated with nuclear chromatin. Purified human protein unwinds DNA in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction, using accessible single-stranded loading regions and showing substrate-dependent activity on forked duplexes, D-loops and selected G-quadruplexes. DDX11 supports replication under stress and sister-chromatid cohesion, with both catalytic and protein-association contributions under investigation. A nucleolar pool participates in ribosomal chromatin regulation. Pathogenic variants cause Warsaw breakage syndrome.

DDX3X is a DEAD-box RNA helicase that binds RNA and uses an ATP-dependent cycle to remodel short RNA duplexes. It promotes translation of selected mRNAs and supports formation of functional 80S initiation complexes through interactions with translation-initiation machinery. DDX3X also performs separable noncatalytic signaling roles: it helps recruit IRF3 to IKKε during antiviral interferon induction and stimulates casein kinase 1 in Wnt signaling. The protein shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm and can enter stress granules and other conditional assemblies. Its cellular effects depend on transcript, stimulus and cell type. Pathogenic DDX3X variants are associated with neurodevelopmental disease.

Desmin is a type III intermediate-filament protein that forms a mechanically resilient cytoskeletal network in muscle cells. Its filaments connect and support myofibrillar structures around Z discs and at cardiac intercalated discs. Desmin self-assembly and interactions with cytoskeletal partners help organize this network; the small heat-shock protein alpha-B-crystallin binds assembly intermediates and modulates filament organization. Disruptive DES variants can impair filament assembly and produce protein aggregates in cardiac and skeletal muscle.

DGAT1 (diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1) is a multi-pass endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme of the membrane-bound O-acyltransferase (MBOAT) family that catalyzes the terminal and only committed step of triacylglycerol (TAG) biosynthesis: transfer of a long-chain acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol (DAG), yielding triacyl-sn-glycerol and CoA (EC 2.3.1.20). The nine-transmembrane-helix MBOAT fold forms a hydrophobic reaction chamber in the ER membrane with an invariant catalytic histidine (His415) and separate entrances for the acyl-CoA and DAG substrates; the enzyme functions as a homodimer or homotetramer. DGAT1 has a broad acyl-acceptor specificity and, besides DAG, can esterify monoacylglycerol (MGAT activity), retinol (acyl-CoA:retinol acyltransferase, ARAT; EC 2.3.1.76, generating retinyl esters), long-chain alcohols (wax ester synthesis), and monoalkylglycerols (ether-lipid synthesis). It is highly expressed in small-intestine epithelium, where its activity is essential for dietary fat absorption, and in liver and mammary gland, where it drives fat storage and milk-fat production; in skin it is the major ARAT maintaining retinoid homeostasis. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause a congenital diarrheal disorder with protein-losing enteropathy (DIAR7).

DGKE is an ATP-dependent lipid kinase that converts diacylglycerol to phosphatidic acid. Its preference for substrates bearing an arachidonoyl chain at sn-2 connects diacylglycerol signaling with phosphatidylinositol recycling. DGKE acts at membrane interfaces and is found in membrane-associated and cytosolic pools. The sn-1 chain preference is more flexible, so stearoyl-arachidonoyl diacylglycerol is not its only efficiently used substrate.

DGUOK encodes a homodimeric mitochondrial deoxyribonucleoside kinase that uses ATP to phosphorylate deoxyguanosine and deoxyadenosine. The precursor has an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence. These reactions initiate purine nucleoside salvage in the matrix and help maintain the nucleotide supply for mitochondrial DNA synthesis. Deoxyinosine and several nucleoside analogues are also substrates. The enzyme favors purine substrates, although low deoxycytidine phosphorylation has been measured in vitro. Disease-associated loss of DGUOK activity can compromise mitochondrial DNA maintenance, causing mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome or progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions.

DHCR7 is a membrane-bound, NADPH-dependent sterol reductase that reduces the C7–C8 double bond of 7-dehydrocholesterol to produce cholesterol. It acts principally at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and also contributes with EBP to microsomal cholesterol-5,6-epoxide hydrolysis. By consuming 7-dehydrocholesterol, a sterol that can interrupt membrane lipid autoxidation, DHCR7 influences cellular susceptibility to ferroptosis. Its association with DHCR24 couples the activities of terminal cholesterol-synthesis enzymes.

DHFR is cytosolic dihydrofolate reductase (EC 1.5.1.3), a small monomeric NADPH-dependent oxidoreductase that reduces 7,8-dihydrofolate to 5,6,7,8-tetrahydrofolate (THF). This is the only route by which dietary folic acid and the dihydrofolate released by thymidylate synthase re-enter the active THF pool, so DHFR sustains the one-carbon reactions that make thymidylate, purines and methionine. A mitochondrial pool has also been reported. During S and G2/M a fraction of DHFR moves to the nucleus, where SHMT1 anchors it with thymidylate synthase to the nuclear lamina and replication forks for de novo dTMP synthesis. DHFR also reduces 7,8-dihydrobiopterin to tetrahydrobiopterin, a salvage reaction with low affinity, and binds its own mRNA to repress translation. It is the target of antifolate drugs such as methotrexate. Biallelic destabilizing missense variants cause DHFR deficiency, with megaloblastic anemia and cerebral folate and tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency that respond to folinic acid.

CYB5R3 is an FAD-containing NADH–cytochrome-b5 reductase that transfers reducing equivalents from NADH to cytochrome b5. Its N-terminally anchored, myristoylated membrane product acts at the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial outer membrane, whereas a shorter soluble product is expressed during late erythroid maturation and supports methemoglobin reduction. Partner redox systems connect this chemistry to lipid metabolism and vascular nitric-oxide handling. Reconstituted CYB5R3–cytochrome-b5–mARC systems also support nitrite reduction, with mARC performing the terminal molybdenum-dependent reaction. Pathogenic variants can impair stability, FAD organization or nicotinamide-cofactor handling and cause recessive congenital methemoglobinemia.

Dyskerin is an RNA-binding pseudouridine synthase and a core protein of H/ACA ribonucleoprotein particles. Guide RNAs position RNA substrates for uridine isomerization during ribosomal and spliceosomal RNA maturation, and dyskerin-dependent pseudouridylation also occurs in human mRNAs. In telomerase, dyskerin binds and stabilizes the H/ACA region of telomerase RNA, enabling assembly and maintenance of the active enzyme while TERT carries out DNA synthesis. Dyskerin occupies nucleolar, nucleoplasmic and Cajal-body pools; a shorter natural product has reported cytoplasmic localization. Pathogenic DKC1 variants cause X-linked dyskeratosis congenita, linking altered RNA biology to telomere dysfunction.

EDAR is a single-pass cell-surface receptor for the EDA-A1 form of ectodysplasin. Its extracellular region recognizes the ligand, while its intracellular death domain couples receptor activation to adaptor-dependent signaling, including NF-kappaB activation. This signaling helps organize the development of ectodermal appendages, including teeth, hair and sweat glands. Pathogenic EDAR variants cause hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia.

DLAT is the dihydrolipoyllysine-residue acetyltransferase (E2) component of the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), EC 2.3.1.12. It carries covalently bound lipoyl cofactors on two lipoyl-binding domains (Lys132 and Lys259) and catalyzes the second step of the overall pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA reaction, accepting the acetyl group from the acetyl-dihydrolipoyl intermediate generated by the E1 component and transferring it to coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA. The C-terminal catalytic (inner) domains of E2, together with the E3-binding protein (PDHX), assemble into a 60-meric dodecahedral core with icosahedral symmetry that forms the structural scaffold of the PDC and to which the peripheral E1 and E3 enzymes and the regulatory kinases (PDK) and phosphatases (PDP) attach. Acting in the mitochondrial matrix, the PDC links cytosolic glycolysis to the tricarboxylic acid cycle by supplying acetyl-CoA. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in DLAT cause pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 deficiency, a rare subtype of PDC deficiency presenting with lactic acidosis, episodic dystonia and neurologic dysfunction. DLAT is also the 70-kDa M2 mitochondrial autoantigen recognized by antimitochondrial antibodies in primary biliary cholangitis.

DLD encodes dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase, a FAD-dependent homodimer that transfers electrons from reduced protein-bound lipoyl groups to NAD+. It regenerates lipoyl cofactors as the shared E3 component of pyruvate, 2-oxoglutarate, branched-chain ketoacid and 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase systems, and as the L protein of the glycine cleavage system. These functions connect carbohydrate oxidation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and amino-acid degradation. The canonical precursor is imported into the mitochondrial matrix; a smaller nuclear OGDH pool supplies succinyl-CoA for KAT2A-mediated histone succinylation. DLD can also display a distinct proteolytic activity under conditions that alter its dimer interface, with physiological deployment less clearly established than its metabolic role. Alternative splicing produces shorter protein forms. DLD deficiency disrupts several metabolic systems, causing variable combinations of lactic acidosis, encephalopathy and liver dysfunction.

DLG3, also called SAP102, is a membrane-associated scaffold with PDZ, SH3 and guanylate-kinase-like domains. It organizes receptor-associated protein complexes at excitatory postsynaptic sites and participates in the trafficking and retention of NMDA receptors. Its synaptic distribution and effects on receptor composition depend on developmental and splice context. DLG3 also participates in junctional organization in polarized epithelia.

DLG4 encodes PSD-95, a membrane-associated guanylate kinase family scaffold concentrated in the intracellular postsynaptic density of excitatory synapses. Its PDZ domains recognize receptor and accessory-protein tails, while its SH3–GK region recruits signaling and scaffold partners, including phosphorylation-dependent ligands. Together these contacts organize neurotransmitter receptors and downstream signaling machinery, support receptor targeting and maintain postsynaptic architecture. The GK-like domain functions in recognition rather than guanylate kinase catalysis. PSD-95 also occupies trafficking, presynaptic and non-neuronal junctional pools in particular contexts. Alternative N termini provide distinct targeting mechanisms, including the palmitoylation-associated alpha and L27-containing beta forms.

DLX1 is a distal-less homeobox transcription factor that functions as a key regulator of GABAergic interneuron specification and migration in the ventral telencephalon. It contains a conserved homeodomain that binds TAAT/ATTA-like DNA motifs at enhancers and promoters to activate or repress developmental gene programs. DLX1 is a nuclear protein that acts in the forebrain as part of the ASCL1→DLX1/2→ARX/LHX6 GABAergic fate specification network. It also plays roles in craniofacial patterning and odontogenic development. The protein can modulate chromatin architecture through promoter-enhancer loop rewiring in a motif-dependent manner. In hematopoietic cells, DLX1 interacts with SMAD4 to inhibit TGF-beta superfamily signaling pathways including activin A, TGF-beta1, and BMP4.

DMD encodes dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein expressed as multiple products that organize links between the cytoskeleton and membrane-associated protein assemblies. Long dystrophins connect actin and intermediate-filament networks to the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex at the muscle sarcolemma, stabilizing the membrane during contraction and positioning associated scaffold and signaling proteins. Alternative promoters and splicing generate shorter products with distinct neural, glial and other cellular distributions. Dystrophin deficiency disrupts muscle integrity and contributes to Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies, with cardiac and neurological manifestations influenced by the affected products.

DMP1 (dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein 1) is a secreted, highly acidic, intrinsically disordered phosphoprotein of the SIBLING family (small integrin-binding ligand, N-linked glycoproteins), encoded in the SIBLING cluster on chromosome 4q21. It is expressed by odontoblasts, osteoblasts and above all by osteocytes, and is deposited in the mineralized extracellular matrix of bone and dentin, largely as proteolytically processed N-terminal (proteoglycan) and C-terminal phosphorylated fragments. Its serine-rich acidic domains are phosphorylated in the secretory pathway, notably by the Golgi casein kinase FAM20C, and bind calcium; in vitro the protein and its C-terminal fragment nucleate hydroxyapatite, while the intact phosphorylated protein and the N-terminal domain can inhibit crystal growth, so DMP1 is regarded as a matrix regulator of biomineralization. It also carries an RGD motif and engages alphaVbeta3 integrin. Loss of DMP1 in mice and humans causes defective osteocyte maturation, hypomineralized bone and dentin, and elevated osteocytic FGF23 expression with renal phosphate wasting (autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets type 1), indicating that DMP1 is also required, by a still undefined mechanism, to restrain FGF23 production. A nuclear, transcriptional role in pre-osteoblasts has been proposed but is less firmly established.

DMRT1 is a sequence-specific transcription factor that regulates gonadal cell identity and germ-cell development. Its DM DNA-binding region recognizes cis-regulatory sequences and forms DNA-dependent homomeric assemblies. DMRT1 acts in the nucleus and can activate or repress transcription depending on target and cellular context. It supports testicular differentiation and maintenance of the male somatic program; in mouse spermatogonia it also restrains premature meiotic entry. Alternative human transcripts encode three predicted isoforms with different C-terminal sequences.

DNAH1 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 1; also HDHC7/DNAHC1, mouse ortholog Mdhc7/Dnah1) is a 4265-residue heavy chain of a single-headed inner dynein arm (IDA) of the motile axoneme. It has the usual dynein heavy chain layout: an N-terminal stem that anchors it within the arm, and a motor head of six AAA modules (four with ATP-binding P-loops) with a coiled-coil stalk that carries the microtubule-binding domain. Like other axonemal dyneins it is expected to use ATP to generate force toward microtubule minus ends, driving doublet sliding. DNAH1 is expressed mainly in testis and trachea. In human sperm it lies along the whole flagellum, and in respiratory epithelium along the full length of the ciliary axoneme, where PCD studies assign it to IDA d. It associates with the axonemal light intermediate chain DNALI1, and with the flagellar proteins TTC29 and ZMYND12; DNALI1, DNAH3 and DNAH12 are each needed for DNAH1 to reach the sperm flagellum. Biallelic DNAH1 loss of function in men causes asthenoteratozoospermia with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF; spermatogenic failure 18), with loss of inner dynein arms, disorganized doublets and frequent loss of the central pair, usually without respiratory disease. One consanguineous family with a homozygous missense variant had primary ciliary dyskinesia (CILD37). Dnah1-null mice are infertile, with poorly progressive sperm and a roughly 50% reduction in tracheal ciliary beat frequency, but their axonemes look grossly normal, possibly because a shorter Dnah1 isoform partly substitutes. DNAH1 therefore acts as a force-generating IDA motor whose loss most strongly affects the sperm flagellum.

DNAH10 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 10) is a 4471-residue axonemal dynein heavy chain. With DNAH2 it forms the two heavy chains of the two-headed inner dynein arm f (I1 dynein; DNAH10 corresponds to the Chlamydomonas 1-alpha subspecies). The arm also contains the intermediate chains DNAI3, DNAI4 and DNAI7 and several light chains. It has an N-terminal stem and a motor head of six AAA modules with ATP-binding P-loops and a coiled-coil stalk with a microtubule-binding domain. Like other axonemal dyneins it is expected to generate minus-end-directed force that drives doublet sliding. DNAH10 is expressed mainly in testis and trachea and lies along the whole sperm flagellum and in respiratory cilia, where it localizes independently of the light intermediate chain DNALI1. Biallelic DNAH10 variants cause asthenoteratozoospermia with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF; spermatogenic failure 56), with loss of inner dynein arms and reduced DNAH2, DNAH6 and DNAH1 in sperm. Other families have primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic respiratory infection, situs inversus and disordered respiratory axonemes. Dnah10 knockout and knock-in mice reproduce male infertility and PCD-like airway disease with hydrocephalus. Zebrafish dnah10 mutants have slower-beating ependymal monocilia and spinal curvature. Later reports link DNAH10 to manchette function during spermiogenesis, through bridging of the UCHL3-PACRG complex, and to primary cilia in skeletal development, but these roles are less well established.

DNAH11 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 11) is a beta-type heavy chain of the outer dynein arm (ODA), the ATPase motor that powers ciliary beating by sliding outer doublet microtubules towards their minus ends. In human respiratory cilia DNAH11 is found only in the proximal part of the axoneme, where it forms proximal (type 1) ODAs with the gamma chain DNAH5; its paralog DNAH9 takes this place in distal ODAs. Its mouse orthologue, left-right dynein (lrd, Dnah11), is present in the motile monocilia of the embryonic node and is needed for the leftward nodal flow that breaks left-right symmetry; iv/iv mice carrying lrd mutations show randomized situs. DNAH11 interacts with CFAP45, which joins a proximal axonemal module with CFAP52 and adenylate kinase AK8 that is thought to regulate local adenine nucleotide levels. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause primary ciliary dyskinesia 7 (CILD7). This is one of the commonest forms of PCD with normal ciliary ultrastructure on standard electron microscopy: tomography reveals only a partial proximal ODA loss, and cilia beat in a stiff, hyperkinetic pattern with reduced amplitude. Situs abnormalities are frequent. DNAH11 is not detected in the human sperm axoneme, and male fertility can be preserved.

DNAH12 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 12, also known as DHC3/DNHD2) is an inner dynein arm (IDA) heavy chain of the sperm flagellar axoneme. It is the shortest member of the axonemal dynein heavy chain family (3092 aa): it keeps the N-terminal stem and the ATP-binding AAA1-AAA4 modules, but lacks a typical microtubule-binding domain at the tip of the stalk. It is expressed in human trachea and testis; human testis single-cell RNA data place its expression mainly in spermatocytes and early spermatids. In mice, Dnah12 is expressed most highly in testis and at lower levels in lung, trachea and oviduct. The protein lies along the sperm flagellum. Rather than acting as an independent force-generating motor, DNAH12 is needed to assemble the sperm IDA. It binds the IDA components DNALI1 and DNAH1 and recruits them to the axoneme. It also binds the radial spoke head proteins RSPH1, RSPH9 and DNAJB13 and helps keep the central pair stable. DNAH12 sits near radial spoke 1, because it is depleted from sperm when the RS1 protein IQUB is lost. The recruitment hierarchy is not fully settled: one patient studied by another group lost DNAH12 and the central-pair protein SPAG6 but kept DNAH1 in the flagellum. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause asthenoteratozoospermia with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), IDA loss and central-pair loss (spermatogenic failure 100, SPGF100). Dnah12 knockout and knock-in mice reproduce this male infertility. In these mouse models, tracheal ciliary beating and morphology were preserved; knockout mice also retained tracheal axonemal ultrastructure and comparable DNALI1 and DNAH1 abundance and localization in trachea and oviduct. The affected men reported no primary ciliary dyskinesia symptoms. These observations support a preferential requirement for DNAH12 in sperm flagella. Affected men and mice can achieve fertilization and offspring by ICSI. The mouse ortholog Dnah12 (MGI:107720, Q3V0Q1, 3086 aa) has the same domain layout. DNAH12 belongs to the inner-arm dynein heavy chain group with DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH3, DNAH6, DNAH7, DNAH10 and DNAH14. One exome study describes it as the closest paralog of DNAH1 (PMID:34089056). Its established relationship with DNAH1 is physical: DNAH12 binds DNAH1 and is needed to recruit it.

DNAH17 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 17; also DNEL2, DNAHL1) is a beta-type outer dynein arm (ODA) heavy chain, the sperm-specific paralog of DNAH9 and DNAH11. It is a 4462-residue motor protein with an N-terminal tail that assembles with other ODA subunits, a ring of six AAA+ domains with the hydrolytic ATP site in AAA1, and a coiled-coil stalk with a microtubule-binding domain, and it generates force towards microtubule minus ends. DNAH17 is expressed in testicular germ cells from early spermatocytes to late spermatids and lies along the sperm flagellar axoneme (midpiece, principal piece and end piece). In human sperm the ODA heavy chains are DNAH17 (beta) and DNAH8 (gamma), whereas respiratory cilia use DNAH5, DNAH9 and DNAH11 and lack DNAH17. Loss of DNAH17 removes the outer arms from sperm, together with DNAH8, DNAI1 and the docking-complex proteins ODAD2 and ODAD4, but leaves the inner arms in place. Bi-allelic variants cause isolated male infertility with asthenozoospermia or asthenoteratozoospermia with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF; spermatogenic failure 39), without respiratory disease. Dnah17-/- mice show MMAF with disorganized axonemes and impaired flagellar assembly in spermatids; Dnah17 knockout rats are infertile, and an in-frame DNAH17 splice deletion in pigs causes MMAF. ICSI outcomes are variable and sometimes require oocyte activation. Candidate DNAH17 variants have also been reported in two families with left-right asymmetry disorders, which is not yet confirmed.

DNAH2 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 2) is a 4427-residue axonemal dynein heavy chain and one of the two heavy chains of the two-headed inner dynein arm f (I1 dynein), the vertebrate counterpart of the Chlamydomonas 1-alpha heavy chain. Its partner heavy chain is DNAH10, and the arm also contains the intermediate chains DNAI3 (WDR63/IC140), DNAI4 (WDR78/IC138) and DNAI7 (CASC1) and several light chains. It has an N-terminal stem that assembles the arm and a motor head of six AAA modules with ATP-binding P-loops and a coiled-coil stalk carrying the microtubule-binding domain. Like other axonemal dyneins it is expected to generate minus-end-directed force that drives doublet sliding. DNAH2 is expressed mainly in testis and trachea and is found along the sperm flagellum and in motile cilia. RNAi knockdown of Dnah2 in mouse ependymal cells paralyses their motile cilia, and loss of the IC138 ortholog Wdr78 removes Dnah2 and the other dynein-f subunits from the cilium. Biallelic DNAH2 variants cause male infertility with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF; spermatogenic failure 45). Patient sperm lose DNAH2 and the inner dynein arms and have disorganized axonemes and midpiece defects. Dnah2-null male mice are infertile with MMAF-like sperm, mislocalized centriolar and annulus proteins and loss of the inner-arm heavy chain DNAH1 from the flagellum, whereas female mice are fertile. Men with DNAH2 variants can father children by ICSI.

DNAH5 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 5) is the gamma-type heavy chain of the outer dynein arm (ODA), the multi-subunit ATPase motor that attaches every 24 nm to the A-tubule of each outer doublet in motile cilia and powers ciliary beating by sliding adjacent doublets. It is a ~4,600-residue protein with an N-terminal tail that assembles with the ODA intermediate and light chains and a C-terminal motor head of six AAA+ modules and a microtubule-binding stalk; it moves toward microtubule minus ends. DNAH5 is present along the whole length of respiratory cilia, where it pairs with the beta heavy chain DNAH11 in proximal (type 1) ODAs and with DNAH9 in distal (type 2) ODAs, and it is also found in ependymal and embryonic nodal cilia. Human sperm flagella use DNAH8 instead. ODAs are preassembled in the cytoplasm with chaperones such as ZMYND10 before transport into the cilium, and DNAH5 is needed for the whole arm to form: without it the intermediate chain DNAI2 is not incorporated. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause primary ciliary dyskinesia 3 (CILD3), the most common genetic cause of PCD with ODA defects. Respiratory cilia are immotile, mucociliary clearance fails, and about half of patients have situs inversus because nodal cilia do not beat. Dnah5 mutant mice reproduce PCD with situs inversus and develop hydrocephalus because ependymal flow is lost.

DNAH8 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 8; mouse Dnahc8) is a gamma-type outer dynein arm (ODA) heavy chain, the sperm-specific paralog of DNAH5. It is a 4490-residue motor protein with an N-terminal tail that assembles with the other ODA subunits, a ring of six AAA+ domains (AAA1 carries the hydrolytic ATP site), and a coiled-coil stalk ending in a microtubule-binding domain, and it generates force towards microtubule minus ends. DNAH8 is expressed in germ cells from early spermatocytes to late spermatids, is detected in the cytoplasm of spermatocytes during dynein preassembly, and in mature sperm lies along the flagellar axoneme, concentrated in the principal piece. In human sperm the ODA heavy chains are DNAH8 (gamma) and DNAH17 (beta), whereas respiratory cilia use DNAH5, DNAH9 and DNAH11 and lack DNAH8. DNAH8 and DNAH17 depend on each other for stable incorporation into the sperm axoneme. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants cause male infertility with asthenoteratozoospermia and multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF; spermatogenic failure 46) without respiratory disease, and Dnah8-knockout male mice are sterile with MMAF; ICSI can achieve pregnancy. Mouse t-haplotype alleles of Dnahc8 contribute to the curlicue sperm-tail phenotype. Knockout and cancer studies also link DNAH8 to androgen signalling (an androgen-regulated gene in prostate cancer, and reduced fetal testosterone in knockout mice), but how an axonemal motor would do this is unexplained.

DNAH9 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 9) is a beta-type heavy chain of the outer dynein arm (ODA), the ATPase motor that drives the beating of motile cilia by sliding outer doublet microtubules towards their minus ends. It has the dynein heavy chain architecture of an N-terminal tail that assembles into the arm and a C-terminal AAA+ motor head with a microtubule-binding stalk. In human respiratory cilia DNAH9 is restricted to the distal part of the axoneme, where it forms type 2 ODAs together with the gamma chain DNAH5 and the intermediate chain DNAI2; the proximal ODAs instead contain its paralog DNAH11, and human sperm ODAs contain a third beta paralog, DNAH17. DNAH9 binds the ODA docking complex subunit ODAD1 (CCDC114) through its N-terminal tail, which is thought to dock distal ODAs onto the doublet. DNAH9 is expressed early in airway ciliogenesis, before cilia appear, and in pit cells of the embryonic node. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause primary ciliary dyskinesia 40 (CILD40). Distal type 2 ODAs are lost, cilia beat more slowly with a subtle waveform defect, and respiratory symptoms are mild, but situs inversus and other laterality defects are common.

DNAI1 is a noncatalytic intermediate-chain subunit of axonemal outer dynein arms. It helps organize the dynein motor complex and supports ciliary beating and flagellated sperm movement. The mature protein is associated with axonemes, while a cytoplasmic pool occupies dynein axonemal particles during motor assembly and deployment. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause primary ciliary dyskinesia with outer-arm defects, which can affect respiratory function, fertility and left-right body patterning.

DYNC1H1 encodes the force-generating heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein-1. Its motor region couples ATP hydrolysis to movement toward microtubule minus ends, while its tail assembles with accessory subunits that connect the motor to cargo and regulatory proteins. Dynein-1 transports organelles and other cellular cargo, including cargo moving toward neuronal cell bodies, and supplies forces for nuclear movement and mitotic spindle organization. Recruitment to the cell cortex helps position the spindle. Long-range processive movement is regulated by dynactin and activating adaptors; the isolated motor is not constitutively highly processive.

DYNC2H1 encodes the force-generating heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein-2, the motor that returns intraflagellar transport trains and cargo from ciliary tips toward the cell body. Its C-terminal motor region couples ATP hydrolysis to movement toward microtubule minus ends, while its N-terminal tail assembles with light intermediate, intermediate and light chains. Dynein-2 activity is controlled by interactions between its two heavy chains and associated subunits. The motor supports the construction and maintenance of sensory and motile cilia. Pathogenic biallelic variants cause skeletal ciliopathies. A short alternative product lacks the AAA motor ring and microtubule-binding stalk.

Dynamin-2 is a widely expressed mechanochemical GTPase that assembles on membranes and couples GTP hydrolysis to membrane remodeling and vesicle scission. Its pleckstrin-homology domain binds membrane lipids, while its proline-rich region engages recruitment and regulatory partners. It supports receptor-mediated endocytosis and recycling-endosome scission during autophagic membrane formation, and participates in cortactin-dependent actin-bundle remodeling. Cytosolic, membrane-associated and specialized neuronal or adhesion pools provide distinct cellular contexts for this machinery.

DNMT1 is a regulated DNA methyltransferase that uses S-adenosylmethionine to methylate cytosine in CpG dinucleotides. It preferentially copies methylation onto newly synthesized DNA opposite methylated template strands, helping preserve epigenetic patterns and transcriptional silencing through cell division. Its RFTS regulatory module recognizes paired ubiquitin marks on histone H3, while a CXXC zinc-binding domain and BAH domains coordinate DNA and chromatin engagement with the catalytic domain. DNMT1 acts predominantly in the nucleus and is recruited to replication-associated and heterochromatic sites. Its abundance, activity and recruitment are regulated by protein interactions and post-translational modifications. Alternative transcripts encode three curated protein products with changes in the amino-terminal regulatory region; functional equivalence across these products is not established. Pathogenic DNMT1 variants cause neurological syndromes that can include sensory neuropathy, deafness, dementia or ataxia.

DNMT3A is a chromatin-associated DNA cytosine C5 methyltransferase that establishes DNA methylation patterns important for development and cellular identity. It methylates CpG sites and can also methylate non-CpG cytosines. With the noncatalytic activator DNMT3L it forms a heterotetrameric DNA methyltransferase complex in which DNMT3A supplies both active sites, and in germ cells it deposits the methylation that establishes maternal and most paternal genomic imprints. Its ADD domain recognizes the histone H3 amino terminus preferentially when lysine 4 is unmethylated, while its PWWP domain recognizes methylated H3 lysine 36. These reader modules, oligomerization and regulatory partners help target and control DNA methylation, including repression at selected promoters. Nuclear and cytoplasmic pools vary with cell type and developmental stage. Alternative transcripts encode products with different amino termini or extensive truncation. Germline and somatic variants can alter growth and neurodevelopment or contribute to hematological malignancy.

DNMT3B is a nuclear DNA cytosine-5 methyltransferase that helps establish DNA methylation patterns and regulate gene expression. Catalytically competent forms prefer CpG sites but also methylate non-CpG cytosines under tested conditions. Association with DNMT3L, other DNA methyltransferases and chromatin regulators influences activity and targeting. A distinct, catalytically inactive splice product, DNMT3B3, binds the nucleosome acidic patch and positions DNMT3A-containing complexes on chromatin. DNMT3B-dependent methylation contributes to repeat stability and transcriptional silencing; pathogenic variants cause a subset of immunodeficiency, centromeric instability and facial anomalies syndrome. Context-specific positive effects on gene expression are also reported. DNMT3B also helps maintain epigenetic repression of D4Z4 repeats. Hypomorphic variants can contribute to somatic DUX4 derepression and digenic facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy type 4 when repeat length and a permissive chromosome 4 haplotype provide the required genetic context.

DOCK2 is a RAC-directed guanine-nucleotide exchange factor enriched in hematopoietic cells. Its DHR2 catalytic region promotes nucleotide exchange, while interactions with ELMO proteins and membrane-associated signaling components regulate substrate access and cellular recruitment. DOCK2 links chemokine and antigen-receptor signals to actin remodeling, immune-cell migration and antigen uptake. Biallelic loss of function causes combined immunodeficiency with impaired cellular responses. Alternative transcripts encode a long catalytic product and a much shorter product whose biological activity remains unresolved.

DPAGT1 is a ten-pass endoplasmic-reticulum membrane phosphotransferase that initiates dolichol-linked oligosaccharide assembly for protein N-linked glycosylation. On the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane, it transfers GlcNAc-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc to dolichyl phosphate, producing GlcNAc-PP-dolichol and UMP. Other enzymes extend this lipid-linked precursor and transfer the completed glycan to nascent proteins. Human DPAGT1 forms dimers, requires magnesium for catalysis and is inhibited by tunicamycin. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause congenital disorders of glycosylation or congenital myasthenic syndromes; defects can involve catalytic activity, protein abundance or RNA splicing. Changes in DPAGT1 expression can alter E-cadherin glycosylation and epithelial junctions. Alternative transcripts encode proteins with different N termini, whose functional properties are not uniformly established.

DPM1 is the catalytic subunit of dolichol-phosphate mannose synthase at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. It transfers mannose from GDP-mannose to dolichyl phosphate, generating the lipid-linked donor used in N-glycosylation, protein O- and C-mannosylation and GPI-anchor synthesis. DPM3 recruits and stabilizes DPM1 at the membrane, and DPM2 supports efficient complex activity. Biallelic defects cause DPM1 congenital disorder of glycosylation.

DPM2 is the small (84-residue), multi-pass endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane regulatory subunit of the dolichol-phosphate mannose (Dol-P-Man) synthase complex, which is composed of the catalytic subunit DPM1 together with DPM2 and DPM3. DPM2 is non-catalytic: it stabilizes the complex and enhances its activity rather than performing the mannosyltransfer itself. DPM2 forms a complex with DPM1 that is required for the correct ER localization and stable expression of DPM1, stabilizes DPM3, and enhances the enzyme's binding of the substrate dolichyl phosphate, increasing Dol-P-Man synthase activity roughly ten-fold. Dol-P-Man is the mannosyl donor used for glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor synthesis, the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor of N-glycosylation, and protein O- and C-mannosylation. DPM2 additionally associates with, and enhances the activity of, the GPI-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (GPI-GnT) complex that initiates GPI-anchor biosynthesis, although it is not essential for that complex. In humans, loss-of-function variants cause DPM2-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type Iu), a muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy with severe epilepsy.

DPM3 is the small (92-residue) membrane-anchoring and stabilizer subunit of the heterotrimeric dolichol-phosphate mannose (Dol-P-Man / DPM) synthase complex, which also comprises the catalytic subunit DPM1 and the regulatory subunit DPM2. DPM synthase transfers mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose to dolichyl phosphate at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane to produce dolichol-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man), the essential lumenal mannosyl donor for GPI-anchor biosynthesis, N-glycan precursor assembly, and protein O- and C-mannosylation. DPM3 is non-catalytic; because the catalytic DPM1 subunit lacks a transmembrane domain, DPM3 (a multi-pass ER membrane protein) tethers DPM1 to the ER membrane and bridges the complex, associating with DPM1 through its C-terminal region and with DPM2 through its N-terminal region. This scaffolding stabilizes DPM1 and is required for assembly and activity of the DPM synthase. Loss of DPM3 function causes DPM3-CDG, an alpha-dystroglycanopathy-type congenital muscular dystrophy (with elevated serum creatine kinase, reduced O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan, and cardiomyopathy in some patients).

DPYD encodes dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase [NADP(+)] (DPD; EC 1.3.1.2), the initial and rate-limiting enzyme of the reductive catabolism of the pyrimidine bases uracil and thymine. It reduces uracil to 5,6-dihydrouracil and thymine to 5,6-dihydrothymine using NADPH as the electron donor. DPD is a large cytosolic homodimeric flavoprotein; each subunit binds two FAD, two FMN and four [4Fe-4S] clusters that shuttle electrons from NADPH to the pyrimidine substrate. It is the principal enzyme that catabolises the fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutic 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and the dihydrouracil it produces is further processed (by dihydropyrimidinase and beta-ureidopropionase) toward beta-alanine. Deficiency of DPD (DPYD deficiency) causes severe, potentially life-threatening toxicity from 5-FU/capecitabine, and more complete deficiency produces thymine-uraciluria with a variable neurological phenotype (seizures, motor and intellectual disability). DPYD is a major pharmacogenetic gene, and DPYD genotyping is used clinically to guide fluoropyrimidine dosing.

DPYS encodes dihydropyrimidinase (DHP/DHPase; EC 3.5.2.2), the second enzyme of the reductive pyrimidine catabolic pathway. Acting downstream of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPYD) and upstream of beta-ureidopropionase (UPB1), it catalyzes the reversible, Zn2+-dependent hydrolytic ring opening of 5,6-dihydrouracil to N-carbamoyl-beta-alanine (3-ureidopropanoate) and of 5,6-dihydrothymine to N-carbamoyl-beta-aminoisobutyrate. It is a binuclear zinc metalloenzyme of the metallo-dependent (cyclic amidohydrolase / amidohydrolase) hydrolase superfamily, hydantoinase/dihydropyrimidinase family, and forms a homotetramer with two Zn2+ ions bridged by a carbamylated lysine per subunit. The enzyme is cytosolic and most highly expressed in liver and kidney. Loss-of-function variants cause dihydropyrimidinase deficiency (dihydropyrimidinuria), an autosomal recessive disorder with a variable neurological phenotype, and impaired dihydropyrimidinase activity increases the risk of fluoropyrimidine (5-fluorouracil) toxicity.

Atrophin-1 is a broadly expressed transcriptional coregulator with nuclear and cytoplasmic pools. Its transcriptional corepressor activity is enhanced by ETO/MTG8, and it can associate with nuclear-matrix structures containing corepressor machinery. Context-dependent coactivation is reported for the mouse ortholog. Atrophin proteins also associate with FAT1 and contribute to directional migration in vascular smooth muscle cells. Expansion of the ATN1 polyglutamine tract causes dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, with altered protein processing, localization and cellular toxicity.

Desmocollin-2 (DSC2) is a single-pass desmosomal cadherin that mediates calcium-dependent adhesion between neighboring cells. Its extracellular cadherin domains bind desmosomal cadherins, and its cytoplasmic tail associates with plaque proteins that connect the junction to intermediate filaments. DSC2 helps maintain the mechanical integrity of cardiac intercalated discs and epithelial junctions and contributes to desmosome assembly and epithelial repair. Alternative splicing produces two forms with shared extracellular regions and distinct cytoplasmic tails that differ in plaque-protein interactions.

PIGP (phosphatidylinositol N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase subunit P; PIG-P) is a small (158 aa) multi-pass endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that is a required, non-catalytic accessory subunit of the GPI-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (GPI-GnT) complex. GPI-GnT catalyzes the first, committed step of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis: the transfer of N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-N-acetylglucosamine onto phosphatidylinositol to give GlcNAc-phosphatidylinositol. The catalytic subunit of the complex is PIGA; PIGP is one of several accessory components (with PIGC, PIGH, PIGQ/GPI1, PIGY and the regulatory protein DPM2) that are together required for enzyme activity, and it interacts directly with PIGA and PIGQ. PIGP is broadly (ubiquitously) expressed. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PIGP cause an autosomal-recessive inherited GPI-deficiency disorder, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 55 (DEE55), characterized by early-onset refractory seizures, hypotonia and profound developmental delay, reflecting reduced surface expression of GPI-anchored proteins.

Desmoglein-2 is a single-pass desmosomal cadherin that supports adhesion in epithelial tissues and heart muscle. Its calcium-binding extracellular cadherin domains engage neighboring cells, and its cytoplasmic region connects to the desmosomal plaque. This transmembrane connection couples extracellular adhesion to the intracellular junctional architecture and helps tissues resist mechanical stress. Its extracellular region also serves as an attachment receptor for selected species B adenoviruses, including types 3, 7, 11 and 14/14a, and supports type 3 entry into human cells. DSG2 also occurs at non-desmosomal cell contacts and surface pools in progenitor, endothelial and pancreatic cells. Its junctional and signalling-associated roles vary with cell context; proteolytic cleavage can release extracellular or intracellular fragments. Human DSG2 variants are associated with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and altered desmosomal structure.

Desmoplakin is a plakin-family structural protein that couples intracellular junctional plaques to intermediate-filament networks. Its N-terminal region engages plaque partners and its C-terminal tail binds filament proteins, organizing desmosomes and supporting the mechanical integrity of epithelial and cardiac tissues. Cytoplasmic assembly particles recruit desmoplakin to cell contacts, and cardiac pools also occupy mixed fascia-adherens-like junctions. Association with EB1 helps organize cortical microtubule ends and promotes connexin-43 localization to cell-cell junctions. Alternative splicing changes the central rod while retaining terminal interaction regions. Pathogenic DSP variants cause skin fragility, keratoderma and cardiomyopathy.

Dentin sialophosphoprotein is a secreted precursor of non-collagenous dentin matrix proteins. Proteolytic processing produces an N-terminal dentin sialoprotein region and an acidic, highly phosphorylated C-terminal dentin phosphoprotein region. Their matrix interactions and effects on mineral deposition support the formation and maturation of mineralized dentin. The phosphoprotein region binds calcium and collagen; evidence from rodent biochemistry and genetics distinguishes promotion of later dentin mineralization from an obligatory role in its initial nucleation. Pathogenic human DSPP variants cause autosomal dominant dentinogenesis imperfecta and dentin dysplasia. Cellular models of disease-associated variants support impaired secretion and retention of coexpressed normal DSPP as a dominant-negative mechanism.

DTYMK is thymidylate kinase (dTMP kinase; EC 2.7.4.9), a small cytosolic P-loop nucleotide kinase that catalyses the ATP- and Mg2+-dependent phosphorylation of thymidine monophosphate (dTMP) to thymidine diphosphate (dTDP) (dTMP + ATP -> dTDP + ADP). This is the common penultimate step in the synthesis of the DNA building block dTTP: the de novo route (dUMP -> dTMP via thymidylate synthase) and the salvage route (thymidine -> dTMP via thymidine kinase) both converge on dTMP kinase, making it the bottleneck for dTTP biosynthesis; dTDP is subsequently phosphorylated to dTTP by nucleoside diphosphate kinase. Because dTTP cannot be generated by any bypass, the enzyme is essential for DNA replication and genome integrity; its expression and activity peak in S phase. The active enzyme is a homodimer and has been crystallised extensively in complex with dTMP/ATP analogues. It also activates thymidine-analogue prodrugs (e.g. zidovudine/AZT monophosphate). Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause a severe childhood-onset neurodegenerative disorder with progressive microcephaly.

DUSP6 (MKP-3, PYST1) is a cytoplasmic dual-specificity protein phosphatase of the MAP kinase phosphatase (MKP) family that selectively inactivates the extracellular signal-regulated kinases ERK1 and ERK2. An N-terminal rhodanese-like domain carrying a kinase-interaction motif docks ERK2, which both confers substrate specificity and allosterically activates the C-terminal catalytic domain (catalytic Cys293), allowing DUSP6 to remove the phosphates from the threonine and tyrosine of the ERK activation-loop TEY motif. DUSP6 has little activity toward JNK or p38. A CRM1-dependent nuclear export signal keeps DUSP6 predominantly cytoplasmic, and through ERK docking it also retains ERK in the cytoplasm. DUSP6 transcription is induced by FGF receptor/ERK signalling through Ets factors, while ERK phosphorylation of DUSP6 promotes its proteasomal turnover, so DUSP6 acts as an ERK-dependent negative-feedback regulator that sets the amplitude and duration of growth-factor-driven ERK signalling. Loss of mouse Dusp6 raises ERK activity and causes FGFR gain-of-function-like phenotypes (dwarfism, craniosynostosis, hearing loss), and human DUSP6 variants are associated with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

DYRK1A is a dual-specificity protein kinase with nuclear, cytoplasmic and cytoskeleton-associated pools. It phosphorylates serine/threonine-containing substrates and undergoes tyrosine autophosphorylation. Its substrate repertoire includes the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, histone H3, Tau and splicing factors, connecting kinase activity to transcription, chromatin regulation, alternative splicing and neuronal function. The histidine-rich C-terminal region contributes to RNA polymerase II targeting. Natural products share the kinase domain but differ in their terminal sequences; the shorter products lack this histidine-rich region. Human pathogenic variants cause an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder commonly including microcephaly and intellectual disability.

Dysferlin is a ferlin-family membrane protein whose C2 domains bind calcium and acidic phospholipids. It participates in skeletal-muscle membrane maintenance and repair and is found at the sarcolemma, T-tubules and internal membrane compartments, with trafficking between the cell surface and endosomes. Alternative splicing changes its N-terminal calcium/lipid coupling, and one truncated product lacks the canonical C-terminal membrane anchor.

EBP, the emopamil-binding protein, is a five-pass integral membrane sterol isomerase that catalyzes a post-lanosterol step in cholesterol biosynthesis. It moves the sterol double bond from the Delta8 to the Delta7 position, converting zymostenol to lathosterol and zymosterol to cholesta-7,24-dien-3beta-ol. EBP acts at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and is also detected at nuclear-envelope membranes and in vesicles during mitosis. It binds several sterol-like and lipophilic inhibitors, including tamoxifen. EBP and DHCR7 cooperate in microsomal cholesterol-5,6-epoxide hydrolysis, although the separate catalytic contribution of each protein remains unresolved. Loss of EBP sterol-isomerase function causes X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata 2, with abnormal accumulation of Delta8 sterol intermediates.

Thymidine phosphorylase (TYMP; EC 2.4.2.4), also known as platelet-derived endothelial cell growth factor (PD-ECGF) and gliostatin, is a cytosolic homodimeric enzyme that catalyzes the reversible phosphorolysis of thymidine (and 2'-deoxyuridine), converting thymidine + phosphate into thymine + 2-deoxy-alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate (and 2'-deoxyuridine into uracil + 2-deoxy-alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate). Through this activity it feeds pyrimidine catabolism and the thymine-to-dTMP salvage pathway, and by controlling systemic levels of thymidine and 2'-deoxyuridine it protects the mitochondrial deoxyribonucleotide (dNTP) pool from imbalance. TYMP additionally has an extracellular moonlighting role as an angiogenic growth factor, promoting endothelial cell growth and chemotaxis. Loss-of-function mutations in TYMP cause mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalomyopathy (MNGIE; mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 1, MTDPS1), in which accumulation of thymidine and deoxyuridine drives mitochondrial DNA instability and depletion, producing gastrointestinal dysmotility, cachexia, peripheral neuropathy, and leukoencephalopathy.

ECHS1 is a short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase in the mitochondrial matrix. It catalyzes reversible hydration of enoyl-CoA thioesters, including crotonyl-CoA in fatty acid beta-oxidation and methacrylyl-CoA in valine catabolism. Human enzyme assays also demonstrate hydration of acryloyl-CoA, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA and, less efficiently, tiglyl-CoA. ECHS1 is synthesized as a 290-amino-acid precursor with a cleaved mitochondrial targeting sequence. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause ECHS1 deficiency, a mitochondrial encephalopathy associated with impaired valine metabolism and accumulation of reactive acyl-CoA intermediates.

EEF1A2 is a cytoplasmic translation elongation factor expressed prominently in brain, heart and skeletal muscle. It uses a GTP-dependent cycle to deliver aminoacyl-tRNAs to the ribosomal A site during protein synthesis, including translation associated with the endoplasmic reticulum. EEF1A2 also binds and activates the lipid kinase PI4KB. Pathogenic variants cause neurodevelopmental disorders, frequently including epilepsy.

EFEMP1, also called fibulin-3, is a secreted extracellular matrix glycoprotein containing EGF-like repeats and a C-terminal fibulin domain. It contributes to matrix integrity and influences the organization and turnover of extracellular matrix networks. In human retinal pigment epithelial cells, loss of EFEMP1 disrupts collagen VI network formation and reduces extracellular MMP2 activity. EFEMP1 also associates with EGFR and stimulates receptor-dependent Akt and ERK signaling in human pancreatic carcinoma cells. Distinct pathogenic variants cause inherited retinal disease or connective-tissue defects, reflecting different effects on folding, secretion and extracellular function.

EFNB1 encodes ephrin-B1, a single-pass type I membrane ligand for Eph receptor tyrosine kinases. Its extracellular domain binds Eph receptors on neighboring cells, initiating signals that control cell adhesion, repulsion and tissue organization. The cytoplasmic tail participates in reverse signaling within the ephrin-bearing cell. Sequential proteolysis can release an intracellular fragment with a distribution distinct from the membrane-bound ligand; developmental and neuronal effects depend on receptor, cell type and presentation context. Pathogenic variants in EFNB1 cause craniofrontonasal syndrome, an X-linked developmental disorder.

EGF encodes a type I transmembrane precursor that is proteolytically processed to release mature epidermal growth factor, a secreted ligand for EGFR-family receptor tyrosine kinases.
