In T cells, BACH2 stabilizes regulatory T cell (Treg) identity by repressing effector gene programs and promotes stem-like/memory CD8+ T cell fates by competing with AP-1 factors at enhancers. BACH2 undergoes regulated nucleocytoplasmic shuttling controlled by PI3K-AKT-dependent phosphorylation at Ser-521 (promoting cytoplasmic localization) and by oxidative stress and SUMOylation (promoting nuclear retention). Haploinsufficiency of BACH2 causes BACH2-related immunodeficiency and autoimmunity (BRIDA/IMD60), and common GWAS variants at the BACH2 locus are associated with multiple autoimmune diseases including type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, celiac disease, and Crohn disease.

ANLN (anillin) is a conserved multidomain scaffold of the cytokinetic contractile ring. It has an N-terminal myosin-binding region and actin-binding domain, and a C-terminal anillin homology region made of a cryptic C2 domain, a Rhotekin-like Rho-binding domain and a PH domain. During interphase it is held in the nucleus. After nuclear envelope breakdown it moves to the cortex and concentrates in the cleavage furrow, then at the midbody. There it binds F-actin, active RhoA, PI(4,5)P2 and septins (and, in Xenopus, nonmuscle myosin II), linking RhoA signalling and the membrane to the actomyosin ring and the septin cytoskeleton. Anillin keeps active myosin in the equatorial plane, stabilizes furrow ingression and is needed for intercellular-bridge maturation and abscission. Its loss causes cytokinesis failure and multinucleation. Anillin is degraded by APC/C-Cdh1 at mitotic exit. It also supports epithelial junction integrity, and missense variants (R431C, G618C) cause familial focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

PIGQ (also known as GPI1 or PIG-Q) is a non-catalytic subunit of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (GPI-GnT) complex, the multi-protein enzyme that catalyses the first, committed step of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis: transfer of N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-GlcNAc onto phosphatidylinositol to form GlcNAc-phosphatidylinositol. Within this complex, PIGA is the catalytic subunit, while PIGQ is a required accessory subunit (together with PIGC, PIGH, PIGP, PIGY and DPM2) that stabilises the complex and supports its activity; PIGQ itself has no independent enzymatic activity. It is a multi-pass integral membrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, where the GPI-GnT complex assembles and acts. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PIGQ cause multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 4 (MCAHS4), an autosomal-recessive inherited GPI-deficiency disorder presenting as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with refractory neonatal seizures, severe global developmental delay, dysmorphism and skeletal, renal and ophthalmic anomalies.

ELAC2 encodes the long tRNase Z endoribonuclease, which removes 3′ trailers from precursor tRNAs to generate their mature 3′ ends. It acts in the nucleus and mitochondria, supporting tRNA maturation in both compartments. In the mitochondrial processing system, association with TRMT10C and SDR5C1 enhances ELAC2 cleavage. Alternative translation initiation contributes to its nuclear and mitochondrial targeting.

BLNK (SLP-65/BASH) is a noncatalytic adaptor that organizes signaling downstream of the B-cell antigen receptor. Its phosphorylated tyrosines and proline-rich motifs recruit effectors including phospholipase Cgamma, VAV, GRB2 and NCK, coupling SYK-dependent receptor-proximal events to calcium mobilization and downstream signaling. Constitutive association with CIN85 and binding to lipid vesicles help assemble cytoplasmic signaling granules that can be recruited to activated receptor sites at the plasma membrane. BLNK supplies docking and spatial organization, while associated kinases and phospholipases perform the enzymatic reactions. Disruption of human BLNK can arrest the transition from pro-B to pre-B cells and cause antibody deficiency.

CIC encodes capicua, a nuclear sequence-specific transcriptional repressor that links RTK/Ras–MAPK signaling to gene expression. Its HMG-box and C1 domains jointly recognize TGAATGAA-like octamers in regulatory DNA, including ETV-family promoters. RTK activation can downregulate CIC and release its target genes from repression. CIC associates with ATXN1 and ATXN1L in repressive complexes and controls developmental gene-expression programs. CIC also functions as a tumor suppressor; somatic mutations, including missense changes in its DNA-recognition domains, recur in oligodendroglioma. In contrast, oncogenic CIC–DUX4 fusions activate CIC target genes in a subset of sarcomas. Loss of CIC disrupts neural maturation and behavior, and human heterozygous loss-of-function variants cause neurodevelopmental disease. Short and long CIC products share the DNA-recognition domains but differ in their N-terminal regions.

Ceramide synthase 1 (CERS1; also LASS1, UOG1), a multi-pass endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme that catalyzes the N-acylation step of de novo ceramide biosynthesis. It transfers an acyl group from acyl-CoA onto the amino group of a sphingoid base (sphinganine in the de novo pathway, sphingosine in the salvage pathway) to form dihydroceramide/ceramide. Among the six mammalian ceramide synthases, CERS1 is highly selective for stearoyl-CoA (C18:0-CoA) and therefore produces predominantly C18-(dihydro)ceramide; the resulting dihydroceramide is desaturated by DEGS1 to ceramide. CERS1 is enriched in brain (neurons, cerebellar Purkinje cells) and skeletal muscle, where its C18-ceramide output contributes to neuronal function and, in muscle, to glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity. Loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy type 8 (EPM8), reflecting the requirement of C18-ceramide for neuronal survival.

BRPF1 is a multivalent chromatin reader and scaffold that assembles and activates histone acetyltransferase complexes containing KAT6A/MOZ, KAT6B/MORF or KAT7/HBO1. It connects catalytic subunits with ING and MEAF6 cofactors and helps direct their activity toward nucleosomal histone H3, including H3K14 and H3K23. Its PZP module recognizes the unmodified H3 amino terminus and supports chromatin engagement, while its bromodomain recognizes acetylated histone ligands. BRPF1 acts principally in the nucleus, with partner-dependent localization observed in expression assays, and supports context-dependent transcriptional regulation. Monoallelic pathogenic variants cause an intellectual developmental disorder associated with deficient histone H3 acetylation.

CD2AP is a multivalent cytoplasmic adaptor that connects membrane-associated protein complexes with the actin cytoskeleton. Its three SH3 domains, proline-rich regions and C-terminal interaction region organize selected receptor, trafficking and junctional partners. Full-length human CD2AP also binds actin filaments and caps their barbed ends in reconstitution experiments, providing a mechanism for stabilizing junctional actin. Its CPI-region peptides also bind heterodimeric actin-capping protein and partially inhibit that complex in biochemical assays, a distinct mechanism from CD2AP itself capping filaments. CD2AP contributes to epithelial junction organization and to podocyte cytoskeletal integrity; its effects on migration and signaling depend on the cellular context and associated proteins. Human loss-of-function variants are associated with glomerular disease.

IFT81 is a coiled-coil core (IFT-B1) subunit of the intraflagellar transport B complex. It forms an obligate heterodimer with IFT74 through their C-terminal coiled coils, and the IFT81/IFT74 pair constitutes the main tubulin-binding module of IFT-B: the N-terminal calponin-homology (CH) domain of IFT81 binds the globular body of alpha/beta-tubulin while the basic N-terminus of IFT74 binds the beta-tubulin acidic tail, together giving micromolar affinity suited to loading tubulin onto anterograde trains. Tubulin binding by IFT81 is required for ciliogenesis in human cells. The C-terminal parts of IFT81/IFT74 also bind GTP-RABL2B, which captures IFT-B at the ciliary base. IFT81 localizes to the ciliary base, along the axoneme and at the ciliary tip, and is required for sperm flagellum assembly in mice. Biallelic IFT81 variants cause short-rib thoracic dysplasia (SRTD19).

Glomulin (GLMN; also known as FAP48/FAP68, FKBP-associated protein) is a ~68 kDa, predominantly alpha-helical cytoplasmic protein (with a HEAT-repeat-like architecture) that functions as a regulatory component of cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL/SCF) complexes. It binds directly to the RING domain of RBX1 (ROC1) through its C-terminal half and masks the surface that RBX1 uses to recruit the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme CDC34, thereby inhibiting RBX1-dependent E3 ubiquitin ligase activity and blocking RBX1-mediated neddylation of CUL1. By sequestering RBX1, glomulin stabilizes assembled SCF/CRL components and controls the auto-ubiquitination and turnover of the F-box substrate receptor FBXW7, thereby influencing the abundance of FBXW7 substrates such as Cyclin E and c-Myc. Glomulin has been found in CRL/SCF assemblies containing RBX1 with CUL1, CUL2, CUL3, CUL4A, and in a CUL7-RBX1-SKP1-FBXW8 complex. Loss-of-function mutations in GLMN cause glomuvenous malformations, cutaneous venous lesions with abnormal smooth-muscle-like glomus cells, reflecting a requirement for glomulin in normal vascular development. An alternatively spliced shorter isoform (isoform 2, FAP48) was originally characterized as a ligand of the immunophilins FKBP12 (FKBP1A) and FKBP52 (FKBP4), and glomulin/FAP68 was also reported to bind the inactive hepatocyte growth factor receptor (MET) and modulate downstream p70 S6 kinase signaling; these immunophilin- and receptor-associated activities predate the discovery of the CRL-regulatory role and are mechanistically distinct from it. In innate immunity, glomulin also binds the RING domains of the cellular inhibitor of apoptosis proteins cIAP1 and cIAP2, inhibits their self-ubiquitination, and acts as a negative regulator of cIAP-mediated inflammasome activation and macrophage pyroptosis; the Shigella effector IpaH7.8 ubiquitinates glomulin to drive its degradation and enhance inflammation. Structurally, glomulin binds RBX1 with high affinity (Kd in the nanomolar range) through a region in its C-terminal half (approximately residues 300-594) that occludes the RBX1 surface used to recruit the E2 enzyme CDC34.

ELOVL4 is a multipass endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme that catalyzes acyl-CoA/malonyl-CoA condensation, the first step of the two-carbon fatty-acid elongation cycle. It supports synthesis of very long-chain saturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids incorporated into specialized lipids, including skin lipids and retinal photoreceptor phospholipids. C-terminal truncating variants associated with Stargardt-like macular dystrophy can disrupt ER retention and redirect wild-type protein into intracellular inclusions. The SCA34-associated W246G missense variant has a distinct effect: in homozygous knock-in rats it reduces skin very-long-chain saturated fatty acids while preserving retinal very-long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids.

ELOVL1 (very long chain fatty acid elongase 1; 3-oxoacyl-CoA synthase ELOVL1, EC 2.3.1.199) is a multipass endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme of the ELO family that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting condensation step of the microsomal very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) elongation cycle. It condenses a long-chain acyl-CoA with malonyl-CoA to yield a 3-oxoacyl-CoA plus CO2 and CoA; this 3-oxoacyl-CoA is subsequently reduced, dehydrated and reduced by KAR (HSD17B12), HACD1/2 and TECR to complete each two-carbon elongation. ELOVL1 is specific for saturated and monounsaturated acyl-CoA substrates and is the principal producer of C24-C26 VLCFAs (extending C22 to C24 to C26), with highest activity toward C22:0-CoA. Its VLCFA products are precursors of membrane lipids and lipid mediators, and are especially important for the synthesis of C24 sphingolipids and ceramides (coordinated with the ceramide synthase CERS2), contributing to myelin and the epidermal permeability barrier. In humans, dominant loss-of-function ELOVL1 variants (recurrent p.Ser165Phe) cause ichthyotic keratoderma with spasticity, hypomyelination and dysmorphic facies (IKSHD).

RDH8 (retinol dehydrogenase 8; photoreceptor outer segment all-trans-retinol dehydrogenase, prRDH) is an NADPH-dependent, membrane-associated short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) of the vertebrate visual cycle. It is expressed specifically in retinal photoreceptor cells and localizes to the outer segments of both rods and cones, where it is tightly associated with the disc/plasma membranes as a multi-pass integral membrane protein. RDH8 catalyzes the NADPH-dependent reduction of all-trans-retinal to all-trans-retinol (EC 1.1.1.300), the first step in clearing all-trans-retinal that is released from photobleached rhodopsin. This reductive step protects photoreceptors from retinaldehyde toxicity and feeds all-trans-retinol back toward the retinal pigment epithelium for regeneration of the 11-cis-retinal chromophore, contributing to visual pigment regeneration especially at high light intensity. Biallelic variants in RDH8 are associated with an autosomal recessive form of Stargardt macular dystrophy (STGD5). Structurally, RDH8 has an N-terminal Rossmann-fold NAD(P)-binding region and is most closely related to 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 1, but its physiologically demonstrated substrate is retinoid, not steroid.

LPIN2 is a magnesium-dependent phosphatidate phosphatase and transcriptional coactivator of the lipin family. Its conserved DXDXT catalytic motif hydrolyzes phosphatidic acid to diacylglycerol and orthophosphate. LPIN2 partitions between cytosolic, endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, and nuclear pools; membrane-associated catalysis supplies diacylglycerol for triacylglycerol, phosphatidylcholine, and phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis. LPIN1 abundance can increase when LPIN2 is depleted, providing compensatory phosphatidate-phosphatase capacity. LPIN2 differs from LPIN1 in phosphatidate binding and phosphoregulation, and its membrane association varies with lipid and cell-state cues. In the nucleus, LPIN2 can coactivate PPAR-responsive transcription through a noncatalytic mechanism. Biallelic loss of LPIN2 causes Majeed syndrome, an autoinflammatory disorder characterized by early chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, dyserythropoietic anemia, and inflammatory dermatosis. In macrophages, LPIN2-dependent lipid homeostasis restrains JNK/c-Jun signaling, P2X7/NLRP3 activation, and excessive interleukin-1 beta production, and also modulates interferon-associated responses. LPIN2 abundance is regulated by β-TRCP-dependent ubiquitination, and lipin-family proteins can oligomerize.

SLC26A6 (putative anion transporter 1, PAT1; CFEX) is an SLC26A/SulP-family, STAS-domain anion exchanger of the apical (brush-border) membrane of small intestine, pancreatic duct and renal proximal tubule epithelia. It operates in several exchange modes, principally chloride/bicarbonate and chloride/oxalate, and also oxalate/formate, chloride/formate and, at low rates in the human protein, sulfate exchange. Its C-terminal PDZ-binding motif links it to NHERF scaffolds, and its bicarbonate transport is regulated by CFTR, cAMP, protein kinase C and carbonic anhydrase II binding. SLC26A6 mediates intestinal oxalate secretion, which limits net absorption of dietary oxalate; Slc26a6-null mice develop hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones, and a heterozygous dominant-negative human variant (p.R507W) causes enteric hyperoxaluria with calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. It also contributes to duodenal and pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and intracellular pH regulation.

ARHGEF9 encodes collybistin, a Dbl-family guanine-nucleotide exchange factor and adaptor associated with inhibitory postsynaptic organization. Its exchange-factor activity promotes CDC42 activation. Through gephyrin and phosphoinositide interactions, collybistin recruits gephyrin to the postsynaptic membrane, helping organize inhibitory receptor scaffolds. This recruitment activity can operate independently of nucleotide exchange and is conformationally regulated through the SH3 and PH domains. Collybistin occupies cytosolic and postsynaptic pools. Pathogenic ARHGEF9 variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with intellectual disability; hyperekplexia and an exaggerated startle response occur in affected individuals.

PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1) is a mitochondrially targeted Ser/Thr protein kinase. Mutations in PINK1 cause autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson disease (PARK6). PINK1 has an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence, a single transmembrane segment and a C-terminal kinase domain with distinctive inserts. It acts as a sensor of mitochondrial damage. In healthy, polarized mitochondria the PINK1 precursor is imported through TOM/TIM23 and cleaved by MPP and the inner-membrane rhomboid protease PARL. The resulting fragment is released to the cytosol and degraded by the proteasome, so steady-state levels are very low. When import is blocked by loss of membrane potential or protein misfolding, full-length PINK1 accumulates at the TOM complex on the outer membrane with its kinase domain facing the cytosol, dimerizes and autophosphorylates. It then phosphorylates ubiquitin at Ser65 (including ubiquitin already conjugated to outer-membrane proteins) and Ser65 in the ubiquitin-like domain of the E3 ligase Parkin (PRKN). Phospho-ubiquitin recruits Parkin and, together with Ubl phosphorylation, relieves Parkin autoinhibition. The resulting feed-forward loop coats damaged mitochondria with phospho-ubiquitin chains that recruit autophagy receptors (OPTN, NDP52/CALCOCO2), leading to mitophagy. PINK1 also phosphorylates other substrates, including the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1, the Miro GTPases (arresting mitochondrial transport) and DRP1 (Ser616, promoting fission). It contributes to mitochondria-derived vesicle trafficking and has broad neuroprotective, anti-apoptotic effects.

DNAJB4 (HLJ1, "human liver DnaJ-like protein"; also DNAJW) is a cytosolic HSP40/J-domain co-chaperone of the DNAJB subfamily and a paralog of DNAJB1. Through its N-terminal J domain it stimulates the ATPase activity of HSP70 (HSPA1A/HSPA1B), binding misfolded client proteins and delivering them to HSP70 to drive their folding, refolding and disaggregation. It is a homodimer, is heat-inducible, and is broadly expressed with high levels in striated muscle, where it localizes to the sarcomeric Z-disc and contributes to myofibril/Z-disc proteostasis. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in DNAJB4 cause an autosomal recessive congenital myopathy with early respiratory failure (CMYO21), reflecting its role as a muscle chaperone. It also interacts with the mu-opioid receptor (OPRM1) C-terminal tail and with aggregation-prone clients such as huntingtin and ataxin-1.

DNAJB6 is a J-domain co-chaperone that suppresses aggregation of client proteins, regulates interactions with HSP70 and helps organize keratin intermediate filaments. Its products occupy nuclear and cytoplasmic pools, with DNAJB6 also detected at muscle Z discs. The serine/threonine-rich client-handling region supports antiaggregation, while the adjacent glycine/phenylalanine-rich region restrains access of the J-domain to HSP70. Disease-associated disruption of these functions or their regulation causes dominant DNAJB6-related myopathy.

DNAJB11 (ERdj3, also HEDJ/ERj3p/ABBP-2) is a soluble, glycosylated, ER-lumenal HSP40/J-domain co-chaperone and the principal J-protein partner of the ER HSP70 chaperone BiP (HSPA5). Through its N-terminal J domain it binds and stimulates the ATPase activity of BiP, and through a cysteine-rich substrate-binding domain it binds unfolded and misfolded peptides directly; it recruits BiP to substrates and then dissociates as BiP engages, promoting proper folding, maturation, trafficking and ERAD-targeted degradation of secretory and membrane proteins. It is a stress (UPR)-inducible component of a large ER chaperone complex (with HSPA5, HSP90B1, HYOU1, PDIA proteins, SDF2L1, UGGT1 and others) and is required for the maturation and trafficking of polycystin-1 (PKD1). Monoallelic loss-of-function variants in DNAJB11 cause an atypical autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD6).

Interleukin-22 (IL-22) is a secreted cytokine of the IL-10 family that plays critical roles in innate immunity, tissue repair, and inflammation at barrier surfaces. Unlike most cytokines, IL-22 acts primarily on non-immune cells (epithelial cells, hepatocytes) through the IL-22R1/IL-10RB receptor complex, activating JAK-STAT signaling to promote antimicrobial defense, epithelial proliferation, and tissue regeneration. IL-22 is produced mainly by activated T cells (Th17/Th22) and innate lymphoid cells (ILC3) in response to infection and inflammation. Its activity is tightly regulated by the soluble antagonist IL-22BP (IL-22RA2), creating a balanced system essential for maintaining barrier integrity while preventing excessive tissue responses.

NAD-dependent protein deacetylase that catalyzes removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues of histones (preferentially H4K16, H3K9, H3K14) and numerous non-histone proteins including p53, NF-kB RelA/p65, FOXO factors, HIF1alpha/HIF2alpha, and PGC-1alpha. The core enzymatic function couples NAD+ cleavage to lysine deacetylation, producing nicotinamide and 2-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose. Functions in transcriptional regulation through heterochromatin formation and as a transcription corepressor. Has broad pleiotropic effects on metabolism, stress responses, DNA damage response, and aging through deacetylation of diverse substrates.

PIGS (phosphatidylinositol-glycan biosynthesis class S protein) is a non-catalytic accessory subunit of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchor transamidase (GPI-T) complex, an endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme complex. GPI-T is an equimolar heteropentamer of PIGK, GPAA1, PIGT, PIGS and PIGU that post-translationally attaches a pre-assembled GPI anchor to the C-terminus of GPI-anchored proteins, replacing their C-terminal GPI-attachment signal peptide. Within the complex, PIGK is the catalytic (cysteine-protease/transaminase-like) subunit and GPAA1 forms the amide bond, whereas PIGS is an indispensable but non-catalytic subunit whose precise molecular role is not fully defined; loss of PIGS abolishes complex activity. PIGS is a multi-pass ER membrane glycoprotein with a large lumenal domain flanked by two transmembrane helices. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause the autosomal recessive inherited GPI-deficiency disorder GPIBD18, presenting with severe developmental delay, seizures, hypotonia and dysmorphic features.

PIGT (GPI-anchor transamidase component PIG-T) is one of the five subunits of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchor transamidase (GPI-T) complex, an endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme complex that attaches the pre-assembled GPI anchor to the C-terminus of GPI-anchored proteins after cleaving their C-terminal GPI-attachment signal peptide. The complex comprises the catalytic subunit PIGK (GPI8) together with GPAA1, PIGS, PIGU and PIGT as an equimolar heteropentamer. PIGT is a single-pass type I ER membrane glycoprotein that acts as a required structural subunit; it forms an interchain disulfide bond with the catalytic PIGK/GPI8 (PIGT Cys182 to PIGK Cys92) and stabilises and holds the complex together, and it also contributes to binding of the GPI lipid substrate. PIGT itself is not an independent enzyme, the transamidation catalysis residing in PIGK. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PIGT cause the inherited GPI deficiency multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 3 (MCAHS3), and germline plus somatic PIGT variants can produce a paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria-like phenotype (PNH2).

GPR101 encodes an orphan class A/rhodopsin-like G protein-coupled receptor. The protein is a multi-pass plasma-membrane receptor with no firmly established endogenous ligand, but evolutionary and structural features support a GPCR signaling role. Increased GPR101 dosage is associated with X-linked acrogigantism and growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma predisposition, consistent with altered pituitary signaling rather than a defined enzymatic activity.

POFUT1 is a GDP-fucose protein O-fucosyltransferase 1 (O-FucT-1; EC 2.4.1.221), the founding member of the CAZy GT65 family. It catalyzes transfer of L-fucose from GDP-beta-L-fucose to the hydroxyl group of a serine or threonine within the consensus C2-X(4,5)-S/T-C3 of epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like repeats, forming an O-linked fucose. Catalysis is strictly dependent on a properly folded, correctly disulfide-bonded EGF domain rather than on the linear sequence alone. Unlike the Golgi type-II membrane fucosyltransferases (FUT1-9), POFUT1 is a soluble enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, retained there by a C-terminal KDEL-like motif, so protein O-fucosylation occurs in the ER during biosynthesis of EGF-repeat-containing secretory and cell-surface proteins. Because it modifies only folded EGF domains, POFUT1 has been proposed to participate in a non-canonical ER quality-control/folding-surveillance step for EGF-repeat proteins. Its principal physiological substrates are the Notch receptors (NOTCH1-4): O-fucose added by POFUT1 primes the EGF repeats for elongation by Fringe beta-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases, and the resulting O-glycans modulate binding of Notch to its DLL and JAG ligands, making POFUT1 essential for canonical Notch signal transduction in mammals. Loss of POFUT1 abolishes Notch signaling and causes embryonic lethality in mice; in humans, heterozygous loss-of-function (haploinsufficiency) causes the autosomal-dominant reticulate pigmentation disorder Dowling-Degos disease 2.

MBTPS2 encodes site-2 protease (S2P), an intramembrane zinc metalloprotease of the M50 family. It is a polytopic membrane protein in the Golgi with cytosolic N- and C-termini, an HEIGH zinc-binding motif, and an Asp ligand buried within membrane-spanning segments. S2P acts after site-1 protease (MBTPS1) in regulated intramembrane proteolysis. Once S1P has trimmed the lumenal domain of a membrane-bound transcription factor, S2P cleaves within its transmembrane helix, which depends on a helix-destabilizing Asn-Pro motif in the substrate. This releases the cytosolic N-terminal bZIP domain, which enters the nucleus. Its principal substrates are SREBP-1 and SREBP-2, which drive cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis and uptake, and ATF6/ATF6B, which induce ER chaperones in the unfolded protein response. S2P also cleaves the CREB3-family factors OASIS (CREB3L1), BBF2H7 (CREB3L2) and CREB-H (CREB3L3). S2P is essential for cholesterol prototrophy and the ATF6 branch of the ER stress response. X-linked hypomorphic variants cause IFAP syndrome, keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans, X-linked Olmsted syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta type XIX. In the bone disease, defective processing of OASIS, ATF6 and SREBP impairs collagen secretion and osteoblast differentiation.

MBTPS1 encodes site-1 protease (S1P, also SKI-1 or PCSK8), a Ca2+-dependent subtilisin-like serine protease of the proprotein convertase family. It is a type I membrane protein with a lumenal peptidase S8 catalytic domain, made as a zymogen whose propeptide is removed autocatalytically in the ER. The mature enzyme acts mainly in the Golgi membrane, and a soluble form is also shed. Unlike the basic-residue-directed convertases, S1P cleaves after hydrophobic or small residues in R-X-hydrophobic-X motifs. It makes the first, lumenal cleavage in the regulated intramembrane proteolysis of membrane-bound transcription factors: SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 (after SCAP escorts them to the Golgi when sterols are low), ATF6 and ATF6B during the unfolded protein response, and the CREB3 family (LUMAN, OASIS/CREB3L1, BBF2H7/CREB3L2, CREB-H/CREB3L3). Site-2 protease (MBTPS2) then cuts within the membrane to release the transcriptionally active N-terminal domains. S1P also processes non-transcription-factor proproteins. Its cleavage of the GNPTAB alpha/beta precursor activates GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase for mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes. It also processes FAM20C, the secretory-pathway kinase, as well as pro-BDNF and arenavirus glycoproteins. Through these substrates S1P controls lipid synthesis, the ER stress response, lysosome biogenesis, collagen export and skeletal development. Biallelic hypomorphic variants cause spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Kondo-Fu type. A mitochondrial pool that stabilizes the ETFA/ETFB complex has also been reported, and variants are linked to CAOP syndrome.

SPINK5 encodes LEKTI (lympho-epithelial Kazal-type-related inhibitor), a secreted multidomain serine protease inhibitor of about 1,064 residues with an N-terminal signal peptide and 15 Kazal-like inhibitory domains, two of them classical three-disulfide Kazal domains and 13 of a two-disulfide variant. It is expressed in differentiated layers of stratified epithelia, most strongly in the granular and upper spinous layers of the epidermis, and in thymus, oral and vaginal mucosa and tonsils. The precursor is N-glycosylated, cleaved by furin after leaving the endoplasmic reticulum into single- and multidomain fragments, transported in epidermal lamellar granules and secreted into the extracellular spaces of the upper stratum granulosum and stratum corneum. Purified and recombinant LEKTI fragments inhibit the epidermal kallikreins KLK5 (its strongest target), KLK7 and KLK14, as well as trypsin, plasmin and other serine proteases; binding to KLK5 is tight at neutral pH and released at acidic pH, so the epidermal pH gradient restricts kallikrein activity to the outermost stratum corneum. By holding these proteases in check LEKTI limits degradation of corneodesmosomal desmoglein 1, profilaggrin processing, cathelicidin processing and KLK5-PAR2-driven inflammatory signalling. Loss-of-function mutations cause Netherton syndrome, a severe ichthyosis with hair shaft defects and atopy, and Spink5-deficient mice reproduce the skin barrier failure.

Gephyrin is a bifunctional (moonlighting) protein that combines an enzymatic and a structural role. As an enzyme it catalyses the final two steps of molybdenum cofactor (MoCo) biosynthesis: its N-terminal G domain has molybdopterin adenylyltransferase activity (adenylylating molybdopterin to adenylyl-molybdopterin), and its C-terminal E domain has molybdopterin molybdotransferase (molybdenum insertase) activity (inserting molybdenum to form MoCo). MoCo is the prosthetic group required by the human molybdoenzymes sulfite oxidase, xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase, aldehyde oxidase and mARC. In the nervous system gephyrin is the master scaffolding protein of inhibitory (glycinergic and GABAergic) postsynapses: it clusters glycine receptors and major subsets of GABA type A receptors at the postsynaptic membrane, anchoring them to the cytoskeleton, and its clustering activity is regulated by palmitoylation. It is a peripheral membrane protein present in the cytosol and, in neurons, at the cytoplasmic face of the postsynaptic membrane in dendrites and dendritic spines. Loss of the enzymatic function causes molybdenum cofactor deficiency type C, whereas disruption of the scaffolding function is associated with hyperekplexia and epileptic encephalopathy.

DNAJC6 (auxilin, auxilin-1) is a neuronally enriched DnaJ/HSP40 co-chaperone that drives the HSC70/HSPA8-dependent uncoating of clathrin-coated vesicles. It is a multidomain protein comprising an N-terminal PTEN-like tensin-type phosphatase domain and a C2 domain (a phosphoinositide-binding membrane-targeting module that is thought to be catalytically degenerate), a long disordered clathrin-binding region, and a C-terminal J domain. Auxilin binds clathrin cages stoichiometrically (one per triskelion) and, through its J domain, recruits HSPA8/HSC70 and stimulates its ATPase activity to dismantle the clathrin lattice, thereby promoting clathrin-mediated endocytosis and the recycling/uncoating of synaptic vesicles at nerve terminals. Loss-of-function mutations cause autosomal-recessive juvenile- and early-onset Parkinson disease (PARK19A/PARK19B) through impaired synaptic vesicle endocytosis in dopaminergic neurons.

DIAPH3 is a Rho-regulated diaphanous-related formin that binds actin and promotes filament assembly. Its FH1–FH2 region supports actin filament growth and bundling, while terminal regulatory regions restrain assembly activity. DIAPH3 also associates with microtubules; mDia2 fragment experiments separate microtubule binding and stabilization from actin assembly. Human DIAPH3 occupies cytosolic and cytoskeletal pools and accumulates at the cleavage furrow and spindle midzone during cytokinesis. Regulated nuclear transport and membrane recruitment provide additional cellular contexts. Increased DIAPH3 activity is associated with auditory neuropathy. Multiple natural splice products differ in regulatory and C-terminal sequences, and their individual activities are not established by the historical engineered constructs.

LPAR6, historically called P2Y5/P2RY5, is a class-A seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor that recognizes extracellular lysophosphatidic acid at the plasma membrane. Human LPAR6 expressed in receptor-null rodent cells responds preferentially to 2-acyl-LPA over 1-acyl-LPA and most consistently activates a G12/13-Rho pathway; Gi-dependent calcium and ERK responses and Gq coupling are also supported in defined heterologous systems. Knockdown of endogenous LPAR6 suppresses LPA-induced contraction of human endothelial cells, providing a bounded native-human link to the recombinant signaling results. Cryo-EM structures of engineered, LPA-bound human LPAR6 with mini-G13 or mini-Gq define the ligand pocket and distinct coupling contacts, with functional mutagenesis supporting both interfaces and stronger G13 coupling. These structures represent activated signaling states rather than constitutive stable complexes. LPAR6 is expressed in human skin and hair follicles, including Henle and Huxley layers of the inner root sheath. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive woolly hair and hypotrichosis, establishing an essential role in hair growth and texture. Several disease-associated missense forms are retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and fail to reach the cell surface, whereas other surface-expressed variants are signaling defective; these are allelic forms, not protein isoforms. Variant-specific rescue by the synthetic agonist alkyl-OMPT and activation by farnesyl pyrophosphate have been observed in expression systems but do not establish general clinical rescue or an alternative endogenous human ligand.

KLB encodes beta-Klotho, a glycosylated single-pass type III plasma-membrane protein whose tandem extracellular glycoside-hydrolase-like domains have lost essential catalytic residues and instead form a high-affinity recognition surface for the endocrine fibroblast growth factors FGF19 and FGF21. KLB associates with FGFR4 and FGFR1-family receptors to assemble ligand-responsive receptor complexes: the KLB ectodomain supplies ligand specificity while the FGFR supplies intracellular tyrosine-kinase signaling. In liver, FGF19-KLB-FGFR4 signaling represses CYP7A1 and limits bile-acid synthesis; KLB also enables tissue-selective FGF21 metabolic signaling.

Sprouty homolog 4 (SPRY4) is a small intracellular, non-enzymatic member of the Sprouty family that acts as an inducible negative-feedback inhibitor of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signalling to the Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade. Its expression is induced by growth-factor/ERK signalling (e.g. downstream of FGFR), and the protein then dampens ERK activation by at least two routes: it limits Ras activation at or upstream of Ras (associating with SOS1 and, with SPRY1, reducing recruitment of GRB2-SOS1 to FRS2 after FGF stimulation; this requires phosphorylation of the conserved N-terminal Tyr75), and it binds RAF1 through its C-terminal cysteine-rich Sprouty domain to block Ras-independent RAF1 activation, e.g. by VEGF. Through the same cysteine-rich domain SPRY4 binds and inhibits the cofilin kinase TESK1, suppressing integrin-mediated cofilin phosphorylation and cell spreading independently of ERK. SPRY4 is mainly cytoplasmic/cytosolic, often in vesicular puncta, and can associate with membranes. It also influences migration and focal adhesion formation (an MDM2-SPRY4-RhoA axis in p53-deficient cancer cells) and its expression correlates with favourable prognosis in some tumours.

CHCHD10 is a small CHCH-domain protein concentrated in the mitochondrial intermembrane space near cristae. It associates with CHCHD2 in human cells, forming heterodimers and higher-molecular-weight complexes. Human control fibroblasts contain CHCHD10-containing complexes of approximately 170 and 220 kDa; differentiated mouse tissues contain complexes of approximately 100–140 kDa and retain CHCHD10 oligomerization after CHCHD2 loss. The two proteins have partly redundant roles in mitochondrial membrane organization and respiratory homeostasis, including control of OMA1-dependent OPA1 processing. CHCHD10 also promotes cytochrome-c oxidase activity in cellular and purified-component experiments, while a secondary nuclear pool participates in CXXC5-dependent repression of COX4I2 expression in human cells. Pathogenic variants differ in aggregation, residual activity and mitochondrial-stress effects.

Interleukin-36 receptor antagonist (IL-36Ra), a secreted cytokine of the IL-1 family that serves as the sole antagonist of the IL-36 signaling axis. Member of IL-36 subfamily which includes three pro-inflammatory agonists (IL-36α/β/γ) and this single antagonist. Encoded as 155-amino acid precursor that requires N-terminal proteolytic processing (removal of initiator Met and adjacent residues by neutrophil elastase) to achieve full antagonist activity - unprocessed form has drastically reduced receptor-binding capacity. Primary molecular function: competitive antagonist of IL-36 receptor (IL-36R/IL1RL2) - binds IL-36R with high affinity (Kd ~5-6 nM, much stronger than IL-36 agonists at 480-1800 nM) and slow dissociation rate, effectively blocking receptor occupancy. Critical mechanistic difference from agonists: IL-36Ra binding prevents recruitment of IL-1RAcP co-receptor, thereby blocking formation of functional signaling complex and preventing downstream MyD88-dependent activation of NF-κB and MAPK pathways. Structurally adopts β-trefoil fold characteristic of IL-1 family but lacks conventional signal peptide - secreted via unconventional pathways (likely microparticles/exosomes or during cell stress). Expressed in barrier tissues (skin keratinocytes, intestinal epithelium) and immune cells (monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells); some cells constitutively express IL-36Ra to maintain basal antagonism preventing spontaneous inflammation. Essential role in immune homeostasis: loss-of-function mutations cause generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP/DITRA), a severe autoinflammatory skin disease with widespread sterile pustules and systemic inflammation, demonstrating that unopposed IL-36 signaling is life-threatening. Patients with processing-defective variant (p.V2F) that cannot be N-terminally cleaved have inactive IL-36Ra despite normal expression, proving proteolytic maturation is mandatory for function. Also implicated in other inflammatory conditions: rare IL36RN mutations found in severe Crohn's disease; IL-36Ra expressed in inflamed synovium in rheumatoid/psoriatic arthritis. Knockout mice show delayed wound healing due to excessive prolonged inflammation and neutrophil accumulation. IL-36Ra limits chemokine production (CXCL1, IL-8) and restrains Th17 responses. In 2022, FDA approved spesolimab (anti-IL-36R antibody) for GPP treatment, validating IL-36 pathway as therapeutic target and confirming IL-36Ra's natural protective role. Beyond immunity, potential context-dependent roles in cancer (may suppress pro-tumor inflammation in some settings). IL-38 (IL1F10) can also antagonize IL-36R but with more restricted activity. Overall, IL-36Ra is paradigmatic cytokine antagonist maintaining immune equilibrium at epithelial barriers by tightly blocking IL-36-driven inflammatory amplification.

TLR7 (Toll-like receptor 7) is an endolysosomal pattern recognition receptor of the innate immune system that detects RNA degradation products, chiefly those of viral single-stranded RNA genomes. It is a single-pass type I membrane glycoprotein: a large leucine-rich-repeat ectodomain faces the lumen of the compartment, a single transmembrane helix crosses the membrane, and a cytoplasmic TIR domain carries the signal. Unlike a simple ssRNA sensor, TLR7 is a dual receptor with two spatially distinct ligand-binding sites on its horseshoe-shaped ectodomain. The first site, at the dimerisation interface and conserved with TLR8, binds a guanosine moiety - guanosine itself, deoxyguanosine, synthetic guanosine analogues and imidazoquinolines such as imiquimod and R-848, and physiologically the guanosine 2',3'-cyclic monophosphate released from RNA. The second site, on the concave surface and unique to TLR7, binds short uridine-containing single-stranded RNA fragments, which raise the affinity of the first site. Both ligands are made in situ by sequential RNA catabolism: the lysosomal endonuclease RNase T2 cuts RNA between purine and uridine residues, and the exonucleases PLD3 and PLD4 release the terminal 2',3'-cyclic GMP and generate the pyrimidine-rich fragments. Occupancy of both sites locks TLR7 into an activated m-shaped homodimer that brings the two TIR domains together, recruiting MyD88 and assembling the myddosome with IRAK4, IRAK1/IRAK2 and TRAF6; this activates canonical NF-kappaB and MAP kinases, driving IL-6, IL-8, TNF and chemokine production, and activates IRF7, driving type I interferon. Newly made TLR7 folds in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and is delivered to endosomes and lysosomes by the chaperone UNC93B1, which engages its transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions; signalling requires endosomal acidification, and this intracellular confinement is what restrains responses to self RNA. TLR7 is expressed most strongly in plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells, and also in monocytes and various epithelial and pigment cells. Loss-of-function variants cause an X-linked immunodeficiency presenting as severe COVID-19 with impaired interferon responses, while gain-of-function variants that increase guanosine sensing cause X-linked systemic lupus erythematosus, driving survival of B-cell-receptor-activated B cells and accumulation of CD11c-positive age-associated B cells in a MyD88-dependent manner.

TLR8 (Toll-like receptor 8, CD288) is an endosomal pattern recognition receptor of the innate immune system and the most highly expressed nucleic-acid-sensing Toll-like receptor of the human myeloid compartment, found in monocytes, macrophages and myeloid dendritic cells. It is a single-pass type I membrane glycoprotein whose horseshoe-shaped leucine-rich-repeat ectodomain faces the endosomal lumen and whose cytoplasmic TIR domain transmits the signal. TLR8 detects the degradation products of single-stranded RNA rather than intact RNA, using two distinct sites: uridine binds a pocket at the interface between the two protomers - the same pocket that accommodates synthetic imidazoquinolines such as R-848 - while a short oligonucleotide binds a second site on the concave LRR surface. Both sites must be occupied for activation. The ligands are generated in the same compartment by the lysosomal endoribonuclease RNase T2, which cleaves single-stranded RNA between purine and uridine residues, supplying catabolic uridine and purine-2',3'-cyclophosphate-terminated oligoribonucleotides. Natural agonists include GU-rich single-stranded RNA sequences from HIV-1, SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 and endogenous RNAs such as microRNAs. Activation has two structural prerequisites: the receptor exists as a pre-formed dimer whose Z-loop, the insertion between leucine-rich repeats 14 and 15, must first be cleaved by furin-like proprotein convertases and cathepsins in endosomes - the uncleaved loop sterically blocks dimerisation - after which ligand binding reorganises the dimer so that the two C-termini and hence the two TIR domains come together. The apposed TIR domains recruit MyD88 and assemble the IRAK4-IRAK1/IRAK2-TRAF6 myddosome, activating canonical NF-kappaB and IRF7 and driving IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-12, TNF and type I interferon. Endogenous TLR8 resides in the early endosome and the endoplasmic reticulum, distinguishing it from TLR7 and TLR9, which occupy endolysosomes; it associates with the chaperone UNC93B1, which is required for its trafficking and signalling. Beyond cytokine induction, TLR8 signalling in CD4-positive regulatory T cells relieves their suppressive activity. X-linked gain-of-function variants, frequently present as somatic mosaicism, cause an inborn error of immunity with refractory neutropenia, lymphoproliferation, autoinflammation, impaired B-cell maturation and in some cases bone marrow failure.

TLR9 (Toll-like receptor 9, CD289) is an endosomal pattern recognition receptor of the innate immune system that senses DNA containing unmethylated CpG dinucleotides, a feature enriched in bacterial and viral genomes. It is a single-pass type I membrane protein with a leucine-rich-repeat ectodomain and a cytoplasmic TIR domain. Newly made TLR9 is folded in the endoplasmic reticulum and trafficked with the chaperone UNC93B1 through the Golgi to endolysosomes, where proteolytic cleavage of the ectodomain generates the functional receptor. CpG DNA binding induces a 2:2 receptor-ligand dimer that recruits MyD88 through the TIR domain, assembling an IRAK4-IRAK1/2-TRAF6 complex that activates NF-kappaB and MAP kinases (pro-inflammatory cytokines) and, in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, IRF7 (type I interferon). TLR9 is expressed mainly in B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and also in epithelial and other cell types; it drives B cell proliferation and antibody secretion, and its intracellular localization limits responses to self DNA.

UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) is a large (~173 kDa) soluble ER-resident enzyme that serves as the central quality control sensor and folding checkpoint in the calnexin/calreticulin cycle. UGGT1 recognizes glycoproteins with minor folding defects (preferentially molten-globule-like intermediates, not fully folded or completely unfolded proteins) and reglucosylates their N-glycans, thereby tagging them for re-engagement with the calnexin/calreticulin chaperone system. Its core molecular function is UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase activity (EC 2.4.1.-), transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to deglucosylated high-mannose N-glycans on misfolded substrates. Structurally, UGGT1 has a seven-domain architecture: four N-terminal thioredoxin-like domains (TRXL1-TRXL4) arranged in an arc that mediate substrate recognition, two beta-sandwich domains (betaS1, betaS2), and the C-terminal GT24 catalytic domain (~20% of the protein) (DOI:10.1073/pnas.1703682114). Substantial interdomain conformational flexibility enables UGGT1 to accommodate diverse client shapes and to glucosylate glycans at least ~40 angstroms from localized disordered regions. UGGT1 writes a site-selective "glyco-code" that determines which ER chaperones engage substrates and when during maturation (DOI:10.1016/j.molcel.2023.11.006). UGGT1-mediated reglucosylation competes with EDEM-family mannose trimming in a "tug-of-war" that determines whether substrates are retained for refolding or committed to ERAD (DOI:10.1101/2023.10.18.562958). UGGT1 activity is modulated by the partner selenoprotein SELENOF/SEP15 (DOI:10.1073/pnas.2315009121). UGGT1 is the dominant mammalian reglucosyltransferase (UGGT2 is ~7-30% of UGGT1 abundance in tested cell lines). Described as a "gatekeeper for quality control" that prevents transport of improperly folded glycoproteins out of the ER (PMID:10694380).

ALG9 is a glycosyltransferase 22 (GT22) family enzyme in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. Its luminal catalytic site uses dolichyl-phosphate-mannose to build the oligomannose core of the lipid-linked precursor for protein N-linked glycosylation. ALG9 adds an alpha-1,2-linked seventh mannose to Man(6)GlcNAc(2)-PP-dolichol (EC 2.4.1.259) and, after ALG12 adds the eighth mannose, adds an alpha-1,2-linked ninth mannose to Man(8)GlcNAc(2)-PP-dolichol (EC 2.4.1.261). Human isoform 1 has 11 transmembrane helices. Reduced ALG9 activity causes accumulation of the Man6 and Man8 lipid-linked intermediates and deficient protein glycosylation. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause ALG9 congenital disorder of glycosylation (ALG9-CDG), including severe Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura skeletal dysplasia with renal and other visceral malformations.

LRPPRC (Leucine-rich PPR motif-containing protein) is a mitochondrial PPR protein that functions as a key regulator of mitochondrial mRNA metabolism. It forms a stable ribonucleoprotein complex with SLIRP (SRA stem-loop interacting RNA-binding protein) and performs three core functions: (1) stabilization of mitochondrial mRNAs by protecting them from 3'-5' exonucleolytic degradation by the PNPase/SUV3 degradosome, (2) promotion of polyadenylation of mt-mRNAs via MTPAP, and (3) delivery of mRNAs to the mitoribosome through direct interaction with mS39 and mS31. Cryo-EM structures (2024) reveal LRPPRC acts as an mRNA "holdase" that maintains proper mRNA folding for efficient translation. Loss of LRPPRC causes the French-Canadian form of Leigh syndrome (LSFC) with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. While predominantly mitochondrial, a fraction localizes to the nucleus where it may participate in nuclear mRNA export via EIF4E.

HID1 is a conserved 788-residue peripheral membrane protein of the HID1/Ecm30 family (PANTHER PTHR21575, subfamily SF12) with no recognised catalytic, lipid-binding or protein-interaction domain. Despite early predictions of transmembrane segments, it is a soluble protein that shuttles between the cytosol and the cytoplasmic face of the medial- and trans-Golgi and the trans-Golgi network (TGN). Membrane association depends on an N-terminal myristoylated glycine and an adjacent polybasic patch, while TGN specificity and function reside in a highly conserved C-terminal domain. In neuroendocrine and endocrine cells HID1 is required for the biogenesis of large dense core vesicles (secretory granules): it supports sorting of soluble and membrane cargo into these granules, formation of the dense core, acidification of the TGN with correct localisation of the V-ATPase a2 subunit, and homotypic fusion of immature granules during their maturation, and so the storage and regulated release of peptide hormones and neuropeptides. Most of this functional evidence comes from rat neuroendocrine cell lines and mouse pancreatic beta cells, whose HID1 orthologs are about 95% identical to the human protein; in humans, biallelic HID1 variants cause an early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with hypopituitarism (DEE105). Its molecular activity is unknown.

ADNP is a zinc-finger and homeobox-containing chromatin regulator that recognizes DNA sequences and assembles the ChAHP complex with CHD4 and HP1 proteins. Its sequence-specific targeting recruits chromatin-remodeling activity to control transcription and local genome organization. ADNP also binds HP1 chromoshadow domains, supporting a complementary mode of recruitment to H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin. In mouse embryonic cells, ADNP controls lineage-gene expression and SINE repression and competes with CTCF at shared binding motifs. ADNP additionally has context-dependent cytoplasmic functions involving beta-catenin, microtubule end-binding proteins and neuronal morphogenesis. Heterozygous pathogenic variants cause Helsmoortel-van der Aa syndrome. The NAPVSIPQ sequence within ADNP is pharmacologically active as an isolated peptide.

Seipin, encoded by BSCL2, is an oligomeric integral endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that organizes lipid droplet biogenesis. Its conserved lumenal domain binds anionic phospholipids, and seipin associates with LDAF1 to define sites where neutral lipids assemble into droplets. Seipin tethers growing lipid droplets to the ER and organizes their membrane contacts, supporting delivery of lipids and proteins and maintaining an organized droplet population. These functions contribute to cellular lipid storage and adipose tissue physiology. Biallelic loss causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy, whereas specific dominant variants that affect folding or glycosylation are associated with motor neuropathy.

ARFGEF2 encodes BIG2 (brefeldin A-inhibited guanine nucleotide-exchange protein 2), a ~202 kDa guanine-nucleotide exchange factor for ADP-ribosylation factor GTPases. Its central Sec7 domain catalyses GDP-to-GTP exchange on class I ARFs, principally ARF1 and ARF3, and this activity is blocked by the fungal metabolite brefeldin A. BIG2 works at two membrane sites: at the trans-Golgi network, where ARF activation recruits the clathrin adaptors AP-1 and GGA - but not the COPI coat - to drive traffic towards endosomes and the cell surface; and on recycling endosomes, where it is required to maintain compartment integrity and to return internalised cargo such as the transferrin receptor and integrin beta1 to the plasma membrane. It is recruited from a large cytosolic pool onto membranes, and its exchange activity is damped by PKA phosphorylation and restored by protein phosphatase 1. Beyond catalysis, BIG2 is an A-kinase anchoring protein: three short amphipathic regions in its N-terminal half bind PKA regulatory subunits, assembling a local cAMP module that also contains phosphodiesterase PDE3A, and a separate non-catalytic C-terminal region binds non-muscle myosin IIA and restrains myosin light-chain phosphorylation, stress fibre formation and cell migration. BIG2 forms homodimers through its DCB and HUS regions and is found in large complexes with its close paralog BIG1, with which it shares trans-Golgi functions while retaining distinct roles - BIG1 maintains Golgi morphology, BIG2 maintains endosomal integrity. It is expressed in placenta, lung, heart, brain, kidney and pancreas, with the Human Protein Atlas reporting tissue-enhanced expression in parathyroid, and in neurons it is concentrated in the trans-Golgi network and in dendritic vesicles, where it contributes to GABA(A) receptor export from the endoplasmic reticulum. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in ARFGEF2 cause autosomal recessive periventricular nodular heterotopia with microcephaly (PVNH2), in which cortical neurons fail to migrate away from the periventricular proliferative zone.

SMOX (spermine oxidase, also known as PAOh1/SMO) is a soluble, FAD-dependent amine oxidase of the flavin monoamine oxidase / polyamine-oxidase family (EC 1.5.3.16). It catalyzes the direct oxidation of the free polyamine spermine to spermidine, releasing 3-aminopropanal and hydrogen peroxide (spermine + O2 + H2O -> spermidine + 3-aminopropanal + H2O2). This reaction constitutes the direct back-conversion arm of polyamine catabolism and, together with spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase (SSAT) and N1-acetylpolyamine oxidase (PAOX/PAO), controls the interconversion and intracellular concentrations of the polyamines spermine, spermidine and putrescine. Unlike PAOX, which acts on N1-acetylated polyamines, SMOX acts preferentially on non-acetylated spermine and does not require prior acetylation. SMOX is a monomeric flavoprotein that binds one FAD per subunit. The enzyme is expressed from at least six alternatively spliced isoforms with differing substrate affinities and is found in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus. Its products link SMOX to oxidative stress: the H2O2 and reactive aldehyde generated by spermine oxidation, particularly when produced in the nucleus, can cause reactive-oxygen-species-mediated DNA damage and apoptosis, and elevated SMOX activity is implicated in inflammation-associated carcinogenesis.

ABHD12 is a membrane-associated serine hydrolase that degrades lysophosphatidylserine and oxidized phosphatidylserine. It is enriched at the endoplasmic reticulum and controls bioactive lipid pools implicated in neural and immune homeostasis. The human enzyme also hydrolyzes monoacylglycerols, including the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol; the importance of this activity depends on cell type and activation state. Its catalytic serine, aspartate and histidine residues and glycosylation support lipid hydrolysis. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause PHARC, a progressive disorder featuring polyneuropathy, hearing loss, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa and cataract.

CFAP61 (Cilia- and flagella-associated protein 61; formerly C20orf26) is a structural scaffold protein and conserved component of the calmodulin- and radial spoke-associated complex (CSC) in motile cilia and flagella. The CSC, composed of CFAP61, CFAP91/MAATS1, and CFAP251/WDR66, connects the radial spokes to the nexin-dynein regulatory complex (N-DRC), mediating mechanochemical signal transduction that coordinates dynein motor activity and ciliary/flagellar beating. CFAP61 is specifically required for the stable assembly of radial spoke 3 (RS3) and contributes to RS2 base formation. In sperm, loss of CFAP61 causes collapse of axonemal architecture with loss of central pair, radial spokes, and inner dynein arms, resulting in multiple morphological abnormalities of the flagella (MMAF) and male infertility (SPGF84). Despite containing a Rossmann-like FAD/NAD(P)-binding superfamily fold (residues 665-998), CFAP61 has no enzymatic activity; this domain serves as a structural scaffold for protein-protein interactions within the axoneme. The protein also has a CFAP61-specific N-terminal domain and a C-terminal dimerisation domain. CFAP61 is expressed in all tissues with motile cilia, including respiratory epithelium, fallopian tubes, and testis, though disease phenotypes from human mutations are restricted to male infertility without classical primary ciliary dyskinesia symptoms.

PANK2 is the mitochondrial isoform of pantothenate kinase, a type II pantothenate kinase that catalyzes the first, committed and rate-limiting step of coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis: the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of pantothenate (vitamin B5) to (R)-4'-phosphopantothenate (EC 2.7.1.33). It is a feedback-regulated homodimer, strongly inhibited by acetyl-CoA and other acyl-CoA thioesters and activated by long-chain acylcarnitines such as palmitoylcarnitine, which is thought to couple CoA synthesis to mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation demand. In humans the enzyme is synthesized as a precursor with an N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide and is proteolytically processed by the mitochondrial-processing peptidase to a mature ~48-kDa protein that resides in the mitochondrial intermembrane space; a dynamic minor pool shuttles to the nucleus in a cell-cycle-dependent manner. The mitochondrial targeting signal is a primate-specific feature (rodent PanK2 is cytosolic). PANK2 is highly expressed in brain, and loss-of-function mutations cause the autosomal-recessive disorder pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN; neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1, formerly Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome), characterized by iron accumulation in the basal ganglia, dystonia, and the 'eye of the tiger' MRI sign.

IFT52 is a core (IFT-B1) subunit of the intraflagellar transport B complex, built from an N-terminal GIFT-like domain, a central domain and a C-terminal region that mediate multiple subunit contacts. IFT52 is a structural hub of IFT-B: it bridges the IFT88/IFT70/IFT52/IFT46 and IFT81/IFT74/IFT27/IFT25/IFT22 portions of the IFT-B1 core and connects IFT-B1 to the peripheral IFT-B2 subcomplex via IFT57/IFT38. As part of anterograde IFT trains moved by kinesin-2, IFT52 is required for ciliary entry of IFT-B and for cilium assembly and length control. IFT52 resides at the ciliary base and within cilia. Biallelic IFT52 variants cause short-rib thoracic dysplasia (SRTD16); patient cells show reduced levels of other IFT-B subunits and impaired ciliogenesis.

ORMDL3 (ORM1-like protein 3) is a conserved, multi-pass transmembrane protein of 153 amino acids that resides in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. It functions as a ceramide-sensitive regulatory subunit of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex (SPTLC1/SPTLC2/ssSPTa/ORMDL3), the enzyme that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis. ORMDL3 acts as a negative regulator of SPT: its N-terminus physically occludes the substrate entry tunnel of SPT, and this inhibitory conformation is stabilized by ceramide binding, thereby implementing a homeostatic negative feedback loop that maintains sphingolipid levels. Structurally resolved by cryo-EM, ORMDL3 has four transmembrane helices and a cytoplasmic N-terminal ceramide-sensing region. The 17q21 locus containing ORMDL3 is the strongest and most replicated genetic risk locus for childhood asthma. Beyond sphingolipid regulation, ORMDL3 has been implicated in ER stress/UPR signaling, ER calcium homeostasis, and autophagy regulation in immune cells, though these may represent downstream consequences of altered sphingolipid metabolism rather than independent molecular functions.

DDRGK1 (DDRGK domain-containing protein 1; also called UFBP1, Dashurin) is a single-pass endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that is an obligate component of the UFM1 ribosome E3 ligase (UREL) complex, together with the E3 ligase UFL1 and CDK5RAP3. DDRGK1 tethers the complex to the ER membrane through its N-terminal transmembrane helix, thereby restricting ufmylation activity to ER-docked ribosomes, and stabilizes UFL1. Following mono-ufmylation of the 60S ribosomal protein RPL26/uL24, DDRGK1 acts as a UFM1 reader, in that its UFM1-interacting motif (UFIM) binds ufmylated RPL26, producing stable association of the 60S subunit with the UREL complex and promoting release and recycling of the large subunit from SEC61 translocons. DDRGK1 is itself a substrate of ufmylation (at Lys-267). Through ER-resident ufmylation it participates in ribosome recycling, reticulophagy (ER-phagy), the response to ER stress and the unfolded protein response (regulating IRE1-alpha/ERN1 stability). Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause Shohat-type spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, reflecting a role in cartilage development via SOX9 stabilization.

SLC52A3 (riboflavin transporter 3, RFVT3; formerly C20orf54) is a multi-pass plasma-membrane transporter of the SLC52 solute-carrier family that mediates cellular uptake of the water-soluble vitamin B2 (riboflavin). Riboflavin is the precursor of the flavin cofactors FMN and FAD, which are essential for numerous oxidation-reduction reactions in carbohydrate, lipid and amino-acid metabolism; because humans cannot synthesize riboflavin, it must be acquired from the diet by intestinal absorption. RFVT3 localizes to the apical (brush-border) membrane of polarized epithelia and is the principal transporter for riboflavin absorption at the intestinal apical surface; it is most highly expressed in testis and is also abundant in small intestine, kidney and prostate. Transport is riboflavin-selective, Na(+)-independent at low pH, and is inhibited by riboflavin analogs (lumiflavin, FMN, FAD) and by methylene blue. The protein has 11 transmembrane helices. Two splice isoforms exist: isoform 1 (SLC52A3a) traffics to the cell membrane and is the functional transporter, whereas isoform 2 (SLC52A3b) is cytoplasmic and transport-deficient. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC52A3 cause riboflavin transporter deficiency, presenting as Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome type 1 and Fazio-Londe disease: progressive bulbar palsy with sensorimotor neuronopathy, sensorineural deafness and respiratory compromise that is responsive to high-dose oral riboflavin.

Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 4 isoform 2 (COX4-2) is a nuclear-encoded, tissue-biased alternative COX4 subunit of mitochondrial Complex IV. COX4I2 is homologous to the ubiquitous COX4I1 subunit and is incorporated into cytochrome c oxidase as a supernumerary, non-catalytic subunit rather than as one of the mtDNA-encoded redox-core subunits. Its annotations should therefore distinguish Complex IV membership and participation in mitochondrial electron transport from independent cytochrome-c oxidase catalytic activity. COX4I2 is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein with intermembrane-space topology and is highly expressed in lung; pathogenic variants cause exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, dyserythropoietic anemia, and calvarial hyperostosis (EPIDACH).

DNAJC5 (cysteine string protein alpha, CSPalpha; also CLN4) is a palmitoylated DnaJ/HSP40 co-chaperone of the presynaptic and secretory-vesicle membrane. It carries an N-terminal J domain that recruits and stimulates the constitutive HSP70 chaperone HSC70/HSPA8 and a central cysteine-string domain whose extensive palmitoylation anchors the protein to vesicle membranes. As a vesicle-localized co-chaperone it maintains the conformational integrity of the SNARE machinery, acting as a co-chaperone for SNAP-25 (with HSC70 and SGTA) and interacting with synaptotagmins, thereby supporting regulated/calcium-dependent exocytosis and the synaptic vesicle cycle and protecting nerve terminals against activity-dependent degeneration. Loss-of-function or aggregation-prone mutations in the cysteine-string domain (Leu115Arg, Leu116del) cause autosomal-dominant adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN4/ANCL, Kufs type).

YAP1 (Yes-associated protein 1) is a transcriptional coactivator and the main nuclear effector of the Hippo signaling pathway. It has no DNA-binding domain. An N-terminal TEAD-binding domain lets it bind TEAD1-4 and form a hybrid transcription factor (TEAD supplies the DNA-binding domain, YAP1 the activation domain). Its WW domains bind PPxY motifs in partners such as p73, angiomotins, PTPN14, LATS kinases and WBP2, and a C-terminal transactivation region and PDZ-binding motif complete the protein. When the Hippo kinase cascade is active, LATS1/2 phosphorylate YAP1 on HXRXXS motifs: phospho-S127 binds 14-3-3 and holds YAP1 in the cytoplasm, and a C-terminal phosphodegron targets it for SCF(beta-TrCP)-mediated degradation. Junctional and polarity proteins also sequester YAP1 according to cell density and mechanical cues. Nuclear YAP1-TEAD activates growth-promoting and anti-apoptotic genes (e.g. CTGF) at enhancers shared with AP-1. Through this program YAP1 promotes epithelial and progenitor proliferation, organ growth and regeneration, influences cell-fate choices such as osteogenic versus adipogenic differentiation, and drives oncogenic growth when deregulated. YAP1 also coactivates p73 proapoptotic genes after DNA damage. It is paralogous to WWTR1 (TAZ). Yorkie/YAP coactivators predate animals. The Capsaspora ortholog binds the Capsaspora TEAD ortholog and activates Hippo-responsive transcription in fly cells. In Capsaspora itself it controls cortical cytoskeletal dynamics and aggregate shape but not proliferation. This suggests that TEAD coactivation under Hippo-kinase control is ancestral, while control of proliferation and organ size was acquired in animals.

SLC19A3 (thiamine transporter 2, ThTr-2/THTR2) is a plasma-membrane solute carrier of the reduced-folate-carrier (RFC; TC 2.A.48) family with 12 transmembrane helices. It mediates high-affinity cellular uptake of thiamine (vitamin B1), coupled to proton antiport, and has no folate transport activity, distinguishing it from its folate-carrier paralog SLC19A1 and functionally paralleling SLC19A2/THTR1. In addition to thiamine, the human transporter also carries pyridoxine (vitamin B6) in an H(+)-dependent, acidic-pH-favoring manner; this pyridoxine activity is species-restricted (present in human but absent in rat/mouse Slc19a3). SLC19A3 is widely expressed, with highest abundance in placenta, kidney and liver, and contributes to intestinal and renal thiamine uptake. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease (BTBGD; thiamine metabolism dysfunction syndrome 2), an autosomal-recessive episodic encephalopathy that responds to high-dose thiamine with or without biotin.

NFU1 encodes a mitochondrial matrix protein of the NifU/NFU family that functions as a late-acting [4Fe-4S] cluster carrier in mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis. The protein dimerizes and ligates a bridging [4Fe-4S] cluster that is transferred to specific client proteins. NFU1 receives two [2Fe-2S] units from upstream donors ISCU2 and ISCA1, which are reductively coupled (with electrons from FDX2) to form the [4Fe-4S] cluster. The primary client is lipoyl synthase (LIAS), which requires the auxiliary [4Fe-4S] cluster for its catalytic activity. NFU1 dysfunction therefore impairs lipoylation of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (OGDH), and the glycine cleavage system, explaining the metabolic features of NFU1 deficiency. Biallelic mutations in NFU1 cause Multiple Mitochondrial Dysfunctions Syndrome type 1 (MMDS1), characterized by early-onset leukoencephalopathy, lactic acidosis, nonketotic hyperglycinemia, and pulmonary hypertension. Alternative splicing produces isoforms with distinct subcellular localizations, with isoform I targeted to mitochondria and isoform II present in cytosol and nucleus.

MRM2 (formerly FTSJ2) is a nuclear-encoded, mitochondrial-matrix S-adenosyl-L-methionine-dependent 2'-O-ribose methyltransferase of the FtsJ/RlmE family. It installs 2'-O-methyluridine at position 1369 (Um1369; U3039 in mtDNA numbering) in the A-loop of 16S mitochondrial large-subunit rRNA, a universally conserved modification in the peptidyl transferase centre; this modification is interdependent with the adjacent MRM3-installed Gm1370. Independently of its catalytic activity, MRM2 is a late-stage assembly factor of the mitoribosomal large subunit. It binds mtLSU intermediates after MTERF4-NSUN4 has exposed the A-loop, and it is released when GTPBP5 completes folding of the region. In its absence, mtLSU particles accumulate as immature intermediates with disordered rRNA domains IV and V and a bound MALSU1:L0R8F8:mtACP anti-association module, mitochondrial translation fails and respiration collapses. Catalytically dead K59A and D154A variants rescue these defects. MRM2 localises to foci near mtDNA nucleoids. A homozygous p.Gly189Arg variant causes a MELAS-like mitochondrial disease (mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 17).

USH1G encodes SANS (scaffold protein containing ankyrin repeats and SAM domain), a 461-residue non-enzymatic multivalent scaffold built from three N-terminal ankyrin repeats, a partly disordered central (CENT) region, a C-terminal SAM domain and a terminal class-I PDZ-binding motif. Its best-established role is in the mechanosensory hair cells of the cochlea and vestibule, where SANS binds harmonin (USH1C) through a bipartite SAM/PDZ-binding-motif interface and binds the MyTH4-FERM cassette of myosin VIIa (MYO7A) through its central region. SANS, MYO7A and harmonin cluster together at the upper tip-link density, the electron-dense plaque that anchors the cadherin-23 end of the stereociliary tip link in the mature hair bundle, where the complex holds the tip link under resting tension and is required for hair-bundle cohesion, hearing and balance. In photoreceptor cells SANS is a scaffold of the ciliary and periciliary protein network: it concentrates at the ciliary base and connecting cilium, associates with microtubules, binds the intraflagellar transport complex B proteins IFT20, IFT52 and IFT57 through its ankyrin repeats and central region, and is needed for their correct positioning at the cilium; a CK2-phosphorylation-dependent interaction between the SANS SAM domain and MAGI2 additionally regulates clathrin-dependent endocytosis at the periciliary membrane facing the ciliary pocket. SANS also shuttles into the nucleus, where it localises to Cajal bodies and nuclear speckles, interacts with SF3B1, SON, PRPF6, PRPF31 and the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP, and mediates transfer of tri-snRNP particles from Cajal bodies to speckles, so that its loss slows spliceosome assembly and alters constitutive and alternative splicing. Additional partners include PDZD7, spectrin beta-V and, by similarity, the tip-link cadherins CDH23 and PCDH15, which recruit SANS to the plasma membrane. Biallelic loss-of-function causes Usher syndrome type 1G (congenital profound deafness, vestibular areflexia and prepubertal retinitis pigmentosa); hypomorphic alleles cause non-syndromic progressive hearing loss.

WHRN encodes whirlin, a multivalent PDZ-domain scaffold protein (two harmonin-N-like/harmonin-homology domains, three PDZ domains, a proline-rich region and a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif) that organizes macromolecular complexes in the sensory cells of the inner ear and retina. Distinct isoforms produced from alternative promoters carry out two spatially and temporally separable roles in cochlear hair cells. The long (full-length) isoform is a component of the transient ankle-link/USH2 complex at the base of developing stereocilia, where its N-terminal PDZ domains bind the cytoplasmic PDZ-binding motifs of the large transmembrane proteins usherin (USH2A) and ADGRV1 (VLGR1/GPR98) and heterodimerize with the paralogous scaffold PDZD7; multivalent interactions among these four proteins drive condensate-like assembly of the ankle-link complex, which maintains hair-bundle cohesion during morphogenesis. The short (C-terminal) isoform localizes to stereocilia tips, where together with the motor MYO15A and the actin regulator EPS8 it forms the tip complex that controls stereocilia elongation and staircase architecture. In retinal photoreceptors, whirlin scaffolds USH2A and ADGRV1 at the periciliary membrane complex adjacent to the connecting cilium, supporting periciliary organization and protein trafficking toward the outer segment, and it also interacts with MPP1/p55, CASK and CIB2. Whirlin self-associates, a property required for its phase-separation-mediated scaffolding. Biallelic loss of the long isoform causes Usher syndrome type 2D (deafness with retinitis pigmentosa), while variants disrupting the C-terminal region cause DFNB31 nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness. Whirlin has additionally been reported at hair-cell and photoreceptor synapses, in neuronal growth cones, and at axonal paranodes.

PARK7/DJ-1 is a multifunctional protein linked to autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson disease (PARK7). It functions as a GSH-independent glyoxalase converting methylglyoxal/glyoxal to lactate/glycolate, an oxidative stress sensor via Cys-106 oxidation, a redox-dependent molecular chaperone that inhibits alpha-synuclein aggregation, a copper chaperone for SOD1, and a transcriptional coactivator. DJ-1 stabilizes NFE2L2/Nrf2 by preventing Keap1-mediated degradation, modulates NF-kappaB signaling via OTUD7B/Cezanne binding, and participates in mitochondrial quality control as part of the PINK1-PRKN-DJ-1 complex. The protein deglycase activity initially attributed to DJ-1 is controversial, with evidence suggesting apparent deglycase activity results from glyoxalase-mediated equilibrium shifts rather than direct deglycation. DJ-1 forms a homodimer with Cys-106 as the critical active-site residue for most activities.

CARD11 (CARMA1) is an intracellular signaling adaptor that couples antigen-receptor stimulation in lymphocytes to canonical NF-kappaB activation. Its CARD and coiled-coil region organize BCL10 assembly, while regulated recruitment of MALT1 and ubiquitin-signaling proteins builds the CBM signalosome at membrane-associated signaling sites. Phosphorylation and intramolecular interactions control access to this assembly platform. CARD11 also supports activation-associated metabolic signaling in T cells. Activating germline variants cause B-cell expansion with NF-kappaB activation and T-cell anergy (BENTA), biallelic loss of function causes combined immunodeficiency, and some heterozygous hypomorphic variants interfere with the normal protein and cause immunodeficiency with severe atopy.

NLRP3 (cryopyrin) is a cytosolic NLR-family protein of myeloid and other innate immune cells that nucleates the NLRP3 inflammasome, the platform that activates caspase-1 and so drives maturation of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 and gasdermin-D-dependent pyroptosis. It is built from an N-terminal pyrin domain, a central nucleotide-binding NACHT domain and a C-terminal leucine-rich repeat. In the resting state it is held as an autoinhibited, ADP-bound, membrane-binding oligomeric cage - reported as a decamer and as a dodecamer by different groups - with the pyrin domains sequestered inside the leucine-rich-repeat shell. Activation converts the NACHT domain to an ATP-bound conformation and assembles an active disc in which the pyrin domains stack into a filament that nucleates unidirectional polymerisation of the adaptor ASC, which in turn recruits procaspase-1. NLRP3 has no established direct agonist ligand. It responds to an unusually wide range of stimuli - pore-forming toxins, extracellular ATP, crystals such as monosodium urate, silica and alum, cell swelling, and mitochondrial and lysosomal damage - and the prevailing view is that it detects a shared downstream cellular perturbation, with potassium efflux and disassembly of the trans-Golgi network as common intermediates, rather than binding each agonist. Recruitment to the dispersed trans-Golgi network occurs through ionic interaction between a conserved polybasic region and phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate, after which microtubule-dependent transport concentrates NLRP3, together with the kinase NEK7, as condensates at the pericentriolar material of the microtubule organising centre. Whether this route is obligatory is disputed: low-molecular-weight, non-cage NLRP3 species can drive a slower, trans-Golgi- and MTOC-distal pathway that dominates in human neutrophils, and raising NLRP3 abundance can make potassium-efflux-driven activation independent of both NEK7 and priming. Gain-of-function mutations, mostly in the NACHT-encoding exon 3, cause the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes - familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome and neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease - which respond to interleukin-1 blockade, and NLRP3 activity contributes to gout, atherosclerosis, silicosis and neuroinflammation. A separate, inflammasome-independent role for NLRP3 as a nuclear transcriptional cofactor that binds the Il4 promoter with IRF4 in T helper 2 cells has been reported in mouse but is not independently corroborated.

DNAJC30 is a mitochondrial inner-membrane member of the DnaJ/HSP40 family that is enriched in neurons, including large cortical pyramidal neurons.
