It helps maintain respiratory-chain function through turnover and replacement of N-module subunits in assembled complex I. DNAJC30 also binds mitochondrial ATP synthase and contributes to regulation of mitochondrial ATP production, with the contribution varying across cellular contexts. The gene lies in the chromosome 7q11.23 Williams-Beuren syndrome interval; its individual contribution does not explain the full multigene-deletion phenotype. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause autosomal-recessive Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.

SUFU (Suppressor of fused homolog) is a 484-residue intracellular protein with no catalytic domain and no enzymatic activity, and the single human member of the Suppressor of fused family. It is the principal negative regulator of the vertebrate Hedgehog pathway acting downstream of Smoothened. SUFU binds full-length GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3 zinc-finger transcription factors through a conserved interface that closes around the SYGHL motif of GLI, and this single interaction accounts for its several documented effects: GLI is held in the cytoplasm and blocked from entering the nucleus, its transcriptional activity is repressed even where the two are bound together on DNA, and it is protected from proteasomal degradation. In the pathway-off state SUFU additionally acts as an adaptor that promotes proteolytic conversion of full-length GLI3 into the GLI3R repressor by recruiting GSK3B to GLI3; the SUFU-GLI3 complex is delivered to the primary cilium, and intraflagellar transport moves it between the ciliary base, where the processing kinases act, and the ciliary tip. Hedgehog signalling releases GLI from SUFU: the Fused-family kinases STK36 and ULK3, the ciliary kinase DYRK2, ERK/MAPK and S6K1 each weaken the SUFU-GLI interface by phosphorylating GLI, and SCF(FBXL17) ubiquitylates SUFU itself at Lys-257 to drive its turnover in the nucleus. SUFU is expressed ubiquitously in adult tissues and is found in the cytoplasm, the nucleoplasm and the cilium. Loss of SUFU raises Hedgehog output: knockout is embryonic-lethal in mouse, germline loss-of-function in humans predisposes to medulloblastoma and causes basal cell nevus syndrome, and hypomorphic recessive missense variants cause Joubert syndrome with cranio-facial and skeletal defects.

ACAP1 is a multidomain, phosphoinositide-regulated GTPase-activating protein for the small GTPase ARF6 and a component of the coat that sorts cargo out of recycling endosomes. Its four domains divide the work unconventionally: an N-terminal BAR domain that oligomerises ACAP1 into a lattice on the membrane rather than binding membrane itself, a pleckstrin-homology domain that binds phosphoinositides and performs the membrane binding and curvature generation a BAR domain would normally perform, a C4 zinc-finger Arf-GAP catalytic domain that accelerates GTP hydrolysis on ARF6 in preference to ARF1 and ARF5, and three ankyrin repeats. GAP activity is stimulated by phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate and phosphatidic acid, so catalysis is coupled to lipid composition. ACAP1 is largely cytosolic at rest and is recruited by ARF6-GTP both to tubular recycling endosomes and to the cell surface during ruffling. On the endosome it forms part of an ARF6-regulated clathrin coat that packages cargo for return to the plasma membrane: it binds clathrin heavy chain directly and captures the cytoplasmic tails of integrin beta-1 and of the glucose transporter GLUT4/SLC2A4, thereby supporting integrin-dependent cell migration and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake. Cargo capture is a switch rather than a constitutive activity. Akt phosphorylation of Ser-554 relieves a local autoinhibition and licenses binding to a sorting signal in the integrin beta-1 tail, which couples growth-factor signalling directly to the recycling step. Because ARF6 also governs peripheral actin, ACAP1 acting on ARF6 dampens membrane protrusions, dorsal ruffles and focal adhesions; the PTB-domain adaptor GULP1 opposes this by sequestering ACAP1 in a complex with GDP-bound ARF6. ACAP1 is expressed most strongly in haematopoietic and lymphoid tissue, and is one of three paralogous human ACAPs together with ACAP2 and ACAP3.

Barttin, encoded by BSND, is an integral membrane accessory subunit of the ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb chloride channels. It associates with these pore-forming subunits and regulates channel activation, surface abundance and polarized membrane sorting. Barttin modifies cooperative channel gating, favoring chloride conductance at physiological potentials; its palmitoylation at Cys54 and Cys56 supports efficient activation. Trafficking and activation can be separated experimentally and by disease-associated variants. ClC-K/barttin complexes support renal chloride reabsorption and potassium recycling in the inner ear. Wild-type human barttin preferentially sorts basolaterally in polarized epithelial models. Loss of barttin function causes Bartter syndrome with sensorineural deafness, while some hypomorphic variants predominantly impair hearing.

PYCARD (ASC; also TMS1) is a small 195-residue cytosolic adaptor protein built from only two death-fold domains - an N-terminal pyrin domain (PYD) and a C-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD) joined by a flexible linker - with no catalytic or ligand-sensing module. It is the shared adaptor of ASC-dependent inflammasomes. On activation, a sensor (NLRP3, NLRP1, NLRP6, AIM2, IFI16 or pyrin/MEFV) nucleates polymerization of the ASC PYD into filaments; the clustered ASC CARDs then nucleate procaspase-1 CARD filaments, bringing procaspase-1 molecules into proximity for autoprocessing. These filaments condense into a single micrometre-scale perinuclear 'speck' (also called the pyroptosome) per cell. Active caspase-1 matures pro-interleukin-1 beta and pro-interleukin-18 and cleaves gasdermin D to execute pyroptosis. ASC thus supplies the connectivity and signal-amplification geometry of the inflammasome rather than any enzymatic step. In resting monocytes/macrophages a pool of ASC is nuclear and must redistribute to the cytosol for inflammasome function; the protein is otherwise cytosolic. Its activity is tuned by post-translational modification (K63 ubiquitination at K174, tyrosine phosphorylation) and by competing pyrin-domain-only proteins (POP1/2/3). Released ASC specks persist extracellularly and propagate inflammation. Beyond the inflammasome, ASC has context-dependent, inflammasome-independent activities reported in apoptosis (as a CARD/pyrin aggregating adaptor engaging caspase-8, caspase-9 and the p53-Bax mitochondrial pathway) and in NF-kB and MAPK signalling, where it can both activate and, via IKK suppression and DUSP10 regulation, dampen downstream cytokine output. PYCARD/ASC is central to the monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes driven by its sensor partners and to IL-1-driven inflammatory disease.

CHEK2 encodes CHK2, an FHA-domain-containing protein serine/threonine kinase that couples DNA damage signaling to checkpoint control, substrate stability and apoptotic responses. ATM-dependent priming and regulated self-association promote activation-loop autophosphorylation. Nuclear CHK2 phosphorylates regulatory proteins including checkpoint phosphatases and factors controlling p53 signaling, transcription and DNA-repair pathway choice. Its action is regulatory rather than direct DNA rejoining. PML-associated nuclear pools and context-dependent extranuclear distributions have been reported. Alternative splicing produces proteins with different domain content and activity; the canonical 543-residue enzyme is not representative of every product.

CD320 (transcobalamin receptor, formerly 8D6 antigen) is a single-pass type I cell-surface glycoprotein that captures transcobalamin carrying vitamin B12 and mediates uptake of this complex by endocytosis. Its extracellular region contains two calcium-coordinating LDL receptor class A domains that contact transcobalamin, separated by an EGF-like region. Calcium stabilizes the receptor-ligand complex, and acidic pH reduces ligand affinity in vitro. CD320 has high selectivity for transcobalamin over the related circulating carrier haptocorrin. Its expression is associated with proliferation, with higher levels in actively dividing cells than in quiescent cells. It thereby supplies cells with cobalamin for subsequent intracellular metabolism. Human variants can impair this uptake and cause transcobalamin receptor deficiency with methylmalonic aciduria. CD320 also supports B-cell proliferation in follicular dendritic cell coculture experiments; this context-dependent activity is distinct from its broadly established nutrient uptake role.

BCAP31 encodes BAP31, a multipass endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein involved in the handling of newly synthesized membrane proteins and in communication between the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. It associates with selected clients and protein translocation machinery, directing misfolded CFTR toward degradation. Its cytoplasmic region also participates in a FIS1-associated platform that recruits procaspase-8. Caspase cleavage generates an ER-localized p20 fragment that promotes calcium-dependent apoptotic signaling. At ER-mitochondria contacts, BAP31 associates with TOMM40 and supports the mitochondrial localization of selected respiratory-chain proteins. Pathogenic BCAP31 variants cause an X-linked disorder with deafness, dystonia, and cerebral hypomyelination.

FBXW7 (also known as hCdc4, SEL-10, FBW7, Archipelago homolog) is the F-box/WD40 substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein) E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex. Its N-terminal F-box domain binds SKP1 (and thereby connects to the CUL1-RBX1 catalytic core), while its C-terminal eight-bladed WD40 beta-propeller forms a phosphodegron-binding pocket that recognizes Cdc4 phosphodegron (CPD) motifs (a high-affinity consensus is pThr-Pro-Pro-X-pSer, with the central phosphothreonine at the P0 position), typically generated by GSK3, CDK1/2, or ERK/MAPK priming-plus-phosphorylation schemes; low-affinity and noncanonical CPDs can also be biologically decisive. By recruiting these phosphorylated substrates to the SCF complex, FBXW7 directs their polyubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. FBXW7 is a major tumor suppressor: it targets a network of oncoproteins and regulatory proteins for destruction, including cyclin E (CCNE1/CCNE2), MYC and N-MYC, the NOTCH1/NOTCH2/NOTCH4 intracellular domains, JUN, MCL1, MLST8, RICTOR, NR1D1 (REV-ERBalpha), presenilin 1, EGFR (via CPD-like motifs in its cytoplasmic tail), the Wnt effectors LEF1 and TCF7L2, and the mitophagy kinase PINK1. FBXW7 functions as a homodimer, which tunes substrate turnover and processivity. Three N-terminally distinct isoforms (alpha/nucleoplasm, beta/cytoplasm, gamma/nucleolus) localize to different subcellular compartments and access partly distinct substrate pools. Through this substrate-receptor activity FBXW7 governs cell-cycle progression (G1/S transition), Notch signaling, MYC-driven proliferation, EGFR/MAPK and Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, lipid and circadian metabolism, mitochondrial quality control, and bone homeostasis. Beyond canonical degradative K48-type ubiquitination, an ATM-phosphorylated SCF(FBXW7) pool can promote non-degradative K63-linked polyubiquitination of XRCC4 at DNA double-strand breaks to facilitate non-homologous end joining. Loss-of-function mutations, frequently clustered in the WD40 substrate-binding arginines (hotspots R465, R479, R505), are among the most common in human cancers, where they stabilize oncogenic substrates and can drive resistance to anti-EGFR and anti-Wnt therapies; germline FBXW7 variants cause an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder (DEDHIL).

DHX30 is an ATP-dependent RNA helicase with cytosolic and mitochondrial populations. It binds RNA and supports mitochondrial large ribosomal subunit assembly in association with mitochondrial RNA granules and nucleoids. Its endogenous RNA substrates and the remodeling step used during assembly remain unresolved. Pathogenic variants can impair RNA-dependent ATP hydrolysis or RNA unwinding, alter stress-granule behavior and disrupt neurodevelopment.

DNAAF11 (LRRC6) is a leucine-rich-repeat and CS-domain protein that supports assembly and axonemal incorporation of the outer and inner dynein arms required for motile-cilia and sperm-flagellar beating. It associates with other dynein assembly factors and localizes to cytoplasmic dynein axonemal particles (DynAPs). Human airway and sperm studies also report ciliary or flagellar localization, with differences between airway preparations. Loss of DNAAF11 disrupts dynein-arm formation and causes primary ciliary dyskinesia, often with laterality defects and impaired fertility.

MCEE encodes methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (also called DL-methylmalonyl-CoA racemase; EC 5.1.99.1), a mitochondrial matrix enzyme of the vicinal-oxygen-chelate (VOC)/glyoxalase superfamily. It catalyses the interconversion of (2R)- and (2S)-methylmalonyl-CoA (D- and L-methylmalonyl-CoA), the epimerisation step that lies between propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT) in the propionyl-CoA catabolic pathway. Propionyl-CoA arising from catabolism of the branched-chain and other amino acids (valine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine), odd-chain fatty acids, and cholesterol is carboxylated by PCC to (2S)-methylmalonyl-CoA, epimerised by MCEE to the (2R)/(S)-isomer that MMUT requires, and rearranged by MMUT to succinyl-CoA for entry into the citric acid cycle. The mature enzyme (after cleavage of an N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide) binds a divalent metal ion, with cobalt modelled at the active site in the crystal structure. Loss-of-function variants cause methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase deficiency (MCEED), a usually mild autosomal recessive methylmalonic aciduria.

CDC73 encodes parafibromin, a nuclear component of the polymerase-associated factor 1 complex (PAF1C). It associates with RNA polymerase II and helps coordinate transcription elongation with recruitment of mRNA 3′-end processing factors. These functions depend on interactions within the transcription machinery rather than an intrinsic RNA-cleavage or histone-modifying activity. Parafibromin also engages beta-catenin and influences context-dependent transcriptional programs, proliferation and differentiation. Loss of CDC73 function underlies hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome and predisposes to parathyroid tumors.

EDEM3 (ER degradation-enhancing alpha-mannosidase-like protein 3) is a soluble endoplasmic reticulum lumenal protein of glycoside hydrolase family 47 (GH47, EC 3.2.1.113), one of three mammalian Htm1/Mns1 homologues (EDEM1, EDEM2, EDEM3) acting in ER-associated degradation of glycoproteins (gpERAD). EDEM3 is an active, calcium-dependent alpha-1,2-mannosidase that accelerates glycoprotein ERAD by catalyzing the downstream mannose-trimming step from Man8GlcNAc2 to Man7GlcNAc2 and further trimming toward Man5GlcNAc2 isomers, generating the demannosylated glycans recognized by the downstream lectin OS-9. It acts mainly at the second trimming step (with EDEM1 contributing to a lesser extent), downstream of the first-step enzyme EDEM2, and, like EDEM1 but unlike EDEM2, it associates with the HRD1 adaptor SEL1L. Beyond misfolded ERAD substrates, EDEM3 may also trim N-glycans on general glycoproteins. It is unique among the EDEMs in containing a protease-associated (PA) domain of unknown function, is induced by the unfolded protein response, and is broadly expressed. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal-recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation (EDEM3-CDG / CDG2V) with neurodevelopmental delay.

NMNAT2 (nicotinamide/nicotinate mononucleotide adenylyltransferase 2) is one of three human NMNAT isoforms and catalyzes the central, committed adenylyl-transfer step of NAD+ biosynthesis: it condenses nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) with ATP to form NAD+ (EC 2.7.7.1), and less efficiently condenses nicotinate mononucleotide (NaMN) with ATP to form deamido-NAD+ (NaAD; EC 2.7.7.18), releasing pyrophosphate in each case. This reaction is shared by the NAD+ salvage and de novo routes. The active enzyme is a Mg2+-dependent monomer. Unlike the nuclear isoform NMNAT1 and the mitochondrial NMNAT3, NMNAT2 is a cytosolic, Golgi/Golgi-derived-vesicle-membrane-associated enzyme; membrane attachment requires palmitoylation, and the protein is trafficked into axons on Golgi-derived vesicles. NMNAT2 is highly expressed in brain and is a labile, short-lived protein. Its continuous supply is a key axon-maintenance/survival factor: by sustaining local NAD+ (and consuming NMN) it keeps the pro-degenerative NADase SARM1 inactive, thereby delaying Wallerian-type axon degeneration; loss or depletion of NMNAT2 triggers axon degeneration and, in mice, perinatal lethality with severe axon defects. In cytosolic NAD+-supply roles it can also support the mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase PARP16, promoting ribosomal-protein MARylation that tunes cytoplasmic translation. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause a human polyneuropathy with skeletal abnormalities.

COQ8A (also known as ADCK3, CABC1, COQ8) is a mitochondrial member of the ancient UbiB family of atypical protein-kinase-like (PKL) enzymes, and is one of two human co-orthologs (with COQ8B/ADCK4) of yeast Coq8p. It is required for the biosynthesis of coenzyme Q (ubiquinone/CoQ10), a lipid-soluble electron carrier of the respiratory chain and a membrane antioxidant. The 647-residue precursor is imported into mitochondria (an N-terminal transit peptide of ~162 residues is removed) and anchors to the inner mitochondrial membrane as a single-pass membrane protein, with its catalytic domain facing the matrix, where CoQ is produced. Although COQ8A adopts a protein-kinase-like fold, several UbiB-specific features suppress canonical protein-kinase activity: an N-terminal KxGQ domain occludes the substrate-binding cleft, and an alanine-rich (AAAS) loop replaces the canonical glycine-rich nucleotide-binding loop, conferring an unusual selectivity for binding ADP over ATP. Biochemically, the protein binds and hydrolyzes ATP (ATPase activity that is enhanced by the KxGQ motif and by coenzyme-Q head-group intermediates and cardiolipin), and it interacts with lipid CoQ intermediates, rather than exhibiting canonical protein-kinase phosphotransfer in trans. Functionally, COQ8A stabilizes and helps assemble the multi-subunit CoQ biosynthetic complex (the "COQ synthome"/complex Q; COQ3-COQ7, COQ9), thereby streamlining CoQ production. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-4 (COQ10D4), presenting as autosomal-recessive cerebellar ataxia (ARCA2/SCAR9) with cerebellar atrophy, exercise intolerance, and variable seizures.

Mitofusin 2 (MFN2) is a dynamin-superfamily GTPase anchored in the mitochondrial outer membrane by a hairpin transmembrane segment, with its N-terminal GTPase domain and helical bundle domains facing the cytosol. Together with its paralog MFN1, MFN2 forms homo- and hetero-oligomeric complexes in trans between apposed mitochondria; nucleotide-dependent dimerization of the GTPase domains tethers the membranes and GTP hydrolysis drives outer-membrane fusion, which is coordinated with OPA1-mediated inner-membrane fusion. MFN2 also concentrates at ER-mitochondria contacts and has been proposed to tether the two organelles, connects mitochondria to the Miro/TRAK transport machinery, and in damaged mitochondria is phosphorylated by PINK1 and ubiquitinated by Parkin, linking fusion arrest to mitophagy. Dominant MFN2 mutations cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A, an axonal peripheral neuropathy.

BCKDK is an ATP-dependent protein serine kinase that controls branched-chain amino acid utilization. In the mitochondrial matrix it associates with the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex and phosphorylates its BCKDHA/E1 alpha subunit, inhibiting oxidative decarboxylation of branched-chain ketoacids. Loss of this inhibition increases amino acid breakdown and can cause depletion of circulating branched-chain amino acids with neurodevelopmental disease. BCKDK also phosphorylates ATP-citrate lyase at human Ser455; biochemical and rodent liver experiments connect this second activity to cytosolic lipid-synthesis regulation.

ATG7 is an E1-like ubiquitin-activating enzyme essential for autophagy. It functions as the common E1 enzyme for two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems: (1) ATG12 conjugation, where ATG7 activates ATG12 for its conjugation with ATG5 via the E2 ATG10; and (2) ATG8/LC3 lipidation, where ATG7 activates LC3/GABARAP proteins for their conjugation with phosphatidylethanolamine via the E2 ATG3. ATG7 forms a homodimer and uses a trans-thioester transfer mechanism across protomers. The catalytic cysteine (Cys572) is essential for forming thioester intermediates with ATG12 and ATG8 family proteins. Both conjugation systems are essential for autophagosome formation and membrane expansion during canonical macroautophagy.

DGAT2 (diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2) is an integral endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme that catalyzes the terminal and only committed step of triacylglycerol (TAG) biosynthesis: transfer of a long-chain acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-3 position of 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol (DAG), producing triacylglycerol and CoA (EC 2.3.1.20). It is a member of the DGAT2/MOGAT acyltransferase family and shares no sequence homology with the MBOAT-family enzyme DGAT1, which performs the same net reaction. DGAT2 is a multi-pass ER membrane protein whose catalytic region faces the cytosol; it concentrates at ER–lipid-droplet contact sites and is also found on the lipid droplet surface and in the perinuclear region. Predominantly expressed in liver and white adipose tissue, DGAT2 is the quantitatively major TAG-synthesizing enzyme and, in liver, preferentially channels endogenously synthesized fatty acids into triglyceride for storage in lipid droplets; it is a therapeutic target in hepatic steatosis. Beyond its principal DGAT activity it displays several related in vitro acyltransferase activities, including acyl-CoA:retinol O-fatty-acyltransferase (ARAT, EC 2.3.1.76), monoacylglycerol acyltransferase activity, and use of monoalkylglycerol as an acyl acceptor to form ether neutral lipids. DGAT2 forms multimeric complexes of its own subunits and interacts with the fatty-acid transporter SLC27A1.

ERLIN1 (SPFH1, ER lipid raft-associated protein 1) is a single-pass type II endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein with a lumenal SPFH/prohibitin (band 7) domain, belonging to the band 7/mec-2 (stomatin-prohibitin-flotillin) family. It associates with lipid-raft-like domains of the ER membrane and functions as a scaffold rather than an enzyme. ERLIN1 forms a large ring-shaped heteromeric complex with its homolog ERLIN2 (SPFH2); the ERLIN1/ERLIN2 complex binds inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) tetramers and, together with the ER ubiquitin ligase RNF170, mediates the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of activated IP3Rs, thereby controlling calcium signaling. The erlins are cholesterol-binding proteins that restrict SREBP activation: they associate with the SCAP-SREBP-Insig machinery to promote its ER retention and thus negatively regulate cholesterol and fatty acid biosynthesis, contributing to cellular cholesterol homeostasis. ERLIN1 also interacts with the ER ubiquitin ligases AMFR/gp78 and SYVN1/HRD1, linking it to sterol-accelerated ERAD. Loss-of-function variants in ERLIN1 cause autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG62).

ARPP21 (ARPP-21, TARPP) is a cytoplasmic R3H-domain RNA-binding protein, first identified as a cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein that PKA phosphorylates and that is enriched in dopamine-innervated striatal neurons. It binds uridine-rich sequences in 3' UTRs and acts as a positive post-transcriptional regulator, interacting with the translation initiation complex eIF4F. In neurons it opposes the miRNA it hosts, miR-128, by co-regulating shared target mRNAs, and promotes dendritic branching. In thymocytes it promotes the expression of target mRNAs that support TCR repertoire diversity. A short isoform has been proposed to inhibit calmodulin-dependent enzymes.

SYNE2 encodes nesprin-2, a family of spectrin-repeat proteins produced from a very large gene by alternative promoters and splicing. The giant isoform (nesprin-2G, NUANCE, ~800 kDa) has N-terminal paired calponin-homology domains that bind F-actin, a long spectrin-repeat rod, and a C-terminal transmembrane KASH domain that anchors it in the outer nuclear membrane. In the perinuclear space the KASH peptide binds trimeric SUN1/SUN2 of the inner nuclear membrane, forming the LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex that transmits cytoskeletal forces to the nuclear lamina. Nesprin-2G assembles with SUN2 into transmembrane actin-associated nuclear (TAN) lines that couple the nucleus to retrograde actin flow, moving the nucleus and reorienting the centrosome in migrating fibroblasts; the formin FHOD1 reinforces this coupling. Its membrane-proximal spectrin repeats also recruit microtubule motors to the nuclear envelope, kinesin-1 through a LEWD motif and dynein-dynactin through the adaptor BICD2, providing the nuclear attachment for motor-driven nucleokinesis in migrating neurons and interkinetic nuclear migration in neural progenitors, and it is required for centrosome migration during ciliogenesis. Shorter isoforms lacking the actin-binding or KASH domains localize to the inner nuclear membrane (where they bind lamin A and emerin), nucleoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum, sarcomeric Z-discs and focal adhesions. SYNE2 variants are associated with Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy.

SYNE1 encodes nesprin-1, a family of spectrin-repeat proteins produced from a very large gene by alternative promoters and splicing. The giant isoform (enaptin, ~1 MDa) has paired N-terminal calponin-homology actin-binding domains, a long spectrin-repeat rod, and a C-terminal transmembrane KASH domain that anchors it in the outer nuclear membrane. In the perinuclear space the KASH peptide binds trimeric SUN1/SUN2 (with a SUN-KASH disulfide) to form LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complexes, which connect the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons, and associated dynein-dynactin and kinesin-1 motors, to the nuclear lamina. Through this bridge nesprin-1 transmits force across the nuclear envelope and functions in nuclear anchorage and positioning (notably of myonuclei and synaptic nuclei), nuclear shape, centrosome-nucleus coupling, and, redundantly with nesprin-2, nuclear migration in developing brain. Shorter isoforms lacking the actin-binding domain (nesprin-1alpha/myne-1, beta) are enriched in muscle and associate with lamin A/C and emerin at the nuclear envelope, while other isoforms localize to the Golgi, sarcomeric Z-lines, or processing bodies. Biallelic SYNE1 loss-of-function causes autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia (SCAR8/ARCA1); SYNE1 variants are also associated with Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy 4 and myogenic arthrogryposis.

NCSTN encodes nicastrin, a single-pass type I membrane glycoprotein and essential non-catalytic subunit of the gamma-secretase complex. Together with a presenilin catalytic subunit, APH1A or APH1B, and PSENEN/PEN-2, nicastrin forms a membrane-embedded intramembrane protease complex that processes substrates including APP and Notch receptors. Nicastrin contributes to complex assembly, maturation, substrate recruitment or presentation, and endoprotease activity rather than acting as the catalytic aspartyl protease itself. It functions in ER/Golgi/endomembrane, endosomal, and plasma-membrane compartments where gamma-secretase substrates are processed.

DICER1 encodes a multidomain RNase III enzyme that cleaves double-stranded RNA and precursor microRNA hairpins into small regulatory RNAs. Its paired RNase III domains, PAZ region and RNA-binding domains coordinate substrate recognition and cleavage. Dicer works with Argonaute proteins and the cofactors TARBP2 or PRKRA in RNA processing and guide loading, linking small-RNA production to post-transcriptional gene regulation. Cytosolic Dicer supports this pathway, with nuclear and perinuclear pools varying by cellular context. Dicer-dependent regulatory RNAs influence development and differentiation, including Schwann-cell maturation and myelination. Alternative splicing produces structurally distinct proteins; t-Dicer has an altered C terminus and asymmetric RNA-cleavage behavior.

Optineurin (OPTN) is a ubiquitously expressed, predominantly cytoplasmic coiled-coil adaptor protein that functions as a selective autophagy receptor. It carries two functional cargo-recognition modules: an LC3-interacting region (LIR motif, residues 176-181, with the critical Phe178) that binds ATG8-family modifiers (MAP1LC3A/B, GABARAP, GABARAPL1, GABARAPL2), and a UBAN (ubiquitin binding in ABIN and NEMO) motif (residues 474-479, with the essential Asp474/Phe475) that binds linear (M1) and K63-linked polyubiquitin chains. By simultaneously engaging ubiquitinated cargo and ATG8 proteins on the nascent autophagosomal membrane, OPTN bridges cargo to the autophagy machinery. Its C-terminus contains a CCHC NOA-type zinc finger (residues 547-577) that coordinates Zn2+. OPTN partners with and is activated by the kinase TBK1, which phosphorylates OPTN at Ser177 adjacent to the LIR, markedly increasing LC3 binding affinity and thereby driving cargo-selective autophagy. Through this mechanism OPTN mediates antibacterial xenophagy of ubiquitin-coated cytosolic bacteria (e.g. Salmonella) and PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy of damaged mitochondria, acting alongside the related receptors SQSTM1/p62 and CALCOCO2/NDP52. As a NEMO-related protein, OPTN also regulates innate immune and inflammatory signaling: it negatively regulates canonical NF-kB signaling (competing for polyubiquitin within the TNFR1 complex) and dampens virus-triggered IFN-beta induction, while recruiting and activating TBK1 at the Golgi after RNA-virus sensing. Independently, OPTN links myosin VI and GTP-Rab8 to the Golgi complex, contributing to Golgi ribbon organization, post-Golgi exocytosis, and Rab8/TBC1D17-dependent endocytic recycling (e.g. of the transferrin receptor). OPTN mutations cause primary open-angle glaucoma (GLC1E; e.g. E50K), normal-pressure glaucoma, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with or without frontotemporal dementia (ALS12; e.g. the UBAN mutant E478G and the truncation Q398X), linking impaired selective autophagy and vesicular trafficking to neurodegeneration.

ARL2BP, also called BART, is a small helical protein that binds the active forms of the ARL2 and ARL3 GTPases. It cooperates with ARL13B in ARL3 nucleotide exchange and stabilizes GTP-bound GTPases. ARL2BP is predominantly cytosolic, with additional mitochondrial, centrosomal, ciliary and nuclear pools. It also binds STAT3 and supports its nuclear retention in human cells. Human variants and mouse loss-of-function studies associate ARL2BP with photoreceptor and sperm ciliary integrity, although the relationship between its GTPase-regulatory activity and ciliary microtubule architecture is not fully resolved.

PLD3 (Phospholipase D3) is a lysosomal enzyme that, despite its name, functions primarily as a 5'-3' exonuclease rather than a phospholipase. The protein is synthesized as a type II transmembrane glycoprotein and traffics to lysosomes where it is proteolytically cleaved to release its soluble catalytic domain. PLD3 degrades single-stranded DNA and RNA from the 5' end at acidic pH, generating nucleoside 3'-monophosphates. This nuclease activity is critical for degrading mitochondrial DNA and other nucleic acids in lysosomes, thereby preventing inappropriate activation of nucleic acid-sensing innate immune receptors (TLR7, TLR9, cGAS-STING). Recent work (2024) has also established that PLD3 synthesizes (S,S)-bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP), a key lipid constituent of lysosomal intralumenal vesicles. PLD3 is highly expressed in brain and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease risk (though this remains controversial) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 46 (SCA46).

CHSY1 is a type-II Golgi membrane glycosyltransferase that elongates the chondroitin backbone of proteoglycans. Its luminal catalytic region alternately adds glucuronic acid through a beta1,3 linkage and N-acetylgalactosamine through a beta1,4 linkage, using UDP-sugar donors. CHSY1 forms functional polymerase complexes with CHPF or CHPF2, which support complex assembly and activity, while CHSY1 supplies both sugar-transfer reactions. The resulting chains can subsequently be modified by sulfotransferases. CHSY1-dependent chondroitin production contributes to extracellular-matrix organization and skeletal development. A soluble CHSY1 pool has also been detected in primary human fibroblast conditioned medium; its processing and the relationship between chondroitin synthesis and altered NOTCH signaling remain incompletely resolved.

AGTPBP1 encodes cytosolic carboxypeptidase 1 (CCP1), a zinc-dependent protein deglutamylase. It hydrolyzes terminal alpha-linked glutamates from polyglutamylated tubulin side chains and from gene-encoded tubulin C termini, generating delta2- and delta3-tubulin. On the tubulin substrates examined, CCP1 shortens glutamate chains without removing the gamma-linked branching glutamate. This activity controls microtubule modification and supports neuronal integrity. CCP1 is predominantly studied in the cytoplasmic microtubule system; nuclear distribution and a mitochondrial-associated pool have also been reported. Reported non-tubulin substrates include myosin light-chain kinase; KLF4 deglutamylation is described in reprogramming studies. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause childhood-onset neurodegeneration with cerebellar atrophy, affecting the central and peripheral nervous systems.

CPAP is a centrosomal and centriolar protein that binds tubulin and organizes its incorporation during centriole construction. Its PN2-3 region recognizes tubulin, while coiled-coil and C-terminal interactions connect this activity to the centriolar assembly machinery, including STIL and CEP135. Reconstitution and cellular experiments support control of microtubule growth and centriole length, with the direction of the growth effect depending on the construct and assay. CPAP also associates with gamma-tubulin-containing complexes and contributes to centrosomal aster formation. Human CPAP has shown STAT5 coactivator activity in a defined reporter system. Pathogenic variants can disrupt centriole formation and cause primary microcephaly or Seckel syndrome.

RRM2B (p53R2) is the p53/TP53-inducible small subunit of ribonucleotide reductase. Together with the large catalytic subunit RRM1 it forms an active ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) that reduces ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) to 2'-deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) via a diiron-tyrosyl free radical center (EC 1.17.4.1), the rate-limiting de novo step supplying dNTPs for DNA synthesis and repair. Unlike the S-phase/cell-cycle-regulated small subunit RRM2, RRM2B is induced by p53 in response to DNA damage and is present in quiescent and post-mitotic cells, where an RRM1/RRM2B complex provides dNTPs for DNA repair and, critically, for mitochondrial DNA synthesis. Ribonucleotide reduction is a cytosolic process; the deoxyribonucleotides produced diffuse to the nucleus or are imported into mitochondria. Loss-of-function mutations cause mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 8 (MTDPS8, encephalomyopathic form, with or without renal tubulopathy) and autosomal-dominant progressive external ophthalmoplegia with multiple mtDNA deletions.

DTNBP1 encodes dysbindin, a coiled-coil subunit of the BLOC-1 complex. BLOC-1 associates with endosomal membranes and shapes tubular carriers that sort cargo toward lysosome-related organelles and other destinations. Dysbindin contributes to melanosome and platelet dense-granule biogenesis and to neuronal vesicle trafficking. It also regulates synaptic vesicle release and dopamine D2 receptor trafficking. Biallelic loss of DTNBP1 causes Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 7, with defects in pigmentation and platelet dense granules. Alternative protein products differ in sequence and have incompletely resolved functional specialization.

BRWD3 is a nuclear protein containing eight WD repeats and tandem bromodomains that participates in regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription. Mammalian studies connect its WD-repeat region to DDB1 binding and recruitment of transcriptional machinery to active promoters during early adipogenesis. The bromodomains are consistent with chromatin recognition, while the physiological histone-mark preferences and effector repertoire of the human protein remain incompletely resolved. Depletion of human BRWD3 alters cell morphology, and loss-of-function variants cause X-linked intellectual disability frequently accompanied by macrocephaly. The single Drosophila family homolog regulates histone deposition and KDM5 abundance; the conservation of its particular ubiquitin-ligase substrates among human BRWD3, BRWD1, and PHIP remains uncertain.

ANAPC7 (APC7) is a tetratricopeptide-repeat (TPR) subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), the E3 ubiquitin ligase that marks cell-cycle regulators and other substrates for proteasomal destruction. APC7 sits in the TPR lobe, where APC16 recruits it to APC3. It binds the C-termini of the coactivators CDC20 and CDH1. Without APC7 the APC/C keeps its structure but cannot stably recruit and ubiquitinate substrates. APC7 is enriched in the nucleus in brain, where APC/C-CDH1 needs it to degrade Ki-67, and its loss causes an intellectual disability syndrome. Loss of APC7 does not lengthen mitosis in human cells.

ADGRV1 (VLGR1, GPR98 or MASS1) is a large adhesion G protein-coupled receptor whose longest human isoform has approximately 6,300 residues. Its extracellular region contains 35 Calx-beta repeats, EAR/EPTP repeats and a pentraxin-like domain, followed by a GAIN/GPS region and seven transmembrane helices. Isolated Calx-beta repeat fragments bind calcium. The receptor supplies an extracellular structural component of transient ankle links between neighboring stereocilia in developing cochlear hair bundles. Its C-terminal PDZ-binding motif docks onto whirlin and PDZD7 in the USH2 protein network, organizing sensory-cell membrane complexes with usherin. In photoreceptors, ADGRV1 localizes around the connecting cilium and supports photoreceptor maintenance. Reported Gs/Gq/Gi coupling is established mainly for the shorter VLGR1a isoform and C-terminal fragments; coupling of intact VLGR1b in native sensory cells remains unresolved. Intracellular ER-associated pools and roles in calcium homeostasis have also been reported. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause Usher syndrome type 2C, with congenital sensorineural hearing loss and progressive retinal degeneration. Neural expression and reported seizure-associated variants provide additional disease context, with less established human causal mechanisms than for Usher syndrome.

CYP39A1 (24-hydroxycholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase; EC 1.14.14.26) is a liver-specific, microsomal (endoplasmic reticulum membrane) heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. It catalyzes the 7-alpha-hydroxylation of (24S)-hydroxycholesterol, a neural oxysterol produced in the brain (by CYP46A1) and exported to the liver, converting it to (24S)-7-alpha-dihydroxycholesterol as the committing step of the alternative (acidic) bile-acid synthesis pathway. Like other P450s it uses molecular oxygen, inserting one oxygen atom into the substrate and reducing the other to water, with two electrons supplied by NADPH via NADPH--cytochrome P450 reductase; catalysis requires a heme cofactor coordinated by an axial iron ligand. CYP39A1 is one of two mammalian oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylases: it is selective for 24-hydroxycholesterol, whereas the related enzyme CYP7B1 acts on 25- and 27-hydroxycholesterol. Through this reaction CYP39A1 contributes to disposal of excess brain-derived cholesterol as bile acids and to sterol homeostasis. In humans, loss-of-function alleles raise serum (24S)-hydroxycholesterol levels, and functionally deficient CYP39A1 variants are associated with exfoliation syndrome and exfoliation glaucoma.

ALPK3 is a muscle-enriched alpha-kinase-family protein that organizes sarcomeric M-band proteins and supports the development and maintenance of functional cardiomyocytes. Human cell studies place ALPK3 at the M band and, in tagged immature cardiomyocytes, at the nuclear envelope, where its loss disrupts myomesin organization. Interactions with M-band proteins connect ALPK3 to sarcomeric protein homeostasis. Its intrinsic protein kinase activity remains disputed: positive recombinant-domain phosphorylation assays coexist with negative catalytic-domain and cellular mutant studies. Loss-of-function variants cause severe pediatric and adult cardiomyopathy.

IL17RD (SEF, "similar expression to FGF genes"; hSef) is a single-pass type I transmembrane glycoprotein with an extracellular Ig-like/fibronectin III region and a cytoplasmic SEFIR domain related to IL-17 receptors. Its expression is induced by FGF signalling and it acts as a negative-feedback inhibitor of FGF receptor signalling to the Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade. The membrane isoform resides at the plasma membrane and Golgi apparatus, associates (by co-immunoprecipitation) with FGFR1 and FGFR2 independently of ligand, and reduces FGFR1/FRS2 tyrosine phosphorylation and downstream ERK activation; in addition it binds activated MEK, retains the MEK-ERK complex at cytoplasmic/Golgi sites and blocks nuclear translocation of active ERK, selectively suppressing nuclear ERK targets. A cytosolic splice isoform (hSef-b) lacks the signal peptide. Despite its name, IL17RD has no demonstrated IL-17 ligand-binding activity, but it associates with IL17RA and modulates IL-17A signalling outputs (via Act1-TRAF6), and its SEFIR domain engages TIR adaptors to restrain Toll-like receptor signalling. Loss-of-function variants cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia (Kallmann syndrome, HH18), often with hearing loss, consistent with a role in fine-tuning FGF8-FGFR1 signalling during GnRH-neuron and olfactory development.

NDE1 (nuclear distribution protein nudE homolog 1) is a coiled-coil dynein regulator of the NudE family, paralogous to NDEL1. Its N-terminal coiled coil dimerizes (and can form mixed complexes with NDEL1) and binds LIS1, while the C-terminal region binds the cytoplasmic dynein intermediate and light chains; NDE1 thereby recruits LIS1 to autoinhibited dynein and promotes LIS1-mediated assembly of active dynein-dynactin-cargo adaptor complexes, dissociating when dynactin binds the intermediate chain; at high levels it inhibits motility. NDE1 is concentrated at the centrosome/mother centriole throughout the cell cycle, on the mitotic spindle and spindle poles, and at kinetochores, where it is recruited by CENP-F and is needed for kinetochore dynein, chromosome alignment and spindle orientation. In late G2, CENP-F bound to the nucleoporin NUP133 recruits NDE1/NDEL1 and thus dynein and LIS1 to the nuclear envelope, keeping centrosomes tethered to the nucleus and, in radial glial progenitors of the developing neocortex, driving apical interkinetic nuclear migration; NDE1, regulated by CDK1 phosphorylation, is specifically required for this step and for subsequent mitotic entry. NDE1 also restrains primary cilium length at the mother centriole, acts as a RAB9 effector linking late endosomes to dynein for retrograde transport to the trans-Golgi network, and contributes to neuronal migration. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause microlissencephaly (lissencephaly 4) and microhydranencephaly, reflecting failed neural progenitor proliferation and neurogenesis.

NDEL1 (nudE neurodevelopment protein 1-like 1, formerly NUDEL) is a cytoplasmic coiled-coil protein of the NudE family and a paralog of NDE1. Its N-terminal coiled coil forms parallel homodimers (and tetramers) that bind the LIS1 (PAFAH1B1) homodimer, and its C-terminal region binds the N-terminus of the cytoplasmic dynein-1 intermediate chain and DISC1. By tethering LIS1 to dynein NDEL1 regulates the minus-end-directed motor, supporting dynein assembly with dynactin and cargo adaptors and dynein function under load, although in purified systems it can also restrain dynein activation. NDEL1 localizes to the centrosome (mother centriole), where it helps anchor microtubules and target pericentriolar proteins, to kinetochores via CENP-F, to the mitotic spindle, and to axons and growth cones. It is required for dynein-dependent processes including nucleus-centrosome coupling and nuclear translocation (nucleokinesis) in radially migrating cortical neurons, retrograde organelle and lysosome transport, Golgi integrity, and chromosome alignment and segregation. CDK5/p35 (and CDK1 in mitosis) phosphorylate its C-terminal region; phosphorylated NDEL1 recruits the microtubule-severing katanin p60 and switches LIS1/dynein regulation. Additional reported roles include neurofilament assembly, DISC1-dependent neurite outgrowth, adhesion at the leading edge of migrating cells, and enhancement of dynamin 2 GTPase activity.

DCLRE1C encodes Artemis, a metal-dependent DNA nuclease with an N-terminal metallo-β-lactamase/β-CASP catalytic region and a regulatory C-terminal region. Artemis cleaves exposed single-stranded DNA and DNA hairpin or overhang structures during nuclear DNA end processing. In cooperation with DNA-PK, it opens coding-end hairpins generated during V(D)J recombination and processes a subset of complex double-strand breaks for nonhomologous end joining. These activities support antigen-receptor assembly and genome integrity. Purified full-length Artemis also exhibits weaker 5′ exonuclease activity on single-stranded DNA, whose physiological contribution is less well established.

SPRED2 (Sprouty-related, EVH1 domain-containing protein 2) is a non-catalytic intracellular negative regulator of receptor tyrosine kinase-Ras-ERK signalling. It has an N-terminal EVH1 (WH1) domain, a central c-Kit-binding domain (KBD) and a C-terminal cysteine-rich Sprouty-related (SPR) domain that mediates membrane association and SPRED homo-/heterodimerization. SPRED2 acts at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane: its EVH1 domain binds the GAP-related region of neurofibromin (NF1) and relocates this Ras GTPase-activating protein from the cytosol to the membrane, so that Ras-GTP is converted to inactive Ras-GDP. Consistently, SPRED2 lowers growth-factor-induced Ras-GTP, fails to block oncogenic RasV12, and dampens RAF1, MEK and ERK1/2 activation downstream of EGF, FGF and other stimuli. Additional reported mechanisms include an EVH1-dependent interaction with NBR1 that routes activated FGF receptors to lysosomal degradation, and SPR-domain binding to the kinase DYRK1A, inhibiting its phosphorylation of substrates such as Tau and STAT3. SPRED2 is also found in the cytoplasm and on vesicles (Rab11/Rab5a-positive and secretory vesicles). Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal recessive Noonan syndrome-like RASopathy with increased and prolonged MAPK activation in patient cells.

Mechanically activated, Ca2+-permeable cation channel of the TMEM63/OSCA (CSC1) family that also acts as a mechanically activated phospholipid scramblase. TMEM63B is an 11-transmembrane protein that, unusually for this structural superfamily, functions as a monomer with a single highly restricted pore, and it gates according to the force-from-lipids principle: membrane stretch or hypo-osmotic swelling opens a small-conductance, high-threshold cation conductance permeable to Ca2+, Na+, K+ and Mg2+. The same protein translocates phospholipids bidirectionally between bilayer leaflets when membrane curvature and thickness change, dissipating plasma membrane lipid asymmetry and altering the distribution of phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin; cryo-EM structures resolve a membrane-spanning lipid pathway that opens in the same groove as the ion pore, and distinct residues form the bottlenecks for ions and for lipids. This dual channel/scramblase behaviour parallels the TMEM16 family, to which TMEM63 proteins are structurally related. TMEM63B is found in the plasma membrane, lysosomal and early endosomal membranes, and the limiting membrane of alveolar lamellar bodies. Physiologically it is required for stretch-evoked pulmonary surfactant and ATP secretion from alveolar type 2 cells, and in rodents it contributes to osmosensing for thirst, to outer hair cell survival and hearing, and to intestinal stem cell homeostasis. Heterozygous de novo missense and in-frame variants clustered around the hydrophobic gate cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with progressive neurodegeneration, often with macrocytic anaemia and haemolysis; several of these variants act by converting the protein into a constitutive scramblase rather than by increasing ion leak. Whether the wild-type scramblase activity is deployed physiologically in vivo, as opposed to being measurable in reconstituted and over-expressing systems, is not yet settled.

PDSS1 (decaprenyl-diphosphate synthase subunit 1; also DPS1/TPRT) is one of the two subunits of the human all-trans-decaprenyl-diphosphate synthase (trans-prenyltransferase, EC 2.5.1.91). Together with PDSS2, it forms a heterotetramer (2 PDSS1 + 2 PDSS2) that performs the first committed, chain-length-determining step of coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) biosynthesis: sequential head-to-tail condensation of (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate (the primer) with multiple isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) units, adding them with trans stereochemistry to build the all-trans C50 decaprenyl (and C45 nonaprenyl) polyisoprenoid diphosphate side chain. This polyprenyl tail is subsequently attached to the quinone ring (by COQ2) to yield ubiquinone-10 (and ubiquinone-9). The enzyme is a Mg(2+)-dependent member of the trans-isoprenyl diphosphate synthase (FPP/GGPP synthase) family and localizes to the mitochondrion, acting at the matrix/inner-membrane face where CoQ is assembled. Loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency type 2 (COQ10D2), a multisystem mitochondrial disorder.

TREM2 is a type I plasma-membrane immunoglobulin-superfamily receptor expressed mainly by microglia and other myeloid-lineage cells. Together with the TYROBP/DAP12 adaptor, TREM2 converts ligand binding at the cell surface into intracellular signaling through kinases and PLCG2-linked pathways that support cell survival, calcium/ERK signaling, phagocytosis, chemotaxis, microglial activation, and lipid handling. TREM2 recognizes lipid-rich and damage-associated ligands, including aminophospholipids exposed on apoptotic cells, lipoprotein particles and apolipoproteins, and amyloid-beta-lipoprotein complexes. Disease-model annotations involving amyloid plaques, synapse pruning, neuroinflammation, osteoclast biology, and dendritic cell maturation are important contexts but are secondary to the core receptor-ligand signaling and phagocytic myeloid-cell functions.

MAP3K20 (ZAK; also MLK7/MRK) is a stress-activated mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAP3K) of the MLK family. As a serine/threonine protein kinase it phosphorylates the MAP2Ks MKK4/MKK7 (activating JNK) and MKK3/MKK6 (activating p38), driving stress-activated MAPK (JNK and p38) signaling that can promote programmed cell death. The principal isoform ZAKalpha is the proximal sensor of the ribotoxic stress response and directly binds the ribosome by inserting its flexible C-terminus into the intersubunit space (contacting helix 14 of 18S rRNA), acting as a sentinel for colliding ribosomes. Ribosome collisions trigger MAP3K20 autophosphorylation and activation; depending on collision severity it either activates the JNK/p38 cascade to promote cell death or activates EIF2AK4/GCN2 to engage the integrated stress response. ZAKalpha also drives the UV-B-induced NLRP1 inflammasome and pyroptosis by phosphorylating NLRP1. A shorter isoform, ZAKbeta, lacks the ribosome-binding C-terminus and does not sense collisions. MAP3K20 localizes mainly to the cytoplasm/cytosol (with reported nuclear pools and histone H3 Ser-28 kinase activity). It has additional reported roles in DNA-damage checkpoint signaling and cardiac stress responses. Biallelic variants cause split-foot malformation with mesoaxial polydactyly (SFMMP) and centronuclear myopathy 6 (CNM6).

AMOTL1 (angiomotin-like 1) is a peripheral membrane scaffold of the angiomotin family, with a central coiled-coil domain, N-terminal PPxY motifs and a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif. It localizes to tight junctions, anchored through multi-PDZ scaffolds, and binds the WW domains of the Hippo-pathway co-activator YAP1 through its PPxY motifs, regulating YAP1 movement between cytoplasm and nucleus. Its abundance is controlled by NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligases and by KIBRA and Merlin. Like other angiomotins it has been implicated in endothelial migration and angiogenesis.

NT5C1A encodes cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 1A (cN-IA; also cN-I / cN1A), a Mg2+-dependent cytosolic enzyme of the 5'-nucleotidase type 3 (haloacid dehalogenase-like phosphatase) family. It catalyzes hydrolysis of ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates to the corresponding nucleoside plus inorganic phosphate. It is AMP-preferring (AMP is the major substrate) but also hydrolyzes dCMP and IMP, and its activity is allosterically stimulated by ADP. By dephosphorylating AMP to adenosine, cN-IA is a principal intracellular source of adenosine during nucleotide (ATP) breakdown, a role that is physiologically prominent in skeletal muscle and in heart, where it can account for adenosine formation during ischemia. The protein is highly expressed in skeletal muscle and at intermediate levels in heart, brain, kidney and pancreas. cN-IA is also a well-known autoantigen: circulating anti-cN1A (anti-NT5C1A) autoantibodies are a serological marker of sporadic inclusion body myositis and related inflammatory myopathies.

NT5C3A (cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 3A; pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase 1, P5'N-1/PN-I; UMP-CMP 5'-nucleotidase; also historically "p36") is a cytosolic, Mg2+-dependent hydrolase of the haloacid dehalogenase (HAD) superfamily that belongs to the pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase family. It dephosphorylates pyrimidine (deoxy)ribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates to the corresponding nucleoside plus inorganic phosphate (EC 3.1.3.5), with a strong preference for pyrimidine over purine substrates; UMP and CMP are the physiological substrates and CMP is the preferred one in vitro. The enzyme uses a two-aspartate HAD catalytic mechanism (Asp88 nucleophile, Asp90 proton donor) with an active-site Mg2+ ion, and also exhibits an associated phosphotransferase activity that exchanges phosphate between pyrimidine monophosphates and pyrimidine nucleosides. NT5C3A is very highly expressed in reticulocytes and mature erythrocytes, where it degrades the pyrimidine ribonucleotides released by RNA breakdown during erythroid maturation so that the resulting nucleosides can be cleared from the cell; this makes it central to erythroid pyrimidine nucleotide catabolism. Loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal recessive hereditary non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia (pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency) featuring marked basophilic stippling and intra-erythrocyte accumulation of pyrimidine nucleotides, and the enzyme is also implicated in the anemia of lead poisoning. An alternatively spliced, N-terminally distinct isoform (isoform 2/p36) is interferon-alpha-inducible and localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum.

AFF4 is the central scaffold of the super elongation complex (SEC), the metazoan assembly that releases promoter-proximally paused RNA polymerase II into productive elongation. Most of the 1163-residue protein is intrinsically disordered and carries short, separately mapped interaction motifs along its length: an N-terminal segment binds the cyclin T1 subunit of P-TEFb without contacting the CDK9 kinase, a central 50-residue "ELLBow" binds the C-terminal domain of ELL2, and further motifs recruit the ENL/AF9 proteins. Because these sites are non-overlapping, AFF4 can hold P-TEFb and an ELL-family elongation factor on the same polymerase, and it does so without any additional partner; this bridging is the molecular activity of the protein itself, whereas the resulting stimulation of elongation is an activity of the assembled complex. Its one folded module, the C-terminal homology domain, mediates AFF4 homodimerisation and AFF1-AFF4 heterodimerisation and carries a surface loop phosphorylated by CDK9. AFF4 acts in the nucleus on transcriptionally active euchromatin, and its loss slows elongation, deepens promoter-proximal pausing and lowers Ser2-phosphorylated polymerase II genome-wide. It is required for Sertoli-cell-dependent spermiogenesis, and it promotes both adipogenic and osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells - the latter in the opposite direction to its paralogue AFF1. It is the shared partner of MLL/KMT2A fusion oncoproteins, and is hijacked by the HIV-1 Tat protein, which folds onto the same cyclin T1 surface to build a Tat-AFF4-P-TEFb complex that transactivates the viral promoter. Missense substitutions in its ALF homology domain that make the protein resistant to SIAH1-directed proteasomal degradation cause CHOPS syndrome, a gain-of-function developmental disorder.

NMNAT1 is the nuclear isoform of nicotinamide/nicotinic acid mononucleotide adenylyltransferase, one of three human NMNAT isoenzymes (NMNAT1 nuclear, NMNAT2 Golgi, NMNAT3 mitochondrial). It catalyses the central, committed adenylyl-transfer step shared by all routes of NAD+ biosynthesis: transfer of an adenylyl group from ATP to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) to form NAD+ with release of pyrophosphate (EC 2.7.7.1), and, with comparable efficiency, to the deamidated substrate nicotinate mononucleotide (NaMN) to form nicotinate adenine dinucleotide (deamido-NAD+/NaAD; EC 2.7.7.18). NMNAT1 therefore sits at the convergence of the de novo (kynurenine), salvage and Preiss-Handler pathways. The enzyme requires a divalent metal cofactor (Zn2+ gives higher activity than Mg2+), assembles into a homohexamer, and is imported into the nucleus via a nuclear localization signal. In the nucleus it supplies NAD+ locally to NAD+-consuming enzymes such as PARP1 and the sirtuin SIRT1, and participates in nuclear ATP generation from poly-ADP-ribose that supports chromatin remodeling. In humans, loss-of-function variants cause Leber congenital amaurosis 9 and the multisystem SHILCA syndrome.

PGAP2 (Post-GPI Attachment to Proteins Factor 2; also FRAG1) is a multi-pass Golgi-membrane protein that carries out the second step of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) fatty-acid remodeling. GPI anchors are made in the endoplasmic reticulum and attached to nascent proteins, then remodeled during transport through the Golgi. In the Golgi, after PGAP3 removes the sn-2 unsaturated fatty acid, PGAP2 is required to reacylate the resulting lyso-GPI intermediate with a saturated (stearic) fatty acid at the sn-2 position; it is annotated as an acyltransferase (EC 2.3.-.-) by similarity, though whether it is the catalytic acyltransferase or an accessory factor required for reacylation is not firmly established. This fatty-acid remodeling generates the mature, detergent-resistant-membrane (lipid-raft)-associating GPI anchor and is required for stable cell-surface expression of GPI-anchored proteins such as DAF (CD55) and CD59. Biallelic hypomorphic PGAP2 variants cause hyperphosphatasia with impaired intellectual development syndrome 3 (HPMRS3), characterized by intellectual disability, hypotonia, and elevated serum alkaline phosphatase.

Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase of the AlkB family, encoded by a nuclear gene and imported into the mitochondrial matrix, with a smaller nuclear and cytoplasmic pool. Its best-established activity is on transfer RNA: it performs the second, oxidative step of wobble-base maturation in mitochondrial tRNA-Met, converting NSUN3-generated 5-methylcytidine at position 34 first to 5-hydroxymethylcytidine and then to 5-formylcytidine (f5C34). That modification allows the single mitochondrial tRNA-Met to decode AUA and AUU as well as AUG under the non-universal mitochondrial genetic code, so loss of ALKBH1 impairs mitochondrial translation and respiratory complex activity. ALKBH1 makes analogous 2'-O-methylated hydroxymethyl- and formyl-cytidines at position 34 of cytoplasmic tRNA-Leu, and it demethylates N1-methyladenosine in cytoplasmic and mitochondrial tRNAs, which modulates tRNA usage and the rate of translation initiation. Additional activities demonstrated in vitro include oxidative demethylation of 3-methylcytosine in single-stranded DNA and in RNA, and an AP (abasic site) lyase activity that arises from an active site distinct from the dioxygenase centre. A widely cited role as the eraser of N6-methyladenine (6mA) in genomic DNA is disputed: ALKBH1 demethylates 6mA efficiently in single-stranded or bubbled DNA but poorly in duplex DNA, and several independent methodological audits attribute most reported mammalian genomic 6mA to bacterial and RNA contamination, antibody cross-reactivity and misincorporation of N6-methyladenosine from the nucleotide salvage pool, while comparative genomics places robust eukaryotic 6mA only in lineages retaining the AMT1 adenine methyltransferase, which animals have lost. In mouse, loss of Alkbh1 causes embryonic lethality with defects in placental trophoblast and neural differentiation.

CEP83 (centrosomal protein of 83 kDa, also CCDC41) is a coiled-coil protein of the distal appendages (ciliary transition fibers) of the mother centriole. It sits at the root of the appendage blades and is the most upstream component of the appendage assembly hierarchy: CEP83 recruits SCLT1 and CEP89, and through SCLT1 the more distal components FBF1 and CEP164. Loss of CEP83 abolishes distal appendages and blocks docking of the mother centriole to ciliary vesicles and the plasma membrane, so that TTBK2 is not recruited, the CP110 cap is not removed and primary cilia fail to form. CEP83 is itself phosphorylated by TTBK2 at the appendage root, which supports vesicle docking and CP110 removal. A minor pool associates with IFT20 at the Golgi. In mouse neural progenitors CEP83-dependent appendages anchor the centrosome to the apical membrane. Biallelic CEP83 variants cause infantile nephronophthisis (NPHP18), often with intellectual disability.

IRAK4 (interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4) is a cytosolic serine/threonine protein kinase of the Pelle/IRAK family and the closest human homolog of Drosophila Pelle. It has an N-terminal death domain and a C-terminal kinase domain. Upon activation of Toll-like receptors (except TLR3) and IL-1 family receptors, MyD88 death domains recruit IRAK4, which in turn recruits IRAK2 or IRAK1 to form the helical Myddosome. Clustered IRAK4 trans-autophosphorylates and phosphorylates IRAK1, IRAK2 and Pellino E3 ligases, leading to TRAF6 activation and downstream NF-kappaB, MAPK and IRF signalling and inflammatory cytokine and type I interferon production. IRAK4 also acts as a kinase-independent scaffold, for example integrating MYD88 and TRIF signals downstream of TLR4. Inherited IRAK-4 deficiency abolishes most TLR and IL-1R responses and causes susceptibility to invasive pyogenic bacterial infections in childhood.

B3GALT6 is a Golgi type II membrane glycosyltransferase, also called galactosyltransferase II. It transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to galactose-beta-1,4-xylose attached to a proteoglycan core protein, forming the second galactose and third sugar of the common glycosaminoglycan linker. This reaction supports efficient synthesis of heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate proteoglycans. Its catalytic domain faces the Golgi lumen, with enrichment in medial Golgi cisternae. Biallelic loss-of-function variants disrupt proteoglycan glycanation and cause skeletal and connective-tissue disorders, including spondylodysplastic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity.

N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS; EC 2.3.1.1) is a nuclear-encoded, mitochondrial-matrix enzyme that catalyzes the formation of N-acetyl-L-glutamate (NAG) from L-glutamate and acetyl-CoA. In mammals, NAG is the obligate allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle; NAGS therefore functions as the regulatory gate of hepatic ureagenesis and ammonia detoxification. Although NAG is not consumed stoichiometrically in the urea cycle, the cycle cannot proceed without it. The enzyme is a homotetramer whose subunits comprise an N-terminal amino-acid-kinase (AAK) domain that binds the allosteric activator L-arginine (which enhances mammalian NAGS activity) and a C-terminal GCN5-related N-acetyltransferase (NAT) domain that is catalytically competent on its own. NAGS is expressed mainly in liver, kidney and small intestine and is imported into the mitochondrion via a cleaved N-terminal transit peptide. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency, an autosomal recessive urea cycle disorder presenting with hyperammonemia (without orotic aciduria) that, uniquely among urea cycle disorders, is specifically treatable with the NAG analogue carglumic acid.

COA6 is a small CHCH-fold protein in the mitochondrial intermembrane space that supports maturation of the copper-containing MT-CO2 subunit and assembly of cytochrome c oxidase. Its disulfide-reductase activity maintains copper-site assembly proteins, including SCO1 and SCO2, in suitable redox states. COA6 associates with these proteins, nascent MT-CO2 and the COX20 chaperone during assembly. Copper-binding capacity has been demonstrated, while its physiological contribution to copper carriage remains unresolved. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 13 (MC4DN13), often with severe infantile cardiomyopathy.

ARID2, also called BAF200, is a nuclear DNA-binding subunit that specifies the PBAF branch of mammalian SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complexes. It supports PBAF assembly and promoter-selective transcriptional regulation while contributing to remodeling powered by the BRG1 ATPase. Its ARID region binds DNA without an established sequence preference. ARID2 also associates with RAD51 and promotes its recruitment during homologous-recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks. ARID2-containing assemblies with and without BRG1 have been recovered, indicating that its repair interactions cannot be reduced to a single fixed complex composition.

ARID1B (BAF250B/p250R) is a nuclear DNA-binding and assembly subunit of canonical mammalian SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complexes. Its ARID region binds DNA without an established sequence preference, and other regions associate with the SMARCA2 or SMARCA4 ATPase and additional complex subunits. ARID1B and ARID1A are mutually exclusive alternatives in these assemblies, coupling DNA engagement and regulatory recruitment to ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling. Human ARID1B also supports steroid-receptor transcriptional coactivation in tested cellular contexts. ARID1B-dependent gene regulation is important in development, and pathogenic loss of function causes Coffin–Siris syndrome.

ARX is a paired homeobox transcription factor that binds cis-regulatory DNA and activates or represses gene expression according to target and cellular context. It acts in the nucleus and participates in neuronal development, pancreatic alpha-cell specification and selected intestinal endocrine lineages. ARX can cooperate with the histone demethylase PHF8 in activating KDM5C. Pathogenic ARX variants cause a spectrum of X-linked neurodevelopmental disorders, including developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, Partington syndrome and lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia.

DCDC2 is a microtubule-associated protein whose long isoform contains tandem doublecortin domains. It binds microtubules, associates with the kinesin-2 machinery and localizes along ciliary axonemes. DCDC2 supports epithelial cilium assembly and controls ciliary growth in sensory-cell contexts. It restrains canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and associates with Dishevelled proteins, although the molecular link between those interactions and Wnt inhibition remains unresolved. Biallelic variants are associated with renal-hepatic ciliopathy and neonatal sclerosing cholangitis. The shorter annotated product lacks both doublecortin domains, and its equivalent ciliary or Wnt-regulatory activity has not been established.

MOCOS is molybdenum cofactor sulfurase (EC 2.8.1.9; also called molybdenum cofactor sulfurtransferase, MoCo sulfurase), a cytosolic, pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme of the class-V (NifS-like) cysteine-desulfurase family. It converts the molybdenum cofactor (MoCo) from its dioxo form into the terminal-sulfido (thio) form. The enzyme is a homodimer of two-domain subunits; the N-terminal NifS-like PLP domain abstracts sulfur from L-cysteine via L-cysteine desulfurase activity (yielding L-alanine and an enzyme-bound persulfide), and the C-terminal MOSC/Moco-binding domain receives the mobilized sulfur and transfers it to the bound Mo-molybdopterin. This sulfurated MoCo is specifically required to activate the molybdo-flavoenzymes xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase (XDH/XO) and aldehyde oxidase (AOX1); the third human molybdoenzyme, sulfite oxidase, uses the non-sulfurated cofactor and does not depend on MOCOS. Loss-of-function variants in MOCOS cause classical xanthinuria type II, an autosomal-recessive disorder with combined XDH and aldehyde oxidase deficiency, marked by xanthine accumulation and urolithiasis, very low uric acid, and inability to convert allopurinol to oxypurinol.

ELP2 is a WD-repeat subunit of the six-subunit Elongator complex that supports assembly of its ELP1–ELP2–ELP3 subcomplex. In the cytosol, ELP2 contributes to Elongator-mediated modification of uridine at the wobble position of tRNAs. ELP3 supplies the catalytic activity that forms carboxymethyluridine, an intermediate in further wobble-uridine modifications important for codon decoding. ELP2 is predominantly cytosolic, with an additional nuclear pool.

Vezatin is a multi-pass integral membrane protein of adherens junctions that couples cadherin-catenin adhesion complexes to the actomyosin cytoskeleton. It has two closely spaced transmembrane helices with cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal regions; the cytoplasmic C-terminal region binds the C-terminal FERM domain of the unconventional motor myosin VIIA (MYO7A), and vezatin also binds the FERM domain of radixin in its open, actin-binding conformation. Vezatin is recruited to cell-cell contacts through the cytoplasmic tail of E-cadherin and the C-terminal region of alpha-catenin, arriving after E-cadherin during junction assembly, so it acts as a maturation and mechanical-stability factor rather than an initiator of adhesion. It is broadly expressed and is found at adherens junctions of most epithelia; junctional vezatin recruits myosin VIIA and thereby generates tension between the junctional membrane and cortical actin, strengthening cell-cell adhesion. In cochlear and vestibular hair cells vezatin occupies two membrane sites, the adherens junctions between hair cells and their supporting cells, and the base of developing stereocilia, where it is a component of the transient ankle-link complex together with ADGRV1/VLGR1, usherin (USH2A) and whirlin, binding the usherin cytoplasmic region directly. Additional vertebrate sites and roles include the acrosome of differentiating spermatids and sperm, the postsynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction where it associates with acetylcholine receptors and promotes postsynaptic maturation and receptor stability, and dendritic spines, where it is needed for spine morphogenesis and functional synapse maturation. Loss of vezatin in mouse is lethal around implantation and causes delocalization of E-cadherin and beta-catenin, while hair-cell-specific loss causes extreme susceptibility to acoustic trauma and progressive hair cell death, indicating that the protein is required for junction integrity under mechanical load. Vezatin proteins are also conserved regulators of dynein-dependent, cargo-selective retrograde transport of late and signalling endosomes in invertebrate and fish axons, and the fungal homolog VezA promotes dynactin assembly. Vezatin has no known catalytic activity; its molecular role is that of a transmembrane adaptor and stabilizer of specialized membrane-cytoskeleton assemblies.

HHAT (Hedgehog acyltransferase) is a polytopic endoplasmic-reticulum membrane enzyme of the membrane-bound O-acyltransferase (MBOAT) superfamily, and the enzyme that lipidates the Hedgehog morphogens. It transfers palmitate from palmitoyl-CoA onto the alpha-amino group of the N-terminal cysteine exposed by autoprocessing of the Sonic, Desert and Indian Hedgehog precursors, forming an amide rather than a thioester bond, and it recognises the conserved Hedgehog N-terminal CGPGR motif with such selectivity that Hedgehog proteins are thought to be its only substrates. The protein comprises ten transmembrane helices and two reentrant loops, with the catalytic aspartate and histidine on opposite faces of the bilayer and a bound heme b that is required for activity; the active site is embedded in the membrane and receives palmitoyl-CoA from the cytosolic leaflet through an internal archway while the Hedgehog peptide enters from the ER lumen, so the enzyme brings together two chemically dissimilar substrates from opposite sides of the membrane. HHAT has also been reported to promote net movement of palmitoyl-CoA to the luminal side of the ER membrane, an activity separable from catalysis in reconstituted liposomes. The palmitate HHAT installs is not decoration: together with the C-terminal cholesterol added by Hedgehog autoprocessing it makes the dually lipidated ligand, and the palmitoyl chain is read directly by the receptor Patched, so palmitoylation is required for both short- and long-range Hedgehog signalling. HHAT is therefore a positive regulator of the pathway that acts entirely upstream of it, on the ligand rather than within the signalling cascade. Loss-of-function variants cause Nivelon-Nivelon-Mabille syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder with progressive microcephaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, skeletal dysplasia and, in some individuals, 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis; the enzyme is also a drug target in Hedgehog-dependent cancers, and small molecules such as IMP-1575 inhibit it by occluding the substrate site. Its closest paralog, HHATL, retains the fold but has lost acyltransferase activity, and its Drosophila counterpart is Rasp.

ALG1 is an endoplasmic reticulum beta-1,4-mannosyltransferase that catalyzes the first mannose addition during dolichol-linked oligosaccharide assembly. It uses GDP-mannose to convert GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol to Man1GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol on the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane, producing the substrate for ALG2. This catalytic step builds the glycan precursor subsequently transferred to proteins during N-linked glycosylation. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause ALG1-CDG, an autosomal recessive disorder with variable multisystem and neurodevelopmental manifestations, including severe early-lethal presentations.

ATP6AP2 is a single-pass membrane protein that acts as a V-ATPase accessory component and as the renin/prorenin receptor. Its endomembrane-associated forms support V-ATPase assembly and endolysosomal acidification, which sustain lysosomal degradation and cellular homeostasis. At the cell surface, ATP6AP2 binds renin and prorenin; receptor association enhances renin catalytic efficiency and can activate ERK signaling independently of angiotensin II. ATP6AP2 also connects V-ATPase-dependent acidification to Wnt signaling. Proteolytic processing produces luminal or extracellular and membrane-associated fragments with distinct localization and interaction properties.

ASXL1 is a nuclear chromatin regulator containing HARE-HTH, DEUBAD and PHD regions. As a noncatalytic component of the BAP1-containing PR-DUB complex, it activates BAP1 and helps position nucleosomal DNA and monoubiquitinated histone H2A for deubiquitination. ASXL1 also participates in transcriptional coactivation and context-dependent nuclear-receptor regulation. These chromatin functions influence developmental gene expression and cellular identity. Pathogenic variants cause Bohring-Opitz syndrome, and somatic alterations occur in myeloid neoplasia.

HSD3B7 (3 beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 7; 3-beta-hydroxy-Delta(5)-C27-steroid oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.1.181) catalyzes the second committed step of bile-acid biosynthesis. Acting on the 7-alpha-hydroxylated sterols generated by CYP7A1/CYP7B1, it oxidizes the 3-beta-hydroxyl group and isomerizes the Delta5 double bond, converting 7-alpha-hydroxycholesterol (and related 7-alpha-hydroxy-oxysterols such as 7-alpha,25-, 7-alpha,26- and 7-alpha,24-triols) to the corresponding 3-oxo-Delta4 intermediates, e.g. 7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one. A single such enzyme feeds all known pathways of bile-acid synthesis. It is specific for C27 bile-acid-precursor sterols and does not metabolize the C19/C21 steroids handled by the steroidogenic paralogs HSD3B1/HSD3B2 (with which it shares only ~34% identity). HSD3B7 is a multi-pass endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane (microsomal) enzyme expressed predominantly in liver. Loss-of-function mutations cause congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 1 (CBAS1), presenting as neonatal cholestasis, progressive liver disease and fat-soluble-vitamin malabsorption. By acting on the oxysterol 7-alpha,25-dihydroxycholesterol, the enzyme also contributes to turnover of the EBI2/GPR183 ligand that positions lymphocytes in lymphoid tissue.

TICAM1 (TRIF, TIR domain-containing adapter molecule 1) is a cytoplasmic signaling adaptor of the MyD88-independent branch of Toll-like receptor signaling. Its C-terminal TIR domain engages the TIR domain of endosomal TLR3 directly after double-stranded RNA recognition, and of TLR4 through the sorting adaptor TICAM2 (TRAM) after LPS-induced receptor internalization into endosomes. From this position TICAM1 recruits distinct effectors through separate motifs: TRAF6 through N-terminal TRAF6-binding motifs (NF-kappaB and MAPK activation via TAK1), TRAF3 and the kinase TBK1/IKBKE (via its N-terminal region), and RIPK1 and RIPK3 through a C-terminal RHIM region (NF-kappaB activation, caspase-8-dependent apoptosis or necroptosis). TBK1 phosphorylates Ser210 in the TICAM1 pLxIS motif, which then binds IRF3 and positions it for TBK1-mediated activation, driving IFN-beta and interferon-stimulated gene expression.
