CEP120 is enriched on daughter centrioles and helps organize the recruitment of distal centriolar components. In quiescent mouse fibroblasts, CEP120 also restrains premature pericentriolar-material accumulation, distinct from centriole construction in cycling cells. Biallelic variants cause ciliopathies including Joubert syndrome and short-rib thoracic dysplasia.

CFAP47 (cilia- and flagella-associated protein 47) is a very large X-linked axonemal protein, built from a chain of ASH/Ig-like domains with a calponin-homology domain, that is highly expressed in testis and sperm. In the sperm flagellum it is the core structural component of the bridge of the axonemal central apparatus: its N-terminal domains bind the C1 microtubule, a central ring formed with the calponin-homology domain binds HYDIN, and its C-terminal region anchors to the C2 microtubule, so that CFAP47 tethers the two central microtubules together. Loss of CFAP47 leaves a hollow bridge in the central apparatus and disrupts sperm flagellum formation and motility. Hemizygous deleterious variants or deletion of CFAP47 cause X-linked spermatogenic failure 3, with asthenoteratozoospermia and multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagellum, sometimes with head, mitochondrial sheath and annulus defects; intracytoplasmic sperm injection is reported to give a good prognosis. CFAP47 variants have also been reported in a few men with primary ciliary dyskinesia features and with cystic kidney disease, where the protein was detected in renal primary cilia.

ANKS6 is an ankyrin-repeat and sterile alpha motif protein that organizes protein assemblies in the proximal ciliary inversin compartment and cytoplasm. It links NEK8, INVS and NPHP3 in a nephronophthisis-associated complex and promotes NEK8 kinase activation. Its SAM domain binds ANKS3 and helps remodel ANKS3-containing BICC1 assemblies. ANKS6 also binds RNA, while its loss can impair YAP abundance and transcriptional output in biliary cells. Biallelic variants cause nephronophthisis with variable laterality, cardiac and hepatobiliary abnormalities.

COX18 (cytochrome c oxidase assembly protein 18, mitochondrial; also known as OXA1L2) is a mitochondrial inner-membrane protein insertase of the OXA1/ALB3/YidC family. It mediates translocation of the C-terminal tail (containing the apo-CuA site) of the newly synthesised, mitochondrially encoded cytochrome c oxidase core subunit MT-CO2 (COX2) across the mitochondrial inner membrane. COX18 acts within the MT-CO2 maturation module, working together with COX20 (which first stabilises nascent MT-CO2) and preceding the SCO1/SCO2/COA6 copper-metallation step, and is required for assembly and stability of respiratory chain complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). It is a multi-pass inner-membrane protein with three transmembrane helices. Loss of function reduces complex IV assembly and activity and causes autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, with disease presentations ranging from neonatal encephalo-cardio-myopathy to an axonal peripheral neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2MM).

AMER1, also known as WTX, is a phosphoinositide-binding scaffold that connects APC and other canonical Wnt signaling proteins to the cytoplasmic surface of the plasma membrane. Its membrane-targeting region and protein interaction regions organize distinct complexes: it can stabilize Axin and promote beta-catenin destruction, while also facilitating Axin-associated kinase recruitment and LRP6 receptor phosphorylation during Wnt stimulation. AMER1 can also stabilize NRF2 by competing for its KEAP1 interaction, and a nuclear pool associates with WT1 and nuclear bodies. Its membrane-associated and nuclear activities vary with cellular context and alternative splicing.

FOXRED1 (FAD-dependent oxidoreductase domain-containing protein 1) is a nuclear-encoded flavoprotein of the mitochondrial inner membrane that functions as a complex I-specific assembly factor (molecular chaperone) required for biogenesis of the respiratory chain NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I). It belongs to the FAD-dependent oxidoreductase (DAO/FAD-NAD(P)-binding) structural family, carries an FAD cofactor, and is annotated as an oxidoreductase (EC 1.-.-.-), but no in-vivo catalytic substrate or reaction has been defined and it is not a structural subunit of the mature 44-subunit holoenzyme. FOXRED1 acts at the mid-late stages of complex I assembly, transiently associating with assembly intermediates and complex I subunits; in its absence, a late (~815 kDa) intermediate fails to mature and instead degrades to a smaller (~475 kDa) subcomplex, and cells accumulate only residual complex I. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 19 (MC1DN19), an autosomal-recessive infantile-onset encephalomyopathy.

COX20 (also known as FAM36A) is a small (118 aa) multi-pass protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane that acts as a non-catalytic assembly chaperone for cytochrome c oxidase (respiratory chain complex IV, CIV), specific to the core catalytic subunit MT-CO2 (COX2). Following its mitochondrial synthesis, MT-CO2 engages COX20, which binds and stabilises the newly synthesised protein during insertion of its N-proximal transmembrane domain and chaperones it through membrane insertion and maturation of its binuclear copper CuA centre by the metallochaperones SCO1 and SCO2 (together with COA6, COX18 and TMEM177), delivering mature MT-CO2 into the assembling CIV holoenzyme. COX20 has no known catalytic activity; its role is to hold and present MT-CO2 to the copper metallation machinery. Loss of COX20 causes a severe, isolated CIV deficiency in which cells accumulate CIV subassemblies containing COX1/COX4 but lacking COX2. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 11 (MC4DN11), an autosomal recessive disorder with childhood/adolescent onset presenting with cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, choreoathetotic movements, dysarthria and muscle hypotonia.

DNAJC21 is a J-domain protein involved in large (60S) ribosomal subunit biogenesis through nucleolar RNA association and cytoplasmic cooperation with the Hsp70 chaperone HSPA8 and assembly factors PA2G4 and ZNF622. It associates with precursor 45S rRNA and supports PA2G4 recycling during subunit maturation. Its N-terminal J domain contains the conserved HPD motif, and the protein contains two C2H2 zinc fingers. DNAJC21 occupies nucleolar and cytosolic pools and redistributes toward the nucleus when ribosomal RNA synthesis is inhibited. Alternative transcripts encode three predicted protein isoforms that differ between the zinc fingers. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause a cancer-prone bone marrow failure syndrome associated with defective ribosome biogenesis.

CARMIL2 is a multidomain cytoskeletal regulator and signaling adaptor. It binds the actin-capping-protein heterodimer and modulates barbed-end capping, helping organize peripheral actin networks. Distinct regions support peripheral membrane association and localization along vimentin intermediate filaments. In human cultured cells, these activities contribute to polarized protrusions, collective migration and invadopodia. Signaling-competent splice forms in lymphocytes also organize CD28-dependent signaling to CARD11 and NF-kappaB through a function separable from capping-protein binding. The predominant leukocyte splice form differs from the longest reported product. Biallelic loss of CARMIL2 causes combined immunodeficiency with defects extending beyond CD28 responses.

CFAP418 (C8orf37) is a small, conserved protein associated with inherited retinal degeneration and Bardet–Biedl syndrome. It is distributed in the photoreceptor cell body, including the inner segment, and has also been detected at ciliary bases. Mouse CFAP418 binds phosphatidic acid and cardiolipin in vitro; loss of the protein disrupts retinal lipid composition, membrane-protein abundance, outer-segment disc organization and mitochondrial morphology. Human CFAP418 interacts with FAM161A, while its precise membrane-associated mechanism and the relationship between lipid binding and photoreceptor maintenance remain unresolved.

IBA57 (Iron-sulfur cluster assembly factor IBA57, mitochondrial) is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein that functions as a late-acting assembly factor in the mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) biogenesis pathway. IBA57 operates in cooperation with ISCA1 and ISCA2 to convert 2Fe-2S clusters into 4Fe-4S clusters. Specifically, IBA57 forms a heterodimeric complex with ISCA2 that contains a bridging 2Fe-2S cluster, which serves as an intermediate in the reductive coupling mechanism that generates 4Fe-4S clusters. The protein is essential for maturation of mitochondrial 4Fe-4S-containing enzymes including respiratory complexes I and II, aconitase, and lipoic acid synthase (LIAS). Pathogenic variants in IBA57 cause multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome 3 (MMDS3) and spastic paraplegia 74 (SPG74), characterized by defects in respiratory chain complexes and impaired lipoylation of pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. The deep research review (IBA57-deep-research-falcon.md) confirms IBA57 functions downstream with ISCA1-ISCA2 during the late step that converts two GLRX5-derived 2Fe-2S clusters into a 4Fe-4S cluster.

Folliculin (FLCN) is a 579-residue cytosolic protein with longin and DENN domains. With FNIP1 or FNIP2 it forms a heterodimer that is the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for the lysosomal Rag GTPases RagC and RagD. When amino acids are scarce, FLCN-FNIP is recruited to the lysosome surface, where it binds GDP-bound RagA/B with Ragulator in the lysosomal folliculin complex (LFC), a state in which its GAP activity is held off. When amino acids return, the LFC disassembles and FLCN stimulates GTP hydrolysis by RagC/D through its catalytic Arg164. GDP-bound RagC/D lets mTORC1 bind and phosphorylate the MiT/TFE transcription factors TFEB and TFE3, which keeps them in the cytoplasm. FLCN is therefore required for this substrate-specific branch of mTORC1 signalling, but not for phosphorylation of S6K1 or 4E-BP1. Loss of FLCN leaves TFEB/TFE3 constitutively nuclear, which drives lysosomal and mitochondrial biogenesis, adipose browning and renal hyperproliferation. FLCN's activity is restrained by sequestration on lipidated GABARAP and by AMPK phosphorylation of FNIP1. Other reported activities are less established: FLCN promotes starvation-induced perinuclear lysosome clustering by loading active Rab34 onto RILP, and it binds and inhibits lactate dehydrogenase A. It is also found at cilia, centrosomes and the mitotic spindle. FLCN is a tumour suppressor, and germline loss-of-function variants cause Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (fibrofolliculomas, lung cysts, pneumothorax and renal tumours).

ANO5 (TMEM16E) is a multipass membrane protein of the anoctamin family with calcium-dependent phospholipid scramblase activity. It resides mainly in the endoplasmic reticulum and reaches the plasma membrane in particular expression and injury contexts. Human ANO5 supports transbilayer lipid redistribution and associated nonselective ion conductance in cell assays. In muscle, ANO5 supports membrane repair and coordinated annexin trafficking after injury; a scrambling-defective chimera can rescue repair, indicating separable functions. Endothelial ANO5 contributes to surface phosphatidylserine exposure. Recessive ANO5 variants cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R12 or Miyoshi muscular dystrophy 3, whereas specific dominant variants cause gnathodiaphyseal dysplasia.

Stimulator of interferon genes protein (STING1/TMEM173) is a polytopic membrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum and the central signalling adaptor of the cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway. Four transmembrane helices anchor it in the ER bilayer and support a cytosolic ligand-binding and signalling domain that forms an obligate dimer. STING1 is the receptor for 2'3'-cyclic GMP-AMP, the second messenger made by cGAS on detection of cytosolic DNA, and it also binds bacterial cyclic dinucleotides such as cyclic di-GMP directly, making it a sensor as well as an adaptor. Ligand binding closes the ligand-binding domain and rotates it relative to the transmembrane domain, driving side-by-side packing of dimers into tetramers and higher-order oligomers. Oligomerisation licenses COPII-dependent exit from the ER to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and the Golgi, where TBK1 is recruited and phosphorylates the STING1 C-terminal tail; phosphorylated STING1 then presents a docking surface for IRF3, which TBK1 phosphorylates to induce type I interferons. From post-Golgi endolysosomal compartments STING1 additionally activates NF-kappaB, a branch that can operate independently of interferon signalling, before being degraded in lysosomes. Oligomerisation and ER exit require membrane lipids as well as cGAMP: phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate, made by PIKFYVE bound constitutively to STING1, together with cholesterol occupies a groove at the interface between adjacent dimers and acts as a molecular glue; phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate binds the same site in vitro. Residue R71, which contacts the lipid 5-phosphate, is part of the common hypofunctional HAQ allele of human STING1. Independently of its adaptor role, the STING1 transmembrane domain conducts protons and deacidifies the Golgi, and this channel activity drives a separable output branch comprising non-canonical LC3B and GABARAP lipidation, inflammasome activation, and TFEB/TFE3-dependent lysosome biogenesis. Autophagy induction is independent of TBK1 and of interferon induction and is the evolutionarily older function of the pathway. Gain-of-function alleles cause the autoinflammatory disease SAVI, and chronic activation of the pathway contributes to senescence, age-related inflammation and neurodegeneration.

WDPCP (fritz homolog, BBS15) is a non-enzymatic WD40 beta-propeller plus alpha-solenoid scaffold protein that forms the CPLANE (ciliogenesis and planar polarity effector) complex with INTU and FUZ. At the ciliary base and transition zone, CPLANE recruits the peripheral IFT-A subunits to basal bodies, and WDPCP is required for transition-zone localization of SEPT2, NPHP1 and MKS1, so its loss impairs cilium assembly and cilium-dependent Hedgehog signaling. A second pool at the cell cortex, on actin stress fibers and at focal adhesions recruits SEPT2 to actin and supports cortical septin organization, cell-shape stability, polarized protrusion and directional migration. Its disordered C-terminal tail binds monophosphorylated phosphoinositides, preferring PI(3)P. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause recessive ciliopathies (Bardet-Biedl syndrome 15; congenital heart defects, tongue hamartomas and polysyndactyly; oral-facial-digital phenotypes).

NDUFAF2 (also known as NDUFA12L, B17.2L, and Mimitin) is a nuclear-encoded, mitochondrially targeted assembly factor for respiratory chain complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). It is a paralog of the structural complex I subunit NDUFA12 (B17.2) but, unlike its paralog, it is not a stable component of the mature holoenzyme. Instead it acts as a molecular chaperone that binds transiently to a large (~830 kDa) late-stage complex I assembly intermediate containing subunits of both the matrix (peripheral) and membrane arms, and is released once assembly is complete. By stabilizing this subassembly it increases the efficiency of complex I biogenesis, although residual assembly can occur in its absence. The protein carries an N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide and a C-terminal disordered region. Loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 10 (MC1DN10), presenting as progressive encephalopathy/leukoencephalopathy and Leigh syndrome. A more recently reported pleiotropic role links NDUFAF2 to primary cilium formation through interaction with the basal-body protein ARMC9.

BBIP1, also called BBIP10 or BBS18, is a small structural subunit of the BBSome, a protein complex that supports ciliary membrane-protein trafficking. In the human BBSome core, BBIP1 contacts BBS4 and BBS8 and helps maintain complex architecture. It localizes to primary cilia and the cytoplasm and contributes to ciliogenesis. BBIP1 depletion also affects cytoplasmic microtubule polymerization and acetylation, and inhibition of the associated deacetylase HDAC6 restores acetylation in depleted cells. The molecular connection between this phenotype and its BBSome role remains unresolved. Loss-of-function variants cause Bardet–Biedl syndrome type 18.

PIGY (PIG-Y) is a small (71-residue) two-transmembrane endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that is a required non-catalytic subunit of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (GPI-GnT) complex. This complex catalyses the first, committed step of GPI-anchor biosynthesis, transferring N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-GlcNAc onto phosphatidylinositol to form GlcNAc-PI. Within the complex, which additionally comprises the catalytic subunit PIGA together with PIGC, PIGH, PIGP, PIGQ and DPM2, PIGY interacts directly with PIGA and acts as a regulatory accessory subunit rather than as an independent enzyme. Loss of PIGY function causes an inherited GPI-deficiency disorder in the hyperphosphatasia with impaired intellectual development / epileptic encephalopathy spectrum (HPMRS6), with reduced cell-surface display of GPI-anchored proteins.

COX14 (formerly C12orf62) is a small (57 aa, ~6.6 kDa) single-pass transmembrane protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane that acts as an early assembly factor for respiratory chain Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX). It is a core component of the MITRAC complex (mitochondrial translation regulation assembly intermediate of cytochrome c oxidase), where, together with COA3 and other MITRAC/assembly components, it associates with the newly-synthesised mtDNA-encoded core subunit MT-CO1 (COX1) and couples MT-CO1 synthesis with its incorporation into the nascent enzyme, thereby regulating the early steps of COX assembly. COX14 is non-catalytic and has no known enzymatic activity; it functions as a scaffolding/regulatory assembly factor. Loss of COX14 destabilises newly synthesised COX1 and impairs COX assembly. In humans, biallelic COX14 variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 10 (MC4DN10), a fatal neonatal, Leigh-syndrome-like disorder with severe lactic acidosis.

Multidomain peripheral protein of early endosomes, built from an N-terminal pseudokinase domain, a central Tre2-Bub2-Cdc16 (TBC) domain and a C-terminal rhodanese-like domain. Despite its name, TBCK is not a protein kinase: the kinase-fold domain lacks the glycine-rich loop and the VAIK, HRD and DFG motifs, purified full-length human protein binds neither ATP nor GTP and hydrolyses neither, placing it among the class I pseudokinases. The catalytically competent module is the TBC domain, which retains the arginine and glutamine fingers of Rab GTPase-activating proteins; TBCK is the catalytic core of a heterotrimer with PPP1R21 and FERRY3 that acts as a GTPase-activating protein for RAB5, and its loss leaves RAB5 constitutively GTP-loaded, enlarges early endosomes and blocks their conversion to late endosomes. TBCK is also one of the five subunits of the FERRY complex, a RAB5A effector that tethers mRNAs and ribosomes to early endosomes, although the mRNA contacts are made by other subunits. Reported effects of TBCK depletion on mTOR signalling, cell size, proliferation and actin organisation are not consistently reproduced across cell types and remain disputed. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause TBCK encephaloneuronopathy (infantile hypotonia with psychomotor retardation and characteristic facies 3), a severe autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder.

ALG14 is the membrane-anchoring, non-catalytic subunit of the bipartite ALG14-ALG13 UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) transferase. ALG14 is a single-pass endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that recruits and anchors the otherwise-soluble catalytic subunit ALG13 to the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane; the resulting heterodimer catalyses the second step of dolichol-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) assembly, transferring a second, beta-1,4-linked GlcNAc from UDP-GlcNAc onto GlcNAc-PP-dolichol to form the chitobiose core GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol. This activity is essential for the biosynthesis of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor used in protein N-linked glycosylation. Neither ALG14 nor ALG13 is active alone: ALG13 provides catalysis but lacks a membrane domain, whereas ALG14 provides the membrane anchor but lacks catalytic residues. In humans, biallelic loss-of-function variants cause ALG14-CDG, a spectrum encompassing congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS15), a myasthenic/myopathic neurodegeneration with progressive cerebral atrophy (MEPCA), and an intellectual developmental disorder with epilepsy and coarse facies (IDDEBF).

DYNC2I2 (WDR34) is a WD-repeat intermediate chain of cytoplasmic dynein-2, the motor that returns intraflagellar transport components and cargo toward the ciliary base. It supplies light-chain, intermediate-chain and heavy-chain contacts that organize the asymmetric motor complex. Its ciliary transport and assembly roles involve basal-body, ciliary-interior and tip-turnaround pools; the severity of ciliary defects varies with the disrupted allele or engineered fragment. Biallelic variants cause skeletal ciliopathies. In human HEK293 cells, WDR34 also associates with TAK1/TAB2/TRAF6 and attenuates IL-1/TLR signaling, a reported nonciliary activity whose relationship to dynein-2 remains unresolved.

C9orf72 is a DENN-family regulator of small-GTPase-dependent membrane trafficking. Its long product forms a stable complex with SMCR8 and WDR41 that helps control GTPase cycling and endolysosomal homeostasis. C9orf72 also recognizes active Rab1A to recruit autophagy-initiation machinery, and purified C9orf72 has been reported to promote Rab39A nucleotide exchange upstream of HOPS-dependent autophagosome–lysosome fusion. The protein is predominantly cytoplasmic, with nutrient-dependent lysosomal association and enrichment in neuronal presynaptic compartments. It also influences stress-granule responses and neuronal actin dynamics. Pathogenic intronic repeat expansions can reduce normal protein expression while generating toxic repeat RNA and dipeptide-repeat products; these are distinct from the normal protein and its alternative products.

D2HGDH is a mitochondrial FAD-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes D-2-hydroxyglutarate to 2-oxoglutarate and limits accumulation of this metabolite. Its catalytic pocket binds substrate adjacent to FAD and a zinc-coordinating site. Human enzyme also efficiently oxidizes D-malate and more weakly D-lactate in purified assays, while their physiological fluxes remain less defined. Loss-of-function variants cause D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria type 1. The 521-residue precursor contains an N-terminal targeting region; two shorter splice products of 307 and 319 residues lack much of the canonical C-terminal substrate-binding region and have not been functionally characterized in the cited assays.

SGMS2 encodes sphingomyelin synthase 2 (SMS2), an integral membrane enzyme that transfers phosphocholine from phosphatidylcholine to ceramide, forming sphingomyelin and diacylglycerol. It acts mainly at the plasma membrane and also at the Golgi, maintaining membrane sphingomyelin and influencing local diacylglycerol and ceramide pools. The enzyme can catalyze the reverse transfer from sphingomyelin to diacylglycerol, regenerating ceramide and phosphatidylcholine. SMS2 also transfers phosphoethanolamine from phosphatidylethanolamine to ceramide and hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine in purified-enzyme assays; the relative activities depend strongly on the membrane or detergent environment. Heterozygous pathogenic variants cause osteoporosis and skeletal dysplasia. Some variants retain catalytic activity but accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, disrupting the normal distribution of sphingomyelin across cellular membranes.

TMEM67 (meckelin/MKS3) is a single-pass transmembrane protein that localizes to the ciliary transition zone and is a core component of the MKS complex (Meckel syndrome complex). Its domain architecture comprises an N-terminal extracellular region containing a cysteine-rich domain (CRD) homologous to Frizzled/ROR receptors (a Wnt-binding module), a beta-sheet-rich domain, an extracellular linker region containing ADAMTS9 cleavage sites, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic tail with coiled-coil features mediating protein-protein interactions (DOI:10.1101/2024.09.04.611229). A major mechanistic advance identifies TMEM67 as a proteolytic substrate of the metalloproteinase ADAMTS9, generating two functional forms: a released N-terminal ectodomain fragment proposed to modulate Wnt signaling, and a C-terminal fragment (Delta342) that localizes to the TZ and supports ciliogenesis/TZ assembly (DOI:10.1101/2024.09.04.611229). This cleavage-based functional partitioning explains how different alleles may differentially affect ciliary gating versus signaling outputs. TMEM67 is essential for primary cilium formation and structure, acting in centrosome migration to the apical cell surface during early ciliogenesis. Loss of TMEM67 or ADAMTS9 reduces recruitment of multiple MKS/B9 module proteins (TCTN1/2/3, TMEM237, CC2D2A, B9D2) to mature basal bodies/TZ, positioning TMEM67 as a central organizer within MKS-related TZ assemblies. TMEM67 functions as a receptor or co-receptor in non-canonical Wnt signaling (interacting with WNT5A and ROR2), and plays a role in epithelial branching morphogenesis. It also participates in endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) of misfolded surfactant protein C (SFTPC), where it acts as an adaptor linking the ER lumenal quality control machinery with the cytosolic degradation apparatus. TMEM67 is the most commonly mutated gene in MKS, accounting for approximately 16-20% of MKS cases (DOI:10.1101/2024.09.04.611229). Mutations in TMEM67 cause a spectrum of ciliopathies including Meckel-Gruber syndrome (MKS3), Joubert syndrome (JBTS6), COACH syndrome, nephronophthisis (NPHP11), Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS14), and RHYNS syndrome. TMEM67 pathogenic variants contribute to around 80% of JS-related disorders featuring liver involvement (DOI:10.54029/2024wir).

TMEM43 (also known as LUMA) encodes a highly conserved integral inner nuclear membrane protein with four transmembrane domains. The protein functions primarily as a structural/adapter component at the inner nuclear membrane (INM), where it interacts with emerin, lamins A/C, and SUN2 to maintain nuclear envelope integrity and contribute to mechanotransduction through LINC complex associations. TMEM43 is required for retaining emerin at the INM. Beyond the nuclear envelope, TMEM43 also localizes to the ER membrane and, in cardiomyocytes, to intercalated discs. In cochlear glia-like supporting cells, it contributes to passive conductance current through gap junction interactions with connexins (Cx26/Cx30). Pathogenic variants cause arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy type 5 (ARVD5, notably p.S358L), Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy type 7 (EDMD7), and autosomal dominant auditory neuropathy (AUNA3). The protein also plays roles in NF-kappa-B signaling downstream of EGFR and modulates innate immune signaling through the cGAS-STING pathway via interaction with RNF26.

DYNLT2B (TCTEX1D2) is a small non-catalytic Tctex-type dynein light chain and the only Tctex light chain unique to cytoplasmic dynein-2, the minus-end-directed motor that drives retrograde intraflagellar transport (IFT) from the ciliary tip back to the base. It forms a 1:1 heterodimer with the Tctex light chain DYNLT1 (or DYNLT3), and this pair binds the dynein-2 intermediate chain WDR60/DYNC2I1, forming the WDR60-TCTEX1D2-DYNLT1/DYNLT3 subcomplex of the dynein-2 tail. Endogenous protein is found at the ciliary base, centrosomal microtubule-organizing centers and mitotic spindle poles, with WDR60-dependent recruitment. Loss of DYNLT2B in human cells and of its Chlamydomonas ortholog Tctex2b impairs retrograde IFT and partially destabilizes the motor, and biallelic loss-of-function variants cause short-rib thoracic dysplasia 17 (Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy). In mouse testis the ortholog is also an axoneme component that associates with inner-dynein-arm intermediate chains and is required for sperm flagellum formation.

CFAP251 (cilia- and flagella-associated protein 251; also known as WDR66) is a large WD40-repeat protein of the motile-cilium and sperm-flagellum axoneme. It is a subunit of the calmodulin- and spoke-associated complex (CSC), together with CFAP61 and CFAP91, and forms part of the base of radial spoke 3 (RS3) on the outer doublet microtubules. In the ciliate Tetrahymena, loss of the ortholog FAP251 removes an arch-like density at the RS3 base, leaves RS3 missing or incomplete, and impairs ciliary waveform and swimming; in the human respiratory axoneme cryo-EM model, RS3 is built on a base of CFAP61, CFAP91 and CFAP251. The CSC links radial spokes to the nexin-dynein regulatory complex and is implicated in calcium/calmodulin-dependent regulation of axonemal dynein activity. CFAP251 is most highly expressed in testis, where it localizes along the sperm flagellum. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause spermatogenic failure 33, a male infertility disorder with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagellum (MMAF) and defective mitochondrial sheath formation; Cfap251 knockout mice reproduce MMAF and also show loss of inner dynein arms in tracheal cilia, although respiratory disease in affected men is not established.

EOGT is an endoplasmic-reticulum glycosyltransferase that adds O-linked N-acetylglucosamine to serine or threonine residues between the fifth and sixth conserved cysteines of folded extracellular EGF-like domains of secretory-pathway proteins. The canonical 527-residue human protein has demonstrated activity on Notch EGF-repeat reporters in a heterologous system. This enzyme is distinct from intracellular OGT. Biallelic EOGT variants cause Adams-Oliver syndrome; the activities and locations of its shorter natural protein products remain incompletely characterized.

DNAAF6 is a 214-residue cytoplasmic assembly factor required for formation of outer and inner axonemal dynein arms. It associates with the dynein intermediate chain DNAI2 and other assembly factors, and is enriched at the trans-Golgi network in human ciliated airway cells. It belongs to the PIH/CS dynein-assembly-factor family and contains a predicted CS-like domain, rather than a distinct PIH domain. Loss of DNAAF6 disrupts ciliary and sperm flagellar motility and causes X-linked primary ciliary dyskinesia, with variable residual dynein arms and laterality phenotypes.

B3GALNT2 is a glycosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.313) whose canonical protein has a single-pass type-II membrane topology. It transfers N-acetylgalactosamine from UDP-GalNAc to terminal beta-linked N-acetylglucosamine, forming a beta-1,3 linkage. Its established physiological role is the assembly of the core M3 O-mannosyl glycan of alpha-dystroglycan in the endoplasmic reticulum. It extends the product of POMGNT2, producing the trisaccharide recognized by the mannose kinase POMK and enabling later glycan elaboration required for extracellular-matrix binding. Cultured-cell studies also support modification of N-glycans on intracellular glycoproteins, although the endogenous substrate range and physiological significance remain incompletely resolved. Biallelic loss of B3GALNT2 function causes dystroglycanopathy with muscle and, in severe cases, brain and eye abnormalities.

NDUFAF6 (C8orf38) is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial assembly factor for respiratory chain complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). The functional isoform (isoform 1) carries an N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide and is imported into mitochondria, where it localizes peripherally on the matrix face of the inner membrane. It acts at early stages of complex I assembly and is specifically required for biogenesis of the mitochondrially encoded ND1 (MT-ND1) subunit, participating in formation/stabilization of the ND1-containing assembly intermediate; loss of NDUFAF6 blocks maturation of late-stage assembly intermediates and leads to a profound decrease in steady-state complex I. Structurally the protein retains an isoprenoid/squalene-phytoene-synthase-like (terpenoid synthase) fold, and although named a "putative phytoene synthase" no catalytic activity has been demonstrated; it is not a structural subunit of the holoenzyme. A shorter splice isoform (isoform 2) lacks the transit peptide and is cytoplasmic/nuclear. Biallelic NDUFAF6 variants cause mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 17 (including Leigh syndrome and bilateral striatal necrosis) and, via a non-coding intronic variant, the Acadian variant of Fanconi renotubular syndrome (FRTS5).

B9D2 (B9 domain-containing protein 2; MKSR2/MKS10) is a small soluble protein with a C2-like B9 domain. It forms the B9 complex with MKS1 and B9D1 (arranged MKS1-B9D2-B9D1), part of the MKS module at the ciliary transition zone. The B9 complex anchors the transmembrane protein TMEM67, and the module acts as a diffusion barrier that keeps the ciliary membrane composition distinct from the plasma membrane; for example, B9D2-knockout cells lose GPR161 from the ciliary membrane. The B9-TMEM67 module also sustains post-translational modification of axonemal microtubules. Earlier, at the mother centriole, B9 proteins promote vesicle docking and CP110 removal to initiate ciliogenesis. B9D2 is not essential for ciliogenesis, but its loss reduces cilium formation and length. Biallelic B9D2 variants cause Meckel syndrome (MKS10) and Joubert syndrome (JBTS34).

ISCA1 is a mitochondrial matrix A-type iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster assembly protein that functions late in the ISC biogenesis pathway, specifically in the maturation of [4Fe-4S] cluster-containing proteins. ISCA1 forms a heterodimeric complex with ISCA2 that acts as an "assembler" of [4Fe-4S] clusters by receiving two [2Fe-2S] clusters from GLRX5 and catalyzing their reductive fusion into a single [4Fe-4S] cluster. This reaction requires the additional factor IBA57 and electrons from the mitochondrial ferredoxin FDX2 and its reductase FDXR. The assembled [4Fe-4S] clusters are then transferred to target apoproteins, with downstream factors NFU1 and BOLA3 mediating insertion for certain targets including lipoic acid synthase (LIAS) and respiratory complex I subunits. ISCA1 is essential for [4Fe-4S] protein maturation but dispensable for [2Fe-2S] proteins. Pathogenic variants cause Multiple Mitochondrial Dysfunctions Syndrome 5 (MMDS5), characterized by infantile-onset leukodystrophy, lactic acidosis, and combined OXPHOS deficiencies.

COQ5 is the mitochondrial 2-methoxy-6-polyprenyl-1,4-benzoquinol methylase (EC 2.1.1.201), a Class I S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferase of the MenG/UbiE family. It catalyzes the sole C-methylation step in the biosynthesis of coenzyme Q (ubiquinone; CoQ10 in humans): using SAM as the methyl donor, it transfers a methyl group onto the C2 position of the polyprenylated benzoquinol ring, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. In humans this converts 2-methoxy-6-(all-trans-decaprenyl)benzene-1,4-diol to the corresponding methylated product en route to CoQ10. The protein is synthesized with an N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide and localizes as a peripheral membrane protein on the matrix side of the mitochondrial inner membrane, where it is a component of the multi-subunit COQ enzyme complex (the CoQ synthome / COQ metabolon) together with COQ3, COQ4, COQ6, COQ7 and COQ9. Loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency (COQ10D9), presenting with cerebellar ataxia and static encephalomyopathy.

An uncharacterized protein of the UPF0711 family containing a DUF4674 domain. Originally identified as upregulated by Hepatitis B virus X protein (hence alias XTP13), this 220 amino acid protein is ubiquitously expressed and conserved in vertebrates. Despite appearing in hundreds of CRISPR screens affecting cell fitness and having numerous potential protein interactions, its molecular function was long unknown. A strong but not-yet-verified lead (an OpenScientist Foldseek run plus recent 2025-2026 literature) identifies C18orf21 as RMP24, a subunit of the human RNase MRP ribonucleoprotein complex, assigning the DUF4674 fold to the RPP21 RNase P/MRP-subunit superfamily; this remains to be confirmed against the primary literature before the annotations are updated.

MAGT1 is an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, thioredoxin-like oxidoreductase and an accessory subunit of the STT3B-containing (post-translocational) oligosaccharyltransferase complex (OST-B). It carries a lumenal thioredoxin fold with a redox-active CXXC (CVVC) motif and is one of two mutually exclusive STT3B-specific accessory subunits (MAGT1 or its paralog TUSC3). Within OST-B, MAGT1 promotes N-linked glycosylation of a subset of acceptor sequons that are near cysteine residues or bracketed by disulfides: in its predominantly oxidized state it forms transient mixed disulfides with the free thiols of nascent glycoprotein substrates, delaying disulfide-bond formation so that the catalytic STT3B subunit can access and glycosylate the unmodified asparagine. It also has oxidoreductase-independent roles in substrate recognition by OST-B. Although historically named "magnesium transporter 1" and reported to support cellular Mg2+ uptake, its principal, best-supported molecular function is the OST-B oxidoreductase role; any contribution to Mg2+ homeostasis appears to be secondary and at least partly a downstream consequence of altered glycosylation. Loss of MAGT1 function causes X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia (XMEN) and a congenital disorder of glycosylation (MAGT1-CDG).

DNAJC12 (also called JDP1) is a small cytosolic "J domain-only" co-chaperone of the DnaJ/Hsp40 (DNAJC) family, consisting of an N-terminal J domain (with the conserved HPD motif) and a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region. As a co-chaperone of the HSP70 family, it binds the cognate Hsp70 chaperone Hsc70 (HSPA8) and, through its J domain, stimulates HSP70 ATPase activity. DNAJC12 is a dedicated chaperone for the biopterin (BH4)-dependent aromatic amino acid hydroxylases, interacting with phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and tryptophan hydroxylases (TPH1, TPH2) and assisting their proper folding and stability. It is diffusely cytoplasmic and is up-regulated by ER stress. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause autosomal-recessive non-BH4-deficient hyperphenylalaninemia accompanied by dopamine and serotonin deficiency, dystonia/parkinsonism and intellectual disability, a condition treatable with BH4 and neurotransmitter precursors.

RUBCN encodes Rubicon (RUN domain Beclin-1-interacting and cysteine-rich domain-containing protein), a negative regulator of late-stage autophagy and endolysosomal maturation. Its middle PI3K-binding region associates with the UVRAG-containing class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex II (Beclin 1-VPS34-VPS15-UVRAG), contacting the Beclin 1 BARA domain, and inhibits VPS34 lipid kinase activity; its C-terminal zinc-cluster Rubicon homology (RH) domain binds GTP-bound Rab7, targeting Rubicon to late endosomes and lysosomes. By restraining PI3KC3-C2 and sequestering UVRAG from the HOPS tethering complex, Rubicon slows autophagosome maturation, autophagosome-lysosome fusion and endosome maturation. Rubicon expression rises with age and under lipid overload, and its loss enhances autophagic flux. In phagocytes Rubicon is also linked to NADPH oxidase-dependent phagosome functions and to feedback inhibition of CARD9 signalling downstream of pattern-recognition receptors.

CEP290 is a large coiled-coil protein at the ciliary transition zone, centriolar satellites and photoreceptor connecting cilium. Its microtubule-binding and membrane-binding domains support ciliary organization and compartmentalization. CEP290 associates with PCM1, CEP131 and CCDC66 at centriolar satellites and helps recruit proteins needed for primary-cilium formation. Its interaction with CP110 contributes to the restraint of ciliogenesis. Conserved transition-zone assembly involves a hierarchy in which the Caenorhabditis elegans RPGRIP1L/RPGRIP1 ortholog MKS-5 recruits CEP-290, which organizes MKS-module proteins. CEP290 also modulates ATF4-dependent transcription in human cells. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause a spectrum including Joubert, Meckel, Senior-Loken and Bardet-Biedl syndromes and Leber congenital amaurosis.

IFT140 (C. elegans CHE-11) is a large WD40-repeat/TPR-repeat subunit of the core of intraflagellar transport complex A (IFT-A), together with IFT122 and IFT144/WDR19; the peripheral IFT-A subcomplex contains IFT43, IFT121/WDR35 and IFT139/TTC21B. IFT-A is carried into the cilium on anterograde IFT trains and then, with cytoplasmic dynein-2, drives retrograde transport of IFT-B, BBSome and membrane cargo from the ciliary tip back to the base. Through its cargo adaptor TULP3, which binds membrane phosphoinositides, IFT-A also mediates ciliary entry of membrane proteins, notably G protein-coupled receptors such as SSTR3, MCHR1, GPR161 and GPR45. IFT140 localizes to the basal body, the axoneme and the ciliary tip. Mutations in IFT140 cause skeletal ciliopathies (Mainzer-Saldino syndrome, Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy / short-rib thoracic dysplasia 9), retinitis pigmentosa and an adult-onset polycystic kidney disease, and mouse Ift140 is required for photoreceptor outer segment development and opsin delivery.

RPGRIP1L (also called NPHP8, MKS5 or FTM) is a large coiled-coil and C2-domain protein of the ciliary transition zone, related to the photoreceptor protein RPGRIP1. It sits at the basal body and transition zone, distal to CEP290, and binds NPHP4 directly as part of the NPHP1-NPHP4-NPHP8 module. RPGRIP1L acts as the upstream scaffold for assembling the transition zone: MKS- and NPHP-module proteins depend on it to reach the transition zone and form the ciliary diffusion barrier. In photoreceptors it binds RPGR at the connecting cilium, and the common A229T variant, which weakens RPGR binding, modifies retinal degeneration. Loss of RPGRIP1L causes Joubert syndrome, Meckel syndrome and nephronophthisis.

CEP164 is a coiled-coil and WW-domain protein of mother-centriole distal appendages, extending toward their outer membrane-docking region. Its N-terminal region directly binds TTBK2 and recruits the kinase to the mother centriole, enabling early events in primary-cilium assembly. The C-terminal region targets CEP164 to appendages and binds Rabin8; CEP164 also supports ciliary membrane organization and centrosomal Rab8 accumulation; recent ultrastructure places its requirement after initial small-vesicle docking, in vesicle enlargement. Rab8 association in cell extracts is distinct from the direct Rabin8 interaction. Biallelic CEP164 variants cause a ciliopathy that can include nephronophthisis and retinal degeneration. Reported nuclear localization and DNA-damage-response functions remain contextually disputed.

INTU (Inturned) is a scaffold protein that functions as a core component of the CPLANE (ciliogenesis and planar polarity effector) complex at basal bodies, where it recruits intraflagellar transport machinery, specifically IFT-A proteins. INTU also serves as an adaptor linking ciliary proteins (NPHP4) to actin-modifying proteins (DAAM1) to control the subapical actin network required for basal body docking and ciliary orientation. Essential for primary cilia assembly and Hedgehog signaling, INTU is mutated in ciliopathies including Oral-Facial-Digital syndrome XVII and Short-Rib Thoracic Dysplasia 20.

KCTD16 is an auxiliary subunit of GABA-B receptors that modulates the pharmacology and kinetics of receptor signaling. It contains an N-terminal BTB/POZ domain that forms an open pentamer and binds to the GABAB2 C-terminal tail in a 1:5 stoichiometry. Unlike KCTD12 which promotes rapid desensitization, KCTD16 generally confers sustained, non-desensitizing GABA-B receptor responses. KCTD16 is enriched in brain regions including thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala, where it shapes postsynaptic inhibitory currents through GIRK channels. Notably, KCTD16 does not function as a Cullin3 E3 ligase adaptor, distinguishing it from other KCTD family members.

WDR35 (IFT121) is a subunit of the intraflagellar transport complex A (IFT-A), built from two N-terminal WD40 beta-propellers followed by a TPR-rich alpha-solenoid, an architecture related to COPI/clathrin vesicle coat proteins. Within IFT-A it belongs to the peripheral subcomplex (IFT43-IFT121-IFT139), where the IFT43-IFT121 dimer connects to the IFT122 core subunit. IFT-A mediates retrograde intraflagellar transport along the axoneme and, with the TULP3 adaptor, the entry of membrane proteins (GPCRs, Smoothened, EVC/EVC2) into the primary cilium; WDR35 is required for ciliary import of many membrane cargoes and for efficient delivery of membrane to the nascent cilium. WDR35 localizes to cilia (axoneme, tip), the basal body and centrosome. Fibroblasts lacking WDR35 fail to form or form short, bulbous cilia, and mouse Wdr35 mutants die at midgestation with Hedgehog-pathway defects. Biallelic WDR35 variants cause short-rib thoracic dysplasia with polydactyly (SRTD7) and cranioectodermal dysplasia (CED2).

CC2D2A (coiled-coil and C2 domain-containing protein 2A, also called MKS6) is a large (1,620 residues) non-catalytic structural protein of the ciliary base. It carries an N-terminal disordered region, central coiled coils, a CC2D2AN-C2 module, a transglutaminase-like (TGL) peptidase fold whose catalytic residues are lost throughout the CC2D2A clade, and a C2 domain. CC2D2A is a core subunit of the MKS/Tectonic module of the ciliary transition zone, together with TCTN1-3, MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, TMEM216, TMEM231 and TMEM67, and also concentrates at the basal body and the subdistal appendages of the mother centriole. Its localization at the transition zone and that of B9D1 and TMEM231 are mutually dependent. Loss of the protein impairs subdistal-appendage assembly, microtubule anchoring and docking of ciliary vesicles at the mother centriole, causing tissue-dependent failure of axoneme extension. Where cilia still form, it is required for the ciliary membrane to retain its distinctive composition (for example Arl13b, adenylyl cyclase 3, Pkd2 and Smoothened) and for normal Hedgehog signalling. In photoreceptors it sits at the connecting cilium and is needed for fusion of opsin-carrier vesicles at the periciliary membrane. It interacts with CEP290 and with NINL, which links it to RAB8-MICAL3 vesicle docking. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause Meckel syndrome 6, Joubert syndrome 9, COACH syndrome 2 and retinitis pigmentosa 93.

CEP152 is a large coiled-coil centrosomal scaffold that organizes centriole biogenesis. With CEP63 it forms a higher-order cylindrical assembly around the proximal region of a parent centriole. Its N-terminal region binds and positions PLK4, and distinct interactions with CPAP/CENPJ support procentriole initiation. CEP152 also participates in the conserved Deup1-dependent machinery for centriole amplification in multiciliated cells. During mitosis, a CEP152–CEP63 complex restrains CEP57-dependent pericentrin recruitment, while CEP152 recruits APC/C and undergoes ubiquitylation associated with release of this restraint. Biallelic CEP152 variants cause primary microcephaly 9 and Seckel syndrome 5.

EPG5 is a 2,579-residue cytoplasmic Rab7 effector that coordinates selective fusion of autophagosomes with late endosomes and lysosomes. It associates with the lysosomal surface through Rab7 and VAMP7/8, binds autophagic STX17-SNAP29-containing SNARE assemblies, and engages LC3/GABARAP proteins through tandem LC3-interacting-region motifs, with preferential binding to the GABARAP subfamily. These interactions organize the fusion machinery and restrict inappropriate fusion with other endocytic vesicles; EPG5 deficiency causes accumulation of undegraded autophagic cargo. EPG5 also supports endosome-to-lysosome delivery of internalized nucleic acids, enabling endosomal TLR9 and TLR7 signaling. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause Vici syndrome and a neurodevelopmental disorder with parkinsonism or other movement abnormalities.

ASXL3 is a nuclear chromatin regulator and noncatalytic partner of the BAP1 deubiquitinase complex PR-DUB. Its DEUBAD region activates BAP1, while a separate BRD4-binding region bridges BRD4 to the BAP1 complex and supports enhancer recruitment in human small cell lung cancer cells. PHD-associated MBD proteins contribute to complex organization. ASXL3 can promote transcription in enhancer-associated contexts and repress nuclear-receptor programs in other settings. Disruption of ASXL3 causes Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome.

SELENOI (ethanolaminephosphotransferase 1, EPT1/hEPT1; also known as Selenoprotein I) is a multi-pass endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme of the CDP-alcohol phosphatidyltransferase class-I family. It catalyzes the final (third) step of the CDP-ethanolamine branch of the Kennedy pathway, transferring a phosphoethanolamine group from CDP-ethanolamine to a diacylglycerol acceptor to produce phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) plus CMP (EC 2.7.8.1); catalysis requires a divalent cation (Mg2+ or Mn2+). It is specific for CDP-ethanolamine (rather than CDP-choline) as the phosphobase donor. In addition to diacyl-PE, it uses 1-O-alkyl-2-acylglycerol acceptors to make ether-linked PE (plasmanyl-/plasmenyl-PE, a plasmalogen precursor), contributing to the pool of ether-linked phospholipids important for myelin. As a selenoprotein, it incorporates a selenocysteine near its C-terminus (residue 387). PE is the second most abundant membrane glycerophospholipid in mammalian cells, and SELENOI-mediated PE and plasmalogen synthesis supports membrane biogenesis, myelination and neurodevelopment. Loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG81) with hypomyelinating white-matter disease.

ARV1 is a conserved multi-pass ER membrane protein. It is a component of the GPI N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (GPI-GnT) complex that initiates glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor biosynthesis: it binds PIGQ and helps the enzyme use phosphatidylinositol. Biallelic ARV1 variants reduce cell-surface GPI-anchored proteins and cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. ARV1 also takes part in cellular sterol homeostasis. Its ARV1 homology domain binds cholesterol and phospholipids, and loss of ARV1 retains cholesterol in the ER and suppresses SREBP signalling. In yeast, however, sterol transport between the ER and plasma membrane is intact without Arv1, and Arv1 instead maintains ER and plasma membrane structure. An alternative model holds that Arv1 helps deliver the GlcN-acyl-PI intermediate to the luminal face of the ER.

MTFMT encodes the nuclear-encoded mitochondrial methionyl-tRNA formyltransferase. Metazoan mitochondria use a single tRNA(Met) for both initiation and elongation; MTFMT transfers a formyl group from 10-formyltetrahydrofolate to part of the aminoacylated Met-tRNA(Met) pool, generating fMet-tRNA(Met), which is preferred by the mitochondrial initiation factor for translation initiation on mitochondrial ribosomes. Formylation is required for efficient synthesis of the mtDNA-encoded respiratory-chain subunits in human cells, and biallelic loss-of-function or hypomorphic variants cause Leigh syndrome with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency (COXPD15) or isolated complex I deficiency.

GNPTAB encodes the alpha/beta-subunit precursor of UDP-GlcNAc:lysosomal enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase (EC 2.7.8.17), the alpha2beta2gamma2 Golgi membrane enzyme complex (with GNPTG) that transfers GlcNAc-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc to mannose residues of high-mannose N-glycans on soluble lysosomal acid hydrolases. This is the first step in generating the mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) recognition marker that directs hydrolases to M6P receptors and thence to endosomes and lysosomes. The alpha/beta subunits are catalytic and also recognise a conformational protein determinant on acid hydrolases; the precursor is activated in the Golgi by site-1 protease cleavage and depends on LYSET/TMEM251 for stability and Golgi retention. Biallelic loss of GNPTAB causes mucolipidosis II (I-cell disease) and, with residual activity, mucolipidosis III alpha/beta.

PAM16 encodes MAGMAS/TIM16, a matrix-facing regulatory J-like cochaperone/adaptor subunit of the TIM23-associated PAM import motor. It forms a Pam18/Tim14 subcomplex, recruits and restrains Pam18 activity, and tunes mtHsp70-driven import of presequence-containing proteins into the mitochondrial matrix.

NADSYN1 (glutamine-dependent NAD(+) synthetase; EC 6.3.5.1) is a cytosolic homohexameric enzyme that catalyzes the final, committed step of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) de novo biosynthesis. It performs the ATP-dependent amidation of deamido-NAD+ (nicotinate adenine dinucleotide, NaAD) to NAD+, using L-glutamine as the physiological nitrogen donor, which is hydrolyzed to L-glutamate. This same reaction is the last step of both the de novo (tryptophan/kynurenine) route and the Preiss-Handler route, which converge at deamido-NAD+. The protein is bifunctional, with an N-terminal carbon-nitrogen (CN) hydrolase / nitrilase-family glutaminase domain that hydrolyzes glutamine to supply ammonia in situ (catalytic nucleophile Cys-175) and a C-terminal NAD synthetase (ligase) domain that carries out the ATP-dependent amidation. NADSYN1 can also use free ammonia as an alternative amide donor, but its low KM for glutamine indicates glutamine is the physiological donor. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants cause a congenital NAD deficiency disorder (Vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 3; VCRL3), an autosomal recessive, often lethal condition with cardiac, renal, vertebral, and limb malformations.

ISCU is the primary scaffold protein of the mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) assembly machinery in human cells. It provides the structural platform upon which nascent [2Fe-2S] clusters are assembled de novo before transfer to recipient apoproteins. The mature mitochondrial form (isoform 1/ISCU2) functions in the mitochondrial matrix as part of a core ISC complex that includes the cysteine desulfurase NFS1-LYRM4-NDUFAB1 subcomplex, frataxin (FXN) as an allosteric activator, and ferredoxin-2 (FDX2) as the electron donor. During cluster assembly, persulfide sulfur is transferred from NFS1 Cys381 to ISCU Cys138, and FDX2 provides reducing equivalents to reduce persulfide to sulfide for [2Fe-2S] formation. ISCU dimerization, mediated by Tyr-35, is critical for de novo cluster synthesis. Following cluster assembly, the HSPA9-HSCB chaperone system catalyzes ATP-dependent cluster release from ISCU for transfer to downstream carriers (GLRX5, NFU1, ISCA1/ISCA2) and ultimately to recipient Fe-S proteins. A cytosolic isoform (isoform 2/ISCU1) participates in cytoplasmic Fe-S biogenesis. ISCU deficiency causes hereditary myopathy with exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis.

NDUFAF3 (also known as C3orf60) is a nucleus-encoded, mitochondrially imported assembly factor for mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). It is not a structural subunit of the mature holoenzyme and has no catalytic activity. NDUFAF3 associates with the mitochondrial inner membrane and acts early in complex I biogenesis, tightly interacting with its partner factor NDUFAF4 and with the iron-sulfur (IP) core subunits NDUFS2 and NDUFS3 to help nucleate and stabilize an early membrane-arm assembly intermediate. Like other complex I assembly factors, it associates transiently with assembly intermediates and dissociates from the fully assembled complex. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in NDUFAF3 cause isolated mitochondrial complex I deficiency (nuclear type 18), with phenotypes ranging from fatal neonatal mitochondrial disease to Leigh syndrome.

COASY is the human bifunctional coenzyme A synthase, a single polypeptide that carries out the last two of the five steps of de novo coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis from pantothenate (vitamin B5). Its N-terminal/central phosphopantetheine adenylyltransferase (PPAT) domain adenylylates (R)-4'-phosphopantetheine using ATP to form 3'-dephospho-CoA, and its C-terminal dephospho-CoA kinase (DPCK) domain then phosphorylates 3'-dephospho-CoA using ATP to generate CoA. CoA and its acyl-CoA thioesters are ubiquitous acyl-group carriers essential for fatty acid metabolism, the TCA cycle, and many other pathways. The enzyme functions predominantly in the cytosol, where the bulk of de novo CoA synthesis occurs, with a minor pool associated with mitochondria. It is expressed in essentially all tissues, with a brain-enriched splice isoform. Loss-of-function mutations in COASY cause neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration, CoPAN/NBIA6) and pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 12.

BBS9 is an integral subunit of the BBSome, an eight-protein complex that contributes to membrane-protein trafficking at cilia. It provides multiple contacts with other BBSome subunits and helps organize assembly of the complex. Its N-terminal region forms a beta-propeller, while other regions participate in subunit association. BBS9 occurs in cytoplasmic and ciliary compartments, including the ciliary base and centriolar satellites. Loss of BBS9 can disrupt BBSome organization and ciliary assembly or trafficking in a manner that depends on the cell and organism studied. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause Bardet-Biedl syndrome, with features that can include retinal degeneration, obesity, polydactyly and renal abnormalities.

NAMPT (nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; also known as pre-B-cell colony-enhancing factor 1, PBEF, and visfatin) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the mammalian NAD+ salvage pathway (EC 2.4.2.12). It catalyzes the condensation of nicotinamide with 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP) to form nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), the immediate precursor of NAD+, thereby recycling the nicotinamide released by NAD+-consuming enzymes such as sirtuins, PARPs, and CD38. The active enzyme is a homodimer, and catalysis is stimulated by ATP-dependent phosphorylation of an active-site histidine (His247). NAMPT exists in an intracellular form (iNAMPT), which supplies NAD+ for cytosolic and nuclear NAD+-dependent processes, and a secreted extracellular form (eNAMPT/visfatin) that circulates as an adipocytokine; the secreted form lacks robust enzymatic activity under extracellular conditions and behaves as a cytokine and adipokine. Through NAD+-dependent regulation of SIRT1 and the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer, NAMPT contributes to circadian oscillation of NAD+ and clock-controlled gene expression. NAMPT is highly expressed in bone marrow, liver, and muscle, and is a well-studied anticancer drug target (inhibited by FK866/APO866).

PSENEN encodes PEN-2, a small multipass membrane protein and essential non-catalytic subunit of the gamma-secretase intramembrane protease complex. Together with a presenilin catalytic subunit, nicastrin, and APH1A or APH1B, PEN-2 promotes presenilin maturation/endoproteolysis, gamma-secretase complex stability and trafficking, and intramembrane cleavage of substrates including APP and Notch receptors. PEN-2 localizes primarily to endoplasmic-reticulum and cis-Golgi membranes, with evidence for cell-membrane and other membrane compartments; additional orthology-based evidence links PEN-2 to energy-stress signaling through V-ATPase/AMPK/TORC1 regulation.

HSPB8 (heat shock protein beta-8, also called HSP22, H11 kinase, E2IG1 or alpha-crystallin C chain) is a member of the small heat shock protein (sHSP / HSP20, alpha-crystallin domain) family, predominantly expressed in skeletal muscle and heart. It is an ATP-independent molecular chaperone (holdase) that binds aggregation-prone and stress-destabilized client proteins. Its central role is in chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA), where together with the co-chaperone BAG3, the Hsp70 chaperones HSPA8/HSC70 and HSPA1A, and the ubiquitin ligase STUB1/CHIP, HSPB8 routes damaged clients (e.g. filamin and polyglutamine-expanded proteins) for autophagic degradation via p62/SQSTM1, a process essential for maintenance of the muscle Z-disk under mechanical stress. HSPB8 forms homodimers and hetero-oligomers with other small HSPs (HSPB1, HSPB2, HSPB7) and DNAJB6. Despite an early report of protein kinase activity, recombinant HSPB8 lacks detectable kinase activity. It localizes to the cytoplasm and nucleus and translocates to nuclear foci during heat shock. Dominant variants (notably at the K141 hot spot) cause distal hereditary motor neuropathy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2L, and myofibrillar/rimmed-vacuole myopathy.

CRBN (cereblon) is the substrate-recognition subunit of a CRL4 cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase, the DCX/CRL4(CRBN) complex composed of DDB1, CUL4A or CUL4B, RBX1 and CRBN. Through an N-terminal Lon-protease-like domain it binds the adaptor DDB1, and through a C-terminal thalidomide-binding (CULT) domain that coordinates a structural Zn2+ ion it recruits substrate proteins for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Endogenous substrates include MEIS2, glutamine synthetase (GLUL) and ILF2, and the complex is required for normal limb outgrowth and FGF8 expression in vertebrates. CRBN also regulates neuronal large-conductance Ca2+-activated potassium (BK) channels via interaction with KCNT1, contributing to presynaptic glutamate release, memory and learning; loss-of-function variants cause autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder. The CULT domain is the direct molecular target of thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide (IMiDs) and of newer molecular-glue and PROTAC degraders, which act as molecular glues that reprogram CRBN substrate specificity to recruit neosubstrates such as IKZF1, IKZF3, SALL4, CK1alpha and GSPT1 for degradation. CRBN is expressed widely and most highly in brain, and localizes to cytoplasm, nucleus and peripheral membranes.

ATP13A2 is a P5B-type ATPase that uses ATP hydrolysis to export polyamines, especially spermine, from late endolysosomal compartments into the cytosol. Its membrane-associated N-terminal region binds phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate, coupling the transporter to its endolysosomal lipid environment. ATP13A2-dependent lysosomal homeostasis affects autophagic trafficking, exosomal secretion and neuronal survival. Loss-of-function variants cause Kufor-Rakeb syndrome and other neurodegenerative phenotypes. Potassium-dependent membrane ATPase activity and cellular potassium-surrogate transport have also been reported.

RFT1 encodes a polytopic endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein of the MOP (multidrug/oligosaccharidyl-lipid/polysaccharide) transporter superfamily that acts on Man(5)GlcNAc(2)-PP-dolichol (M5-DLO), the lipid-linked oligosaccharide intermediate of the N-glycosylation pathway. The protein spans the membrane roughly 12-14 times with both termini facing the cytosol, is not itself N-glycosylated, and is essential for viability in yeast and mammalian cells. Purified human RFT1 reconstituted into proteoliposomes translocates M5-DLO across the bilayer by an ATP-independent, bidirectional (scramblase-like) mechanism, with selectivity for the Man5 over shorter Man3 intermediates. Whether this translocase activity is the essential physiological role of the protein remains actively disputed: M5-DLO flipping persists in Rft1-depleted microsomes and in vesicles reconstituted with Rft1-free ER protein, Rft1-null Trypanosoma brucei is viable and glycosylates normally, and a yeast mutant engineered to block the lipid portal still supports robust growth, leading to an alternative model in which RFT1 acts as an M5-DLO chaperone that routes the intermediate for luminal completion. What is not in dispute is the pathway step at which the protein is required: loss of RFT1 function stalls dolichol-linked oligosaccharide assembly at M5-DLO and causes RFT1-CDG (CDG-In, OMIM 612015), a severe multisystem congenital disorder of glycosylation with neurodevelopmental abnormalities, hypotonia, epilepsy and sensorineural deafness.

SLC52A2 encodes riboflavin transporter 2 (RFVT2; formerly RFT3/hRFT3), a ~445-residue multi-pass plasma-membrane protein of the SLC52 (e-RFT, TCDB 2.A.125) solute carrier family. It mediates Na+-independent, moderately pH-sensitive cellular uptake of the water-soluble vitamin B2/riboflavin, with a submicromolar affinity (KM ~0.33 uM) and selectivity for riboflavin over FMN and FAD. Because mammals cannot synthesize riboflavin, RFVT2-mediated uptake is required to supply cells with the precursor of the flavin cofactors FAD and FMN that drive numerous oxidation-reduction reactions of energy, lipid, carbohydrate and amino-acid metabolism. RFVT2 is most highly expressed in brain, fetal brain and salivary gland and, in polarized epithelia, is one of several riboflavin transporters contributing to vitamin handling. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in SLC52A2 cause Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome type 2, a childhood-onset axonal sensorimotor neuronopathy with sensorineural deafness, optic atrophy, bulbar palsy and respiratory insufficiency that is responsive to high-dose oral riboflavin.

CC2D1A, also called Freud-1 or Aki1, is a multidomain regulatory protein with nuclear and cytoplasmic functions. In the nucleus it participates in sequence-dependent transcriptional repression, including regulation of HTR1A with cell-dependent chromatin-remodeling partners. In the cytoplasm it coordinates PDK1 and Akt in an EGF-responsive signaling complex without supplying their kinase activity. CC2D1A also associates with CHMP4B and localizes to centrosomes. Biallelic loss of function causes a complex neurodevelopmental disorder.

TUSC3 (Tumor suppressor candidate 3; N33) is an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that functions as an accessory oxidoreductase subunit of the STT3B-containing oligosaccharyltransferase (OST-B) complex. It is a multi-pass membrane protein whose lumenal, N-terminal thioredoxin-like domain carries a redox-active CXXC motif (Cys99-Cys102). Within OST-B, TUSC3 promotes N-linked glycosylation of a subset of asparagine acceptor sites that are near cysteine residues or that are otherwise skipped during co-translational glycosylation; in its oxidized form it is thought to form transient mixed disulfides with a free thiol in a glycoprotein substrate, delaying disulfide-bond formation and giving the catalytic STT3B subunit access to the unmodified sequon. TUSC3 is the close paralog of MAGT1, the two being mutually exclusive and functionally largely redundant subunits of OST-B, and is the metazoan orthologue of yeast Ost3/Ost6. Biallelic loss-of-function of TUSC3 causes autosomal-recessive non-syndromic intellectual disability. A role in cellular magnesium uptake has been proposed by analogy to MAGT1, but the established, mechanistically supported function is the ER OST-B oxidoreductase activity.

PNPO is pyridoxine-5'-phosphate oxidase (pyridoxine/pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate oxidase; EC 1.4.3.5), an FMN-dependent flavoenzyme that catalyzes the terminal, rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the catalytically active form of vitamin B6. It oxidizes either pyridoxine 5'-phosphate (PNP) or pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate (PMP) to PLP, using molecular oxygen and generating hydrogen peroxide. The enzyme binds one FMN cofactor per subunit and functions as a homodimer, with each subunit binding one molecule of the product PLP tightly, giving product inhibition. PNPO acts in the cytosol and is broadly (housekeeping) expressed, with highest levels in liver, skeletal muscle and kidney. Because PLP is the essential cofactor for dozens of enzymes, including those of neurotransmitter metabolism, PNPO is critical for maintaining PLP supply; loss-of-function variants cause pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-responsive neonatal/early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy (PNPO deficiency).

PYCR2 is one of three human pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase isozymes (PYCR1, PYCR2, PYCRL) and catalyzes the final, NAD(P)H-dependent step of proline biosynthesis: reduction of (S)-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) to L-proline (EC 1.5.1.2). It is a mitochondrial enzyme that assembles into a homodecamer built from five homodimers, and it acts chiefly in the glutamate-derived route to proline, using the mitochondrial P5C pool generated by P5C synthase. Like its close paralog PYCR1 (84% identical), PYCR2 can use either NADH or NADPH; at physiological substrate concentrations it shows higher specific activity with NADH, while the historically characterized erythrocyte activity has higher affinity for NADPH and is competitively inhibited by NADP+, leading to the proposal that in some cell types the enzyme also contributes to redox balance by regenerating NADP+. Beyond proline supply, PYCR2 supports mitochondrial membrane potential and resistance to oxidative-stress-induced apoptosis. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PYCR2 cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 10 (HLD10), an autosomal recessive disorder with postnatal microcephaly, severe psychomotor delay, hypomyelination and reduced cerebral white-matter volume, indicating a non-redundant role for PYCR2 in the developing central nervous system.

LRIF1 is a 769-amino-acid nuclear chromatin-associated regulatory protein, also known as C1orf103, RIF-1, and HBiX1. No experimentally determined LRIF1 structure or catalytic activity is known. UniProt predicts disordered segments at residues 378-400 and 528-562; the C-terminal region contains the HP1-binding LRVCL motif at residues 580-584, two nuclear-localization signals, and a terminal coiled coil. Through direct motif-dependent HP1 binding and association with SMCHD1, LRIF1 links HP1-marked and XIST-associated domains on the human inactive X chromosome and recruits HP1alpha to mitotic centromeres to support mitotic sister chromatid segregation. In a distinct locus and disease context, LRIF1 binds D4Z4, while loss or knockdown of the long isoform contributes to D4Z4 relaxation and DUX4 derepression in muscle; the binding assay was not isoform-resolved and the D4Z4 recruitment mechanism remains unresolved. LRIF1 also binds RARalpha and other nuclear receptors at the nuclear matrix and represses ligand-dependent transcription partly by recruiting histone deacetylases. The short isoform lacks residues 1-536 but retains the HP1 motif, nuclear-localization signals, and coiled coil by sequence; this retention is not evidence that it executes the same functions as the long isoform. LRIF1 is distinct from the replication-timing factor RIF1 (Q5UIP0).

ARHGEF28 (RGNEF, p190RhoGEF) is a large Lbc-family Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor with an N-terminal IPT/TIG region, a DH/PH catalytic module and a long C-terminal region with coiled coils. Its DH/PH module activates RhoA but not Rac1 or Cdc42; the full-length protein is autoinhibited in vitro, and its PH domain binds active RhoA and Rac1, which promotes its access to RhoA-GDP. Endogenous protein is cytosolic, along microtubules, and at RhoA-rich plasma membrane regions. Downstream of fibronectin-integrin engagement it activates RhoA and, through a GEF-independent scaffolding role, recruits and activates FAK at early adhesions, supporting focal adhesion formation and cell migration. Its C-terminal region binds the neurofilament light chain mRNA, and RGNEF has been implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

IFT172 is the largest IFT protein (~198 kDa), composed of N-terminal WD40 beta-propellers and an extended C-terminal TPR-like domain, and is a peripheral (IFT-B2) subunit of the intraflagellar transport B complex; it dissociates from the IFT-B core at high salt. As part of IFT-B, IFT172 travels on anterograde IFT trains and is required for cilium formation and maintenance; work in model organisms implicates it in IFT turnaround at the ciliary tip and membrane association of trains. IFT172 localizes to the axoneme and around the ciliary base. Biallelic IFT172 variants cause short-rib thoracic dysplasia 10 (Jeune and Mainzer-Saldino syndromes), Bardet-Biedl syndrome 20 and isolated retinitis pigmentosa 71; patient fibroblasts show disturbed ciliary composition, and Ift172 mouse mutants lack cilia and Hedgehog signalling.

DNAAF3 is a cytoplasmic dynein assembly factor required for maturation of outer and inner dynein arms before their deployment in motile cilia. Deficiency disrupts respiratory ciliary beating and can alter left–right organ patterning, causing primary ciliary dyskinesia. The conserved protein concentrates in dynein assembly particles in multiciliated cells. Ortholog genetics, dynein mass spectrometry and structural comparisons support a candidate role in arginine methylation during dynein maturation; intrinsic human methyltransferase activity and its separation from noncatalytic assembly functions remain unresolved. Alternative transcripts encode five predicted products with distinct sequence boundaries.

KIF7 is a 1343-residue member of the kinesin-4 family and the vertebrate counterpart of Drosophila Costal-2, with which it shares PANTHER family PTHR24115 as a sister subfamily. It has an N-terminal kinesin motor domain, a coiled-coil stalk that supports homodimerisation, and a long C-terminal region carrying the GLI-binding and NPHP1-binding determinants. Despite the intact motor domain, KIF7 is not a transport motor: purified KIF7 binds microtubules with high affinity but shows no detectable movement, because it cannot release ADP in response to microtubule binding. Instead it binds the plus ends of growing microtubules, where it slows growth and promotes catastrophe in an ATP-hydrolysis-dependent manner. In cells this makes KIF7 the organiser of the distal tip of the primary cilium: it limits cilium length, keeps the axoneme correctly modified and stable, and creates a single tip compartment. KIF7 concentrates at the ciliary base when Hedgehog signalling is off and redistributes to the tip when the pathway is activated, and it tethers the GLI transcription factors together with their inhibitor SUFU at that tip; it also delivers the prolyl hydroxylase P4HA2 there. Through this one scaffolding activity KIF7 acts in both directions on the pathway downstream of Smoothened - restraining ligand-independent GLI2 activation and preventing ectopic activation of GLI-SUFU complexes scattered along the axoneme, while also promoting signalling by driving SUFU turnover and SUFU-GLI dissociation and by protecting full-length GLI3 from processing into its repressor form. It is not required for intraflagellar transport or for entry of pathway components into the cilium. In humans, loss of KIF7 causes a group of ciliopathies - acrocallosal syndrome, hydrolethalus syndrome 2, Joubert syndrome 12 and Al-Gazali-Bakalinova syndrome - with polydactyly, corpus callosum and other brain malformations, and skeletal defects, and KIF7 missense alleles act as modifiers across the wider ciliopathy spectrum.

DNAAF1 is a leucine-rich-repeat protein that supports cytoplasmic assembly of the outer and inner dynein arms needed for motile cilia. Loss of DNAAF1 disrupts dynein-arm incorporation and causes primary ciliary dyskinesia with respiratory and left–right patterning abnormalities. Human protein has also been observed in cilia and at mitotic spindle poles, and depletion in cultured renal epithelial cells impairs primary-cilium formation. Alternative transcripts encode three predicted products with different repeat or C-terminal regions.

SEPSECS (O-phosphoseryl-tRNA(Sec) selenium transferase, also known as selenocysteine synthase / Sec synthase / SepSecS, and historically as the SLA/LP soluble liver antigen) is a pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the terminal step of selenocysteine (Sec) biosynthesis. In archaea and eukaryotes, Sec is uniquely synthesized on its cognate tRNA(Sec): seryl-tRNA(Sec) is phosphorylated by PSTK to O-phospho-L-seryl-tRNA(Sec), which SEPSECS then converts, using selenophosphate (produced by SEPHS2) as the selenium donor, into L-selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) (EC 2.9.1.2). The charged Sec-tRNA(Sec) is subsequently delivered by the specialized elongation factor EEFSEC to recode in-frame UGA codons during translation of selenoprotein mRNAs. SEPSECS assembles into a homotetramer comprising a catalytic dimer and a non-catalytic dimer that acts as a binding platform orienting two tRNA(Sec) molecules for catalysis; the PLP cofactor is covalently bound through a Schiff base to the active-site lysine (Lys284). The enzyme acts specifically on phosphoserine attached to tRNA(Sec), not on free phosphoserine. It localizes to the cytoplasm/cytosol and can associate with other components of the selenocysteine-synthesis machinery (SEPHS1, SEPHS2, TRNAU1AP/SECp43). Loss-of-function mutations in SEPSECS cause autosomal recessive pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 2D (progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy), underscoring the requirement for selenoprotein biosynthesis in the developing nervous system.

CFAP70 (cilia- and flagella-associated protein 70) is a large tetratricopeptide-repeat protein of motile cilia and sperm flagella. It is a structural component of the C2a projection of the axonemal central apparatus, where it forms a homodimer and assembles interdependently with CFAP65, MYCBPAP and CCDC108; its N-terminal half targets it to the cilium. Loss of CFAP70 collapses the C2a projection, destabilises the central pair and alters the ciliary beat, so that ependymal and airway cilia beat abnormally (hydrocephalus and sinusitis in knockout mice) and ciliary beat frequency falls. In the testis, CFAP70 is required for sperm flagellum biogenesis and normal sperm head shaping: it helps stabilise QRICH2, supports cytoplasmic preassembly of the calmodulin- and radial spoke-associated complex, and influences manchette localisation of axonemal proteins. Biallelic CFAP70 variants in men cause spermatogenic failure 41, an oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagellum. An early model placing CFAP70 at the base of the outer dynein arm has been superseded by localisation to the central apparatus.

TARS2 encodes the nuclear-encoded mitochondrial threonyl-tRNA synthetase, a homodimeric class II aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase imported into the mitochondrial matrix. It activates L-threonine with ATP and transfers it to mitochondrial tRNA(Thr), and its editing domain hydrolyses serine mischarged onto tRNA(Thr) (post-transfer proofreading). The resulting Thr-tRNA(Thr) is required for translation of the thirteen mtDNA-encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunits.
