Biallelic TARS2 variants reduce charged mitochondrial tRNA(Thr) and cause an early-onset mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with multiple respiratory-chain defects (COXPD21).

NAA15 (N-alpha-acetyltransferase 15, NatA auxiliary subunit; also NARG1, NATH, Tubedown-1) is the large, non-catalytic auxiliary subunit of the NatA N-terminal acetyltransferase complex. It dimerizes with the catalytic subunit NAA10, where its TPR-repeat-rich solenoid wraps around NAA10, anchoring the complex to the ribosome near the exit tunnel and orienting nascent polypeptide N-termini for co-translational acetylation. NAA15 itself has no acetyltransferase catalytic activity; rather it activates and confers ribosomal targeting and substrate specificity on NAA10, and is required for NatA-type N-terminal acetylation in vivo. It also serves as the scaffold for the NatA-associated factors HYPK and NAA50 (forming NatE). NAA15 is predominantly cytoplasmic with a nuclear pool, and a nuclear NAA15-containing complex with the Ku70/Ku80 (XRCC6/ XRCC5) heterodimer has been reported to up-regulate transcription from the osteocalcin promoter. NAA15 (as Tubedown-1) has additional reported roles in endothelial/retinal vascular biology, and NAA15 variants are associated with neurodevelopmental and congenital heart phenotypes.

CEP57 is a coiled-coil centrosomal protein that binds microtubules and helps organize pericentriolar material and the mitotic spindle. Its distinct interaction regions anchor centrosomal proteins, including pericentrin, and support the integrity of the centrosome and centriole engagement. Human CEP57 can self-associate; purified constructs form condensates that concentrate tubulin, while cellular perturbations disrupt microtubule organization. CEP57, also called translokin, binds the 18-kDa form of FGF2 and supports its intracellular trafficking toward the nuclear vicinity in mammalian cell models. The relative contribution of its proposed kinetochore checkpoint role varies across experimental systems. Biallelic CEP57 variants cause mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome (PMID:21552266).

PNPLA2 encodes adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL; also desnutrin, iPLA2-zeta, PEDF-R), a patatin-domain serine hydrolase that catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of intracellular triacylglycerol hydrolysis, converting triacylglycerol to diacylglycerol and a fatty acid. ATGL acts on the surface of cytoplasmic lipid droplets in adipocytes and many non-adipose cells, including skeletal and cardiac muscle, and its activity is strongly stimulated by the co-activator ABHD5/CGI-58 and limited by inhibitory partners and ubiquitin-dependent degradation. Purified ATGL also shows acylglycerol transacylase activity, which generates fatty acid esters of hydroxy fatty acids, and minor phospholipase A2 and retinyl ester hydrolase activities. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause neutral lipid storage disease with myopathy, with triacylglycerol accumulation in muscle, heart and leukocytes.

EFTUD2 encodes Snu114, the GTP-binding 116-kDa subunit of the U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle. Together with PRPF8 and other U5 proteins, it organizes spliceosomal machinery used in major and minor pre-mRNA splicing. The protein is predominantly nuclear, with a smaller cytoplasmic pool associated with U5 particle assembly. Its conserved nucleotide-binding fold and RNA contacts support this ribonucleoprotein role; an active GTP-hydrolysis cycle in the human spliceosome remains unresolved. Pathogenic variants cause mandibulofacial dysostosis with microcephaly.

ALG13 encodes alternatively spliced proteins, including the short isoform 2 that supplies the catalytic subunit of the ALG13–ALG14 UDP-N-acetylglucosamine transferase. At the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum, this complex transfers the second, beta-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-GlcNAc onto GlcNAc-PP-dolichol, forming GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol during assembly of the lipid-linked glycan precursor for protein N-linked glycosylation. ALG14 anchors the soluble catalytic subunit at the membrane, and the active enzyme requires their association. Human isoform 2 is 165 amino acids long; the 1137-amino-acid isoform 1 did not bind ALG14 or display this transferase activity in comparative cellular and biochemical assays. The long protein contains an OTU domain, but its physiological molecular function remains unresolved. Pathogenic ALG13 variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; several variants reduce transferase activity even when routine transferrin glycosylation measurements are near normal.

SECISBP2 (SECIS-binding protein 2, SBP2) is the essential trans-acting factor for co-translational selenocysteine incorporation into selenoproteins. It is an L7Ae/L30-family RNA-binding protein whose C-terminal half comprises a Sec-insertion domain (SID) and an RNA-binding domain (RBD) that recognizes the kink-turn (K-turn) motif of the SECIS element, a stem-loop located in the 3'-untranslated region of selenoprotein mRNAs. When an elongating 80S ribosome encounters an in-frame UGA codon, the SBP2-SECIS complex binds the 40S subunit (contacting ribosomal protein eS31/RPS27A and 18S rRNA) and forms a docking platform that recruits the selenocysteine-specific GTPase elongation factor EEFSEC together with selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec); after GTP hydrolysis and accommodation, selenocysteine is incorporated at the UGA codon rather than terminating translation. Through this recoding activity SBP2 is required for synthesis of essentially all selenoproteins (glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases, iodothyronine deiodinases, selenoprotein P, and others). The full-length isoform localizes to the nucleus and functions at cytoplasmic ribosomes, while an alternatively spliced isoform bearing an N-terminal transit peptide (mtSBP2) localizes to mitochondria. Loss-of-function variants cause a multisystem selenoprotein deficiency syndrome featuring abnormal thyroid hormone metabolism, growth retardation, myopathy, photosensitivity, and azoospermia.

LRP12 is an 859-residue type-I single-pass plasma-membrane protein of the low-density-lipoprotein-receptor-related family. Its extracellular region contains two CUB domains and five LDL-receptor class A repeats, followed by one transmembrane helix and a long cytoplasmic tail. The tail binds α4 integrins and interferes with talin engagement, restraining integrin activation and balancing nascent-adhesion turnover and cell migration; it also interacts with RACK1, NMRK2/MIBP, and ZFYVE9/SARA. Mouse developmental studies link Lrp12 to neuronal arborization, migration, and cortical lamination. Two named human protein isoforms differ by a short N-terminal deletion. Noncoding CGG-repeat expansions in the LRP12 5-prime untranslated region cause oculopharyngodistal myopathy 1 and, at shorter pathogenic repeat lengths, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 28.

ALG11 is an endoplasmic reticulum membrane alpha-1,2-mannosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.131) of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) assembly pathway. Using GDP-mannose as donor, it adds the fourth and fifth mannose residues onto Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol to produce Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol, the final cytoplasmic-face LLO intermediate; this glycan is then flipped into the ER lumen (by RFT1) for continued assembly and eventual transfer to nascent proteins during protein N-linked glycosylation. It is a single-pass ER membrane protein whose catalytic domain faces the cytosol and belongs to the glycosyltransferase group 1 family (GT4 subfamily). Loss of function causes ALG11-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ip), a multisystem disorder with under-glycosylated serum glycoproteins.

ARMS2 is a small (107-residue), primate-specific protein encoded at the 10q26 age-related macular degeneration (AMD) locus. Although it lacks a signal peptide, it is secreted by an unconventional route that recruits the cytosolic lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin and bypasses the Golgi. It is found in the extracellular matrix of the choroid and binds matrix proteins such as hemicentin-1. ARMS2 binds apoptotic and necrotic cell surfaces and recruits the complement activator properdin, promoting C3b opsonization for phagocytic clearance. Its intracellular location is disputed: one study reported a mitochondrial association, another found it cytosolic and not mitochondrial. The AMD-risk haplotype carries a 3' UTR indel that destabilizes ARMS2 mRNA, so risk homozygotes make no detectable protein.

DNAAF19, formerly CCDC103, is a small self-associating microtubule-binding protein that supports axonemal dynein-arm assembly and attachment in motile cilia. Conserved cytoplasmic and axonemal pools support dynein incorporation, enabling ciliary beating and normal left–right patterning. Purified human protein binds and stabilizes microtubules and forms oligomers; native human respiratory material contains apparent dimers. Its precise native polymer arrangement and dynein interface remain unresolved. Human variants cause primary ciliary dyskinesia with variable dynein-arm and laterality defects. Alternative transcripts encode a full-length 242-residue product and a predicted 98-residue product with a distinct short C terminus.

ATXN8 encodes a short, nearly pure polyglutamine protein translated from the antisense (CAG) strand of the spinocerebellar ataxia type 8 (SCA8) CTG-CAG repeat locus, which is bidirectionally transcribed with the noncoding ATXN8OS. In SCA8 the expanded repeat yields a polyglutamine protein that forms intranuclear inclusions in cerebellar Purkinje and brainstem neurons, contributing to toxic gain-of-function pathogenesis alongside the CUG-expansion RNA. ATXN8 protein has been detected only in SCA8 patients, and no normal function is known.

SMPD4 (neutral sphingomyelinase 3, nSMase3) is a magnesium-dependent, neutral sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase (EC 3.1.4.12) that hydrolyses membrane sphingomyelin to ceramide and phosphocholine. Despite its name it is a distinct enzyme unrelated by sequence to the SMPD2/SMPD3 (nSMase1/nSMase2) extended-calcineurin-like family. It is a C-tail-anchored, single-pass integral membrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, and it also resides at the outer nuclear envelope where it associates with nuclear pore complex proteins (it was independently identified as the nuclear envelope transmembrane protein NET13). Its catalytic activity is Mg2+-dependent with a neutral pH optimum, is stimulated by phosphatidylserine and by tumour necrosis factor, and is inhibited by scyphostatin. By generating ceramide from sphingomyelin, SMPD4 contributes to membrane sphingolipid homeostasis and to endoplasmic reticulum organization and ER-to-nuclear-envelope crosstalk, and it participates in stress-response signalling (DNA damage, TNF) linked to apoptosis and cell-cycle/mitotic progression. It is highly expressed in heart and skeletal muscle, where it mediates TNF-stimulated oxidant production. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in SMPD4 cause an autosomal-recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies (NEDMABA).

NDUFAF8 (formerly C17orf89) is a small (74 aa) soluble mitochondrial protein that acts as an assembly factor for respiratory chain Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). It is not a structural subunit of the mature holoenzyme and has no known catalytic activity. NDUFAF8 carries a twin CX9C / CHCH domain stabilized by two intramolecular disulfide bonds, the hallmark of substrates of the mitochondrial MIA40/CHCHD4 disulfide-relay import system; it reaches the mitochondrial matrix via a two-step import pathway in which a weak targeting sequence drives slow TIM23-dependent matrix import while allowing en-route oxidation by the intermembrane-space disulfide relay. In the matrix it binds and stabilizes the early Complex I assembly factor NDUFAF5, which is required for maturation of the Q module during early Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) biogenesis. Loss of NDUFAF8 destabilizes NDUFAF5 and stalls Q-module assembly, producing an isolated Complex I deficiency; bi-allelic loss-of-function variants cause a mitochondrial Complex I deficiency (Leigh syndrome, MC1DN34).

CFAP221, also called PCDP1, is a conserved ciliary and flagellar protein associated with the axonemal central apparatus. Ortholog biochemical studies establish calcium-dependent calmodulin binding, providing a molecular connection to control of ciliary beating. Human airway cells lacking detectable CFAP221 form motile cilia but show abnormal circular waveforms and impaired mucociliary transport. The requirement for flagellar assembly is context dependent: mouse loss-of-function disrupts sperm flagellar maturation, whereas a reported human patient retains sperm motility. CFAP221 also localizes to spermatid and sperm structures and has been detected at primary cilia and their tips. Its precise coupling of calmodulin to the dynein-driven beat and the functional differences among its alternative products remain unresolved.

COA5 (C2orf64; also called PET191) is a small (74-residue) nuclear-encoded mitochondrial assembly factor for cytochrome c oxidase (respiratory chain complex IV). It belongs to the PET191 family and is a twin CX9C-motif protein with a CHCH domain, features typical of intermembrane-space proteins imported and oxidatively folded via the MIA pathway. COA5 acts at an early step of complex IV assembly and participates in the copper/heme metallochaperone machinery that matures the MT-CO1 (CuB) and MT-CO2 (CuA) catalytic metal centers, and it can transiently bind copper. It is a non-catalytic factor rather than an enzyme. COA5 localizes to the mitochondrial intermembrane space, closely associated with the inner membrane where the metallochaperone reactions of complex IV biogenesis take place. Loss-of-function variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 9 (MC4DN9), a fatal infantile disorder with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (fatal infantile cardioencephalomyopathy phenotype).

TMEM231 is a conserved two-pass transmembrane protein of the MKS (tectonic) module of the ciliary transition zone, found only in ciliated organisms. It reaches the basal body early in ciliogenesis, before and independently of intraflagellar transport, in a septin-dependent manner, and becomes a biochemical component of the MKS complex with B9D1, B9D2, MKS1, TCTN1-3, CC2D2A and TMEM17. TMEM231 and B9D1 are needed for each other's transition-zone localization and for that of TMEM67 and MKS1, so TMEM231 helps organize the MKS part of the transition zone. Through this it maintains the ciliary diffusion barrier and the ciliary membrane composition (ARL13B, ADCY3, PKD2, INPP5E), supports tissue-dependent ciliogenesis and is required for Sonic hedgehog signalling. Variants cause Joubert syndrome 20, Meckel syndrome 11 and oral-facial-digital syndrome type 3.

CRPPA is a cytosolic cytidylyltransferase that synthesizes CDP-ribitol from D-ribitol 5-phosphate and CTP. This activated donor supplies ribitol phosphate for elaboration of the O-mannosyl glycan on alpha-dystroglycan by FKTN and FKRP, enabling its extracellular-matrix ligand-binding function. Recombinant human CRPPA forms a homodimer and also accepts ribose and ribulose phosphates in vitro. Loss of CRPPA activity causes dystroglycanopathies with muscular and variable brain and eye involvement. The enzyme is distinct from the bacterial IspD function in the methylerythritol isoprenoid pathway.

PET100 is a small (73 aa) single-pass mitochondrial inner-membrane protein that functions as a Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX)-specific assembly chaperone. It is the human ortholog of yeast Pet100p and belongs to the PET100 family. PET100 is non-catalytic; it promotes incorporation of the early nuclear-encoded COX subunits (the COX7/COX8 group, exemplified by its conserved interaction with COX subunit VIIa, COX7A2) into an early COX assembly intermediate, forming a ~300 kDa subcomplex with Complex IV subunits in the mitochondrial inner membrane. Loss of PET100 function causes isolated mitochondrial complex IV deficiency (mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 12; Leigh syndrome), with reduced COX levels and activity.

PET117 (Protein PET117 homolog, mitochondrial) is a small (81 aa) nucleus-encoded mitochondrial assembly chaperone for cytochrome c oxidase (COX; mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV). It is the conserved human ortholog of yeast PET117 and carries an N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide (aa 1-22) and a single Pfam PET117 domain (PF15786; InterPro IPR031568), adopting a small coiled-coil fold. PET117 is non-catalytic; it acts at an early step of COX biogenesis to assist assembly of the mtDNA-encoded core subunits, functioning together with the related PET100 chaperone (and MR-1S), and it stabilizes the COX1 translational activator TACO1 to support synthesis of the mtDNA-encoded COX1 core subunit. It localizes to the mitochondrion, associated with the inner membrane where COX assembly occurs. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 19 (MC4DN19), an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with global developmental delay and developmental regression.
